Research outputs may be shared with the public, source entities, and federal regulators, creating a risk of broader dissemination than individuals may expect even when direct identifiers are removed.
Indefinite retention of computer and paper records increases the time window for misuse, breach, or secondary use of personal data.
Aggregating previously unavailable data and generating new data about individuals may create profiling or inference risks even when the system says it does not track individual habits.
Limit collection and use of biometric and health information to only cases where it is necessary for the research purpose, and apply heightened safeguards to those records.
Strip direct identifiers from research datasets as early as possible and keep direct identifiers in a separate, tightly controlled environment.
Use de-identified copies of matched datasets for research and analysis after matching is complete.
Limit use of record locators to the minimum necessary for updates, and remove them from analytic files once the update or supplement is complete.
Provide direct notice to individuals where feasible when their information is collected from external sources for Market Research.
Require source organizations to document and verify that notice and sharing disclosures were provided before data is accepted.
Review research outputs before release to ensure they contain no direct identifiers and do not disclose sensitive details through small cells or other re-identification risks.
Adopt and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
Use the matching and weighting methods only for the stated research purposes and avoid creating unnecessary derived profiles about individuals.

Individuals may be re-identified or singled out from loan-level records even though the dataset does not include direct identifiers. The system says users may isolate a single record, which can still expose sensitive mortgage and property details about a specific person or household.

The public can use the dataset to infer sensitive financial and demographic information about applicants and borrowers, including possible denial reasons and protected-class monitoring data. Even without names, the dataset includes enough detail to reveal private circumstances about a household's mortgage application.

Public access and downloadable/API access increase the risk of large-scale copying, reuse, and secondary disclosure by outside parties. Because the dataset can be queried, filtered, downloaded, and shared, third parties can redistribute it in ways that the CFPB does not control.

Long retention of the public-use dataset extends the period during which privacy harms can occur. The records will remain available until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA, which leaves the data accessible for an open-ended period.

The CFPB does not independently verify the dataset before republishing it, which could allow inaccurate or incomplete information to be exposed publicly. If errors remain in the public dataset, they may unfairly affect the privacy and reputation of the individuals represented in the records.
Continue and strengthen redaction of fields before publication, and apply additional disclosure controls to reduce the chance that single records can be linked back to individuals.
Limit the precision of location and loan fields where possible, and review the public-use fields for sensitivity before republication.
Apply stronger controls on bulk download and sharing features, such as rate limits, API monitoring, and clear terms of use restricting misuse of the dataset.
Establish and publish a specific NARA-approved retention schedule for the republished dataset as soon as practicable.
Add validation and quality review before republication so that obvious errors, omissions, or integrity issues are detected before the data is made public.

The system collects highly sensitive personal information, including SSNs, financial data, health information, and data about vulnerable populations, increasing the harm if the data are exposed or misused.
Matching records and combining administrative data with response data can create new, more revealing profiles about respondents that they may not expect from a research survey.
External sharing of research products can still reveal individuals through re-identification or small-cell disclosure, even when direct identifiers are removed.
Direct identifying information is retained and used for scheduling, follow-up, compensation, and matching, which creates a risk of unnecessary exposure if it is not tightly separated and minimized.
The system relies on non-automated transfers through contractor systems, vendor websites, and encrypted email, which creates exposure during data movement and handling by third parties.
Contractors, vendors, and external researchers may access or process the data, creating a risk of broader disclosure if access controls or agreements fail.
Indefinite retention of computer and paper records increases the risk that personal data will remain available longer than necessary and be exposed in future misuse or breaches.

Using administrative data to identify survey recipients and analyze nonresponse bias can reveal participation patterns or other inferred information about people who did not consent to the research itself.
Keep direct identifying PII stored and secured separately from research data and limit collection to what is necessary for the research task.
Use de-identified copies for analysis after record matching is complete and avoid retaining the linked dataset in identifiable form.
Continue and strengthen disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation, rounding, exclusion of variables, and exclusion of observations before any external release.
Limit access to direct identifiers to the smallest necessary set of staff and use separate storage for those identifiers.
Continue using encrypted tunnels and encrypted email for transfers, and reduce manual transfers where possible.
Use legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements for all outside collaborators and restrict their access to only the data needed for the approved task.
Adopt and implement an approved records disposition schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
Use consent and disclosure-protection procedures before any external use of direct identifying PII or any administrative-data-based output that could identify individuals.

The system can contain direct identifiers and sensitive information, creating a risk that individuals could be identified or re-identified from Market Research datasets or outputs. This is especially concerning because the data can include names, addresses, SSNs, financial account numbers, biometric information, and health or medical information.

Matching records across datasets can create new linked profiles about people and increase the risk of inference or re-identification. Even if direct identifiers are removed later, the matching step itself can combine information from multiple sources into a more revealing record.

The CFPB may contact potential survey recipients using direct identifying PII, which could expose individuals to outreach they did not expect and reveal their association with consumer financial products or services. This creates a privacy risk because the system uses identity data to solicit additional information about consumer experiences.

Individuals generally do not receive notice when their information is collected or shared through supervisory or enforcement activity, limiting transparency and their ability to understand or challenge the use of their data. The system relies on constructive notice instead of direct notice in those cases.

The system may share information under Routine Uses of applicable SORNs and with federal financial regulators, which creates a risk of broader downstream disclosure beyond the original collection purpose. Even if outputs are aggregate, the underlying system still contemplates sharing information in some circumstances.

Records are retained indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which increases the risk that personal information will be kept longer than necessary. Long retention extends the window for unauthorized access, secondary use, or future linkage.

Because the system includes demographic information and uses it to weight and proxy datasets, there is a risk of profiling or inference about protected characteristics. This can reveal or amplify information about race, gender, age, education, income, or other traits.
Strip direct identifying PII before Market Research use and keep only de-identified copies for analysis and reporting.
Limit record matching to the minimum necessary and use de-identified copies after matching is complete.
Use direct identifying PII for survey contact only when necessary and limit it to contacting potential recipients, not broader analysis or reporting.
Provide constructive notice through the PIA when direct notice cannot be given and rely on applicable federal law, regulations, discovery rules, and court orders to govern use and disclosure.
Share only non-identifying aggregate Market Research products with the public and federal financial regulators, and apply SORN routine uses and CFPB disclosure rules to any other sharing.
Dispose of records according to an approved NARA records disposition schedule as soon as one is available, rather than retaining them indefinitely.
Use demographic information only for the stated weighting, proxying, and generalization purposes, and avoid producing reports on individuals.
Matching response data with administrative or credit data can create new sensitive information about a participant and increase the chance of re-identification or misuse.
The system collects and may store direct identifiers and other personal data that could be retrieved by name or Social Security number, creating a risk of identity exposure if access is misused.
The system collects sensitive financial, demographic, biometric, and health-related information, which could expose participants to privacy harm if disclosed or analyzed beyond what is needed.
Information collected directly from participants and from third parties may be used for purposes beyond the individual's immediate participation, creating secondary-use privacy risk.
Online activity data such as IP address, timestamps, browser details, pages viewed, and referral address can enable tracking of website visitors and reveal browsing behavior.
Sharing response data with the public, other agencies, or researchers could expose participants if de-identification or aggregation is insufficient.
Internal and external access to the data creates a risk of unauthorized viewing or over-broad access if need-to-know controls or agreements are not followed.
Non-automated transfers through encrypted tunnels or encrypted email still create a risk of interception, misrouting, or handling errors during data movement between systems.
Indefinite retention of computer and paper records increases the amount of time sensitive participant information remains exposed to breach, misuse, or unintended disclosure.
Keep direct identifying PII separated from Participants’ Response Data and use de-identified copies after matching is complete.
Limit retrieval and access to direct identifiers to situations needed to facilitate participation or matching, and use the applicable Privacy Act systems of records coverage.
Collect only the information necessary for recruitment, scheduling, comparison, or analysis, and store direct identifying PII separately when needed.
Use informed consent before matching or collecting third-party information, and give participants notice and choice when sharing response data.
Collect website and tool usage information in aggregate form and avoid direct identification in online analytics.
Apply disclosure-protection techniques such as aggregation, generalized sentiments, rounding, exclusion of some variables, and exclusion of observations before releasing products or response data.
Restrict access to CFPB personnel with a need to know and use legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements for outside collaborators.
Continue using encrypted tunnels and encrypted email for system transfers, and add transfer validation checks to confirm correct recipients and completeness.
Adopt and implement an approved records disposition schedule so records are not kept indefinitely once NARA approves the schedule.
Primary data collection in real-world consumer financial settings may collect personal information from people who are not expecting it or do not understand how it will be used for research.
Consumer data may be shared with third parties involved in collaborations, creating a risk of broader access than participants expect.
If the CFPB contracts with a third party to conduct research, that contractor may mishandle personal information or use it beyond the intended research purpose.
Because the system involves longer-term field research, personal information may be retained or exposed for an extended period, increasing the chance of misuse or unauthorized access over time.
Research data could be linked back to individuals if it is not adequately protected, even though the stated purpose is not to make determinations about individuals.
Participants may have limited ability to understand, access, or correct information collected about them unless notice, access, and redress are meaningfully provided.
Provide clear notice and, where appropriate, consent before or at the time of field data collection.
Use written agreements that define roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms for every external collaborator.
Apply the CFPB's standard privacy protections and security controls to contractors and require them to follow the same controls.
Limit retention to the shortest period needed for the research and dispose of data when it is no longer needed.
Apply strong privacy and security controls to reduce the chance that research data can be linked to individuals.
Provide participants with practical access and redress processes so they can review and correct information when appropriate.
The system collects detailed mortgage application and loan data about individuals, which creates a risk of exposing sensitive financial and housing information if mishandled.
The system receives data about applications, originations, and purchases from covered institutions, creating a risk of collecting more personal information than is necessary for a given filing.
Multiple federal agencies can receive the data, increasing the risk of broader dissemination and access beyond the CFPB.
The system supports reporting and disclosure of mortgage data, creating a risk that individuals' information could be reused or exposed beyond the original reporting purpose.
Because the platform has no public participation component, individuals may have limited ability to notice, correct, or challenge how their information is handled.
The system relies on electronic submission of loan/application registers, which creates a risk of interception, transmission errors, or unauthorized access during data transfer.
Apply the CFPB's standard privacy protections and security controls to all HMDA data.
Limit collection to the HMDA fields required by Regulation C and the 2017/2018 HMDA file specifications.
Restrict access and sharing to the Federal HMDA agencies identified for the program.
Use the data only for the HMDA purposes stated in the system overview.
Provide a public-facing correction or inquiry process for HMDA submissions.
Require secure electronic submission and validation of loan/application registers under the HMDA file specifications.

Public disclosure of mortgage data could allow people to infer or re-identify applicants or borrowers, especially when combined with other available information. Even though direct identifiers are not required, the dataset still contains detailed loan and demographic information that can be linkable.

The collection of age, credit score, and disaggregated race and ethnicity creates a sensitive profile of applicants and borrowers. If exposed or misused, this information could reveal financial status and protected characteristics.

Sharing HMDA data with multiple federal agencies expands the number of systems and personnel that can access the information, increasing the chance of unauthorized access or inconsistent protection. The broader the recipient set, the greater the exposure surface.

Annual and quarterly reporting of loan/application register data creates repeated transfers over time, which can increase the chance of interception, transmission errors, or accumulation of more complete personal profiles. More frequent reporting also means more opportunities for mistakes.

The system relies on lenders to collect and submit the information, including self-identified race and ethnicity, which can lead to inaccurate or overbroad collection if institutions mishandle the process. Incorrect or unnecessary data collection can harm privacy and reduce data quality.
Apply a strong disclosure review process before any public release to suppress or aggregate fields that could enable re-identification.
Limit collection and disclosure of sensitive fields to what Regulation C specifically requires and ensure they are protected with heightened access controls.
Apply the stated CFPB privacy protections and security controls consistently across all recipient agencies and require secure handling agreements for interagency sharing.
Use secure electronic submission channels and transmission safeguards for annual and quarterly filings.
Provide clear collection instructions and validation checks for lenders so self-identified race and ethnicity data are gathered consistently and only for covered reporting purposes.

The tool collects identifiable contact information about entity contacts, creating a risk of exposing names, phone numbers, and email addresses if the system is breached or mishandled. This is especially sensitive because the contacts are tied to regulated financial entities.

Free-text responses and attachments may accidentally include more personal information than intended, increasing the chance of unnecessary disclosure of PII. Because the fields are optional and open-ended, submitters may include names, contact details, or other sensitive context.

The system imports Bureau employee and contractor information, which expands the set of people whose personal data is stored and exposed to the tool. This creates a risk that internal staff information could be accessed beyond what is necessary for the assessment process.

The tool is used to create internal dashboards for data analytics, which may lead to identifiable information being reused beyond the original collection purpose if aggregation is not strict enough. If dashboards are not properly limited, users could infer details about specific entities or contacts.

The system relies on voluntary assessments submitted by external entities, so there is a risk that submitters may not fully understand what personal data they are providing or how it will be used. This can undermine informed participation and increase unnecessary disclosure.
Limit collection to the stated contact fields and apply strong access controls, encryption, and standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls to protect stored contact PII.
Add clear instructions and validation to discourage entering unnecessary PII in free-text fields and attachments, and review submissions for excessive personal data before processing.
Import only the minimum Bureau employee and contractor details needed for administration, and restrict access to those records to authorized users with a business need.
Ensure dashboards and annual reporting use only aggregated or de-identified outputs, with checks that prevent display of individual-level data.
Provide prominent notice to submitters about what PII may be collected, how it will be used, and how to avoid entering unnecessary personal data.
The system may expose personally identifiable information in request records or released documents to unauthorized people if access controls fail.
The system may disclose information about Bureau staff or other third parties when documents are retrieved or generated during request processing.
The public-facing portal could expose account and request data during online submission, access, or communication if the Login.gov-linked portal is not secured properly.
The system may retain more request-related personal data than necessary because it supports the full lifecycle of FOIA and Privacy Act requests.
Bureau staff entering request information can inadvertently introduce or expose unnecessary personal data in the system.
Using a third-party vendor-created system may increase the risk of privacy exposure through vendor access or vendor system weaknesses.
Apply strict role-based access controls, audit logging, and release review procedures before any records are disclosed.
Require redaction and third-party review before releasing documents that contain information about requestors, staff, or others.
Enforce strong authentication, secure session management, and transport encryption for the public portal and Login.gov connection.
Set and enforce retention schedules that delete request records when no longer needed for FOIA or Privacy Act administration.
Train Bureau staff on data minimization and accurate data entry for request processing.
Limit vendor access to the minimum necessary and require contractual privacy and security obligations for the third-party system.
A cloud-hosted, third-party-operated system could expose inquiry data if the hosting environment is compromised or mismanaged.
Staff access to inquiry records could reveal confidential personal information if access controls fail or are too broad.
Separating contact information from the inquiry record creates a risk that email, mail, or voicemail notes could be exposed in their original storage locations.
The system may collect more identifying information than necessary when a person chooses to provide their name.
Inquiry summaries may contain sensitive details about a person's dealings with the Bureau, creating a risk of disclosure of more information than intended.
The Office's independent outreach activity may involve processing information about individuals in a way that expands collection beyond one-off inquiries.
Using the data for administrative purposes could create secondary uses that are broader than the original inquiry resolution purpose.
If the Office lacks effective retention limits, inquiry and outreach records could be kept longer than needed.
Require strong security controls, vendor oversight, and periodic assessment of the third-party hosted environment.
Restrict access to authorized Ombudsman’s Office staff and use the secure web interface for controlled access only.
Protect separately stored contact information with the same confidentiality safeguards and minimize retention of the original source records.
Continue allowing anonymous inquiries and keep the record limited to first and last name only when identification is necessary.
Limit inquiry summaries to the minimum detail needed to manage the case and redact unnecessary sensitive facts.
Apply the same privacy review and access controls to outreach records as to inquiry records.
Restrict administrative use to clearly defined internal operations and document those uses in the PIA and SORN.
Establish and enforce a retention schedule for inquiry and outreach records, including deletion of unnecessary source records.

Consumer complaint and inquiry information may be disclosed to outside companies or other agencies beyond what the consumer expects when the Bureau forwards the matter. Because complaints can include sensitive personal experience with financial products or services, these transfers can reveal private information to additional recipients.

Complaints and other mailed documents may be exposed during vendor processing and digitization before they are scanned into the system. This creates a risk that sensitive information in physical mail is seen, copied, or mishandled by vendor staff.

Consumers who call the contact center may have their voice communications captured and recorded, which can expose sensitive personal details in real time voice interactions. The system’s telephony functions also include call recording and similar voice-type services.

Consumer complaints and inquiries may be analyzed with advanced data analytics, which can create privacy risk if the analysis reveals patterns or inferences about individuals beyond the original complaint handling purpose. Even if the data are used for performance or operational improvement, analytics can expand the visibility of personal information.

Staff identity information used for authentication could be misused if access controls are weak, allowing unauthorized access to consumer complaint records. Since staff email is used for system access, compromise of those credentials could expose large volumes of consumer data.

Consumers who speak with vendor staff may not realize that those staff are working on behalf of the Bureau, which could affect informed disclosure of personal information. The direct interaction with vendor staff creates a risk of over-sharing if roles and handling practices are not clearly communicated.
Limit complaint sharing to the minimum necessary recipient and purpose, and provide clear notice to consumers when their complaint may be sent to a company, another agency, or another Bureau office.
Require vendor staff processing mailed complaints to follow strict handling, confidentiality, and scanning procedures, with immediate scanning and restricted access to physical mail.
Provide notice at the start of calls that voice communications may be captured or recorded, and restrict recording to calls where it is operationally necessary.
Use analytics only on de-identified or aggregated data whenever possible, and limit access to analytic outputs to authorized staff for operational purposes.
Enforce strong authentication and role-based access controls for staff accounts, and protect the staff email credentials used to access the CRC system.
Clearly identify vendor staff to consumers and explain that they are working on behalf of the Bureau when consumers call the contact center.

The platform can collect a broad mix of sensitive and identifying information, including military information, date of birth, sex, race/ethnicity, and place of birth, which increases the harm if the data is misused or exposed.

The system supports collecting PII from many channels and uploading data submitted by mail, email, or phone, which can increase the chance of collecting more information than is needed for a particular purpose.
Internal users may access PII for a wide range of business functions, so without tight role controls there is a risk of unauthorized internal access or use beyond a user's job need.

The platform processes name and email address for internal authentication and external users must log in with email, password, and multi-factor authentication, so compromised credentials could expose PII and account access.

Salesforce integrates with other CFPB-authorized third-party cloud environments for storage and archiving, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure or loss of control as data moves between systems.
Applications may share information with external entities on a need-to-know basis, creating a risk that data could be disclosed more broadly than intended if sharing is not tightly limited.

The system supports creating, managing, and reporting case records and legal matters, so there is a risk that sensitive complaint, supervisory, enforcement, or litigation information could be used for purposes beyond the original collection purpose.
The platform enables trend, pattern, and correlation analysis of large data sets, which can reveal more about individuals than they expect and create privacy risks from inference or profiling.
Records may be retained indefinitely until NARA approves disposition schedules, which increases the risk that PII will remain available longer than necessary.
Limit each application to the minimum PII needed for the authorized use case and apply field-level review before collection.
Standardize intake forms and review uploaded submissions so staff collect only the data elements required for the specific process.
Restrict access by role and enforce least-privilege permissions for internal users who build, manage, or use Salesforce applications.
Continue using multi-factor authentication and provision access through authenticated identity management for all user accounts.
Require assessment and authorization of every connected third-party cloud environment before data is stored or exchanged.
Document each external disclosure in application-specific PIAs and limit sharing to the identified need-to-know recipients.
Review each application’s purpose and privacy impact before deployment to ensure case and legal data are used only for authorized functions.
Limit analytics to approved datasets and use privacy review before trend or correlation analysis is enabled.
Archive and dispose of records according to approved NARA schedules instead of retaining them indefinitely.
The system collects identity and contact details that may be more than is necessary for access management, increasing the amount of personal information stored and exposed if misused or breached.
The system may store personal cell numbers and home addresses for people who work from home, creating a risk of revealing sensitive location or contact information.
The centralized ICAM hub aggregates identity and access data from multiple sources, creating a single repository that could expose many individuals' records if compromised or overused.
The system receives data from external federal systems and other internal systems, which increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure or data integrity problems during transfers.

The system creates a digital ID and manages authentication and authorization for access to CFPB resources, so an access-control failure could expose PII and other sensitive systems to unauthorized users.
Privileged accounts present a heightened privacy risk because elevated access can reveal or alter PII across CFPB environments if not tightly controlled.
The system shares identity data with external federal sources and supports authorized external individuals, which can broaden disclosure beyond CFPB staff and increase the chance of secondary use.
Limit collection to the minimum identity attributes needed for verification and access management, and avoid collecting optional personal details unless they are required.
Allow home address and personal cell number to be collected only when necessary for remote work and protect them with stricter access controls.
Apply role-based access controls, monitoring, and regular review of who can view identity and access records in the centralized hub.
Use only secure transmission methods and validate inbound data feeds to protect data in transit and reduce the risk of tampering.
Continue to enforce authentication, authorization, and standard privacy and security controls for all access to CFPB systems.
Require Rules of Behavior and Privilege User Access Requests for privileged accounts and review them before granting or renewing elevated access.
Limit data sharing with external individuals and external systems to the minimum necessary for credentialing and access provisioning.

The system may collect more personal information than necessary because it can gather PII from supervised entities, consumers, complaints, CFPB employees, and other agencies or public sources. This broad collection increases the amount of personal data exposed if the system is misused or breached.

The system may collect consumer PII indirectly from supervised entities and directly from consumers, complaints, and CFPB employees, creating a risk that people are not fully aware of how their information enters the system. This can reduce transparency and make it harder for individuals to understand or challenge the collection.

The system may involve sharing personal and supervisory information with external entity representatives and state regulators through the CFPB Supervision Portal. If access is misconfigured or overbroad, sensitive information could be disclosed to parties that do not need it.

The system stores compliance rating information and Examination Reports, which could reveal sensitive supervisory assessments about institutions and related individuals. If this information is accessed improperly, it could harm reputations or expose internal regulatory judgments.

The system may use consumer PII to contact consumers for additional information, which could reveal their involvement in a supervisory matter or lead to unwanted contact. This creates a privacy risk if outreach is not minimized or carefully handled.

Because the SES resides in a cloud platform and supports automated collection, concurrent collaboration, and document review tracking, there is a risk that more staff than necessary can access or combine personal data during supervisory work. This can increase internal exposure of PII beyond the minimum needed for a task.

The system may retain PII and supervisory records longer than necessary if retention is not narrowly controlled, increasing the amount of historical personal information available for access or disclosure. Long-lived records also expand the impact of any future breach or unauthorized access.
Limit collection to the minimum PII needed for supervision activities and prefer information already available from other agencies or reported publicly before requesting additional data.
Provide clear notice about the different ways PII is collected and from whom, including direct collection from consumers and indirect collection from supervised entities and complaints.
Restrict portal access to authorized entity representatives and state regulators and review permissions before allowing any file exchange or response capability.
Apply strict access controls and handling rules to Examination Reports and compliance ratings so only users with a supervisory need can view them.
Minimize consumer outreach and use the smallest amount of PII necessary when contacting consumers for verification or follow-up.
Enforce role-based access and need-to-know controls for internal collaboration, automated requests, and document review tracking in the cloud platform.
Establish and enforce a retention schedule that deletes or archives PII once it is no longer needed for supervision and legal obligations.

The system may expose consumers to harm if complaint records and supporting documents are disclosed to companies, other government agencies, or other CFPB offices beyond what is necessary to resolve the complaint.
The system may collect more sensitive personal data than is needed because Social Security Numbers can be submitted and used to validate identity even though they are not required for all complaints.

The system may retain detailed complaint narratives and supporting documents that contain sensitive personal information in a centralized system of record, increasing the impact of any unauthorized access or breach.
Using a vendor-provided cloud platform may create confidentiality and access-control risks if the vendor environment is not tightly managed.
Complaint data may be used for analysis and trend identification in ways that go beyond the consumer’s original complaint purpose, creating a secondary-use privacy risk.
Limit disclosures to companies, other agencies, and other CFPB offices to the minimum information needed to resolve or route the complaint.
Collect Social Security Numbers only when strictly necessary and clearly explain that they are optional and why they are being requested.
Apply strong access controls and role-based permissions to complaint records, details, and supporting documents in the CRS.
Require the vendor-provided cloud platform to use strong security controls, monitoring, and contractual safeguards for the CRS.
Use complaint data for trend analysis in a way that minimizes identifiers and limits access to aggregated or de-identified outputs where possible.
Sensitive personally identifiable information may be exposed because CFPB records are maintained in a contractor-owned environment rather than solely in CFPB-controlled systems.
Large volumes of records can be ingested, analyzed, and organized in ways that expose more personal information than is necessary for a given case.
Metadata and duplicate-document review can reveal additional personal information and relationships that are not apparent in the document content itself.
Keyword-based redaction and automated flagging may miss protected information or flag the wrong material, leaving personal information disclosed or over-processed.
Forensic collection from external entities can capture personal information from storage media in a way that is broader than the immediate legal need.
Storing collected information for litigation and hearings creates a retention and reuse risk if data is kept longer or used more broadly than necessary.
Transmitting and maintaining records across cloud-based solutions and vendor-owned tools increases the chance of unauthorized disclosure during data flow between systems.
Trial and investigative hearing support can expose personal information to broader audiences if exhibits are displayed in court or during hearings.
Restrict contractor access to CFPB records through least-privilege permissions, contractual handling requirements, and monitoring of contractor activity.
Limit ingestion and review to the minimum record set needed for the specific investigation or litigation matter.
Apply strict rules for metadata review and duplicate handling so reviewers only access metadata when necessary for the case.
Require attorney review and validation of automated redaction and keyword flagging before any disclosure decisions are made.
Use court-authorized forensic collection procedures that scope extraction narrowly to the requested data and preserve chain-of-custody controls.
Enforce case-based retention limits and secure deletion or return of records when they are no longer needed.
Use strong access controls and secure transmission protections across on-premises, vendor-owned, and cloud-based environments.
Redact or limit exhibits containing personal information before they are used in hearings or trial presentations.
The system collects personal business contact information that could identify users or points of contact if exposed or mishandled.
If real applicant or associated-person data were entered during beta-testing, the system could collect sensitive lending information beyond the intended fake-data scope.
The system is intended to support fair-lending enforcement and community analysis, which can create privacy risk from secondary use of lending data beyond the original collection context.
The system may receive data from covered financial institutions that is derived from applicants' lending activity, creating risk if those institutions fail to exclude prohibited personal identifiers.
The collected lending dataset can reveal business characteristics and demographics that may enable inference about women-owned, minority-owned, and small businesses.
Apply the stated standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls to the user profile data.
Restrict beta-testing to fake data beyond user or POC business contact information and prevent entry of real applicant data.
Limit access and reuse of lending data to the stated purposes of fair-lending enforcement and community/business development analysis.
Require covered financial institutions to exclude applicant PII before disclosure to the CFPB and validate submissions for compliance.
Use the stated opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress to give affected parties visibility and a way to challenge or correct improper use.

Covered orders and uploaded documents may expose sensitive third-party PII, including consumers, respondents, counsel, officers, and contact persons, because the system accepts copies of orders and related records that can contain personal details.

The public registry may disclose non-confidential information more widely than needed, allowing members of the public and other regulators to view registry data and potentially infer details about individuals named in orders.
Information may be shared with other CFPB programs and with other federal, state, tribal, and local regulators, creating a risk of secondary use beyond the original collection purpose.
The system may retain records indefinitely because there is no approved retention schedule, which increases the long-term exposure of personal information in the registry.
The system collects and maintains account credentials and usernames/passwords for nonbank users and CFPB staff, creating a risk of unauthorized access if credentials are compromised.
The helpdesk feature collects names, email addresses, and questions from members of the public and nonbank users, which may reveal more personal information than necessary to resolve the issue.
The system collects and stores audit/access records for CFPB staff, which can create internal privacy risk if those logs are overused or accessed without need.
Documents may be inadvertently uploaded even when they are not relevant to the Orders Rule, causing unnecessary collection of sensitive information.

Because the system resides in a cloud-based Salesforce environment and uses external-facing web forms, it is exposed to typical online access and transmission risks if those channels are misconfigured or abused.
Require redaction of all nonpublic portions of covered orders before upload and remove any irrelevant or inadvertently uploaded documents from the registry.
Use sole CFPB discretion to publish only non-confidential information and format publication to protect confidential information.
Share registry information only under existing information-sharing agreements and protocols, and only as needed for the receiving agency's mission purpose.
Obtain and implement a NARA-approved retention schedule for NBR records and dispose of records when authorized.
Require password creation and multi-factor authentication for user accounts and restrict access to authorized users only.
Collect only the minimum helpdesk information needed to answer the question and use the secure web form for submissions.
Limit access to staff with assigned duties, require acceptable-use compliance, and require privacy training on onboarding and annually.
Have CFPB staff routinely review uploaded documents and remove any that are not relevant to the Orders Rule.
Maintain the portal as a secure web form and continue using the CFPB Salesforce environment's secure portal features for registration and submission.
The system may collect and retain more personal data than is necessary because enforcement files can include a wide range of PII and full case documents from many sources.
Using information collected for enforcement matters for other internal reporting and market-monitoring purposes can create secondary-use privacy risk for people named in the records.
Internal access by multiple CFPB groups can expose sensitive matter information to a wider audience than a subject would expect.
Sharing enforcement records with FTC staff through the shared portal can expose personal data across agencies and increase the risk of broader disclosure or misuse.
Providing personal information to court reporting vendors for scheduling and documenting testimony creates a disclosure risk to third parties outside the government.
Reporting fines, penalties, and other amounts to the IRS can reveal identifying tax-related information about entities and individuals.
Collecting and storing TINs creates a risk of tax identifier exposure if the data is accessed or disclosed inappropriately.
The system may disclose personal information in response to FOIA requests, which can expose case participants and staff to public release of sensitive records.
Collecting information from complaints, whistleblower tips, public sources, and other agencies can lead to inaccurate or unverified records about individuals and entities.
Limit collection and retention to information that is directly relevant and necessary to the matter, and avoid storing unnecessary personal details in linked documents.
Restrict non-enforcement reporting to aggregated or de-identified outputs unless a specific need for identifiable data is documented.
Enforce role-based, need-to-know access reviews for all internal users and reports, with periodic audits of who can view matter data.
Limit FTC access to the smallest necessary set of fields and require authorized-user controls in the shared portal.
Share only the minimum witness and contact information needed with court reporting vendors and use contractual or procedural safeguards for that disclosure.
Limit IRS reporting to the specific tax-reporting fields required and transmit them only for the stated reporting purpose.
Protect TINs with stricter access controls and use them only when necessary to meet tax reporting obligations.
Apply FOIA review procedures to redact exempt personal information before release.
Verify and annotate source information before it is used in enforcement records, especially when it comes from complaints, tips, or public sources.
The system stores sensitive consumer PII in geospatial form, so unauthorized access or misuse could expose home addresses, demographic attributes, and loan details tied to individuals or businesses.
Internal sharing across programs, teams, contractors, and additional users increases the chance that data will be accessed by people who do not need the full dataset for their work.
Allowing administrators to add users to private folders and enabling multi-user groups creates a risk that outputs are shared more widely than intended.
Storing data in GIS components and connected cloud environments creates a risk of unauthorized access or leakage through the desktop, enterprise server, data store, or AWS-hosted environment.
Geocoding and mapping can make it easier to infer identities or sensitive traits from location patterns, especially when consumer data is layered with census and other public datasets.
The system may publish aggregated outputs externally, and if aggregation or de-identification is insufficient, individuals could still be indirectly identified from maps or trend analyses.
Staff identity and access data are retained for the life of the account, which creates a long-term privacy risk if account records are no longer needed or are compromised.

PII remains on the GIS server until final output is transmitted and is then deleted within a week, so temporary retention still creates a window where data could be exposed or retained longer than necessary if processes fail.
Use role-based access controls so staff only access the system and information necessary and relevant to their assigned duties.
Require a business purpose or need to know before granting access to geocoded data.
Keep outputs in private folders accessible only to the user and GIS administrators unless additional access is specifically approved for collaboration.
Maintain the secure, browser-based enterprise system and authentication controls, including Single Sign-On, for controlled access to stored data.
Limit GIS processing to the location data needed for the analysis and avoid generating new PII from public layers.
Publish only aggregated and de-identified outputs after they are transmitted back to a CFPB on-premise server for review and contextualization.
Use the records retention schedule process to define and limit how long staff PII and audit logs are kept.
Delete PII from the GIS server within a week after the final output is transmitted to permanent program-appropriate storage.
The database contains sensitive identifiers that could expose individuals to identity theft or other misuse if disclosed improperly.
People may not receive actual notice when their information is collected from third parties or other agencies.
The system relies on third-party and government sources without always verifying accuracy, which can create incorrect records about people.
The system combines data from multiple sources, including public complaints and social media, which can create privacy harm through broader profiling than the individual expected.
Internal reports may expose personal information to employees who do not need all of it, increasing the risk of unnecessary internal access.
External sharing with supervised institutions and other agencies creates a risk of disclosure beyond the CFPB, even when limited.
Future connections or imports from other systems could expand exposure if not assessed and controlled before implementation.
Keeping records indefinitely until a disposition schedule is approved increases the period during which personal data could be exposed or misused.
Employee access credentials and training reduce risk, but if not enforced consistently, unauthorized personnel could gain access to the database.
Restrict access to the minimum necessary users and protect reports and records with secure transmission and storage controls.
Provide constructive notice through the PIA and SORN when actual notice is not feasible.
Verify information where practicable by contacting supervised institutions and individuals or using third-party data sources, and allow Privacy Act correction requests.
Limit use of third-party, social media, and complaint-derived information to confirming information gathered from other sources.
Continue enforcing need-to-know access for internal reports and connected systems.
Use secure channels and data sharing agreements before any external disclosure.
Document and review any future external-facing connections in updated PIAs before deployment.
Adopt and implement a NARA-approved records disposition schedule as soon as possible.
Require non-transferrable access codes and passwords, and maintain confidentiality and privacy training for authorized users.
Users may unintentionally disclose directly identifiable contact information or other personal details when using the public website.
User-submitted comments, videos, links, or images may reveal sensitive personal details or be publicly exposed through the website.
Information about consumer financial products used by a user and others may expose financial behavior or associations beyond the individual user.
The site may collect demographic information that could be used to profile visitors or reveal characteristics they did not intend to share.
Website usage data may enable tracking of user behavior across visits or sessions, creating a privacy risk even without direct identifiers.
Information entered through the site may flow into the online complaint intake system, increasing the number of systems that handle the data.
Google Analytics processing may expose aggregate web traffic data to an external service provider.
The site may make some user-provided information public, which can lead to unintended disclosure and loss of control by the user.
The system collects directly identifiable PII when users knowingly provide it, which still creates privacy risk if users do not understand the consequences of disclosure.
Provide clear, prominent notice before submission and minimize required fields so users can avoid sharing unnecessary personal information.
Warn users not to include sensitive personal information in comments, videos, links, or images and review submissions for public-posting risks.
Limit collection of consumer financial product information to what is necessary for the site’s educational purpose and redact unnecessary details before publication or sharing.
Collect demographic information only when needed and make it optional unless required for a specific function.
Use only aggregated website-usage analytics and avoid retaining user-level identifiers in analytics data.
Apply strict access controls and data-handling rules when information moves from ConsumerFinance.gov to the online complaint intake system.
Disclose the use of Google Analytics clearly and configure it to collect the least amount of data necessary for aggregate traffic analysis.
Give users a clear preview of what will be made public and let them choose whether to publish each item.
Strengthen the informed-consent notice so users understand what directly identifiable PII will be collected and how it will be used.
The system collects and stores highly sensitive identifiers, including Social Security numbers, which creates a risk of identity theft or serious harm if exposed.
Accident management collects extensive third-party personal and sensitive information, including health records and credit card data, which increases the impact of any unauthorized disclosure.
The system creates and aggregates new data about individuals across accident and sales processes, which can expand profiles beyond the original source documents.
Accident and sales data are shared with external federal systems and vendors, creating exposure during transmission and increasing the number of parties with access.
Accident documents are moved into EDMS and accessed by authorized users there, so a compromise of the connected document system could expose personally identifiable information.
Vehicle sales data, including Social Security numbers, are transmitted to Experian for credit-worthiness checks, creating a risk of unnecessary disclosure to a private-sector organization.
The system logs employee and contractor transactions, which can reveal user activity and create privacy concerns if audit logs are accessed without need.
Individuals involved in accidents may have limited ability to refuse collection of required information, which can pressure disclosure of personal data.
The system keeps large volumes of accident and sales records, so retained data may remain available longer than necessary and increase exposure over time.
Continue limiting collection to only the information needed for the stated purpose and use encrypted transmission and storage for Social Security numbers.
Restrict accident data collection to what is needed for police reports, insurance claims, and recovery, and keep access limited to authorized users.
Apply a data minimization review before combining accident, sales, and user registration data, so only necessary fields are aggregated.
Use the stated AES-256 encryption for transfers to OCFO and maintain the formal agreement governing sharing with external federal recipients.
Keep EDMS access restricted to authorized users and ensure files remain encrypted during transmission to the document repository.
Limit the use of Social Security numbers in the sales process to the stated credit-worthiness purpose and retain the transmission controls used for Experian.
Limit audit log access to personnel with a need to review security or system activity, and review logs only for authorized purposes.
Provide the Privacy Act Statement and the access/amendment process so individuals understand why the information is required and how to reach AMC.
Apply retention limits and periodic review so accident and sales records are deleted when no longer needed for the stated purposes.
The system stores highly sensitive identifiers and financial data that could cause serious harm if exposed.
The system stores communications and documents that may contain additional PII about constituents and other people, increasing the scope of exposure.
Linking all inquiries submitted by or on behalf of the same constituent can create a consolidated profile that reveals more than any single inquiry.
Staffer, congressional, and OLA representative contact information is retained in case files and could be exposed if the system is compromised.
The system receives and stores information about people who are not the requesting staffer, including constituents and other third parties, which may be disclosed without their direct involvement.
Inquiry records are routed to appropriate OPM program offices and may be shared with other federal agencies, creating a risk of unnecessary internal and external disclosure.
Using cloud-based Microsoft services for case tracking and document storage increases the risk of unauthorized access or data exposure through the hosting environment.
The CS Portal allows staffers to submit inquiries, messages, and documents, so improper account access could expose sensitive case materials even though the portal itself does not retain them.
Minimize collection of sensitive identifiers and financial data by requiring staffers to submit only the specific fields needed to resolve the inquiry.
Apply strict document-handling rules to limit uploads and stored attachments to materials directly relevant to the inquiry, and redact unnecessary PII before storage.
Restrict access to linked constituent histories to staff with a demonstrated need to know and log each access to linked records.
Protect staffer, congressional, and OLA contact information with role-based access controls and audit logging.
Provide notice and obtain or verify authorization before processing constituent or third-party information, and limit use to the specific inquiry.
Limit routing and reporting to the minimum necessary data and apply access controls to program offices and any other recipients.
Enforce strong cloud security configuration, encryption, and vendor access restrictions for Microsoft Dynamics 365, Dataverse, and SharePoint Online.
Maintain multifactor authentication and approval for portal accounts, and review account access regularly.

ROVR collects and maintains a broad set of personally identifiable enrollment and health-related data about many people, creating a risk of overcollection and unnecessary exposure of sensitive information.
The system links records over time into person-level longitudinal files, which increases the risk of re-identification and deeper profiling of individuals across plan changes.
ROVR may reveal erroneous or exceptional dual enrollments, which could expose enrollment mistakes or special coverage circumstances to unauthorized or inappropriate scrutiny.
ROVR analyzes claims, utilization, providers, geography, and disease conditions, creating a risk of detailed health profiling and inference about individuals or small groups.
The system includes pharmacy manufacturer payments and rebate information, which could expose commercially sensitive and potentially personal prescription-related details if mishandled.
Using the data to detect fraud, waste, and abuse or to investigate specific individuals creates a risk of secondary use beyond routine benefits administration.
ROVR receives data from multiple internal and external systems and agencies, which creates a risk of disclosure errors or inconsistent safeguards during data sharing.
Service use and cost data from CMS about Medicare-enrolled family members may be combined with FEHB data, increasing the risk of cross-program linkage and broader exposure of health information.

Because OPM uses identifiable data for longitudinal and analytical purposes, there is a risk that data collected for administration will be reused in ways that exceed what individuals reasonably expect.
Limit collection and retention to the minimum data needed for FEHB and PSHB administration and analysis.
Use de-identified or aggregated data whenever identifiable person-level records are not necessary.
Restrict review of dual-enrollment cases to authorized staff and use the data only to resolve enrollment issues permitted by OPM rules.
Apply strong access controls and cohort-size review rules before releasing or analyzing detailed subgroup, geographic, provider, or disease-condition outputs.
Treat pharmacy payment and rebate data as sensitive administrative data and restrict access to staff with a need to know.
Confine fraud, waste, and abuse review to cases where OPM suspects or has confirmed improper activity and document the basis for each use.
Use data sharing agreements to define permitted uses, retention, and storage protocols for each source and recipient.
Limit CMS-linked data to the minimum needed for Medicare-related FEHB analysis and keep the linkage confined to authorized administrative uses.
Enforce the stated rule that ROVR data are not disclosed outside OPM unless permitted under the Privacy Act.

The system stores highly sensitive personal identifiers and debt information, including SSNs, mailing addresses, and debt amounts, which could expose individuals to identity theft or financial harm if mishandled.
Many USDA agencies can access the data, which increases the chance that more users than necessary could see debtor information or use it beyond the minimum needed.
The system shares debtor information with external federal systems and a records contractor, creating additional disclosure points outside the originating agency.
Contractors at a local facility convert payroll reports into PDF files and transmit them onward, which creates handling and transfer risk during file preparation.
Individuals do not have direct access to ABCO data, which limits their ability to review, correct, or verify information held about them.
ABCO retains mainframe data indefinitely, which increases the long-term exposure of personal and debt information beyond the period needed for collection and reporting.
The system relies on agency-provided data and periodic updates, so incorrect or stale debt records could be used to bill or report on the wrong amount or status.
Debt-related notices are generated from personal data and used by agencies to notify individuals, so any inaccuracy or disclosure in those notices could affect the wrong person or reveal debt status.
Limit collection and display of SSNs and other direct identifiers to the minimum necessary for billing and debt collection, and mask them wherever full values are not required.
Continue enforcing least-privilege access and periodic access reviews so each user retains only the minimum agency data needed for their duties.
Use formal data-sharing agreements and role-based restrictions for each external recipient to limit what data is exchanged and for what purpose.
Require contractor handling of reports to follow documented secure processing procedures and verify encryption before any transmission.
Provide individuals a controlled process to request their records through the responsible agency and to seek correction of inaccurate debt information.
Apply records disposition rules to eliminate or archive mainframe data when no longer needed, rather than retaining it indefinitely.
Strengthen reconciliation and validation checks with routine exception review for mismatched or stale records before they are used for billing.
Add a notice quality review step before debt notices are sent so reports are checked for correct recipient, amount, and status.
The system may over-collect PII from correspondence, including extra details that individuals voluntarily include even when they are not needed to process the request.
Historical correspondence can be searched and analyzed with NLP and machine learning, which may surface or infer more personal information than is necessary for the current business purpose.
The centralized workflow lets multiple users and user groups access package records and track movement, creating a risk of unnecessary internal exposure of PII.
The system maintains physical and email addresses and phone numbers for correspondence, so unauthorized or excessive access could expose direct contact information to misuse or unwanted contact.
Reports, dashboards, and search data about workflow status and congressional inquiries may reveal sensitive correspondence patterns or case details beyond the original contact information.
Limit collection and retention to the minimum correspondence details needed to process the request, and redact or exclude unnecessary volunteered personal information before storing it.
Restrict NLP and ML search and analysis to approved use cases, and suppress or mask unnecessary personal details in returned results and reports.
Enforce the stated role-based access controls so users can access only the package records and metadata needed for their specific duties.
Apply access controls and handling rules to physical addresses, email addresses, and phone numbers so they are used only for correspondence purposes.
Restrict dashboards, reports, and workflow metadata views to authorized staff and minimize the detail shown in status and inquiry reporting.
The system holds sensitive civil rights complaint records that could expose complainants if accessed improperly.
Contractor access creates a risk that non-federal personnel could view or mishandle complainant PII.
Internet-connected hosting increases the chance of unauthorized remote access or interception of complaint data.
The system may retain complaint records longer than necessary if destruction is not tightly controlled.
Collecting information by mail, email, telephone, and interviews can expose data during intake if those channels are not protected.
Broad access by approved users and management could lead to unnecessary internal exposure of complaint details.
Using complaint data for tracking and reporting could reveal individuals through trends or case patterns if reports are not sufficiently aggregated.
Restrict complaint records to designated users only and apply strict access logging and review.
Apply contractor-specific least-privilege access, confidentiality obligations, and periodic access recertification.
Encrypt data in transit and harden the Internet-facing gateway and firewalls with continuous monitoring and patching.
Define a specific retention schedule and automate deletion when the approved retention period ends.
Use secure intake procedures for mail, email, telephone, and interviews, including verification before entry and secure handling of paper and electronic submissions.
Limit access by role so users see only the minimum complaint information needed for their duties.
Publish only aggregated or de-identified reporting outputs and suppress small-cell counts where necessary.
Users can enter unrestricted free-text personal information in the "About Me" field, which may lead to collection of unnecessary or sensitive personal data.
Optional profile photos combined with a name create identifiable personal profiles that increase the risk of unnecessary identification and exposure.

The system collects address information and miscellaneous identification numbers such as parking permit and building permit numbers, which could expose location or permit-related details if mishandled.
User information is shared across multiple USDA administrative domains through dashboards and reports, creating a risk of broader internal dissemination than necessary.

Transmitting data to the USDA Data Lake and then publishing Tableau dashboards creates a risk of secondary use or aggregation of personal data beyond the original parking-permit and service-request purposes.
Department contractors can access the system, which creates a risk of unauthorized viewing or misuse if access is not tightly limited to the minimum necessary.
The system retains records under a general records schedule based on subject matter, which may keep personal data longer than needed for the specific user purpose.
Because the system is web-based and cloud-based, personal data is exposed to the risks of cloud or web application compromise if security controls fail.
Restrict or remove the free-text "About Me" field, or implement validation and guidance to prevent entry of unnecessary personal or sensitive information.
Keep profile photos optional and provide clear notice that photos are PII when combined with a name.
Limit collection of address information and permit numbers to only what is necessary for parking permits and request handling.
Apply role-based access controls and publish only the minimum necessary data in Tableau dashboards and reports.
Before loading data into the USDA Data Lake, segregate or redact personal data that is not needed for reporting.
Require that contractors retain security clearances and specific authorization, and limit their access to the lowest level needed for their duties.
Apply subject-matter-specific retention and destruction procedures to ensure records are deleted when no longer needed.
Maintain strong cloud and web security controls for the hosted system, including secure transmission methods already used for data transfers.
The system collects and maintains a broad set of identity and employment data for cardholders and visitors, which increases the privacy impact if the data is misused or exposed.

Visitor background-check and registration data may be collected for USDA NCR Headquarters visitors, creating a privacy risk for non-employees who may not expect their information to be used beyond entry control.
Manual collection of non-authoritative data at card issuance can lead to inaccurate or inconsistent records, which may cause improper access decisions or incorrect identity records.
Internal sharing of card read activity and employee status for executive management and credit card disabling creates a secondary-use risk beyond the original physical-access purpose.
Daily transfer of limited ePACS data to EDAPT and delivery of the Fleet report by email increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure during internal transmission or downstream dashboard use.
Contractors with access to the system could view sensitive access-control records, creating a risk of insider misuse or excessive access.
Rare external sharing of ePACS data still creates a risk that personal information could leave USDA and be exposed or used in ways not anticipated by the data subject.
Retaining live and archived access records for 5.5 years increases the duration of exposure and the amount of historical movement data available if the system is breached or misused.
Limit collection and retention to the minimum fields needed to issue and validate physical access credentials.
Restrict visitor data collection to the NCR Headquarters rollout and apply the same access controls and approval limits used for other ePACS data.
Validate manually collected issuance data against authoritative sources before it is stored or used to make access decisions.
Use only summary or aggregated access-activity outputs for executive management and disable credit cards only from the minimum employee-status data needed.
Replace email delivery of the Fleet report with a secure file transfer or similarly controlled channel and restrict dashboard access to authorized users only.
Apply role-based, need-to-know access reviews for contractors and remove contractor access when it is no longer required.
Keep the existing director and Office of General Counsel approval requirement for any external disclosure and document the routine use basis before release.
Periodically review whether the 5.5-year retention period is still necessary and purge records at the end of the approved schedule.
The system collects personally identifiable information from USDA employees, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of employee travel and identity data.
Enterprise-wide use and shared access by authorized USDA agency users increase the risk that more people than necessary can see travel and voucher data.
Transmitting authorization and voucher data to FMMI creates a risk of disclosure or compromise while the data moves between systems.
The system's retention of user and billing data for years creates a risk that personal information will remain available longer than needed and be exposed in a later breach.
The system analyzes traveler preferences and creates predictive patterns, which can reveal behavioral profiles about employees beyond the immediate travel transaction.
Storing traveler preferences in profiles for future reference creates a risk that sensitive preference data will be reused in ways the employee did not expect.
Limit collection and access to only the PII needed for travel, booking, and voucher processing, and protect it with the existing role-based and transport protections.
Enforce least-privilege role assignments so users only see the travel data needed for their job.
Continue to encrypt and authenticate all data transfers to FMMI and other systems using the stated TLS and session protections.
Periodically review retention to ensure only records required by the approved schedule are kept and delete expired records promptly.
Provide clear notice and user controls for preference-based profiling, and limit predictive use to the stated travel convenience purpose.
Allow travelers to review and edit stored preferences and remove them when no longer needed.

Travel, authorization, voucher, and bill-related personal data could be exposed to unauthorized users because the system is used enterprise-wide and supports access by authorized USDA agency users and internal users.
Personal and financial travel data could be intercepted or disclosed in transit when shared to other systems, including the financial management system.
The system retains user and bill-related information for long periods, which increases the impact of any later misuse, breach, or unauthorized internal access.
The system creates and retains predictive patterns from traveler preferences, which could reveal behavioral details about employees beyond the original travel transaction.
Mobile and web access expands the attack surface for account compromise and unauthorized access to travel records.
Limit access to the minimum necessary through restrictive roles and periodic access reviews.
Protect all data transfers with strong encryption and authenticated transport controls.
Apply and enforce the approved NARA/USDA retention schedule and delete records when the retention period ends.
Provide a clear privacy notice and limit preference-based profiling to travel-booking functions only.
Harden web and mobile access with multifactor authentication and session protections.
The system holds highly sensitive personal and financial data that could expose individuals to identity theft or financial fraud if accessed improperly.
The system's debt-collection and payroll functions could lead to unfair or harmful decisions if the recorded data is inaccurate or incomplete.
Keeping the data for 10 years increases the period during which the information can be exposed, misused, or breached.
Using the system to record, process, and report personnel and payroll data for multiple agencies can create a risk of unnecessary internal disclosure across organizations.
Collecting statistical information alongside identifiable records may create a risk that individuals are re-identified from supposedly aggregated data.
Restrict access to the sensitive personal and financial fields to authorized personnel only and apply strong authentication and auditing.
Implement data quality checks and a human review process before debt-collection or payroll actions are taken.
Periodically review records during the 10-year retention period and delete or archive information when it is no longer needed under the approved schedule.
Limit interagency reporting to the minimum necessary data elements and document the purpose of each disclosure.
Use de-identified or aggregated statistical outputs whenever possible so individuals are not directly identifiable in reports.
The system retains appellant and case information indefinitely, which increases the chance of unnecessary long-term exposure of personal data.
The system stores audio files and case determinations together with personally identifiable information, creating a risk of exposing sensitive case content if the system is misused or breached.
Appellants can view their transaction history and submitted documents through the eFile portal, which exposes residence and contact information to any account holder who gains access to the portal.
Only a secure login page is mentioned for collection and access, so unauthorized access remains a risk if authentication or account controls are weak.
Contractor employees have access to the system, which broadens the number of people who can view appellant data and increases insider access risk.
Reports generated from the system may expose personally identifiable information to management, creating a risk of unnecessary internal disclosure through analytics or review outputs.
The system collects data from public eFile submissions, so appellants may provide more personal information than is necessary for case tracking.
Establish and enforce a retention schedule that limits storage to the minimum period needed for case tracking and reporting, with secure deletion after that period.
Apply role-based access controls and encryption to audio files, determinations, and PII so only authorized personnel can access sensitive case content.
Limit the eFile portal to the minimum information needed for appellants to track their own appeal and protect access with strong authentication and session controls.
Add stronger authentication and account monitoring for the secure web interface, including measures such as multi-factor authentication and login anomaly detection.
Apply least-privilege access reviews for contractor accounts and periodically validate that contractor access remains necessary for their duties.
Restrict report distribution and suppress or mask PII in management reports unless the data is required for a specific operational need.
Provide clear submission guidance and form design that discourages appellants from entering unnecessary personal information in eFile requests.

The system holds highly sensitive personal and employment data, including names, SSNs, time and attendance records, teleworking agreement information, and payroll data, so a breach or misuse could expose individuals to identity theft or improper disclosure of work and payroll details.

Multiple parties can access or enter data on behalf of individuals, including HR staff, agency payroll/personnel offices, contractors, and system/security officers, creating a risk of unauthorized or overbroad access if role controls fail.

WebTA shares PII with other USDA systems and transmits certified time and attendance data to the PPS TIME application, which creates a risk that data will be disclosed more broadly than necessary across internal systems.
Agencies determine the use and sharing of the information, so privacy protections may vary by customer agency and create inconsistent handling of the same records.
Users may run predefined and custom reports against the data, which can reveal more information than needed if report access is not tightly limited.
Information is retained under NARA schedules and customer agency requirements, which may keep PII available for long periods and increase the impact of any later misuse or breach.

Limit collection and display of SSNs and other sensitive fields to only what is required for time, attendance, and payroll processing, and mask them wherever full values are not operationally necessary.
