Continue enforcing role-based access with least privilege and unique user credentials for all users, including HR staff and contractors, and periodically review those roles for necessity.
Restrict inter-system sharing to only the fields required by each receiving system and document each transfer so that downstream systems receive the minimum necessary PII.
Apply a uniform agency-wide privacy and access standard for WebTA data handling, rather than relying solely on each customer agency's discretion.
Restrict custom reporting to authorized personnel and apply output controls so reports expose only the data elements needed for the approved purpose.
Periodically review retained records and purge or archive them according to the approved records schedule and customer agency requirements as soon as they are no longer needed.

Customer PII may be exposed when it is transmitted internally by email to SME contacts, because email is a less controlled sharing channel than the core system. This creates a risk of misdelivery or unauthorized disclosure of names, addresses, phone numbers, and case details.

PII may be exposed through internal sharing to all USDA Mission Areas for escalated inquiries, which broadens access beyond the original contact center need. This increases the number of people who can see sensitive contact and inquiry information.

The system retains information for at least seven years, which can preserve personal data longer than needed for a customer inquiry process. Long retention increases the impact of any later misuse, breach, or unauthorized access.

There is currently no purging or archiving setup for the PII available through third-party websites or applications, so personal data may accumulate without timely deletion. This can leave older records exposed even when they are no longer operationally necessary.

The system allows contractors to have access, which creates a risk that more people than necessary can view customer PII. Even with role-based controls, contractor access expands the population with potential access to sensitive records.

PII is collected through multiple channels, including webform, email, chat, and phone, which increases the chance of inconsistent handling across intake paths. Different channels can create uneven privacy protections for the same personal information.

The system collects a combination of name, address, and phone number in Salesforce, which can directly identify customers and link them to inquiry history. If accessed improperly, this set of data could reveal both identity and the nature of the customer's contact with USDA.
Replace or supplement email transmission of PII with a secure internal case-sharing workflow that keeps the information inside the authenticated Salesforce environment and logs access.
Limit internal sharing of PII to only the specific mission area personnel needed for each escalated inquiry, rather than all USDA Mission Areas.
Apply a records retention schedule that deletes or archives customer inquiry records as soon as the approved business need ends, rather than keeping them for the full minimum period by default.
Implement automated purging or archiving for third-party application data on a recurring schedule and verify it before the pilot phase ends.
Tighten contractor access approvals and periodically review role-based permissions and EEMS access assignments to confirm contractors retain only the access needed for their duties.
Standardize privacy controls and disclosure notices across webform, email, chat, and telephony intake so each channel handles customer information consistently.
Minimize collection to only the contact details needed to resolve the inquiry and avoid retaining unnecessary combinations of identity and case information.

The system creates broad surveillance of employees, contractors, visitors, and passersby across USDA facilities and nearby areas, which can chill movement and activity even when no wrongdoing is suspected.
The cameras may capture sensitive personal data beyond ordinary video, including facial images, license plates, and driver’s license information such as names, addresses, and dates of birth.

The system can record people on public streets and use zoom, low-light, and tracking features to follow individuals, which expands surveillance beyond USDA-controlled spaces and can capture bystanders who are not the focus of security operations.
Video may be used for disciplinary actions as well as criminal investigations, creating a secondary-use risk that footage collected for security could be repurposed against employees or others.
Footage can be shared outside USDA with federal agencies and local law enforcement, which increases the risk of broader dissemination and loss of control over who sees identifiable video.
Contractors and select non-employees may access the system, which creates an insider-access risk if access is broader than necessary or if non-employees view footage unrelated to their duties.

Footage is retained for up to six months and may be kept longer when tied to suspected criminal activity, which increases the risk of prolonged exposure and secondary use of historical surveillance data.

Because the system can identify individuals through video and other captured data such as license plates, there is a risk of mistaken identification or overreliance on footage in investigations and prosecutions.
Limit camera placement and viewing practices to security-relevant areas only and continue avoiding locations where people have a reasonable expectation of privacy.

Apply data minimization controls such as limiting zoom, masking where feasible, and restricting use of captured license-plate or identity details to cases where they are needed for security or investigations.
Constrain manual tracking, automatic tracking, and low-light monitoring to documented security incidents or active threats, with oversight of when those features are used.
Restrict exports and secondary use of footage to documented criminal or disciplinary matters with supervisory approval and a stated need-to-know.
Share footage externally only in response to formal requests and only the minimum relevant segment needed for the specific investigation or prosecution.
Keep contractor and non-employee access tightly limited to approved roles, and review access regularly to ensure it remains necessary.
Enforce the six-month automatic deletion limit except for footage formally preserved for an active investigation, with supervisor approval for any extension.
Use footage as investigative leads only and require corroboration before making decisions based on identity matches from video or license-plate data.
Customer feedback can include directly identifying information, creating a risk that people are identifiable from comments or associated metadata even when the tool is meant for feedback collection.
The system may collect more identifying information than needed for general feedback, increasing the risk of unnecessary exposure of personal details.
Broad internal sharing of dashboard data across leadership and program staff could expose sensitive feedback to more employees than needed.
A small number of users can access all data across all mission areas, which increases the risk of cross-program overexposure and unnecessary linkage of feedback.
Contractors may have access to the system, which raises the risk of disclosure beyond federal staff with a mission need.

The system supports migration from multiple existing USDA tools into one cohesive product, which creates a risk of combining data in ways that increase identifiability or reuse beyond the original context.
Using demographic and geographic analysis of feedback could lead to profiling or inference about groups or individuals from customer sentiment data.
Retention governance is incomplete because the retention period has not been approved, creating a risk that data may be kept longer than intended or inconsistently disposed of.

The system relies on role- and permission-based access controls, but the presence of broad dashboards and all-data access means misconfiguration or excessive permissions could expose PII to unauthorized users.
Limit collection of name, email address, and zip code to only cases where follow-up contact is explicitly requested, and keep PII out of standard feedback fields.

The system keeps producers’ election-related records permanently, increasing the chance that older personal data will remain available longer than needed.
County office staff enter producer data, so mistakes or incomplete entries could cause incorrect eligibility decisions or inaccurate election records.
The system uses producer information to identify who may vote in committee elections, which could reveal a producer’s participation or eligibility status in a sensitive local election process.
The system stores the current organizational structure of elected COC members and election results, which could expose governance information about individuals if accessed inappropriately.
Although the system says it does not share outside USDA, any unauthorized disclosure outside the department would expose producer data beyond the intended use.
Limit access to race and ethnicity data to only personnel with a documented need to know and enforce role-based access controls.
Review whether all permanent records must remain indefinitely and, where permitted by the records schedule, minimize retention to the approved period.
Implement validation and review checks for county office data entry before records are used for eligibility or ballot generation.
Limit visibility of eligibility lists and related election data to authorized election staff and use the information only for the stated election purposes.
Apply access controls and audit logging to committee member and election result records so only authorized users can view or change them.
Maintain the stated boundary of no external disclosure and monitor for unauthorized export or transmission of producer records.
The system stores highly sensitive identifiers and financial information, so a breach or misuse could expose people to identity theft or financial harm.
Because the warehouse combines farm, loan, commodity, human resources, and financial data into one reporting environment, it increases the impact of any unauthorized access or misuse.
Internal sharing of PII across multiple agencies and through batch processes can disclose more information than needed or expose data during transfer.
External disclosures to other entities, including IRS, Treasury, a university, and Dunn and Bradstreet, create a risk of secondary use or disclosure beyond the original collection purpose.
The system uses data for congressional, program level, and end user reporting, which may reveal personal details to users who do not need full-identifiable information.
Retaining the data under the NARA schedule for an extended period may keep personal information available longer than needed, increasing the chance of later misuse or breach.
Encrypt sensitive identifiers and account data at rest and in transit, and restrict access to users with a documented need to know.
Apply role-based access controls and field-level access restrictions so users only see the data needed for their specific reporting function.
Use secure batch-transfer controls, including integrity checks and access logging, for all internal data exchanges.
Require data-sharing agreements and data minimization for each external disclosure, especially for one-time or validation-only exchanges.
Provide reporting users with aggregated or de-identified outputs whenever identifiable data is not necessary.
Periodically review retained records and delete or archive them according to the approved NARA schedule and any approved deviations.

The system stores sensitive identity and financial data that could cause significant harm if exposed or misused, including SSN/TIN, bank account numbers, routing numbers, and signatures. This creates a high-impact privacy risk because the data supports payments, debt collection, and tax reporting for many individuals.

Public-facing and producer-accessible applications increase the risk of unauthorized access to personal financial information. If authentication or session protections fail, producers or outsiders could view payments, collections, debt, or banking information.

County office employees and producers can view financial information in the same format, which can expose more detail than necessary to users who only need limited information. This raises a risk of overexposure of personal financial records within the USDA environment.

Contractors have access to the system, which creates a risk of insider misuse or accidental disclosure of personal data. Even with need-to-know controls, contractor access expands the number of people handling sensitive records.

The system sends delinquent debt status to commercial credit bureaus, which can affect individuals' creditworthiness and expose debt information beyond the original payment context. This creates a privacy risk because debt data is used for a secondary purpose with external reporting consequences.

The system transmits payment and debt information to Treasury for offset, wage garnishment, and referral to collection agencies, which may reveal financial distress and debt status. These disclosures can affect individuals' privacy and financial standing outside the originating program.

Permanent retention of records increases the risk that outdated or unnecessary personal information will remain available indefinitely. Long-term retention magnifies the impact of any future breach, misuse, or unauthorized access.

The system stores and processes images and faxed or scanned materials, which may include full financial documents and signatures. Document imaging and manual ingestion can create a risk that sensitive information is captured more broadly than needed or retained in image form longer than expected.

The system generates letters and statements for producers, including debt and tax-related notices, which may be exposed if mailed or handled improperly. This creates a risk of disclosure through correspondence containing personal financial information.
Limit access to sensitive fields to only users with a demonstrated need to know and maintain role-based approval for access.
Use strong authentication and tightly controlled update permissions for the public-facing banking and assignment functions.
Apply role-based access controls so county office employees can only see the minimum financial detail needed to assist producers.
Continue mandatory background investigations, eAuthentication, and nondisclosure obligations for contractors before granting access.
Restrict credit bureau reporting to only the delinquent debt information necessary for the authorized purpose and maintain encrypted transmission.
Limit Treasury and collection-related disclosures to the minimum information needed to perform offsets, garnishment, and referrals.
Implement periodic review and disposal controls for records that no longer need to be retained, even if the schedule allows permanent retention.
Apply strict handling controls to scanned, faxed, and imaged documents, including limiting who can upload and retrieve them.
Use secure mailing and statement controls for producer letters and tax notices so only the intended recipient receives the information.

The system stores identifiable employee information that could be exposed if access controls are weak or misconfigured. Even limited fields like name and mailing address can create privacy harm if unauthorized users can view authorization records.

The system maintains authorization data about employees’ roles, groups, offices, and attributes, which could reveal sensitive access patterns or job relationships if improperly accessed. That information can be used to infer internal responsibilities and system privileges.

The system retains information indefinitely, increasing the chance that outdated or unnecessary employee information remains available longer than needed. Long-term retention also expands the window for unauthorized access or secondary use.

Administrators can manage security access rights in real time, which creates a risk of excessive privilege or mistaken role assignment affecting employee data access. If role changes are not carefully controlled, users may gain access they should not have.

The system is designed to support access to business applications, so any compromise of the role-based access control function could broaden access across multiple applications. A failure in this central authorization service could therefore affect many users’ privacy at once.
Enforce least-privilege access and strong authentication for all users who can view or administer authorization records.
Limit visibility of role, group, office, and attribute data to personnel with a documented need to know, and log all access to those records.
Periodically review whether permanently retained records are still required and archive or suppress access to records no longer needed for operations.
Require approval workflows or dual review for high-impact role changes and regularly reconcile assigned roles against authoritative personnel records.
Harden the central authorization service with monitoring, change control, and periodic security testing because it supports access to business applications.

The system stores highly sensitive personal data, so any unauthorized access or exposure could cause significant harm to individuals. The data includes direct identifiers and especially sensitive categories such as financial, health, biometric, and criminal history information.

Permanent retention increases the privacy impact of any breach or improper access because the records remain available indefinitely. Long-term storage also increases the chance that outdated or unnecessary personal information will persist beyond operational need.

Browser-based client access to stored images can create a risk of unauthorized viewing if access controls are weak or misconfigured. Because users can retrieve images from a network device managed by the server, improper authorization could expose records to staff who do not need them.

Workflow functions can expose personal data to more people or systems than are necessary for simple storage and retrieval. When the system controls workflows associated with financial information, data may be routed through multiple processing steps, increasing the chance of internal overexposure.

Imported faxed, scanned, and emailed documents may contain inaccurate, incomplete, or misdirected personal information, which could lead to improper storage or retrieval of the wrong record. If the wrong document is imaged or indexed, individuals may be associated with incorrect financial or identity information.

The system holds historical archive images, including records that are no longer actively updated, which may increase the chance of unnecessary continued access to old personal information. Historical records can still reveal sensitive details about debtors, claims, and check images long after the original business need has passed.

The system stores financial records, debts, debtors, and other information, so unauthorized disclosure could enable financial fraud, identity theft, or reputational harm. The presence of account-related and debt-related data makes the consequences of exposure especially serious.
Restrict access to the sensitive imaging records to only authorized users with a documented need to know, and enforce role-based permissions for the different subsystems and document types.
Implement a records review process to confirm whether any subsets of the indefinite-retention records can be archived, minimized, or disposed of when no longer required by the approved schedule.
Require strong authentication and least-privilege authorization for browser-based retrieval, and log all image access so unauthorized viewing can be detected and investigated.
Limit workflow visibility so each user or role can see only the records needed for that workflow step, and separate workflow functions from broader retrieval permissions where possible.
Add validation and quality checks for scanned, faxed, and emailed documents before they are indexed, including verification of document-to-person matching and correction of indexing errors.
Apply stricter access controls and periodic access reviews for historical archive systems so only users with a specific archival or investigative need can retrieve old records.
Protect financial and debt records with encryption and monitoring controls for storage and retrieval, especially for the server and database components that manage document indexes and workflow.

Users may see more personal information than is necessary for the PSS task because the system includes names, addresses, application and contract identifiers, and multiple eligibility and status fields tied to individual records.
Exporting work lists to Excel can create uncontrolled local copies of personally identifiable information on user devices.
E-mail alerts can disclose personally identifiable information through a channel that may be forwarded, stored, or accessed outside the system.
Users with access to PT-FM can reach FA Tracker data, so a broader-than-necessary access grant could expose records to people who only need limited information.
Contractors may access the system and therefore view PII, creating a risk of misuse or accidental disclosure by non-federal users.
The system relies on data replicated from SCIMS, so any stale or inaccurate copied information could affect individuals’ records and work-list decisions.
The system includes demographic-related information from SCIMS, which can increase sensitivity if used or viewed beyond the stated conservation-program purpose.
Long retention of records increases the period during which personal information remains available for internal access, disclosure, or breach.
Limit the work lists to the minimum fields needed for PSS intervention and keep the current minimal-display approach.
Restrict or disable Excel export for records containing PII, or require stronger controls such as approved secure storage and audit logging for any exported file.
Limit e-mail alerts to the smallest possible data set and avoid including direct identifiers where feasible.
Keep access tied to role-based, need-to-know authorization and verify that FA Tracker roles are narrower than PT-FM access where possible.
Continue requiring background investigations, Level 2 eAuthentication, NDAs, and Rules of Behavior for contractors, and enforce those conditions with periodic review.
Use procedures to reconcile replicated data against the source system and flag records that may be outdated before they are used in work lists.
Restrict access to demographic reports and related SCIMS-derived fields to authorized users with a documented need.
Apply records disposition schedules consistently and delete records when the approved retention period ends.
External users can access and review their program information through the public interface, creating a risk that weak authentication or authorization could expose other participants' data.
The system holds tax identification numbers and payment bank information, which are sensitive financial identifiers that could be misused if disclosed or accessed inappropriately.
Reports and nightly files are used by internal teams and submitted to auditors and other departments, creating a risk of over-disclosure beyond the minimum necessary information.
Department contractors have access to the system, which creates a risk of unauthorized access, misuse, or secondary disclosure by non-federal personnel.
The system retains information indefinitely, increasing the chance that data will be exposed, misused, or kept longer than needed for the original purpose.
Enforce strong role-based access controls and authentication for the public interface so users can only enter and review their own program information.
Limit access to tax identification numbers and payment bank information to only personnel who need it, and mask or redact those fields in reports and screens where full values are not required.
Apply data minimization and disclosure review before generating or distributing reports and nightly files to ensure only necessary fields are included.
Require contractor access to be limited by least privilege and subject to monitoring and periodic access reviews.
Use a records review process to confirm that permanently retained records remain necessary and are protected with strong safeguards over time.

Uploaded files may contain highly sensitive personal data, so unauthorized disclosure could expose identity, financial, employment, criminal, or signature information. Because the system stores documents rather than collecting only narrow fields, a single file can reveal extensive PII.

Internal and external collaboration can expose PII to more people than necessary if sharing is not tightly limited to a need-to-know basis. The system is intended to support sharing with employees, contractors, affiliates, partners, and customers.

Manual sharing of files creates a risk of human error, such as sending or granting access to the wrong file or recipient. Since sharing is performed by authorized users rather than automatically controlled by the system, mistakes may be harder to detect.

External partners and contractors may access PII through the system, which increases the risk of disclosure outside USDA if access is misused or improperly managed. The system explicitly allows access for partners and contractors consistent with their roles and responsibilities.
PII stored in a third-party cloud service may be exposed if the vendor mishandles security or access controls. The agency states that third-party PII will be maintained and secured by the vendor.

PII available through third-party applications is not periodically purged, which can leave sensitive information exposed longer than necessary. Longer availability increases the chance of unauthorized access over time.

Long retention periods can keep personal data available for years after it is no longer needed for a current purpose. The system retains information for five to ten years, and in some cases as long as the individual qualifies for conservation programs.

User profile information derived from LDAP may be inaccurate or outdated if users do not update it, which can cause incorrect identity or access records. The system also allows users to update their own PII, which could introduce inconsistent records if not validated.
Restrict file access with role-based authorization and strong encryption for stored and transmitted documents.
Limit sharing to authorized users with a need-to-know and enforce role-based access controls for collaboration.
Add stronger sharing safeguards such as mandatory recipient verification or approval before a file can be shared externally.
Constrain contractor and partner access to the minimum permissions needed for their assigned tasks and review those permissions regularly.
Require the vendor to maintain documented security controls and oversight for any PII hosted in the third-party service.
Implement periodic purging of PII stored in third-party applications when it is no longer needed.
Apply and enforce records schedules so files are deleted or archived as soon as the approved retention period ends.
Validate profile updates before they are accepted, especially when users modify their own PII.

User information is transmitted through the portal to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov, creating a risk that sensitive application data could be exposed if those communications are intercepted or mishandled.
The system stores a producer’s DOL case number for 90 days, which can create a link between a user and their inquiry even if the system says it does not store other PII.
Because the portal is a single entry point to multiple agencies, users may not clearly understand which organization is collecting and using their information at each step.
The system depends on third-party federal services for authentication and processing, so privacy protections may vary across Login.gov, DOL, and USCIS rather than being controlled solely by USDA.
Although the system says no PII is stored, it still expects PII to be present within the system boundary, which creates a risk of accidental logging, caching, or other unintended retention.
Continue to require HTTPS for all communications between FPAC CASP / H2A and the external agencies, and verify that strong TLS configurations are enforced end to end.
Minimize the stored case-number record by keeping it only as long as needed for the inquiry workflow and then deleting it promptly at the end of the 90-day period or sooner if no longer needed.
Provide a clear notice at the single entry point explaining which agency collects each piece of information and how it will be used before the user is routed onward.
Limit the data shared with Login.gov, DOL, and USCIS to the minimum needed for authentication and application processing, and document those interfaces.
Prevent accidental retention by ensuring that logs, caches, and temporary files do not capture user PII or other transmitted application data.

DRMS contains highly sensitive personal and financial information that could expose individuals if access controls fail or are misused. The stored records can include SSNs, tax IDs, bank routing numbers, deposit account numbers, and other detailed PII in scanned documents.

TeamMate+ contains audit materials about programs, administrative areas, and customers that may include personal and operational details, creating a privacy risk if those records are exposed. The system may hold information from many FPAC divisions and external parties, including private individuals and other governments.

Many staff can upload and search DRMS documents, which creates a risk of unnecessary internal access to personal records. Although access is role-based, the system states that all staff can search documents within their organizational role and rights.

Specialized DRMS users can perform unconstrained searching for legal and audit purposes, which increases the risk of overbroad access to personal information. This capability is specifically available for records managers and legal staff.
The system allows contractor access, which raises the risk of privacy harm from a larger population of users handling PII. Contractors are explicitly permitted access if they have a need-to-know.

DRMS retains records for long periods and many applications retain information indefinitely, which increases the risk of unnecessary prolonged exposure of PII. The retention strategy includes permanent records and retention that can extend beyond ten years.

TeamMate+ audit records can be uploaded directly by customers or by auditors, which creates a risk that incorrect or excessive personal information could be entered into the system. The system relies on human upload paths rather than only controlled automated ingestion.
Continue enforcing need-to-know access controls and least-privilege authorization for all users handling DRMS and TeamMate+ records.
Limit audit record access to the Internal Auditing Branch and keep TeamMate+ information for internal use only.
Maintain role-based permissions so staff can only upload and search documents within their organizational role and rights.
Restrict unconstrained searching to records managers and legal staff only, and require it only for approved audit, legal discovery, litigation hold, or FOIA purposes.
Apply the same documented access control procedures and need-to-know review to contractors before granting access.
Retain records only for the approved NARA schedule and avoid indefinite retention unless a specific records schedule requires it.
Require review of uploaded audit materials to ensure only necessary information is entered and that incorrect completion or incompleteness is corrected before use.

The system holds highly sensitive identifiers, including SSNs and EINs, which would create significant harm if exposed through any compromise of the platform or its applications. Because the platform hosts many HVA applications, a breach could affect a large amount of identity-linked crop insurance data at once.

Data is shared with an internal fraud-analysis group, creating a risk that PII will be used more broadly than needed for eligibility, claims, or reimbursement purposes. Even legitimate investigative access can expand exposure if not tightly limited.

External sharing with Approved Insurance Providers exposes PII outside USDA, increasing the chance of unauthorized disclosure or misuse by non-federal entities. The system sends SSNs and EINs back to the same entities that collected them, so any weakness at the AIP side affects the data subjects.

The system retains most application records indefinitely, which increases the duration of exposure and the amount of historical personal data available if the system is breached or misused. Long retention also raises the chance that data will outlive its original need.

The system relies on multiple contractors and many applications, which can broaden access to PII and make least-privilege enforcement harder. More users and more components increase the chance of unauthorized internal access or accidental disclosure.

The system uses hard copy forms and e-forms submitted through AIPs, which creates collection and transmission risk before the data reaches the platform. Paper and intermediary handling can lead to loss, misrouting, or incomplete security controls.

Because the system uses PII to determine eligibility and payment calculations, inaccurate data could cause improper benefit decisions or incorrect reimbursement amounts. Errors in submitted policy data could affect producers, agents, and loss adjusters financially.

The system shares data for actuarial trend analysis and program viability, which can create a risk of using personal information for purposes beyond the individual’s immediate insurance transaction. Even if permitted, this increases privacy sensitivity because data may be repurposed for broader program analytics.
Enforce strong role-based access controls and encryption for SSNs, EINs, and other sensitive identifiers, with regular review of who can view or export them.
Limit the fraud-analysis team to the minimum data necessary and log all queries, exports, and case reviews for periodic oversight.
Continue to require encrypted transmission to AIPs and verify that AIP access is controlled and limited to the policies they collected.
Apply records-management rules to purge or archive data when no longer required, instead of retaining all applications indefinitely.
Use least-privilege access for contractors and separate duties across applications so contractor access is limited to specific functions and datasets.
Standardize secure submission procedures for hard copy and e-form intake, including validation and secure handling by AIPs before transmission to RMA.
Continue and strengthen validation and review of submitted policy data so errors are detected before eligibility or payment decisions are made.
Document and limit analytic use of PII to the stated program purposes, and prefer de-identified or aggregated data for actuarial trend analysis where possible.

The system may collect identifiable personal information from people who interact with CFPB on social media, creating a risk of unnecessary exposure of names, usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, geographic information, or demographic information.
Because the system uses social media platforms that are controlled by third parties, users’ information may be subject to privacy practices and exposure outside CFPB’s direct control.
Public interactions on social media can reveal PII in a way that makes individual users more visible to others, including through posts, comments, usernames, or other platform metadata.
Collected PII could be retained or reused in ways that extend beyond the immediate social media interaction if not tightly limited to the stated purpose and SORN coverage.
If users do not clearly understand when PII is collected through social media, they may share more information than intended or without fully informed participation.
Limit collection and use of PII to only what is necessary for social media engagement.
Apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls to all social media interactions and collected data.
Provide clear notice to users that social media interactions may be public and may expose their information to others.
Use the System of Records Notice to govern any collected PII and keep it subject to the CFPB.006 records controls.
Offer opportunities for consent, access, and redress so users can understand and respond to CFPB’s handling of their information.
Public release of agency personnel names and contact details can expose individuals to unwanted contact, profiling, or other privacy harms because the dataset is openly available.
The locator tool and API let users download or share the dataset in multiple formats, which can make it easier to copy, aggregate, and republish the information at scale.
Third-party developers or lenders can build their own applications from the API, creating downstream uses of the public data that CFPB does not control.
ZIP codes entered by locator-tool users are collected and used for analysis, which creates a record of a user's search behavior and approximate location.
Consumerfinance.gov collects usage analytics such as visit timestamps, browser version, operating system, pages viewed, and time on site, which can support tracking or profiling of site visitors.
ZIP codes and analytics are being kept as permanent records until a retention schedule is approved, increasing the period during which user activity data can be exposed or misused.
Limit the public dataset to the minimum contact and organizational details needed for locating housing counselors, and keep the existing read-only access model.
Keep the tool's design that always returns ten closest results and prevent record-level isolation through the locator interface.
Publish clear reuse terms and developer guidance for API consumers so downstream applications handle the public data consistently and lawfully.
Collect only the ZIP code needed to return nearby counselors and avoid retaining it beyond the immediate search function unless needed for approved analytics.
Use only the non-identifying analytics necessary for website functionality, security, and usability evaluation, and avoid adding more detailed tracking data.
Approve and implement a NARA disposition schedule for consumerfinance.gov ZIP codes and analytics as soon as possible, then dispose of them according to that schedule.

The system can collect directly identifying and highly sensitive information, so a data breach or misuse could expose names, contact details, financial account numbers, biometric information, or health information. Even if some datasets are later stripped of direct identifiers, the remaining data can still be sensitive and personally revealing.

Matching records across datasets and using unique record locators can create new profiles or re-identify people from data that was not originally direct-identifying. This increases the risk that individuals become more identifiable than the source datasets intended.

The system uses PII to proxy population characteristics, weight samples, and generate survey frames, which can create inferred data about individuals or groups beyond the original collection purpose. Those inferences may affect how people are represented in research outputs even when the CFPB says it does not track individual habits.

Individuals may not receive notice from the CFPB because the data is collected from third parties, commercial sources, and public databases rather than directly from consumers. This creates a transparency risk because affected people may not know their information is being used for Market Research.

The system may share research results with the general public, the source of the data, and federal financial regulators, which creates a risk that supposedly aggregate outputs could still reveal information about small groups or unique cases. Even without direct identifiers, disclosure of detailed results can enable inference.

The CFPB may share information under applicable Privacy Act routine uses, which expands the potential for secondary disclosure beyond the core research purpose. This creates a risk that data could be used in ways not originally expected by the individuals whose information is included.

The records are retained indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which increases the chance of unnecessary long-term exposure, stale data, and future misuse. Longer retention also increases the window in which the data can be breached or repurposed.

The system includes information about the public, consumers, federal employees, contractors, and consultants, so data from different populations may be combined in one system. Mixing these groups can create context confusion and increase the risk that information about one group is used or interpreted in another group's context.
Limit collection to the minimum necessary and continue stripping direct identifiers before analysis whenever possible.
Use record matching only when necessary and keep matched datasets de-identified for research and analysis after linkage is complete.
Restrict use of PII-driven proxying and weighting to cases where it is necessary for the research purpose, and rely on aggregate outputs rather than individual-level outputs.
Provide CFPB notice or public-facing collection notices where feasible, rather than relying only on third parties to decide whether notice is required.
Review public and external research outputs to ensure they remain aggregated and cannot reasonably identify individuals before release.
Apply the disclosure limits in the CFPB’s confidential-information rules and applicable SORN routine uses before any external sharing.
Approve and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
Continue limiting access to personnel with a need to know and separate access controls by dataset or population where feasible.

People in the dataset could be re-identified or singled out because the public can query, filter, and download loan-level records even though direct identifiers are removed. The dataset includes detailed loan and property information that may still be linkable to a person or household.

Sensitive loan, property, and demographic-related information about applicants and borrowers is made public, which can expose financial circumstances and housing activity to anyone. The dataset includes application year, loan purpose and amount, action taken and denial reason, HOEPA flag, rate spread, and census tract information.

Location information in the dataset can reveal where a person lives or sought credit, increasing the risk of household identification and unwanted profiling. The inclusion of census tract, county, state, and property type makes geographic inference easier.

Because the CFPB republishes the dataset without independently verifying its accuracy and completeness, individuals may be exposed to incorrect or misleading public information about their loan activity. Errors could affect how the public interprets a person's borrowing history or denial reasons.

The dataset is available to the public, including federal and state agencies and private sector organizations, so third parties can reuse it for their own purposes without any authorization process. This broad redistribution increases the chance of secondary uses that may be adverse to the data subjects.

The system retains the dataset until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA, which may prolong exposure of public loan-level information. Longer retention increases the window for re-identification and secondary use.

The public API enables users to retrieve the dataset for their own applications or systems, which can facilitate bulk harvesting and automated reuse of the data. That increases the scale at which individuals' loan records can be copied and analyzed.
Continue and strengthen the redaction and modification of fields before publication to reduce the chance that a single record can be linked back to a person.
Limit the public dataset to only the information needed for the publication purpose and avoid adding any new fields or derived data that would increase sensitivity.
Keep geographic detail as coarse as possible in the published dataset and preserve the existing privacy redactions for location fields.
Use automated and manual quality checks before republication to catch errors in the source dataset and flag known limitations to users.
Publish clear user notices that the dataset is public and may be reused by third parties, along with guidance on the privacy limits of the data.
Adopt a NARA-approved retention schedule as soon as possible and delete or archive the dataset according to that schedule.
Maintain access controls and infrastructure protections for the non-public database layer that supports the API.

The system collects highly sensitive direct identifiers and special-category information, so a breach or misuse could expose respondents to identity theft, stigma, or other harms. The inclusion of SSNs, biometric information, and health or medical information increases the sensitivity of any disclosure.

Matching records and combining administrative data with response data can create new, more revealing profiles about respondents. Even if the final research dataset is de-identified, the linking process itself increases the chance of re-identification or unintended inference.

The system may use administrative data to identify potential survey recipients and to analyze nonresponse bias, which means people can be contacted or profiled based on third-party data they did not directly provide for this research. This creates a risk of using information beyond respondents' expectations or without sufficient notice.

Some systems and contractor/vendor transfers occur outside direct CFPB integration, which increases the risk of unauthorized access or transmission errors during data movement. Although encrypted tunnels and encrypted email are used, non-automated transfers still create exposure points.

External sharing of research products could still reveal respondents indirectly if aggregation, rounding, variable exclusion, or observation exclusion is insufficient. This is especially relevant when results are disseminated to the general public or when case studies or quotes are shared with consent.

The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which prolongs the period during which sensitive information could be accessed, breached, or repurposed. Long retention also increases the chance that data will outlive its original necessity.

The system includes populations such as lower-income and vulnerable consumers, older consumers, students, and people with health or public-benefits information, which raises the risk of disproportionate harm if data are disclosed or misused. These groups may be more affected by stigma, financial harm, or coercion.

The system may collect and use direct identifiers for follow-up, compensation, and matching, which creates a risk of function creep if identifiers are later used beyond those stated purposes. Any expansion of use would increase exposure without clear necessity for analysis.
Store direct identifying PII separately from research data and keep it secured with strict access controls.
Use de-identified copies of matched datasets for research and analysis after matching is complete.
Obtain respondent consent before collecting additional information from third parties and limit third-party data use to the stated research purposes.
Continue using encrypted tunnels and encrypted email for transfers between contractor/vendor systems and CFPB systems.
Apply disclosure-protection procedures to all external outputs, including aggregation, rounding, exclusion of some variables, and exclusion of observations.
Dispose of records according to an approved NARA records schedule as soon as the applicable schedule permits.
Apply disclosure-protection procedures and limit externally shared content so that sensitive population characteristics are not unnecessarily exposed.
Limit direct identifying PII to scheduling, follow-up, compensation, and record matching, and keep it separate from analysis data.
Individuals generally do not receive notice when their information is collected or how it will be used or disclosed, which reduces transparency and informed awareness.
The system can contain direct identifiers and sensitive information, creating a risk of unauthorized identification or re-identification if data are mishandled or linked.
Matching records across datasets and updating datasets can create more detailed profiles about individuals than any single source contains.
The Bureau may contact potential recipients of surveys using direct identifying PII, which could expose individuals to outreach they did not expect.
Market Research outputs may be shared with the general public and federal financial regulators, creating a risk of disclosure if aggregation is insufficient or if context allows inference.
The system retains records indefinitely until a NARA-approved disposition schedule exists, increasing the time during which data could be exposed or misused.
The system includes biometric and health or medical information, which could cause heightened harm if disclosed or used beyond the intended purpose.
Provide direct notice to individuals whenever practicable, and otherwise make the constructive notice more prominent and specific about collection, use, and disclosure.
Continue stripping direct identifying PII from Market Research datasets and limit access to only personnel with a need to know.
Limit record matching to cases where it is necessary for the stated research purpose and use de-identified copies after matching is complete.
Use direct identifying PII for survey outreach only when necessary and minimize the data used for contact to the smallest set needed.
Release only aggregate Market Research products and continue excluding direct identifying PII from public-facing outputs.
Adopt and obtain approval for a records disposition schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
Apply heightened safeguards and stricter access controls to biometric and health or medical information, including limiting its use to cases where it is necessary for the research purpose.

Direct identifiers and matching data could be used to link a person’s survey or response data back to them, revealing sensitive financial, demographic, or other personal information. The system explicitly contemplates matching records such as credit scores to response data and using direct identifiers for scheduling and matching.

The system may collect and process sensitive information, including biometric information and health or medical information, which could cause harm if disclosed or used beyond the stated purpose. It also includes financial and demographic information that can be highly sensitive when combined.

Third-party information from financial product or service providers can expand the amount of personal data held about participants and create privacy risks if the participant does not fully anticipate all linked information. The system says it may collect information from third parties with consent.

Information may be shared in un-aggregated form in some cases, which could expose response data to recipients and increase the chance of re-identification or misuse. The system says participants are notified and can choose whether to participate when such sharing occurs.

Products disclosed to the public may still be indirectly identifying if aggregation and suppression are insufficient, especially for small or unusual subgroups. The system states that public products may use aggregation, rounding, exclusion of variables, or exclusion of observations, but residual disclosure risk remains.

Records are retained indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which increases the duration over which personal information could be exposed, misused, or subject to future incompatible uses. The retention language indicates the records may remain in both computer and paper form for an extended period.

Website and online-tool usage data such as IP address, timestamps, browser version, operating system, pages viewed, and linked address can be used to profile or indirectly identify visitors if combined with other data. The system says this information is collected to enhance usability, protect against misuse, and understand decisions driving use of resources.

Access by CFPB personnel, contractors, or collaborating researchers could expose information beyond what each user needs if need-to-know and contractual controls are not effectively enforced. The system includes multiple internal and external collaborators and data transfers.
Keep direct identifying PII stored separately from response and administrative data, and perform matching only after obtaining the participant’s informed consent.
Limit collection to the information needed for the stated consumer education purpose and store any necessary direct identifiers separately from analysis data.
Collect third-party information only with the individual’s consent and document the consent basis before using it for matching or research.
Provide notice before any un-aggregated Response Data sharing and let participants choose whether to participate when that sharing would occur.
Apply disclosure-protection techniques such as aggregation, generalized sentiments, rounding, exclusion of some variables, and exclusion of observations before public release.
Dispose of records according to an approved records schedule as soon as NARA approves it, rather than retaining records indefinitely.
Keep online-use information in aggregate form and use it only for usability, misuse prevention, and understanding resource use.
Restrict access to CFPB personnel with a need to know and use legal agreements and non-disclosure agreements for external collaborators.
Use encrypted tunnels and encrypted email client transfers for pushed, non-automated data exchanges between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems.

Primary data collection in consumer financial markets may collect personal information from people who are not expecting their information to be used for research, creating a risk of privacy intrusion through direct collection.
Collaboration with third parties can increase the chance that personal information is shared beyond CFPB and used by outside entities with different privacy practices.

Accepting collaboration proposals from third parties creates a risk that outside parties may shape the collection or use of personal information in ways that are not aligned with the Bureau's privacy expectations.
The system's broad research purpose could lead to collecting more personal information than is necessary for any single study, increasing the impact if data are exposed or misused.
The promise of notice, consent, access, and redress is only general, so participants may not receive clear enough information or meaningful control over how their data are collected and used.
If data are retained for longer-term field research, there is a risk that personal information remains available longer than needed, extending the window for unauthorized access or secondary use.
Provide clear notice and obtain consent where appropriate before collecting personal information from participants.
Use written agreements with third parties that define roles, responsibilities, and accountability mechanisms for any data sharing.
Require each third-party collaboration proposal to be reviewed against Bureau research or policy goals and specified standards and procedures before any data are used.
Apply data minimization so that only information needed for the specific research question is collected and retained.
Provide study-specific privacy notices that explain what data are collected, how they are used, who receives them, and how participants can exercise access and redress rights.
Set and enforce retention limits tied to the research need, and delete or de-identify data when the study is complete.
Detailed mortgage application and loan data can expose sensitive financial and housing-related information about individual consumers.
The system may enable inference or re-identification of individuals from reported HMDA records even though the purpose is not to make determinations about individuals.
Mandatory disclosure of HMDA data to multiple federal agencies increases the number of entities that can access the information and expands exposure risk.
Electronic submission and platform-based reporting create a risk of unauthorized access or interception during transmission or storage.
The platform lacks a public participation component, which limits transparency and may reduce individuals' ability to understand or challenge how their data is handled.
Limit collection, storage, and internal access to only the HMDA fields required by Regulation C and the 2015 HMDA Rule.
Apply de-identification or disclosure controls before any data is made available for broader use or reporting.
Use role-based access controls and data-sharing agreements for the Federal HMDA agencies that receive the data.
Encrypt electronic submissions and stored HMDA records and monitor access to the platform.
Provide clear public notices about the HMDA Platform's data handling and recipient agencies even without a public participation component.
Public disclosure of HMDA data could expose borrowers' mortgage activity and allow outsiders to infer sensitive financial and housing information about individuals.
The system collects more sensitive attributes such as age, credit score, race, and ethnicity, which can increase the privacy impact if the data are misused or re-identified.
Requiring applicants and borrowers to self-identify using disaggregated ethnic and racial categories can expose detailed demographic information.
Annual and, for larger institutions, quarterly submission of loan/application registers expands the amount and frequency of sensitive data flowing to federal agencies.
Sharing HMDA data with multiple Federal HMDA agencies broadens the number of government recipients that can access the information.
The collection of mortgage application and loan data from institutions may still create a risk of indirect identification even though direct identifiers are not required.
Limit public disclosure to the minimum data required by Regulation C and suppress or aggregate fields that could enable re-identification.
Apply stronger privacy review and masking controls to age, credit score, and other sensitive fields before storage, analysis, or release.
Use the least granular demographic categories necessary for the stated HMDA purpose and restrict access to the raw self-reported race and ethnicity data.
Retain standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls, and extend them to cover the increased annual and quarterly reporting cadence.
Limit access at each recipient agency to staff with a need to know and maintain recipient-specific accountability for use of HMDA data.
Continue to avoid collecting direct identifiers such as names or Social Security numbers in HMDA submissions.

The tool collects contact PII and may also capture additional PII in free-text responses or attachments, creating a risk of collecting more personal data than is necessary for the assessment. This increases the chance that sensitive or irrelevant personal information will be stored and processed without need.

The system collects entity contact information needed for onboarding and access, which creates a risk that personal contact details could be exposed if access controls are not sufficiently restricted. Because the data is used to onboard contacts to gain access, a compromise could affect both identity and contact details.

The tool imports Bureau employee and contractor information, creating a risk of internal personnel data being exposed in a system primarily used to collect external entity assessments. This broadens the privacy footprint beyond the regulated entities submitting assessments.

The system uses voluntary assessments for internal dashboards and an annual report to Congress, which creates a risk that personal data included in submissions could be reused in ways data subjects may not expect. Even if the report is aggregated, underlying PII in the system could still be accessible for analytics.

Because the tool is built on Salesforce Communities and collects information through websites, portals, and forms, there is a risk of unauthorized disclosure through the online collection interface or misconfiguration. This is especially relevant because the system handles PII submitted by external financial entities.
Limit the free-text fields and attachment handling to the minimum necessary and instruct users not to include unnecessary personal information.
Apply strict role-based access controls and strong account onboarding verification for entity contacts.
Segregate Bureau employee and contractor records from external assessment data and limit imports to only the fields needed for system administration.
Use de-identified or aggregated outputs for dashboards and congressional reporting, and prevent direct use of raw PII in analytics.
Harden the Salesforce Communities collection environment with secure configuration, access restrictions, and transmission protections.

Request files may contain personally identifiable information about requestors, Bureau staff, and other people, creating a risk that sensitive information is exposed through FOIA or Privacy Act processing.

A public-facing portal that lets users create accounts, submit requests, access records, and communicate with the Bureau increases the risk of unauthorized access to request and record data if account protections fail.
Using Login.gov and a third-party vendor-created system creates a risk that requestor data and communications flow outside the Bureau to external service providers.
The system may retain more request-related information than necessary because the context does not describe specific retention limits for accounts, requests, or retrieved records.
Staff-entered request information can create accuracy and completeness risks if Bureau staff enter or generate incorrect data about requestors or others.
The system’s communications feature may expose status updates or request content to unintended recipients if messages are not carefully scoped to the requester.
Apply standard Bureau privacy protections and security controls to all request files, including review and redaction before release.
Require strong Login.gov-based authentication and session protections for account creation, request submission, record access, and communications.
Limit external sharing to the minimum necessary for portal operation and ensure the Bureau’s privacy and security controls extend to vendor-handled data.
Establish and document specific retention schedules for request records, account data, and generated documents, and delete data when no longer needed.
Use validation and review procedures for staff-entered request information before records are used or released.
Restrict status communications to the authenticated requester and avoid including unnecessary personal details in messages.
Inquiry records may expose identifiable personal information and the substance of a person's issue if they include first and last name plus a summary of the inquiry.
Contact information kept outside Entellitrak in original-source form may be more exposed than the case record itself.
Because Entellitrak is hosted by a third-party service provider, inquiry data could be exposed through the vendor environment or vendor access.
Cloud-based access to the system could lead to unauthorized disclosure if access controls are weak or credentials are compromised.
The system may retain or process more information than necessary for the Ombudsman’s stated purpose if collection and use are not tightly limited.
Information collected for inquiries and outreach could be reused for administrative purposes beyond the original contact purpose, creating secondary-use privacy risk.
Individuals may have limited visibility into how their information is used or how to exercise privacy rights if notice and access/redress are not effective in practice.
Independent outreach activity in the same system could create a risk of mixing outreach records with inquiry records and exposing information beyond the intended audience.
Continue limiting inquiry records to only the minimum PII needed, and allow anonymous submissions when possible.
Apply the same confidentiality and access controls to contact information stored outside Entellitrak, and move it into a controlled repository if feasible.
Require contractual and security safeguards for the third-party host, including confidentiality, least-privilege access, and monitoring.
Keep the secure web interface restricted to Ombudsman’s Office staff and enforce strong authentication and access logging.
Limit collection and retention to information necessary for inquiry handling and outreach, and review records periodically for deletion of unneeded data.
Restrict administrative use to clearly defined internal functions and document who may use the data for those purposes.
Provide clear, accessible notice and a simple process for access and redress requests tied to the SORN and PIA.
Segregate outreach records from inquiry case records with role-based access and separate views or folders.
Consumer complaints and inquiries may contain sensitive personal information, and the system collects them through multiple channels that can capture more detail than needed.
Consumer submissions may be exposed to vendor staff when physical mail is processed and scanned into the system.
Complaint information may be disclosed to the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint.
Complaint information may be shared with other government agencies, including through referrals from other agencies, the White House, and Congressional offices.
Complaint information may be routed to other offices in the Bureau for further administrative action, creating internal access beyond the original consumer response function.
Voice communications may be captured and processed through telephony tools, which can record or transcribe sensitive consumer statements.
Enhanced processing of voice communications and natural language processing may analyze consumer statements beyond immediate complaint handling.
Advanced analytics may use complaint data to assess performance and identify operational improvements, which could create secondary use of consumer information.
Bureau staff authentication data such as email addresses are used for access control, so compromised staff credentials could expose complaint records.
Minimize collection to only the information needed to answer questions, handle complaints, and document the case, and redact unnecessary sensitive details before further use.
Limit vendor staff access to the minimum necessary for mail scanning and require strict handling and confidentiality controls for physical mail processing.
Share complaint information with the subject company only when necessary to resolve the complaint and limit the disclosure to the minimum relevant content.
Use data-sharing agreements and role-based access controls for referrals to other government entities so only authorized recipients receive the complaint information needed for the referral.
Route submissions to other Bureau offices only when needed for administrative action and limit access to staff with a direct need to know.
Apply recording notices, retention limits, and access restrictions to telephony data, including any call recordings or transcripts.
Limit automated voice and language processing to the minimum necessary for service delivery and avoid retaining derived data longer than needed.
Use complaint data for analytics in aggregated or de-identified form whenever possible.
Strengthen staff authentication for CRC access, such as requiring stronger credentials and limiting access to authorized staff only.

The system may expose sensitive personal data because it collects and maintains a broad set of PII, including military information, date of birth, sex, and race/ethnicity, across many CFPB use cases. If that data is mishandled, the impact to affected individuals could be significant.

Unauthorized access could occur because the platform stores PII in a cloud environment used by multiple internal users and connected applications. If access controls fail or are misconfigured, consumer, staff, and legal-matter information could be viewed by people without a need to know.

External users may gain access to applications that contain PII, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure if credentials are compromised or authentication is weakened. The system supports email, password, and multi-factor authentication for external users, which still leaves the possibility of account abuse if controls are not enforced correctly.

Data shared with other CFPB-authorized cloud environments could be exposed during integration, migration, or archiving. Moving data between systems increases the chance of accidental disclosure, unauthorized access, or loss of integrity.

Information sent through emails, texts, web forms, voicemail, and other communications may be collected or stored in ways that exceed what is needed for the specific purpose. This can lead to overcollection or retention of unnecessary personal information about consumers and other stakeholders.

The system may retain personal information indefinitely until records schedules are approved, which increases the risk that data will remain available longer than needed. Longer retention raises the chance of secondary use, breach impact, or disclosure in response to future access.

The platform supports collection and management of legal matters, whistleblower tips, and supervisory or enforcement information, which could reveal highly sensitive allegations or proceedings. Improper disclosure could harm individuals involved in legal processes or discourage reporting.

The system’s analytics and reporting functions could create privacy risks by enabling trend, pattern, and correlation analysis across large datasets. Even if individual records are protected, combining data can reveal new information about consumers, staff, or other subjects.

The system can share information with external entities on a need-to-know basis, which creates a risk of disclosure beyond what is necessary if sharing decisions are too broad or inconsistent. This is especially important because the specific external recipients are determined in application-specific PIAs rather than at the platform level.
Limit collection to the minimum PII needed for each specific application and use case, and review each proposed collection for authorized purpose before deployment.
Restrict internal access by role and continue using centralized identity and access management for internal users.
Require multi-factor authentication for external users and enforce strong account controls for any application that exposes PII externally.
Assess each connected third-party cloud environment before use and only allow integrations that have been authorized through the CFPB’s assessment and authorization process.
Standardize forms and collection methods to reduce duplicative or incorrect information and limit unnecessary data capture.
Apply approved records schedules and dispose of records according to the applicable retention schedule rather than keeping them indefinitely.
Limit access to legal and investigative records to authorized personnel and maintain them within the application-specific privacy and records controls described for each program.
Review analytics outputs and reporting access so that trend and correlation analysis is limited to authorized business purposes and does not expose unnecessary individual-level detail.
Document and approve each external sharing relationship at the application level so that only recipients with a specific need receive the minimum necessary information.

The system may collect personal contact details and profile preferences that are not strictly necessary for identity and access management, increasing the amount of personal information held about each person. This includes preferred pronouns, job title, and home contact information for remote workers.

The system aggregates identity information from multiple internal and external sources, creating a centralized hub that could expose more information if compromised or misused. Centralization increases the sensitivity of the profile because it links employment, staffing, credentialing, and identity records.

The system transmits personal information through APIs, secure data transmission methods, and flat text files, which creates risk of interception, leakage, or transfer errors during data exchange. Any weakness in these connections could expose identity data outside the intended systems.

The system manages all staff identification, authentication, and access privileges to CFPB systems, so excessive or mistaken access could expose PII and other sensitive resources to unauthorized users. Privileged access management especially raises the impact of any access-control failure.

The system provides insight into who has access to systems and PII based on role and responsibility, which means access metadata about individuals is itself collected and maintained. If that metadata is overbroadly viewed or retained, it can reveal work patterns and authority relationships.

The system provisions access for authorized external individuals, which broadens the number of people whose identity data is processed and increases the chance of inappropriate access or disclosure. External access management can create privacy risk if authorization is not narrowly limited.
Limit the profile fields to the minimum necessary for identity and access management, and avoid collecting optional personal details unless they are required for a documented business need.
Apply strict access controls and segregation of duties to the centralized identity hub so only personnel with a need to know can view linked records.
Use secure, authenticated, and monitored interfaces for all system-to-system transfers, and avoid flat text file exchanges where possible.
Require role-based approval for access changes and periodic review of access privileges, especially for privileged accounts and access to PII.
Restrict access to access-metadata and logs to authorized administrators and retain only what is needed for accountability and security purposes.
Apply the same privacy and security controls to external-user provisioning as to staff accounts, with explicit authorization checks before access is granted.

The system may collect more personal information than necessary because it gathers PII from supervised entities, consumers, consumer complaints, and CFPB employees for supervision activities. This creates a risk of over-collection and unnecessary retention of sensitive personal data.

The system may contact consumers directly to verify information, which can expose their personal information to additional handling and communication risk. This can increase the chance of mistaken outreach or disclosure during follow-up collection.

The Supervision Portal allows external entity representatives and state regulators to view and respond to requests, creating a risk of overbroad or mistaken access to PII and supervisory records. If authorization is not tightly controlled, external parties could see more information than necessary.

Because SES resides in a cloud platform and supports concurrent collaboration and document review tracking, there is a risk that PII could be exposed through shared workflows, misconfiguration, or access errors. Cloud-based repositories can broaden the impact of a security failure.

The system serves as an information repository for compliance rating information, which could affect consumers indirectly if supervisory records are improperly disclosed or used outside the intended oversight context. Even if not used to make a direct determination about an individual, the records still contain sensitive regulatory assessments tied to entities and their personnel.
Apply strict data minimization so the CFPB collects only the PII needed for supervision and prefers information from other agencies or public sources before contacting supervised entities.
Use a controlled consumer-contact process with verification steps and limited disclosure of PII when collecting or confirming information by phone, email, or other outreach.
Limit portal access to authorized users only and review provisioning of entity representatives regularly to ensure they can view only the requests and files needed for their role.
Maintain and enforce the stated privacy and security controls for the cloud environment, including access controls, logging, and review of collaborative document activity.
Restrict access to compliance rating information to staff with a supervision need and apply retention limits so supervisory records are not kept longer than necessary.
Complaint records may contain sensitive personal information and supporting documents that could expose consumers' financial and identity-related details if improperly accessed or disclosed.
Collecting Social Security Numbers for some complaints creates a risk of unnecessary exposure of a highly sensitive identifier.
Sharing complaints with the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint can disclose consumer information beyond what is needed to handle the issue.
Referring complaints to other government agencies, the White House, or Congressional offices can expand access to consumer data beyond the original collection purpose.
Using a vendor-provided cloud platform to operate the system can expose complaint data to third-party service risks if the platform is misconfigured or not tightly controlled.
Limit access to complaint records and supporting documents to authorized staff with a need to know, and protect the stored records with strong security controls.
Collect Social Security Numbers only when necessary for identity validation or account matching, and avoid requiring them for all complaints.
Minimize the information sent to the company or financial service provider and share only the complaint details needed to resolve the matter.
Apply data-sharing rules that limit referrals to the minimum information necessary for the receiving agency or office to act on the complaint.
Require the vendor-provided cloud platform to use strong security, access control, and monitoring protections for CRS data.
