Highly sensitive personal and evidentiary information may be exposed because the system ingests and stores large volumes of records, including ESI and paper, in a contractor-owned environment.
Metadata and embedded information in documents may reveal more personal information than intended during review and production.
Protected or privileged personal information may be disclosed if redaction and keyword-based flagging miss relevant content.
Duplicate documents may be retained and reviewed unnecessarily, increasing the amount of personal information exposed during litigation support.
Forensic collection from external entities may capture more information than is needed for the legal purpose, including unrelated personal data on storage media.
Trial and investigative hearing support may expose personal information to broader audiences when exhibits are displayed in court or hearings.
Cloud-based or vendor-owned tools may create additional confidentiality risk because CFPB records are processed and maintained in systems not directly owned by the Bureau.
Contractor personnel may have access to CFPB records and personal information, creating a risk of unauthorized internal disclosure or mishandling.
Store and process CFPB records in a secure and forensically sound manner with access limited to authorized personnel.
Review metadata during document processing and use it to identify sensitive content before disclosure.
Use attorney-selected keyword searches and automated flagging to identify protected information for manual review before production.
Identify and eliminate duplicate documents during review to reduce unnecessary handling of personal information.
Limit forensic collection to data authorized by the court and use triage to narrow the material that must be reviewed.
Use specialized trial presentation tools to control how exhibits are displayed during hearings and trial.
Apply the same privacy coverage and controls to the contractor-owned and vendor-owned tools used in the LTST suite.
Restrict contractor access to the minimum necessary for eDiscovery and litigation support tasks.

The system collects identifiable business contact information for users or points of contact, creating a privacy risk if that information is exposed or misused. Even though the beta-testing scope is limited, full name, business email, phone number, and mailing address are still personal data that can identify and contact a person.

If beta-testing data entry is not strictly constrained, the system could end up holding real applicant or associated-person information even though the stated intent is to use fake data only. That would expand the privacy impact to actual individuals whose lending data is not supposed to be collected in beta-testing.

The program is intended to receive detailed small-business lending data from covered financial institutions, which can create privacy risk through aggregation and re-identification even when direct applicant PII is excluded. Fields such as census tract, revenue, industry code, workers, time in business, and number of principal owners can still make businesses easier to identify or profile.

The system is designed to support disclosure and use of lending data by communities, governmental entities, and creditors, which creates a risk of broader secondary use than the data subjects expect. Even if the purpose is legitimate, wider access increases the chance of misuse or overexposure.

The system relies on general privacy protections and security controls, but the input does not describe data minimization, masking, or role-based restrictions specific to this system. Without more specific controls, there is a risk of unauthorized access or overcollection beyond what beta-testing requires.

Users may not fully understand what information is collected and how it will be used, because the system depends on access through Login.gov and a profile-creation flow but the input does not describe system-specific disclosures. That creates a notice risk for people entering contact information or fake test data.
Apply strong access controls and security protections to the user profile data, and limit use of the contact information to account administration and beta-testing support.
Enforce beta-testing rules that block submission of real applicant or associated-person data and require only fake data beyond user or POC business contact information.
Limit collection to the minimum fields needed for the statutory purpose and suppress or aggregate outputs where feasible to reduce re-identification risk.
Restrict access to lending data to authorized recipients only and provide clear purpose limitations for any sharing with communities, governmental entities, and creditors.
Add system-specific privacy controls such as role-based access, logging, and periodic review of what data are collected during beta-testing.

Provide a clear system-specific notice at login and profile creation that explains what information is collected, why it is collected, and that beta-testing submissions beyond contact information must be fake data.

Uploaded covered orders and related documents may disclose more personal information than is necessary, including information about consumers, respondents, counsel, officers, or other representatives.
Public publication of registry information could expose personal information to anyone viewing the public registry or website.
Sharing registry information with other federal, state, tribal, and local regulators can spread personal data beyond the CFPB and create additional disclosure risk.
The helpdesk feature collects names, email addresses, and issue descriptions from members of the public and nonbank users, which may reveal unnecessary personal details in support requests.
User accounts and credentials for nonbank representatives and CFPB staff create a risk of unauthorized access if passwords or usernames are compromised.
Records are currently unscheduled and considered permanent, which increases the risk that personal information will be retained longer than necessary.

The system may maintain personal information about individuals named in public orders even when they are not the direct registrant, creating a risk of secondary collection without direct participation.
Internal access by CFPB employees, contractors, and consultants could expose personal data more widely than necessary if role-based limits are not tightly enforced.
Continue requiring nonbanks to redact nonpublic portions of covered orders before submission and remove any inadvertently uploaded or irrelevant documents.
Limit publication to non-confidential information and use a publication format designed to protect confidential information.
Share registry information with other regulators only under existing information-sharing agreements and protocols.
Limit helpdesk collection to the minimum needed to respond and keep using secure web forms for submissions.
Require multi-factor authentication for account creation and access, and maintain audit logs to verify compliance with privacy and security policies.
Obtain and implement a NARA-approved records retention schedule for NBR records.
Keep requiring the nonbank to upload only the final public covered order needed for registration and avoid collecting unrelated documents.
Restrict internal disclosure to CFPB employees, contractors, or consultants whose assigned duties require access, and continue mandatory privacy training and acceptable-use obligations.

The system can expose sensitive enforcement-matter information to too many people because it contains detailed records and reports that may include PII, confidential matter status, and legal documents.
Sharing matter records with FTC staff creates a risk of unnecessary disclosure or editing of CFPB enforcement information across agencies.
Providing information in response to FOIA requests could disclose personal or confidential enforcement information to the public.
Sharing witness names, entity affiliations, and contact information with court reporting vendors creates a risk of disclosure to third parties outside the agency.
Reporting tax information such as TINs to the IRS creates a risk of unnecessary exposure of highly sensitive identifiers if collection or sharing is broader than needed.

The system may hold personal information about people who are only indirectly involved in a matter, such as consumers, witnesses, opposing counsel, and government employees, creating a risk of collecting more data than each person expects.

The system may retain and link large numbers of source documents, such as complaints, tips, transcripts, correspondence, and legal filings, which can concentrate sensitive personal information in one place.
Internal access by multiple CFPB offices for coordination can broaden exposure of matter data beyond the primary enforcement team.
Limit reports to the minimum information needed for the specific business purpose and keep confidential matter-status details restricted to users with a demonstrated need to know.
Use the secured CFPB-FTC Matter Sharing Community module and restrict FTC access to authorized users only.
Apply FOIA review and redaction before release so personal and confidential matter information is withheld when permitted by law.
Share only the limited participant and contact information needed for scheduling and documenting testimony with court reporting vendors.
Restrict TIN collection and IRS reporting to cases where it is necessary for tax reporting obligations and use it only for that purpose.
Collect only information that is directly relevant and necessary to the enforcement matter or contract activity.
Use the integrated document storage system to avoid duplicating records and keep linked source documents in controlled repositories.
Keep internal access limited to CFPB staff with a demonstrated need to know for their assigned responsibilities.
Geocoded consumer records can expose sensitive location and loan-related PII if accessed by users who do not need it for their duties.
Sharing maps, CSVs, or outputs across teams and groups increases the chance that sensitive data will be copied or exposed beyond the original purpose.
Granting additional users access to private folders can expose outputs to more people than originally intended.
Publishing geospatial outputs could allow re-identification if aggregation or de-identification is insufficient for the underlying location data.
The system retains PII long enough for analysis that could increase exposure if the data are not deleted on schedule.
Staff account data and audit logs create a record of employee identity and activity that could be misused if accessed improperly.
Contractors and employees both have access, which can broaden the insider-threat surface for sensitive consumer and staff data.
Use role-based access controls so staff only access the system and information necessary and relevant to their assigned duties.
Restrict sharing to approved internal users and keep outputs in private folders unless a business need for broader sharing is documented.
Require administrator review before any additional user is added to a private folder, and limit that access to the specific collaboration need.
Publish only aggregated and de-identified outputs and review them before release to confirm no identifying information is included.
Delete PII from the GIS server within a week after the final output has been transmitted to permanent program-appropriate data storage.
Limit staff account data and audit logs to what is necessary for authentication, support, billing, and compliance monitoring, and protect those logs with access controls.
Apply the same role-based access controls and need-to-know review to contractors as to employees before granting GIS access.

The database contains highly sensitive identifiers that could cause harm if disclosed or misused, including SSNs and other government identifiers tied to names and contact information. Because the system is searchable by personal identifier, a compromise could expose individuals to identity theft or unwanted tracking.

The system may collect personal information from third parties and other agencies without individuals receiving actual notice. This creates a risk that people will not know what data CFPB holds about them or how it is used.

The CFPB currently gathers information from federal, state, and local sources and does not take steps to verify accuracy or completeness of such data. Inaccurate records could affect supervision, enforcement, or other decisions about the people and organizations in the database.

The system may share PII externally with institutions and other state and federal agency employees, which creates a risk of broader disclosure beyond CFPB staff. Even if shared through secure channels, more recipients increase the chance of secondary misuse or unauthorized access.

The Directory Database is a central repository and other CFPB systems may connect to or derive information from it, which can spread PII across multiple internal systems. This increases the risk of overexposure or inconsistent access controls once data is reused elsewhere.

The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves the disposition schedule. Keeping PII longer than necessary increases the chance of future misuse, breach, or disclosure of outdated records.

Because reports can include names and contact information, internal or external recipients could use the data for purposes beyond the minimum needed for their job functions if access is not tightly controlled. This creates a risk of unnecessary exposure of individuals' business and contact details.
Restrict access to authorized personnel only, using non-transferrable access codes and passwords, and limit access to the minimum needed for assigned duties.
Provide constructive notice through the PIA and the SORN, and where practicable obtain information directly from individuals so they have a better opportunity to know what is collected.

Verify accuracy and completeness where practicable by contacting supervised institutions and individuals or using third-party data sources, and allow individuals to amend or correct records under the Privacy Act.
Share external reports only through secure channels and only when supported by appropriate data sharing agreements.
Restrict connected-system access on a need-to-know basis and document any future external-facing connections in future PIA updates.
Dispose of records according to the applicable NARA-approved schedule once available, rather than keeping them indefinitely.
Continue limiting internal distribution of reports to employees with a bona fide need and ensure external reports are appropriately protected and securely transmitted.
Users may disclose directly identifiable contact information on a public-facing site and have it exposed if they provide it knowingly or without understanding the consequences.
User-submitted comments, videos, links, and images may reveal sensitive personal details or opinions beyond what the user expects.
The site may make some collected information public, creating a risk of broader disclosure of user-provided data.
The site collects demographic information and information about consumer financial products used by users and others, which could create profiling or inference risks.
Website usage data and analytics may enable tracking or linkage of user activity across pages or sessions.
Data shared with Google Analytics may be disclosed to an external recipient outside the CFPB.
Consumer complaint intake routed through the site may transmit personal information into another system, increasing exposure across systems.
Continue limiting collection of directly identifiable PII to information users knowingly provide, and present clear notice before submission.
Warn users not to include personal or sensitive information in comments, videos, links, or images, and provide submission guidance before posting.
Give users a clear choice about what information is public and default to the least public setting possible.
Minimize collection of demographic and consumer financial product information to what is necessary for the site’s public education purpose.
Use only aggregate web-traffic analytics and avoid retaining or using page-level identifiers longer than needed for site improvement.
Apply a data-sharing agreement and privacy controls for Google Analytics to limit use of traffic data to aggregate measurement.
Provide a privacy notice and security safeguards before users are transferred from ConsumerFinance.gov to the online complaint intake system.

Continue to redact EIN/TIN and encrypt other PII before sharing with review panelists, and limit sharing to panelists involved in the grants process.
Apply least-privilege role-based access and review contractor access regularly so contractors only have the access needed for their assigned support tasks.
Validate and reconcile data received from FMMI, CIR, ECP, and Grants.gov before it is used in official records or decisions.
Restrict manual entry to approved users and apply review or audit checks for user-entered changes to official files.
Enforce the stated retention schedule and archive or dispose of records when the approved retention period ends.

The database aggregates highly sensitive SNAP participant information from all states into one place, creating a large concentration of personal, transactional, and financial data that would be valuable if improperly accessed or exposed.
Collecting data from 2000 to present may retain far more information than is necessary for current integrity checks, increasing privacy exposure over time.
Automated matching and scripts can generate false positives, which could wrongly flag participants as ineligible, duplicate, or fraudulent and lead to improper adverse action or investigation.
Sharing information with state agencies for investigations can disclose sensitive eligibility and immigration-related information beyond the original collection context.
The system performs immigration status checks, which can expose highly sensitive information about participants and their household members if handled or matched incorrectly.
Household composition and age validation can reveal intimate family information and create privacy harm if the data are inaccurate or shared more broadly than needed.
Using lawfully shared internal and interagency data across multiple federal agencies creates a risk that data collected for one purpose will be reused for other purposes without clear limits.
Restrict database access to authorized personnel only and keep transfers limited to secure channels and the authorized AWS environment.
Apply data minimization and retention limits so only the historical data needed for integrity checks is retained.
Use matching algorithms designed to minimize false positives and require human review before any adverse action is taken.
Limit disclosures to state agencies to cases that are necessary for investigation and consistent with the notice and law.
Limit immigration-status access and use to the specific fraud-prevention check and protect it with strict access controls.
Validate household and age data carefully and limit use of those fields to the stated integrity checks.
Document and enforce purpose limitations for all interagency data matches so data are used only for SNAP integrity checks and related investigations.

The system stores personally identifiable information about non-employee affiliates, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of names, business contact details, and affiliate identifiers.
Only NRCS employees can access the system, so insider misuse or excessive employee access could expose affiliate records without the affiliates' direct control.
Affiliate information is linked to Level 2 eAuth accounts and used to assign roles, which could lead to improper access if the linkage is wrong or abused.
NRCS employees enter the information provided by affiliates, so transcription or validation errors could create inaccurate records that affect access control decisions.
The system shares affiliate information with zRoles, creating an internal disclosure path that could expand exposure if that connected system is compromised or misused.
The records are retained for long periods, increasing the chance that outdated personal information remains available longer than necessary.
Retention tied to program participation may keep records after an affiliate no longer needs access, which can preserve unnecessary personal data.
Limit collection and storage to the minimum personal information needed for access administration and protect it with strong access controls.
Enforce role-based access controls and periodic review of employee access to the Affiliates system.
Require verification of the affiliate-to-eAuth linkage and role assignment before access is granted.
Use a second-person review or validation step for manually entered affiliate data.
Protect the interface and data exchange with zRoles using authenticated, authorized, and logged system-to-system controls.
Apply records management controls to purge or archive records when they are no longer needed under the approved schedule.
Periodically review retained affiliate records to confirm the person still qualifies for the program need that justifies retention.

The system stores a large amount of sensitive personally identifiable information, including tax IDs and social security numbers, which increases the harm if the data is exposed. The combination of identity, policy, and farm-related details can make individuals highly identifiable.

The system exposes personal data to multiple internal organizations and limited OIG users, creating a risk of unnecessary or mistaken disclosure beyond the minimum needed for a user's role. Broader sharing increases the number of people who can see sensitive records.

Authorized external users, including Approved Insurance Providers, can access data associated with their policies, which still creates a risk of disclosure if access controls are bypassed or misconfigured. Web-based access also increases exposure to account compromise.

The system relies on eAuthentication and HyDRA authentication for access, but the PIA does not describe additional safeguards such as least-privilege review or multi-factor authentication. If credentials are compromised, sensitive records could be disclosed.

The system keeps the information for the life of the project, which creates a retention risk because personal data may remain available long after the original operational need has passed. Long retention increases the window for unauthorized access and secondary use.

The system consolidates annual RMA databases into a single production database, which can concentrate many years of personal information in one place. That aggregation increases the impact of any unauthorized access or breach.

The system uses ETL and cleansing steps that alter source files to remove characters and standardize records, which creates a risk of inaccurate or mismatched personal data if transformation logic is wrong. Inaccurate data can affect individuals in analysis and reporting.

The system uses weather data to validate claims and supports research and fraud analysis, which creates a risk of secondary use beyond the expectations of the original data subjects. Individuals may not expect their information to be used in broad analytics and fraud-related review.
Limit the data stored and displayed in HyDRA to the minimum necessary fields, and mask or redact tax IDs and social security numbers wherever full values are not required.
Restrict sharing to role-based, need-to-know access and periodically review whether each internal recipient still needs access to the specific reports or records.

Enforce least-privilege authorization for external users so AIPs can access only the specific policy records needed for reporting, and regularly validate that access boundaries are working as intended.
Add stronger account protections such as periodic access reviews and multi-factor authentication for web access to reduce the risk of credential compromise.
Apply a shorter retention schedule for working copies and purge or archive records once they are no longer needed for the project or required by the approved records schedule.
Segment the production database or tightly control access to historical years so users only retrieve the minimum historical data needed for a task.
Strengthen validation of ETL and cleansing scripts with change control, test cases, and exception review to ensure transformations do not alter identity or policy data incorrectly.
Document and limit secondary uses of the data to approved purposes, and ensure users understand that analytics and fraud-related review are restricted to the authorized program purpose.
Unauthorized users or insiders could access user profile PII because the system is Internet-based and supports access for multiple user groups, including contractors and partners.
Authorized contractors and partners may see more personal information than necessary if role-based access is not tightly scoped to job duties.
Users can modify their own profiles, which could lead to inaccurate or unnecessary personal data being stored if changes are not validated.
PII is retained for as long as the application remains in production, which may keep personal data longer than needed.
Disabled accounts may still leave residual profile data in the system after a user leaves, creating unnecessary persistence of personal information.
The system maintains personal contact details such as email, phone, and company address, which could expose users to unwanted contact or identification if improperly accessed.
Restrict access to CoLab to authenticated users with approved need-to-know access and periodically review those permissions.
Limit contractor and partner access to the minimum roles required for their responsibilities and review those roles regularly.
Validate and audit user-edited profile changes before they become authoritative records.
Delete application-specific PII when it is no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit, or other operational purposes.
Disable accounts promptly when users leave and ensure associated profile data is reviewed for deletion or archival according to retention rules.
Collect and retain only the contact fields needed to establish and manage CoLab access.

Vendor PII is retained in the IDEA DataMart, which creates a risk of unnecessary persistence and exposure if the data is kept longer than needed for reporting. Even minimal names and contact information can create privacy harm if retained in a reporting store without strict minimization and deletion controls.

Because the system allows contractors access, vendor PII could be viewed by users who do not need it for a specific report or task. This raises the risk of internal overexposure of contact information.

The use of read-only web service calls from SCIMS and periodic refreshes creates a risk that outdated or incorrect vendor PII may be used in reports. Inaccurate contact information can lead to privacy harm through misdirected communications or decisions based on stale data.

Reports can be produced using selectable criteria from drop-down menus, which could allow users to generate outputs that reveal more vendor-related PII than intended for a given business need. Even if the system does not search by personal identifier, broad report parameters can still increase exposure.
Apply strict data minimization and automatic deletion controls to the IDEA DataMart so vendor PII is removed as soon as it is no longer needed for report generation.
Restrict contractor access to the minimum set of reports and records needed for assigned duties, and review access regularly to ensure the need-to-know limitation is enforced.
Use a more frequent synchronization schedule or validation checks for SCIMS-derived PII so reports rely on current vendor names and contact information.
Limit report parameters and output fields to the minimum necessary for the costing and budgeting purpose, and review report templates to prevent unnecessary disclosure of vendor PII.

The system can expose sensitive customer identifiers that may be linked to SSNs or tax IDs, creating a risk of identity theft or improper re-identification if accessed or returned beyond what is needed.
The system transmits customer data between multiple client applications, databases, and adjacent systems, which increases the chance of unauthorized disclosure across internal interfaces.
API responses are returned in JSON format, which may disclose more personal data than the requesting application or user needs if response controls are not tightly limited.
Contractors can access the system, so there is a risk of insider misuse or unnecessary viewing of customer information by non-employee users.
The system relies on a single external-facing gateway as the entry point for requests from outside the firewall, which creates a concentration risk if that control is bypassed or misconfigured.
Core Services accesses a replicated copy or view of SCIMS data, so privacy-sensitive customer data may be exposed in multiple places and become harder to govern consistently.
The system stores administrative and transactional information even though it does not store PII, which may still reveal customer activity or case handling details if not properly protected.
Limit exposure of customer identifiers by returning only the minimum identifier fields needed for the specific business function and masking or truncating identifiers whenever possible.
Continue enforcing secure transmission controls for all internal API and database traffic and restrict each interface to only the systems that require it.
Apply response filtering so each JSON payload includes only the fields required by the requesting application and user role.
Keep the need-to-know restriction and mandatory background investigations for contractors, and review contractor access regularly to ensure it remains justified.
Harden and continuously monitor the CA API Gateway because it is the single point of entry, including strict access control and threat protection rules.
Use eAuth-based access controls and periodic access reviews for all users who reach SCIMS data through NPAD or replicated views.
Apply retention limits and logging review to administrative and transactional records so they are kept only as long as needed for the service purpose.

Emergency Action Plans contain personal contact and location information that could expose responders and property owners if disclosed beyond the intended emergency purpose. The data includes names, home addresses, and telephone numbers, which are identifiable and potentially sensitive when linked to dam emergencies.

The system allows disclosure of PII in hardcopy or electronic form during review cycles or when an EAP is activated, creating a risk of accidental or unauthorized exposure during transmission or handling. Because the information leaves the system in these forms, it can be copied, lost, or intercepted outside DamWatch.

State and local emergency responders receive the PII in the EAPs, so more organizations than NRCS may see the personal data. Each additional recipient increases the chance that the information will be further disclosed or handled inconsistently.

NRCS personnel and contractors can access EAPs containing PII on a need-to-know basis, which still creates insider-access risk if access is excessive, misused, or not properly monitored. The system also includes contractors, which broadens the set of authorized users handling the data.

The system retains the information for potentially long periods, which increases the chance that outdated PII remains available after it is no longer needed. Long retention also lengthens the window in which the data could be exposed by a security incident or improper access.

Because the system uses both publicly accessible information and information voluntarily submitted by individuals or organizations, there is a risk that people may not fully understand how their personal data will be used in emergency planning. This can create transparency and notice concerns, especially for telephone numbers that may not be publicly listed.
Limit EAP PII to the minimum necessary fields required for execution, and review whether every name, address, and phone number is essential for each dam site.
Use secure transmission and controlled distribution procedures for all hardcopy and electronic EAP copies, including logging who receives each copy and when.
Limit external sharing to only the specific state and local emergency responders assigned to the relevant dam site, and ensure they receive only the EAP information needed for activation.
Maintain the documented access control procedures and enforce need-to-know access for NRCS personnel and contractors, with background investigations for contractors as already required.
Apply records management reviews to remove or archive EAP PII when it is no longer needed for an active dam owner, operator, producer, or participant, consistent with approved schedules.
Provide clear notice to responders and property owners about what PII is collected, the sources used, and that the information is used only for EAP execution.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers, so a compromise or misuse could expose individuals to identity theft, financial fraud, or other harm.
Because the system is searchable and supports retrieval of records, users may access more information than is necessary for their duties.
Authorized FPAC staff and contractors can access the records, so insider misuse or accidental disclosure is possible.
Contractor access increases the number of people and organizations that can handle the records, which raises the risk of improper handling or unauthorized disclosure.
Scanned paper records and metadata are bulk transferred into the system, creating a risk that records could be captured, indexed, or stored with incorrect or excessive information.
Long retention periods increase the amount of time sensitive records remain available, which extends the window for misuse or breach.
Individuals do not have direct access to DRMS, so they may be less able to review or correct their own records promptly.
Continue encrypting the documents and restrict access to only those with a documented need-to-know.
Enforce the documented access control procedures so search and retrieval are available only to users with a valid need-to-know.
Keep requiring Level 2 eAuth credentials and need-to-know authorization for all access.
Require mandatory background investigations for contractors before granting access and maintain that control for all contractor users.
Review bulk-scanned records and extracted metadata for accuracy and necessity before they are loaded into the metadata stores.
Apply the NARA-approved retention schedules and dispose of records as soon as they are no longer required.
Use the published SORN request process to let individuals request access to records about them and seek corrections through authorized staff.
The system holds highly sensitive personal and financial information, so unauthorized access could expose names, addresses, tax IDs, SSNs, bank routing numbers, and farm ownership details.
Authorized access by multiple user groups creates a risk of insider misuse or accidental disclosure of documents beyond what each user needs.
Contractors and technical service providers may receive or access PII outside USDA, creating a disclosure risk if authorization is too broad or not properly limited to the stated purpose.
The system uses address and name data from FSA SCIMS to determine the correct producer, which creates a risk of misidentification or matching the wrong individual's records.
Individuals do not have direct access to DMS, which can make it harder for them to see, correct, or challenge inaccurate or improperly held information.
Records may be retained for long periods, increasing the amount of time sensitive PII remains available and the chance of exposure over time.
Because documents are stored in PDF files and viewed with Adobe PDF plug-ins, there is a risk that document content or metadata could be exposed through the file format or viewing environment.
Limit access to the sensitive documents strictly to users with a documented need-to-know and apply role-based controls for the specific locations and documents they are authorized to handle.
Enforce least-privilege access reviews and periodic user recertification for NRCS employees and conservation district employees who can access DMS.
Require written authorization for each external disclosure and document the specific purpose and data elements shared with contractors or technical service providers.
Use additional verification checks when matching SCIMS data so that name and address alone do not determine the correct producer in cases of ambiguity.
Provide a clear, timely correction and access request process so individuals can obtain information about records pertaining to them and request updates through the designated contact path.
Apply records disposition rules to delete or archive records as soon as the applicable retention period ends, rather than keeping them longer than required.
Harden the PDF viewing environment and restrict plug-in use to approved, patched versions only.

The system holds highly sensitive borrower financial and identity information, so unauthorized access could expose personal and financial details about distressed borrowers. This could cause privacy harm because the data includes names, tax IDs, loan information, and security property.

Because the system is used by field office employees to evaluate debt restructuring, there is a risk that access could be broader than necessary for the specific employee role. If users can see more borrower information than they need, privacy exposure increases.

Manual data entry by FSA field agents creates a risk of inaccurate or incomplete borrower records, which could lead to incorrect restructuring decisions and improper handling of personal information. Errors in financial or identity data can affect the borrower directly.

The system accesses other internal databases and reference tables, which can increase the amount of personal data aggregated in one place and expand the privacy impact if the system is misused or compromised. Combining records can create a fuller profile of a borrower than any single source alone.

Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the long-term privacy risk because sensitive data remains available far beyond the period needed for servicing. The longer the records are kept, the greater the chance of misuse, breach, or outdated information being used.
Restrict access to authorized agency officials and field office employees who need the data to perform restructuring duties, and enforce strong authentication and audit logging for all access.
Apply role-based access controls so each user can view only the borrower information necessary for their assigned servicing function.
Add validation and review procedures for manually entered borrower data before it is used in restructuring calculations.
Limit cross-system data retrieval to the minimum fields needed for the calculation and document the necessity of each linked data source.
Review whether all permanent records truly need indefinite retention and, where allowed by the approved schedule, apply records disposition controls to remove data when no longer required.
The system holds highly sensitive borrower PII and financial data, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse if the application or database is compromised.
Borrowers' name and Tax ID are shared with an external credit bureau, which creates a privacy risk from third-party disclosure and downstream handling outside the agency.
The system makes creditworthiness determinations using borrower data, which can expose applicants to adverse decisions based on financial and credit information.
Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the risk that personal data will remain available longer than necessary and be exposed in future misuse or breach.
County office staff enter data collected from borrowers, which creates a risk of inaccurate or incomplete records affecting privacy and loan decisions.
Restrict access to borrower PII and financial records to only authorized users who need it for loan processing, and enforce strong authentication and audit logging.
Minimize the data sent to Microbilt to only the name and Tax ID needed for creditworthiness, and document the disclosure purpose and recipient handling requirements.
Provide a review and correction process for borrowers to challenge inaccurate credit or financial information before it is used in eligibility decisions.
Apply a documented retention schedule to delete or archive records when they are no longer needed for the loan program, rather than storing them indefinitely.
Use validation checks and staff review procedures when county office staff enter borrower data to reduce errors in the records.
The system collects and maintains highly sensitive borrower identifiers that could be exposed if improperly accessed or disclosed.
Borrower account information is broadly shared with multiple internal and external recipients, increasing the chance of over-disclosure.
Using name or Social Security Number for online queries and batch processing can expose borrower records to unauthorized access if those identifiers are misused.
Reporting delinquent borrower information to Treasury, IRS, HUD, and credit bureaus creates a risk of secondary use beyond the original loan-account purpose.
Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the duration of privacy exposure and the chance that outdated information remains accessible.
The stated future customer self-service work could create a public-facing exposure risk if borrower data becomes accessible outside the agency.
Limit collection and display of Social Security Numbers to the minimum necessary and mask them wherever full display is not required.
Apply role-based access controls and data-sharing restrictions so each recipient only receives the borrower information needed for its specific purpose.
Require strong authentication, logging, and audit review for all name- and SSN-based queries and batch access to borrower records.
Provide only the specific data elements required for each reporting or offset function and document the legal basis for each disclosure.
Implement records review and disposition controls to delete or archive records according to an approved schedule instead of keeping all records indefinitely online.
Before any public-facing customer self-service release, perform a privacy and security review to ensure only the minimum borrower data is exposed.
The system stores identifiable contact information that could be exposed if internal users access it without a need to know or if access controls are weak.
Manual entry by multiple FLP staff increases the chance of inaccurate or incomplete records being entered and then used in appraisal processing.
The system centralizes appraisal information for broad FLP use, which increases the impact if a user accesses more information than needed for their role.
Keeping records indefinitely increases the long-term exposure of personal data and the chance that outdated information remains available longer than necessary.
The system’s web-based design creates a general risk of unauthorized access through the application or database if technical safeguards fail.
Enforce role-based access controls and least-privilege permissions so staff can only view the contact information needed for their appraisal duties.
Add validation checks and supervisory review for manually entered records before they are finalized in the system.
Limit each user’s view to only the appraisals and fields needed for their specific county, state, regional, or national role.
Apply records disposition controls and periodic review to confirm indefinite retention remains necessary for each record class.
Use strong authentication, secure session management, and routine security monitoring for the web application and database.

The system collects and maintains highly sensitive personal and financial information, including SSNs/TINs, race, ethnicity, gender, credit reports, and employment history, which could expose borrowers to identity theft or discrimination if misused or breached.

The system relies on data from multiple external sources, including credit reporting agencies, tax records, courthouse records, and other lenders, which may contain inaccurate or incomplete information that can affect loan decisions.

The system uses personal and financial data to determine credit worthiness and restructure debt, creating a risk of unfair or opaque profiling if borrowers cannot understand or challenge the analysis.
Permanent retention of the records increases the long-term privacy impact of any unauthorized access, secondary use, or future disclosure because the data never ages out of the system.

Field office staff and authorized agency officials can access and manually enter borrower data across web-based applications, which creates insider misuse and accidental disclosure risk if access is broader than necessary.
The system consolidates data from several applications into a unified view for loan processing and servicing, which can increase exposure if a user sees more information than needed for their task.

Limit collection and storage to the minimum personal and financial data necessary for loan processing and servicing, and mask or tokenize SSNs/TINs and credit card numbers wherever full values are not required.
Validate third-party and cross-system data before it is used in decisions, and provide a process for borrowers to review and correct disputed information.
Provide clear notice of how creditworthiness and restructuring decisions are made, and require documented human review for adverse or high-impact decisions.
Apply a records lifecycle review and archive or segregate older records so only necessary personnel can access them, even if the records must remain permanent.
Enforce least-privilege role-based access controls and audit logging for all field office and agency users who process or service loans.
Use field-level permissions or task-based views so personnel only see the borrower data needed for the specific loan-making or servicing action they are performing.

PII is kept permanently, which increases the chance of long-term exposure, misuse, or secondary use beyond the original need. Indefinite retention also makes any future breach or unauthorized access more consequential because the data never ages out.

The system holds personally identifiable information about individuals involved in loan oversight, trainee tracking, and directives workflows, creating privacy risk if internal users access more data than needed for their role. Even without external sharing, broad internal visibility can lead to unnecessary disclosure.

Data is entered by county offices, state offices, and state personnel, so the system may store inaccurate or outdated personal information if those sources enter incorrect names or addresses. Inaccurate records can affect oversight, training, and workflow decisions about the individuals named in the system.

The system collects names and mailing addresses for some applications even though the described purposes are oversight, training, and directives management, which suggests a risk of collecting more personal data than necessary. If mailing addresses are not essential to every workflow, retaining them broadens privacy exposure without clear benefit.

SDMS collects information from the public on directives or policies that have not yet been approved by OMB, which could expose public submitters' personal information in an approval workflow not yet finalized for public release. That creates a risk that sensitive submissions are handled before the underlying directive is approved.
Replace indefinite retention with the shortest retention period allowed by records requirements, and periodically review whether permanent retention is still necessary for each application.
Restrict access to PII by role and need-to-know within USDA, with periodic access reviews for District Directors, State Offices, and other users.
Validate and periodically review records entered by county and state offices to correct inaccurate names and addresses.
Limit collection of mailing addresses to the applications and workflows that truly require them, and omit them where names alone are sufficient.
Apply stricter handling controls to public submissions in SDMS, including review before wider use and clear separation from routine internal workflow data.
The system stores highly sensitive identifiers that could cause identity theft or other harm if exposed.
Sharing Farm Record and Business Partner data across USDA agencies increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure or secondary use beyond the original collection purpose.
Long-term retention of historical records increases the amount of personal data exposed if the system is breached or misused.
Maintaining historical data from 1999 to the current program year creates privacy risk because old records may no longer be necessary but remain available.
The system’s geospatial farm, tract, and field boundaries can reveal location-related information about producers' operations.
Centralizing customer and farm data as the system of record creates a high-value target if access controls fail.
Limit collection and retention of sensitive identifiers to only what is required for the specific program purpose, and mask or suppress them when full values are not needed.
Apply role-based access controls and sharing agreements that restrict agency access to only the data needed for program delivery.
Encrypt all inter-agency transmissions and verify that encryption is enforced for every shared data flow.
Implement and enforce data retention schedules that delete or dispose of records once they are no longer required.
Review archived historical records periodically and purge data that is no longer needed for legal or program purposes.
Limit access to geospatial boundary data to users who need it for farm record administration and program delivery.
Continuously monitor access to the system of record and audit use of customer and farm data for inappropriate access patterns.
The system retains producer information permanently, which increases the risk that personal data will be exposed or misused long after it is needed for the program purpose.
Contractors can access the system, creating a risk of unauthorized viewing or mishandling of producer data by non-federal personnel.

Information is disclosed to internal shared services and external systems for certain NAP and TAP functions, which creates a risk that producer data will be exposed beyond the original application boundary.
The system stores producer names and street addresses for many programs, so a compromise of the database would expose direct contact information for affected farmers and ranchers.
The system stores payment, overpayment, premium, and debt-related information, which could reveal a producer's financial status or disputes with the program if improperly accessed.
Some components generate letters that are physically mailed, which creates a risk of disclosure through postal handling or delivery to the wrong address.

County office users can enter and manage producer information in several applications, creating a risk of inaccurate or excessive data entry that could affect the producer's privacy and program records.
Apply records disposition rules to avoid keeping producer records indefinitely when a shorter approved retention period is sufficient for the program need.
Limit contractor access to need-to-know roles, require background investigations, Level 2 eAuthentication, NDAs, and enforcement of the no-download/no-share/no-store/no-print rule.
Minimize disclosures through shared services by limiting them to the specific data needed for the receiving system and keeping internal interfaces restricted to authorized uses.
Restrict access to producer identity and address fields to authorized users only and protect those records with strong authentication and access controls.
Restrict access to payment, overpayment, premium, and debt records to staff who need them for program administration and payment processing.
Use address verification and secure print/mail handling controls for letters that are physically mailed to producers.
Use validation and review procedures for county office data entry so producer information is collected only as needed and entered accurately.
The system stores highly sensitive identity and financial information, so a breach or misuse could expose producers to identity theft or fraud.
Indefinite retention of permanent records increases the chance that personal data will be exposed or used long after it is needed for program operations.
A shared database accessible to a limited number of employees creates insider-access risk if users can view or export more producer data than they need.
The system relies on SCIMS data being displayed and used in FPISS, which can create accuracy and context risks if outdated or incorrect identity data is pulled into eligibility or payment decisions.
The system uses producer information to determine eligibility and identify sign-up participants, which creates a risk of using more personal data than necessary for the stated purpose.
Restrict viewing and export of SSN/EIN, addresses, and payment amounts to only users with a documented need to know, and mask or truncate these fields wherever full values are not required.

Implement a records review and deletion schedule so permanent retention is limited to the minimum period required by the approved records schedule, with periodic reassessment of whether each data element still needs to be kept.
Apply role-based access controls, audit logging, and periodic access reviews for the shared database used by National, State, and County Office employees.
Validate and periodically reconcile SCIMS-sourced identity data before it is used in FPISS workflows that affect eligibility or payments.
Minimize the personal data displayed in FPISS to only what is necessary for the specific eligibility or sign-up task, and suppress fields not needed for that transaction.

County office users can access farmers' and producers' PII to search for specific people, creating a risk of unnecessary exposure or misuse of names, addresses, email, phone, demographic data, and EIN/SSN.
Using SSN as a second authentication method creates a risk of identity theft or account compromise if the SSN is exposed or improperly handled.
Contractors supporting FSCOMS/FSAfarm+ may be able to access PII, creating a risk of broader insider exposure than necessary.
Although the system says PII is not stored, there is still a residual risk that PII remains in memory or cache if logout clearing does not work as intended.
FSAfarm+ depends on receiving PII from SCIMS, so any weakness in that internal data flow could expose or corrupt the personal data used by county office users.
Restrict county office user access to only the minimum PII needed for the specific search task and log access to PII lookups.
Replace SSN-based second authentication with a less sensitive authentication factor and avoid displaying SSN except when strictly required.
Apply least-privilege role-based access for contractors and require background checks, training, and audit logging for contractor access to PII.
Verify that logout clearing reliably wipes session memory and cache and test that no PII persists after session termination.
Secure the SCIMS-to-FSAfarm+ data retrieval path with strong authentication and encryption and monitor for unauthorized access or tampering.
The system holds sensitive demographic information, including ethnicity and race, which could expose producers to privacy harm if mishandled or accessed improperly.
The system retains producers’ information indefinitely, increasing the chance that outdated records remain available longer than necessary.
County office staff enter data collected from producers at the county office, creating a risk of inaccurate or incomplete records being stored and used for election eligibility and ballot mailing.

The system uses producer information to determine who is eligible to vote in committee elections and to send ballots, which could reveal participation-related information if access is not tightly controlled.
The system maintains election results and COC member data, which could expose producers’ voting-related or organizational participation history if records are accessed inappropriately.

The system builds and sends county-specific lists of eligible producers for printing onto ballot self-mailer forms, which could expose mailing addresses if the lists are mishandled during preparation or printing.
Restrict access to ethnicity and race fields to only staff with a documented need to know and apply strong access logging and review.
Periodically review whether all retained records remain necessary and, where permitted by the approved schedule, remove or archive records that are no longer actively needed.
Use validation checks and supervisor review for county office data entry before records are used for eligibility, ballots, or reports.
Limit access to eligibility lists and committee-code data to authorized election personnel and keep those lists segregated from unrelated records.
Apply role-based access controls to election results and COC member records and monitor access to those records.
Protect ballot mailing lists during generation and printing by limiting who can handle them and ensuring secure handling of the printed forms.

The warehouse concentrates highly sensitive personal and financial data in one place, increasing the impact of any unauthorized access or breach. The stored data includes direct identifiers and account information, so a compromise could expose many people at once.

Broad internal reporting access may expose personal data to more personnel than necessary for any one business need. The system provides information to national, state, and county personnel and supports end user reporting.

Batch transfers from source systems into the warehouse create a risk of interception, corruption, or unintended disclosure while data is moving between systems. The data flow includes extraction from multiple sources and loading into Oracle DB.

Sharing PII with other federal agencies and external parties can disclose personal data beyond the original collection purpose. The context shows sharing with NRCS, RD, RMA, IRS, Treasury, and others.

External disclosure for identity or address validation may expose data to entities that do not need full records, creating unnecessary privacy risk. The system notes a share with Dunn and Bradstreet for name and address validation.

The system supports reporting and analysis beyond the original point of collection, which can lead to secondary use of personal data for purposes not obvious to the data subject. It is used for Congressional, program level, and end user reporting.

Retention of large historical data sets for an extended period can increase the chance of outdated or unnecessary personal data remaining available. The system retains information according to the NARA schedule and allows deviations when defined.
Limit access to the warehouse to authorized users only and apply role-based access controls to sensitive fields such as TIN/SSN and account numbers.
Enforce least-privilege permissions and separate reporting views so personnel only see the minimum data needed for their job.
Protect batch and ETL transfers with encryption in transit and integrity checks to prevent interception or tampering.
Use formal data-sharing agreements and disclose only the minimum necessary information to each recipient.
Limit validation exchanges to the specific fields needed for name and address matching, and avoid sending full records when not required.
Document and review each reporting use to ensure it is consistent with the stated purpose of meeting reporting needs and complying with law.
Apply the NARA retention schedule strictly and delete or archive records when they are no longer required.

The system holds highly sensitive personal and financial data, so any unauthorized access could expose identity, banking, payment, debt, and tax information. This creates a significant risk of identity theft or financial harm if the data is mishandled.

Public-facing and producer-accessible functions increase the chance that users can view more financial detail than they need. Because producers and county employees can access the Financial Inquiry and Financial Services functions, a mistake in access control could expose detailed payment and debt records.

Contractors with system access may mishandle USDA-specific data despite restrictions, creating a disclosure risk. Even with need-to-know access, the system allows contractor access to sensitive financial records and images.

The system generates and transmits letters, statements, and reports about debt and payments, which could reveal sensitive information if intercepted, misdelivered, or handled improperly. This is especially sensitive for delinquent debt, bankruptcy, and collection-related notices.

Debt information is shared for collection and creditworthiness purposes, which can harm privacy if delinquent debt status is disclosed too widely or in error. The system also sends delinquent debt status to commercial credit bureaus.

The system retains records indefinitely, so sensitive personal data remains available far longer than necessary for routine operational use. Long-term retention increases the impact of any future breach or unauthorized access.
Restrict access to sensitive financial and identity data to need-to-know users and require strong authentication and background screening for all authorized users.
Limit FI access so producers and county employees see only the minimum necessary fields and summaries needed for their tasks.
Enforce the existing contractor rules that prohibit downloading, sharing, storing, or printing USDA data, and monitor contractor activity for violations.
Use secure delivery controls for letters and statements, and verify recipient addresses before mailing or printing debt-related notices.
Continue using encrypted transmission for delinquent debt disclosures to credit bureaus and limit such disclosures to only the data required for the stated purpose.
Periodically review whether all permanent records still need indefinite retention and archive or segregate older records to reduce routine exposure.
The system permanently retains identifiable employee information, which increases the risk of long-term exposure or use beyond what is necessary for access control.
The system collects and maintains employee name and mailing address information, which could expose personal contact details if the authorization database is misused or compromised.

The system stores detailed authorization data about users’ roles, groups, offices, and attributes, which could reveal sensitive employment and organizational relationships if accessed inappropriately.
Administrators can manage security access rights in real time, so privileged users could over-assign or remove access in ways that expose employee information or enable unauthorized access.

The system is an online application that lets users submit security requests and track status, which creates a risk that access-request information could be exposed through the application if controls are weak.
Apply a periodic records review and purge or archive records that are no longer needed for current access-control purposes, consistent with the approved records schedule.
Limit access to employee name and mailing address information to users with a demonstrated need for role-based access administration.
Restrict viewing of roles, groups, offices, and attributes to authorized administrators and business users whose duties require that information.
Require strong administrative access controls and audit logging for all role, group, and attribute changes.
Protect the online request and status functions with access controls that ensure users can only view their own authorized requests and statuses.

The system holds highly sensitive personal data, so a breach or misuse could expose identity, financial, health, biometric, and criminal-history information. Because the records include images and signatures, harm could extend to impersonation and fraud.

Centralized browser-based access to stored images can expose records to unauthorized viewing if access controls are weak or misconfigured. The system allows client access from desktop browser to stored images on a network device managed by the server.

The system ingests information from faxed, scanned, email, and desktop-scanner sources, which increases the chance that the wrong document or too much information is captured and stored. That can lead to inaccurate or excessive PII being retained in the imaging repository.
Workflow functions can expose sensitive records to staff who only need limited information to perform their jobs. The system controls workflows associated with the financial information being imaged.

Importing Federal Reserve Bank images into the system creates a risk that external-source records are brought in without sufficient validation or minimization. Those imported images may contain more personal data than needed for the stated purpose.
Permanent retention increases the privacy impact of any future breach or misuse because records never age out of the system. The information is retained indefinitely.

A centralized SQL database for document indexes and workflow data creates a metadata privacy risk even if the underlying images are protected. Indexes can reveal who the records are about, what they concern, and how cases move through the system.
Enforce strict role-based access controls and audit logging for all sensitive record types, with special restrictions for records containing health, biometric, financial, and identity data.
Require strong authentication and least-privilege access for browser users, and review permissions regularly for the network device and server-managed image repository.
Add intake validation and quality-control checks for faxed, scanned, email, and manually entered documents before they are stored.
Constrain workflow visibility so users only see the minimum document content needed for their task, and limit workflow routing to authorized roles.
Apply source-validation and data-minimization review to imported Federal Reserve Bank images before they are stored in the repository.
Implement a documented retention review process to confirm permanent retention is still necessary for each record class and to segregate records that no longer need broad access.
Restrict access to document indexes and workflow metadata separately from image content, and log all metadata searches and changes.

Users may see more personal and eligibility-related information than is necessary for the immediate PSS task, because the system displays detailed contract and status fields and provides links to additional details in PT-FM. This increases the chance of unnecessary internal exposure of sensitive records.

Exporting work lists to Excel can create uncontrolled copies of PII on users’ devices, increasing the chance of loss, unauthorized sharing, or retention outside the system. This is especially sensitive because the export contains the same work-list data.

E-mail alerts can disclose PII beyond the application boundary and may be forwarded, stored, or accessed by unintended recipients. Because the alerts contain record deltas, they can reveal changes over time as well as the underlying personal data.

Client-side filtering and sorting may expose sensitive records on the user’s device or browser session, especially if the device is shared or compromised. This creates a risk that PII remains visible or recoverable outside the intended session.

Because access depends on existing PT-FM permissions, any overly broad or misconfigured role could expose FA Tracker records to users who do not need them. The system relies on inherited access controls rather than describing additional fine-grained restrictions within FA Tracker itself.

Contractors with PT-FM access may also obtain FA Tracker access, creating a risk of insider misuse or accidental disclosure of USDA-specific data. Even with onboarding controls, contractor access expands the set of people who can view the records.

The system includes race, sex, national origin, and disability reporting capability through the shared SCIMS source, which raises sensitivity if such data is exposed or used beyond the intended program purpose. Even if FA Tracker does not list these fields directly, the source system supports them and the data flow can carry sensitive customer information.

The system depends on replicated SCIMS data and encrypted web-service transfers, so any weakness in replication, web-service security, or authentication could expose customer information in transit or in copied databases. This creates a risk of unauthorized access to the underlying source records.
Limit the work-list view to the minimum fields needed for PSS intervention and keep detailed PT-FM data behind stricter access checks.
Restrict or disable Excel export unless there is a documented need, and require device-level safeguards for any approved export.
Send e-mail alerts only to authenticated, authorized users and limit the content to the minimum necessary fields, or replace e-mail with in-app notifications where feasible.
Keep client-side filtering and sorting limited to non-persistent session data and avoid storing results locally in the browser or on the device.
Perform periodic access reviews to confirm that zRoles and PT-FM permissions remain aligned with least privilege for FA Tracker users.
Continue enforcing need-to-know approvals, mandatory background investigations, Level 2 eAuthentication, and NDA requirements for contractors.
Apply heightened access controls and review for any reports or queries involving demographic or disability information drawn from the shared SCIMS source.
Maintain encryption for web-service transfers and enforce established security rules through eAuth for access to replicated SCIMS data.

External users can access their program information over the Internet, so a compromised account could expose contact, tax identification, and payment bank information belonging to exporters and financial institutions.
Contractors have access to the system, which increases the risk of unauthorized viewing or misuse of participant and employee contact information.
Nightly files and ad hoc reports create additional copies of system data, increasing the chance that personal or financial information could be exposed through report handling or downstream storage.

Internal reports are submitted to auditors and other federal departments, which creates a risk that more information than necessary could be disclosed to recipients outside the original operational need.
The system retains information indefinitely, so personal and financial data remain exposed for a very long time if the data is ever breached or improperly accessed.
The system stores tax identification numbers and payment bank information, which are highly sensitive identifiers that could be misused for fraud or financial harm if disclosed.
The system collects names, email addresses, and phone numbers for multiple external parties, creating a risk of unwanted contact or exposure of business relationships if those details are disclosed.
Require strong authentication and role-based access controls for the public GSM interface so users can access only their own program records.
Limit contractor access to the minimum necessary and review contractor permissions regularly.
Restrict report and file access to authorized users and protect nightly extracts and ad hoc reports with access controls and secure handling procedures.
Minimize report content before submission to auditors and other departments so only the information needed for the stated purpose is disclosed.
Apply periodic records review and purge any records that are no longer required under the approved schedule.
Protect tax identification numbers and payment bank information with encryption and strict access restrictions.
Restrict access to contact information to users who need it for program administration and monitor for inappropriate lookup or export activity.

The system can hold highly sensitive personal information in uploaded files, so a breach or improper access could expose identifiers, financial data, criminal history, signatures, and other private records.
Authorized users, contractors, affiliates, and partners can access shared files, creating a risk of overbroad internal or external disclosure beyond what a data subject expects.
External collaboration through a third-party cloud platform can expose PII to vendor-side handling or compromise, especially because the system says the vendor maintains and secures some PII.
PII shared through third-party applications is not periodically purged, increasing the chance that stale records remain available longer than necessary.
The system retains records for long periods, which can prolong exposure of personal information even after the original business need has ended.
Users can upload documents and photos and manually store information from public web applications, so there is a risk that more PII than necessary will be collected and retained in file form.
Continue using encryption in transit and at rest for stored files, and keep strong access controls around sensitive uploads.
Enforce need-to-know access through role-based authorization and audit access to shared files.
Require the vendor to maintain strong contractual and security safeguards for any PII handled through the third-party cloud service.
Implement periodic purge or records-review processes for third-party application data so stale PII is removed when no longer needed.
Apply records schedules and disable accounts promptly when users leave so retained data and access do not persist longer than necessary.
Limit uploads to only the documents needed for the mission and provide user guidance on minimizing PII in shared files.
Information sent through the system to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov could be intercepted or exposed in transit, revealing user data involved in H2A applications.
Using a single common entry point concentrates access to multiple federal services, increasing the privacy impact if the entry point is misused or compromised.
The retained DOL case number could still be linked to a producer’s inquiry and reveal participation in the H2A process if improperly accessed.
The system relies on data collected by external services, so users may not have clear visibility into what information is collected and how it is handled once it leaves FPAC CASP.
Continue to require HTTPS for communications between FPAC CASP / H2A and the external services, and ensure the same protection is applied to all related transmissions.
Limit the pass-through entry point to only the minimum functions needed to route users to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov, and avoid storing any additional user data.
Keep the DOL case number retention strictly limited to the stated 90-day period and delete it promptly afterward.
Provide clear notice that data is transmitted to DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov and that FPAC CASP does not assess or perform actions on the data.

The system stores highly sensitive PII, including SSNs, tax IDs, bank account details, and employment or producer records, which increases the harm if the data are misused or exposed. DRMS and TeamMate+ both contain records that can identify individuals and reveal financial or operational details.

Broad internal access and search capabilities could expose records to more staff than necessary if role restrictions are misapplied or too permissive. DRMS allows all staff to upload and search documents, and specialized roles can perform unconstrained searching for certain purposes.

The system's support for audit, legal discovery, litigation holds, and FOIA inquiries creates a risk that personal information will be disclosed more broadly than the individual expects. Those functions can surface records for non-routine purposes and may expose sensitive content in responses or reviews.
Contractor access introduces additional privacy risk because non-federal personnel may handle sensitive records. The system states that contractors will have access as part of their assigned duties.

Administrator access, even though limited, concentrates powerful privileges in a small number of people and could allow broad exposure if misused. TeamMate+ administrators can access the application remotely and local access may be possible for administrative and configuration purposes.

The long retention period, including records kept indefinitely, increases the chance that personal data will remain available long after it is needed. DRMS and TeamMate+ retain information under NARA schedules and most applications may be retained permanently.

TeamMate+ contains audit documentation about programs, controls, and errors that can implicate individuals or entities in improper payments, contracts, agreements, or eligibility determinations. If those records are mishandled, they could reveal sensitive findings about specific people or organizations.
Continue to enforce encryption for the stored documents and limit access to the minimum necessary users with need-to-know rights.
Tighten role-based access controls so staff can only upload and search the records needed for their official duties, and periodically review those roles and rights.

Apply additional approval and logging controls for records used in legal discovery, litigation holds, and FOIA requests, and limit unconstrained searching to authorized records managers and legal staff only.
Require contractors to receive the same need-to-know access review, training, and oversight as federal staff before they are granted access.
Keep administrator access restricted to the smallest possible number of approved users and monitor remote administrative activity closely.
Regularly review retention schedules and delete or archive records in line with the approved NARA schedule rather than keeping data longer than necessary.
Limit access to audit reports and supporting records to authorized audit personnel and apply redaction where possible before sharing findings with customers or other stakeholders.
The system holds highly sensitive personal identifiers, including SSNs and EINs, which creates a risk of harm if the data is exposed or misused.

The system appears to collect and use data about multiple classes of people, including producers, agents, loss adjusters, employees, affiliates, and other persons, increasing the scope of privacy impact.
Internal sharing for forensic data mining could expose PII beyond the original operational need and create secondary-use privacy risk.
