Apply strong access controls and data governance to the USDA Data Lake and Tableau outputs so only authorized users can retrieve PII.
Enforce role-based access controls that limit each contractor and employee to the smallest set of records needed for their assigned duties.

Centralized storage of detailed identity and access data creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse affecting many USDA employees, contractors, and visitors if the database is compromised or improperly accessed.

Visitor registration and background checking can collect more information than is necessary for a simple meeting visit, creating a risk of over-collection and heightened privacy intrusion for visitors.
Manually collected non-authoritative data at card issuance can be inaccurate or incomplete, leading to incorrect access decisions or erroneous records about individuals.
Internal sharing of card read activity and employee status for executive management and credit card services creates a risk that access data will be used for purposes beyond physical access control.
Daily transfer of personal data to EDAPT and reporting by email to the Credit Card Service Center creates a risk of disclosure during transmission or in downstream analytics and reporting tools.
Contractor access to ePACS creates a risk that non-federal personnel could view or misuse sensitive identity and access information.
Long retention of live and archived records increases the risk that personal data will remain exposed for longer than necessary and be available for future misuse.
The system’s use of multiple authoritative HR sources and a staging table creates a risk that identity data may be combined, propagated, or synchronized incorrectly across systems.
Sharing only under a pending SORN creates a risk of insufficiently clear notice or legal basis for some collected or disclosed data until the routine uses are finalized.
Limit access to authorized users on a strict need-to-know basis and keep data encrypted in storage and transmission.
Minimize visitor data collection to only what is necessary for scheduling and entry, and restrict the background checker to approved use cases.
Validate and review manually collected card-issuance data before it is stored or used to make access decisions.
Restrict internal sharing to the minimum fields needed for each recipient and document the permitted purpose for each report or dashboard.
Use secure transfer methods for all outbound data and limit downstream recipients' access to the smallest dataset needed.
Continue granting contractor access only after background checks and security clearances, and review contractor permissions regularly.
Enforce the approved retention schedule and purge archived records when the 5.5-year period ends.
Keep the staging table and consolidated identity feeds protected with strong access controls and data-quality checks before dissemination.
Finalize the SORN and ensure external disclosures occur only under the approved routine uses and legal review.

Travel and voucher information may be exposed to too many users because the system is used enterprise-wide and authorized agency users access it the same way as internal users. Even with roles, broad internal access increases the chance of unauthorized viewing or misuse of employees' travel data.

Personal and financial travel records are retained for a long time, which increases the risk of secondary use, breach impact, or unnecessary exposure after the data is no longer needed for the trip. Bill-related data retained for six full years can still reveal travel history and spending patterns long after the travel event.

The system profiles travelers by analyzing retained preferences to predict preferred airline seating, rental car companies, and hotel details. This creates a privacy risk because travel behavior can be inferred and reused beyond the immediate transaction.

Travel authorization and voucher data are transmitted to another financial system, creating a disclosure risk during data sharing. Even though the transfer is for validation, it still moves personal travel and spending information outside the original application.

The system depends on centralized authentication and cloud/mobile access, which increases the impact if credentials or session controls are compromised. If an attacker gains access through the web browser or mobile app, they could reach employee travel records and preferences.
Keep restrictive roles and audit checks in place, and limit access further to only the users who need each record for a specific travel or financial task.
Apply the approved NARA and USDA records schedule consistently and delete or archive records as soon as the retention period ends.
Allow travelers to control whether preference data is retained for future reference and used for predictive patterning.
Continue to validate authorization and voucher data with audit checks before transmission to FMMI, and ensure the transfer remains encrypted end to end.
Maintain multifactor authentication, VPN protections, and session-authenticity controls for browser and mobile access to reduce the chance of unauthorized account takeover.
The system retains traveler preference data and uses it to create predictive patterns, which can reveal personal habits and enable profiling beyond the immediate travel transaction.
Enterprise-wide access creates a risk that more users than necessary can view USDA employee travel and voucher information.
Sharing authorization and voucher data with FMMI exposes employee travel information to another system, creating additional disclosure and linkage risk.
Long retention of user and billing data increases the risk that personal information will remain available longer than needed and be exposed in a future incident or misuse.
Because the system is accessed through web browsers and mobile applications, travel data may be exposed if endpoints or sessions are compromised.
Limit traveler preference retention to the minimum necessary and provide a clear way for users to review and delete stored preferences.
Continue enforcing restrictive role-based access and periodically review role assignments to ensure users only have access to the data needed for their duties.
Apply data minimization and field-level access controls before transmitting authorization and voucher records to FMMI, so only required data elements are shared.
Enforce the approved retention schedule and conduct periodic data disposition reviews to delete records when they are no longer required.
Maintain strong session and endpoint protections for browser and mobile access, including multifactor authentication and encrypted transport.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial data, so unauthorized access or disclosure could expose employees' identities and banking information.
The system appears to combine multiple personal data elements in one administrative environment, increasing the risk of overexposure if access is broader than necessary.
The system's use for debt collection could lead to inappropriate disclosure or use of delinquent-debt information about individuals.
Personnel and payroll data may be used for purposes beyond the original collection context, creating a risk of secondary use that is broader than necessary.
The 10-year retention period extends the time the system holds personal data, increasing the window for unauthorized access or stale-data exposure.
Restrict access to the sensitive personal and financial fields to authorized staff with a need to know, and protect the data with strong technical and administrative safeguards.
Apply role-based access controls and separate duties across the different administrative functions so users only see the data needed for their specific task.
Minimize the debt-collection information displayed or shared to only what is necessary for the collection task, and log access to delinquent-debt records.
Limit routine use and reporting to the specific personnel and payroll purposes stated, and review any sharing with other Federal agencies for necessity and authorization.
Apply the approved retention schedule consistently and delete or archive records when the 10-year period ends.

The system stores a broad set of personally identifiable and case-related information, including audio files, which could expose appellants and other participants if the data is mishandled or overexposed.
Only OHA-NAD personnel and contractors can access the electronic case tracking system, so insider misuse or unnecessary access could expose appellant data.
Contractor access creates a risk that non-federal users could improperly view or handle personal case information if controls are not consistently enforced.

Public e-filers can view their appeal transaction history and submitted documents, which could expose residence and contact information if account access is compromised or if the portal reveals more than intended.
Reports generated for management review may disclose PII beyond the minimum needed for oversight, creating a secondary exposure path for personal data.
Information is retained forever even though it is not the official record, which increases the long-term risk of unnecessary exposure, stale data, and future misuse.
The system collects data through a web interface behind a secure login page, so any weakness in authentication or session protection could expose case information during online submission and access.
Minimize the data collected and stored to only what is necessary for case tracking and reporting, and apply strong access controls to audio files and PII.
Limit internal access to only personnel with a demonstrated need to know and review access permissions regularly.
Apply the same authentication, authorization, and monitoring controls to contractors as to federal employees, including periodic access reviews.
Require strong authentication for the eFile portal and limit the portal to only the appellant's own case data and submitted documents.
Continue displaying PII warnings on reports and restrict report contents to the minimum needed for management review.
Establish and enforce a finite retention schedule, with periodic deletion or archival review, even if the system is not the official record.
Harden the secure web login page with strong session management, multi-factor authentication, and continuous security monitoring.

The system holds sensitive employee identity and payroll-related records that could be exposed if access controls fail. The collected data includes names, SSNs, time and attendance information, teleworking agreements, and payroll data.

Agency personnel and HR staff may enter or access data on behalf of individuals, which creates a risk of unauthorized or mistaken disclosure of an employee’s information. The system relies on multiple human intermediaries rather than only direct self-service by the data subject.

Access is determined by agencies and supervisors, so users may receive broader access than necessary if least-privilege controls are not strictly enforced. The system explicitly allows access to profiled data based on agency requests and access privileges.

WebTA shares certified time-and-attendance and payroll data with other USDA systems, which increases the number of places where personal data can be accessed or misused. Each additional system connection expands the disclosure surface.

Data is transmitted between agencies and systems over network connections, so interception or misrouting could expose PII in transit. Although secure methods are described, the system still depends on correct use of those channels.
Contractors may have access to the system, which creates a risk that non-government personnel could view or mishandle employee data. Contractor access broadens the set of people who can reach PII.

Individuals may access their data through assigned user IDs and passwords, so account compromise could expose personal records. If credentials are stolen or weakly protected, an attacker could view time, attendance, and payroll information.

The system retains records for periods governed by records schedules and agency requirements, so personal data remains available for a long time. Longer retention increases the window in which an access or breach incident could affect individuals.
Limit collection and display of SSNs and payroll details to only what is necessary for time-and-attendance processing, and protect those fields with strict access controls.
Require logged, authorized workflows when HR staff enter information on behalf of individuals and verify the subject’s identity before updates are made.
Enforce least-privilege access reviews so users only retain the minimum access needed for their duties and specific profiled data.
Restrict inter-system sharing to approved business purposes and document each downstream recipient’s access and use of the shared data.
Continue to require secure transmission methods such as SFTP over VPN and HTTPS for all data exchanges, and verify that no unencrypted channels are used.
Grant contractors access only when a valid role is approved and review contractor privileges regularly to ensure they remain necessary.
Require strong password practices and account protection for assigned user IDs, and limit access to the user’s own data unless a separate authorization exists.
Apply the approved records schedule consistently and remove records when their retention period ends.

Customer contact information and inquiry details may be exposed to a wide internal audience when escalated inquiries are shared across USDA Mission Areas. This increases the chance that staff who do not need the information could see names, addresses, phone numbers, email addresses, and case history.

PII may be disclosed in transit when sent by email to SME contacts or passed through Cisco telephony integration. These transfer methods can create exposure if messages are misaddressed, intercepted, or handled outside the intended workflow.

The system may retain customer PII longer than necessary because no purging or archiving is currently configured. Long retention increases the amount of data available if the system is compromised and extends the period during which old contact details remain exposed.

The system stores directly identifying contact information together with inquiry and case history, which could reveal sensitive details about a person's interaction with USDA programs. Even if the data is not inherently highly sensitive, combining identity and case information can create a fuller profile of the individual.

Authorized users with valid Linc Pass credentials can access PII in the Salesforce environment, so a compromised or misused account could expose customer data. The system relies on user authentication and role-based access, but the PII is still available to internal authorized users.
Limit escalated inquiry access to only the specific mission area staff needed to resolve the case, rather than sharing PII with all USDA Mission Areas.
Use secure, approved transmission methods for PII instead of ordinary email, and apply safeguards to the Cisco telephony integration to minimize disclosure during transfer.
Implement automatic purging or archiving rules tied to the approved retention schedule so records are removed or archived when no longer needed.
Minimize the case details stored with contact records by collecting only what is needed to resolve the inquiry and separating identity data from narrative case history where possible.
Enforce role-based access controls and periodic access reviews for all authorized users and contractors, with prompt removal of access when it is no longer required.

The system creates broad surveillance of employees, contractors, and visitors as they enter and move through USDA facilities, which can reveal their movements and associations over time. This can chill ordinary activity and expose sensitive presence information even when no wrongdoing is suspected.

The cameras can capture highly identifying details beyond simple video, including facial images, license plates, and information from drivers licenses such as names, addresses, and dates of birth. This increases the chance of identifying and tracking individuals across places and events.

Some cameras use zoom, manual tracking, and automatic tracking to follow a single individual or capture text on belongings, which can intensify surveillance beyond general security monitoring. This raises the risk of intrusive focus on particular people without a specific need.

Footage may be used and exported for criminal or disciplinary actions, creating a secondary-use risk that the data will be applied beyond simple facility security. People recorded by the system may face consequences based on footage collected for monitoring purposes.

The system shares video with internal and external organizations, including federal agencies and local law enforcement, which increases the risk of broader dissemination and loss of control over the footage. Once shared, the footage may be used for investigations and prosecutions beyond USDA's direct oversight.

Contractors and select non-employees can access the system, so more people than USDA staff may view sensitive footage. This expands the number of authorized users and the chance of misuse or unauthorized viewing.

Although the system intends a six-month retention period, footage may be kept longer when storage, camera counts, or suspected criminal activity require it. Extended retention increases the amount of historical surveillance data available for later access or misuse.

The cameras record passersby on public streets and people accessing secured areas, so the system may collect information about individuals who are not the primary focus of security monitoring. This can capture bystanders and people with no connection to a specific incident.
Limit camera placement and viewing to security-relevant areas and avoid unnecessary coverage of routine movement areas where possible.
Restrict capture of identifying details to situations where they are needed for security or investigation, and avoid using zoom or plate-reading features unless justified by an incident.
Require documented justification and supervisory approval before using manual tracking or zoom on a person or vehicle, except during an active security incident.
Use footage for criminal or disciplinary actions only when there is a documented investigative need and limit exports to the minimum relevant segments.
Share footage only in response to formal requests and only with recipients whose need is tied to a specific investigation or prosecution.
Keep access limited to screened personnel and apply least-privilege access so contractors and non-employees can view only what they need.
Enforce the six-month automatic deletion rule and require documented approval for any extension tied to suspected criminal activity.
Use camera placement and operational review to minimize capture of passersby and unrelated individuals where feasible.

The system may collect identifiable customer information in feedback channels, creating a risk that customers are identified when they did not expect to provide PII. The tool explicitly allows collection of names, email addresses, and zip codes in free-form comments.

The system may reveal sensitive or identifying information through free-form feedback that is later analyzed and retained. The tool collects both structured and unstructured feedback from multiple channels, which can contain personal details beyond the listed PII.

Combining feedback across USDA mission areas can create a broader profile of an individual’s interactions and preferences. The system is designed to collect and analyze data across all mission areas and offices and to migrate existing tools into one cohesive product.

Geographic, demographic, and ethnographic analysis can create privacy risks by inferring characteristics about customers from their feedback. The system explicitly uses data to gather such insights for improvement purposes.

A small number of users with access to all data across mission areas creates a risk of excessive internal access. This broad access could expose more customer information than is necessary for a user’s role.

Contractor access creates a risk that non-federal personnel may see customer feedback and any included PII. The system states that contractors will have access, but does not describe separate limits in the provided text.

Permissioning and access control weaknesses could expose data to unauthorized users if role-based restrictions are not consistently enforced. The system relies on mission need, permission levels, licensing, and documented permissions.

The retention program is not fully approved, which creates a risk that records may be kept longer than intended or not governed consistently. The PIA states the retention period has not been approved by the component records officer and NARA.
Minimize collection of direct identifiers and only request PII when a customer explicitly asks for follow-up contact.
Review and redact free-form submissions before they are used broadly in dashboards or analysis.
Limit cross-mission-area access to only users with a demonstrated mission need and keep views aggregated where possible.
Use the geographic, demographic, and ethnographic outputs only in aggregated form and suppress small cells or outliers.
Restrict all-data access to the smallest possible number of users and review those privileges regularly.
Apply the same privacy and security training, licensing, and documented permission controls to contractors as to federal users.
Enforce role-based access controls and permission reviews before granting or renewing access.
Obtain formal approval of the retention schedule from the component records officer and NARA.

The system collects more personal information than appears necessary for account provisioning, including contact numbers, which increases the amount of PII exposed if the cloud system is compromised or misused.
Users cannot decline to provide mandatory account fields, so individuals have no practical choice about providing their name, email address, and username to use the system.
PII is stored in a third-party cloud service hosted outside the ACFO-SS-FMS boundary, which creates exposure to cloud-provider security or administrative risks.
Contractors can access the system, which may broaden access to employee PII beyond USDA staff who strictly need it.
Access is granted through customizable workflows and approvals, so there is a risk that users may receive more access than necessary if access controls are not tightly configured.
The system retains PII for 75 months, which extends the time personal data remains available and increases the window for misuse or breach.
Minimize collection by removing contact numbers unless they are strictly required for account provisioning or a documented business need.
Provide a less-privileged alternative account or workflow for users who cannot or should not supply the mandatory fields, where operationally feasible.
Apply and verify strong cloud security controls, including encryption, access restrictions, and vendor oversight for the hosted environment.
Limit contractor access to only those accounts and functions necessary for their assigned duties and review contractor access regularly.
Enforce least-privilege access settings and periodic access reviews to ensure customized workflows do not grant unnecessary permissions.
Review whether the 75-month retention period is the minimum necessary and purge records as soon as the approved retention schedule allows.

The system holds highly sensitive personal data, including SSNs/TINs, handwritten signatures, salary data, and legal names, so a breach or misuse could expose applicants, grantees, vendors, and personnel to identity theft or financial harm.
GIMS data may be shared outside USDA with a broad set of external parties, which creates a risk of unnecessary disclosure of applicant and awardee information beyond the original collection purpose.
Information may be disclosed in common office formats or hard copy, which can lead to accidental forwarding, printing loss, or other unauthorized exposure of personal data.

Review panelists can receive encrypted PII, and although some identifiers are redacted, other personal information still flows to external reviewers, creating a risk of over-disclosure during the grants review process.
Contractors have access for backup, support, and account management, which creates a risk that non-government personnel could access or mishandle sensitive records.
The system ingests data from external systems and manual user entry, so inaccurate or mismatched records could lead to incorrect award, vendor, or collection decisions that affect individuals.
The system retains GIMS and FMAT information for six years after closeout or final payment/cancellation, which may keep personal data longer than needed and extend the window of exposure.

Because the system supports reporting to internal users and external reporting approved by the Grants Director, reports may reveal more personal or program information than intended if not tightly controlled.
Encrypt sensitive PII before distribution and keep the data out of primary key fields used for tracking or identity matching.
Limit external sharing to approved disclosures and require Grants Director approval before any release outside USDA.
Apply stronger handling controls to exported files and paper copies, such as restricting distribution and using encrypted electronic delivery where possible.
Continue limiting PII sharing to review panelists and redact unnecessary identifiers such as EIN/TIN before distribution.
Keep contractor access restricted to the specific support functions listed and maintain direct supervision of computerized files.
Validate and reconcile incoming data from external systems and manual entries before using it for matching, awards, or vendor creation.
Review whether all retained records still need to remain in primary storage for the full retention period and archive them according to approved records schedules.
Restrict report generation and external reporting to approved users and disclosures only, with the Grants Director controlling release.
Centralizing detailed SNAP participant information in one database increases the impact of any unauthorized access or breach because the system aggregates sensitive data from all states in one place.
The system collects highly sensitive eligibility and financial details, which could reveal intimate information about participants if accessed or used beyond the intended checks.
Sharing data across federal and state systems can expose participant information to multiple agencies, increasing the number of places where privacy controls must be enforced.
Using automated scripts, queries, and matching algorithms to make integrity determinations can produce false positives that wrongly flag participants as ineligible, duplicate, or fraudulent.
Collecting data from 2000 to the present creates a long historical record that may include people whose older information is no longer necessary for current program integrity checks.
The system's immigration status checks create a risk that highly sensitive citizenship or immigration-related information will be used in ways that participants may not expect.

Cross-state duplicate enrollment detection may link records about the same person across jurisdictions, increasing the chance of incorrect identity matching or unnecessary exposure of participation history.
Store the data only in the authorized FNS AWS environment and maintain strong access controls and monitoring around the centralized database.
Limit collection and use to the data required for the stated integrity checks and avoid any unrelated secondary use.
Share information only when permitted by law and consistent with the notice, and only with state agencies when necessary to investigate and rectify improper enrollments or transactions.
Use the described matching algorithms and add human review before any adverse action is taken on a participant record.
Apply a retention schedule that limits how long historical participant data is kept and deletes records when they are no longer needed for integrity checks.
Restrict access to immigration-status-related data to personnel with a need to know and document the purpose for each use.
Use data-matching rules designed to minimize false positives and verify matches before treating records as duplicates across states.
The system stores identifiable contact information about non-employee affiliates, so a breach or misuse could expose names, business addresses, contact information, and affiliate IDs.
NRCS employees are the only users of the application, so any misuse or unauthorized access by an employee could expose or alter affiliate records.
The application shares affiliate information with zRoles to assign roles, creating a risk that incorrect or excessive access could be granted to affiliates in other NRCS systems.

Because affiliates provide their information to an NRCS employee and the employee enters it into the system, data entry errors or outdated information could cause inaccurate records and incorrect access decisions.
The records may be retained for a long time, which increases the chance that unnecessary personal information remains available after it is no longer needed.

The system stores affiliate records as long as a person qualifies for conservation programs, which could keep personal information tied to an individual for an extended period beyond immediate access-control needs.
Restrict access to the Affiliates database to authorized NRCS employees only and enforce least-privilege access controls.
Require role-based access review, audit logging, and periodic monitoring of NRCS employee activity in the application.
Validate affiliate records before they are used by zRoles and require periodic review of assigned roles for appropriateness.
Confirm the affiliate's submitted information with the affiliate before entry or when records are updated.
Apply records disposal rules so affiliate data is deleted or archived when the approved retention period ends.
Review whether all retained fields are still necessary for access-control purposes and minimize stored data where possible.

The warehouse holds highly sensitive personal and financial-identifying information, so a compromise could expose producers, agents, and adjusters to identity theft or other misuse. The stored data includes tax IDs, social security numbers, addresses, phone numbers, policy numbers, and location-linked farm information.

The system centralizes data from multiple years into a single production database, increasing the amount of personal information exposed if access controls fail or the database is breached. Consolidation also makes it easier to link records over time and build detailed profiles.

Authorized users in multiple organizations can access the data, creating a risk of overbroad internal disclosure or misuse beyond the minimum necessary. The system shares information with FSA, RMA, OIG, and authorized users in AIPs.

External Approved Insurance Providers can access information tied to their policies, which creates a risk that sensitive policy data could be disclosed outside USDA more broadly than intended. Even limited access still exposes personal and policy details to non-federal entities.

Users access the system through a web application on the RMA Extranet, so unauthorized access or interception of transmitted data could expose personal information. The need for dual authentication helps, but the web-based access path still presents a privacy risk if credentials are compromised.

The data is retained for the life of the project, which increases the amount of time personal information remains exposed to security incidents or inappropriate use. Long retention also increases the chance that data will be used beyond the period originally expected by the individuals.

The system uses data mining and analysis to support fraud and abuse detection, which can create privacy risk if individuals are profiled or decisions are influenced by incorrect or overly broad inferences. The warehouse combines many data elements for research and analysis purposes.
Limit access to the most sensitive fields, such as tax IDs and social security numbers, to only users with a documented need and mask or tokenize those fields in routine reports.
Keep annual datasets segregated where possible and restrict cross-year joins or exports to approved analytical uses only.
Enforce least-privilege role-based access reviews for FSA, RMA, OIG, and other authorized users, with periodic recertification of who still needs access.
Apply contract and account-level controls so AIPs can only retrieve the specific policy records they are authorized to see, and log all external access for review.
Maintain strong authentication for HyDRA, require secure transport, and monitor for suspicious login activity or credential abuse.
Apply a documented retention schedule that minimizes storage to the shortest period compatible with the project and return or dispose of data when no longer needed.
Review data-mining outputs for necessity and accuracy before release, and document limits on how analytical results may be used to avoid unsupported inferences about individuals.

CoLab stores identifiable user profile information, including names and personal contact details, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse if the system is compromised or access controls fail.
Because access is granted to authorized contractors and partners, there is a risk that more people than necessary can view or modify user profiles, increasing insider misuse or accidental exposure.
CoLab uses PII obtained from eAuth to establish and update user profiles, so errors or outdated information in the source or profile can lead to inaccurate identity and contact records.
User profile information is retained for the life of the application, which creates a risk that personal data will remain longer than needed and increase exposure over time.
Although the system says accounts are disabled when a user leaves, there is still a risk that departed users' profile data may persist unless it is actually erased or deleted when no longer needed.
Limit the profile to the minimum contact fields needed for authorization and project administration, and restrict editing and viewing to authorized roles only.
Enforce least-privilege RBAC reviews for contractors and partners so their access remains limited to the duties they need to perform.
Allow users to review and correct their own profile information and verify eAuth-derived identity data before it is used to create the profile.
Delete application-specific PII when it is no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit, or other operational purposes, rather than keeping it for the full life of the application.
When a user leaves, disable the account and also remove or archive any associated profile data according to the approved records schedule.

Vendor PII is retained in the IDEA DataMart, which increases the risk of unauthorized access or exposure compared with purely transitory processing. The retained data includes names and contact information used for reporting.

Contractors can access the system, which creates a risk that vendor PII could be viewed or misused by personnel beyond direct government staff. The access description does not specify technical limits on what contractors can see.

Periodic refreshes from SCIMS create a risk that stale or unnecessary PII may remain available between updates or after it is no longer needed. This can increase the chance of retaining more personal data than necessary for reporting.

Report generation using selectable criteria could allow users to infer or view vendor PII in outputs if access controls are weak. Even though the system says it does not retrieve records by personal identifier, reports still use vendor information.

Keeping application-specific information while the application remains in production may extend the life of PII longer than necessary if deletion is not timely. Long retention increases the window for misuse or breach.
Limit the DataMart to the minimum vendor fields needed for report generation and apply strict access controls and auditing to the stored PII.
Enforce least-privilege role-based access for contractors and review contractor access regularly.
Delete refreshed PII from IDEA when it is no longer needed for reporting and verify that periodic updates do not preserve obsolete records.
Constrain report criteria and output so users only receive vendor information necessary for their assigned reporting task.
Apply the approved NARA deletion schedule promptly when the data is no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit, or operational purposes.

Core Services can expose highly sensitive customer identifiers because it handles a customer ID that can be associated with a Social Security number or tax identification number, along with names, addresses, and partial bank account numbers. If access controls fail, this data could be disclosed to unauthorized users or systems.

Returning data to client applications in JSON can expose personal information to any client or user that receives the response, increasing the chance of over-disclosure if the request is not properly authorized or scoped. This is especially sensitive because the system responds to multiple applications and legacy systems.

Core Services moves USDA application data and metadata between several internal systems, creating a broader internal sharing surface where data could be exposed through one of the connected applications, databases, or adjacent systems. More integrations increase the chance of unauthorized access or accidental disclosure.

Requests from outside the NRCS firewall enter through a single external-facing gateway, so a compromise of that entry point could affect multiple downstream systems and the personal data they retrieve. This creates a concentration risk at the gateway layer.

Contractors with need-to-know access may see personal information as part of their duties, which creates insider-access risk if their access is broader than necessary or if controls are not tightly enforced. Even with background investigations, contractor access increases the number of people who can view the data.

Core Services relies on replicated or copied access to SCIMS data rather than direct control of the source system, so stale or inconsistent data could be returned or used for the wrong person. That can cause privacy harms such as misidentification or disclosure of one customer’s information in response to another customer’s request.

The system depends on authentication and established security rules for access to customer data, so any weakness in eAuth or authorization rules could allow unauthorized viewing of personal information. Because access is mediated across several systems, a control failure in one layer could open access broadly.

Limit returned identifiers to the minimum necessary and mask or suppress sensitive fields such as customer IDs, bank account fragments, and any values associated with SSNs or TINs unless they are strictly required for the specific request.
Apply response-level data minimization and authorization checks before generating JSON output so each client application receives only the fields needed for its approved function.
Use least-privilege interface permissions and periodic review of each internal system connection so only approved systems can exchange the specific data they need.
Harden and continuously monitor the external-facing CA API Gateway with strong threat protection, logging, and alerting, since it is the single entry point for outside requests.
Restrict contractor access to the minimum necessary, enforce periodic access reviews, and keep the required background investigations current for all contractor users.
Validate replicated SCIMS data against the source system and monitor for synchronization errors before returning records to users or downstream applications.
Enforce strong authentication, role-based authorization, and regular review of security rules governing access through eAuth and related interfaces.

Emergency Action Plan records contain names, home addresses, and telephone numbers, so a breach or improper disclosure could expose private contact and location information for responders and property owners.
PII is shared with state and local emergency responders and disclosed in hardcopy or electronic copies, creating a risk of wider dissemination than intended during review cycles or activation.
Contractors and multiple responder roles can access EAPs on a need-to-know basis, so there is a risk of unauthorized internal access or overbroad access if controls are not strictly enforced.
The system retains records for long periods, which increases the chance that outdated PII will remain available after it is no longer needed for an EAP or after a person’s role changes.
Some telephone numbers may not be publicly listed, so collecting them from individuals or organizations can reveal nonpublic contact information that the person may not expect to be broadly retained.
Continue using secure communications methods for all hardcopy and electronic disclosures of EAPs, and limit distribution to controlled documents only.
Restrict disclosure of EAP PII to authorized emergency response situations and review cycles only, and avoid any sharing outside the stated emergency purpose.
Enforce documented access controls and need-to-know authorization for all users, including contractors and responders.
Require mandatory background investigations for contractors before granting access to DamWatch.
Apply the approved NARA retention schedule and remove records when they no longer qualify for conservation program purposes.
Treat nonpublic telephone numbers as especially sensitive and collect or retain them only when necessary for EAP execution.
The system stores highly sensitive personal data, so a breach or unauthorized access could expose Social Security numbers, tax IDs, bank account details, and other sensitive records.
Bulk scanning and metadata extraction can capture more information than needed, including personal details embedded in paper records that were not originally intended for broad digital access.
Because DRMS is a cloud-based system run by a contractor, cloud or contractor access failures could expose records to unauthorized parties or misuse.
Authorized staff and contractors can access records on a need-to-know basis, so excessive internal access could lead to insider misuse or unnecessary viewing of personal information.
Individuals do not have direct access to DRMS, which can make it harder for them to review or correct their own records and may leave inaccurate PII in the system.
Long retention periods increase the chance that outdated personal information will remain stored longer than necessary, expanding exposure over time.

The system holds records about owners, operators, producers, and participants in conservation programs, so disclosure could reveal participation in government programs and related property or farm details.
Limit access to encrypted documents containing sensitive identifiers to only authorized users with a documented need-to-know, and enforce strong authentication and audit logging.
Minimize bulk scanning and metadata extraction to only the records and fields needed for business and records-management purposes.
Maintain contractor security requirements, including mandatory background investigations and least-privilege access, for all contractor personnel with system access.
Review and recertify user access regularly so staff and contractors retain only the access needed for their current duties.
Provide a clear, timely process for individuals to request their records and correction of inaccuracies through the designated field office or records office.
Apply records schedules and dispose of records when the approved retention period ends, rather than keeping them indefinitely.
Restrict search and retrieval capabilities to operational, legal, and records-management uses, and avoid broad retrieval of records beyond the stated business need.

DMS may expose highly sensitive personal and financial data if a document repository is accessed inappropriately, because it stores a wide range of PII including SSNs, tax IDs, bank routing numbers, and deposit account numbers.
Direct document uploads by NRCS users can introduce incorrect, unnecessary, or overly sensitive information into DMS without a structured data-entry review step.
Information transmitted from multiple source systems into DMS could be intercepted or mishandled during transfer, especially because the system relies on web services and user uploads.
Using address and name from FSA SCIMS to identify the correct producer creates a risk of mismatching records and associating the wrong person with a document.
Authorized NRCS employees, conservation district employees, and contractors may view documents beyond what is strictly necessary if access controls are too broad for their roles.
External disclosure to contractors or technical service providers could reveal PII outside USDA if the written authorization or purpose limitation is not properly enforced.
Because individuals do not have direct access to DMS, they may have limited ability to review their records and detect privacy errors or misuse promptly.
Long retention of records can keep personal data in the system for years after it is no longer needed for active processing, increasing exposure over time.
Restrict document access to authorized users with a need-to-know and maintain encryption for stored and transmitted documents.
Require upload review and minimize retained content by rejecting documents that contain unnecessary sensitive information.
Keep the web-service transfers encrypted and controlled for all source-system exchanges and user uploads.
Use additional identity verification or matching checks before linking SCIMS data to a producer record.
Enforce role-based, least-privilege access reviews so users only see the documents needed for their assigned duties.
Require and verify written authorization before any disclosure to contractors or technical service providers, and limit use to the stated purpose.
Provide a clear, timely request process for individuals to obtain information about records pertaining to them and to seek corrections through the designated office.
Apply the approved records schedule and delete records when the retention period ends.

The system holds sensitive borrower financial and identity data that could be exposed if access controls are weak or misused. The data includes loan, financial, and security property information tied to identifiable borrowers.

Manual entry by field agents can introduce privacy risks from input errors or unnecessary collection. Because the system relies on staff-entered data, mistakes could place incorrect borrower information into restructuring decisions.

The system’s access to other internal applications and databases can broaden exposure of borrower information across systems. Cross-system access increases the number of places where the data can be viewed or mishandled.

Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the risk that personal data will remain available longer than necessary. Long-term storage raises the chance of future misuse, breach, or secondary use.

The system is used to make debt restructuring decisions, so inaccurate borrower data could lead to unfair or incorrect servicing outcomes. Errors in cash flow, loan status, or security property data could affect repayment plans.
Restrict access to authorized agency officials and field office employees only, with role-based permissions and audit logging for all borrower record access.
Add validation and review controls for manually entered borrower data before it is saved or used in calculations.
Apply strict access controls and least-privilege rules to all connected internal databases and web applications, and limit data pulled from them to what is needed for restructuring.
Implement a records review process to confirm that permanent retention is still required for each record set and to segregate archived records with strong protections.
Use data quality checks to verify borrower cash flow, loan status, and related inputs before restructuring calculations are performed.
The system stores highly sensitive personal, financial, and credit information that could cause significant harm if improperly accessed or disclosed.
Sharing name and Tax ID with an external credit vendor creates a risk of unnecessary external exposure of identifying data.
Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the long-term risk of misuse, breach, or access beyond the original loan purpose.
Collecting and maintaining credit reports and credit numbers can expose borrowers to sensitive credit-history privacy harms if the data is accessed or used beyond eligibility decisions.
The system’s use of borrower data for loan making and servicing creates a risk of function creep if information is reused beyond the stated loan-assessment purpose.
County office staff enter borrower data, so inaccurate or incomplete entry could lead to incorrect financial or eligibility decisions that affect the borrower’s privacy and interests.
Restrict access to borrower records to only personnel with a need to know and apply strong authentication and audit logging for all access to sensitive fields.
Minimize the data shared with Microbilt to only the specific fields required for creditworthiness checks and document the purpose of that exchange.
Apply and enforce a records schedule that deletes or archives borrower records when they are no longer needed for the approved retention period.
Limit access to credit reports and related credit identifiers to staff directly involved in eligibility and servicing decisions.
Define and enforce purpose-specific use rules so the collected information is used only for loan eligibility, loan making, and loan servicing activities described in the PIA.
Validate borrower-entered information with the borrower before final processing and use data quality checks to reduce entry errors.
The system stores highly sensitive borrower identifiers and account information, including Social Security Numbers, which creates risk if the data is exposed or misused.
Borrower data can be accessed through online queries and batch processing using name or Social Security Number, increasing the chance of unauthorized lookup or overbroad access.
The system shares borrower information with a wide set of internal organizations and support personnel, which expands the number of people who can see personal data.
Borrower information is disclosed externally to multiple agencies and private entities, creating risk of secondary use or disclosure beyond the original collection purpose.
The system reports borrower information to IRS and credit bureaus, which can adversely affect borrowers through tax refund offsets and credit reporting if the data is inaccurate or outdated.
Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the risk that personal information will remain available long after it is needed for active servicing or reporting.
The stated work on a public-facing Customer Self Service capability could expose borrower information to a broader audience if not carefully controlled.
Limit collection and display of Social Security Numbers to the minimum necessary and mask or truncate the number wherever full display is not operationally required.
Restrict online queries and batch access to role-based, need-to-know users and require additional verification before searching by Social Security Number.
Apply least-privilege access controls and logging for internal users, support staff, and developers who can access borrower records.
Use data-sharing agreements and disclosure controls for each external recipient so only the minimum necessary borrower information is sent for the stated purpose.
Validate and reconcile account data before IRS and credit bureau reporting, and provide a process to correct disputed borrower information promptly.

Review whether all permanent records truly require indefinite retention and, where permitted by records schedules, delete or archive records that are no longer needed for operational or legal purposes.
Design the public-facing Customer Self Service feature with strong authentication, authorization, and data minimization before it is launched.

PII could be exposed to too many internal users because the system is available to County, State, Regional, and National FLP staff and stores contact information. Broad internal availability increases the chance that staff with no need to know could view or misuse names and contact details.

The system may retain PII longer than necessary because the information is kept indefinitely as permanent records. Long-term retention increases the amount of historical contact information available for misuse or accidental disclosure over time.

Manual system input can introduce inaccurate, incomplete, or unnecessary personal data into the record. If staff enter incorrect contact information, it can affect appraisal processing and create privacy harm by maintaining wrong data about individuals.

Centralizing appraisal-related information in a single enterprise web application can create a larger concentration of PII than a distributed process. If the system is compromised or misused, the impact could extend across many loan cases and staff levels.
Enforce role-based access controls so each FLP staff level can only view and edit the records needed for its duties.
Apply periodic records review and purge or archive PII that no longer needs to remain active, consistent with the approved records schedule.
Add validation and supervisory review for manually entered contact information before it is finalized in the system.
Segment the database and apply strong administrative controls, logging, and monitoring around access to the centralized appraisal records.
The system collects and stores highly sensitive identifiers and financial data, creating a significant risk of harm if those records are accessed improperly or compromised.
The system includes race, ethnicity, and gender data for loan processing, which creates a risk of sensitive demographic information being exposed or used inappropriately.
The system aggregates borrower information from many internal, government, and private sources, increasing the risk that inaccurate or outdated data will affect loan servicing and credit decisions.

The system uses external financial and property-related sources such as credit reporting agencies, tax records, and courthouse records, which creates a risk that data collected for one context will be used more broadly than borrowers expect.
The system retains information indefinitely, creating a long-term privacy risk because sensitive borrower data remains available far longer than the active loan relationship may require.
Field office staff and county office staff can process, service, and analyze borrower information, creating an insider-access risk if access is broader than necessary or not carefully controlled.
Borrowers can access their FLP account information through the web-based system, which creates a risk of unauthorized account access if authentication or session protections fail.
The system uses manual input for debt restructuring and business-plan data entry, creating a risk of human error or inconsistent handling of sensitive borrower information.
The system combines financial, employment, and business-planning information to determine credit worthiness and loan eligibility, creating a risk of overly broad profiling of borrowers.
Restrict access to SSNs, TINs, credit reports, and other sensitive fields to staff with a documented need to know, and apply strong authentication and audit logging for all access.
Limit demographic fields to the minimum necessary for program administration and mask them in routine views and reports.
Validate, reconcile, and periodically review data received from other FSA applications and third-party sources before it is used in servicing or restructuring decisions.
Limit use of external source data to clearly defined loan-processing purposes and document why each source is necessary for the specific decision being made.
Apply records schedules that delete or archive records when no longer needed for operational purposes, even if some records are authorized as permanent.
Use role-based access controls for field office and county office staff and review access rights regularly.
Require strong user authentication and session protections for producer access to FLP account information.
Use data-entry validation and supervisory review for manually entered restructuring and business-plan information.
Limit the fields used in credit-worthiness and eligibility analysis to those directly needed for the loan decision and avoid retaining unnecessary analytical outputs.
Personal data is retained indefinitely, which increases the chance of unnecessary long-term exposure, misuse, or secondary use over time.
The system holds personally identifiable information that is used across multiple web-based applications, creating a risk of internal overexposure if access is not tightly limited.

SDMS collects information from the public on directives or policies that have not yet been approved by OMB, which could expose individuals to premature disclosure or handling of information tied to unapproved materials.
The system stores mailing addresses for FLOTrack and SDMS users, which creates a risk of unnecessary collection if those addresses are not essential to the stated oversight and workflow purposes.
Replace indefinite retention with a documented retention schedule that deletes or archives records when they are no longer needed for operations, subject to records requirements.
Enforce role-based access controls so users can only see the names and addresses needed for their specific oversight, training, or workflow duties.
Do not collect or publish public input tied to directives or policies until the OMB approval process is complete, or clearly segregate unapproved material with limited access.
Minimize collection of mailing addresses unless they are necessary for the specific application purpose, and remove them where names alone are sufficient.
The system collects and maintains direct identifiers and contact information that could expose farmers, ranchers, and business partners if mishandled.
The system stores a very large volume of records, increasing the impact of any unauthorized access or disclosure.
Farm, tract, and field boundary data can reveal detailed location and property information about participants.
Historical retention of customer and farm records increases the period during which outdated or unnecessary personal information remains exposed to risk.
Sharing Farm Record and Business Partner data across USDA agencies creates a risk of broader internal exposure than is needed for a single program purpose.
Role-based access failures could allow users to view or change records beyond what their job requires.
Limit collection and display of direct identifiers and contact information to only what is required for program administration, and protect it with strong access controls.
Apply least-privilege access and monitoring to the full dataset so only authorized personnel can access records needed for their duties.
Limit access to geospatial farm boundary data and ensure it is used only for the stated farm-record purpose.
Review retention schedules regularly and archive or dispose of records according to the shortest applicable retention period for each data type and program.
Use data-sharing agreements and need-to-know controls for interagency transfers so each recipient receives only the information necessary for program delivery.
Continuously review and test role assignments and approval workflows to confirm users can only create, edit, and view records consistent with their responsibilities.
The system keeps producer information permanently, which increases the risk of long-term exposure, secondary use, or breach impact over time.
County office users and contractors can access producer data, creating insider misuse or overexposure risk even when access is intended to be limited.
NAP notifications are physically mailed, which creates a risk that names and addresses could be exposed through printed letters or mail handling.
The system discloses NAP data to other internal systems, which can expand access beyond the original collection purpose and increase the chance of unnecessary sharing.
Producer information is pulled from SCIMS rather than directly from the producer, which creates a risk that outdated or incorrect source data could affect eligibility or payment decisions.
Payment, overpayment, premium, and revenue-related records can reveal financial status and disaster impacts, creating a sensitivity risk if accessed or inferred by unauthorized parties.
The system stores and uses producer name and street address across many programs, which increases the amount of identifiable information exposed if any component is compromised.
Apply records minimization and periodic review so only records that must be kept indefinitely remain accessible, with archived records tightly restricted.
Keep the stated need-to-know approval, background investigation, Level 2 eAuthentication, and NDA controls for all contractor access.
Limit mailing to the minimum necessary information and use controlled print-and-mail handling procedures for NAP letters.
Restrict disclosures to only the internal systems that need the data and document the purpose of each disclosure.
Validate SCIMS-derived data before use and provide a correction process when producer information appears inconsistent.
Apply stronger access controls and audit logging to payment, overpayment, premium, and revenue-related records.
Protect names and street addresses with role-based access and avoid unnecessary duplication across components.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial data that could cause harm if exposed, including names, mailing addresses, SSNs/EINs, farm tract numbers, and payment amounts.
The system may expose PII to a broad internal user base because it is accessible to National, State, and County Office FSA employees through a shared database.
Because ARC/PLC displays PII retrieved from SCIMS rather than collecting it directly, errors in the source data could be shown to users and affect eligibility or sign-up decisions.
Permanent retention of records increases the long-term exposure of personal data and the chance of future misuse or breach.
The system’s use of payment history and earnings-related records can reveal detailed financial behavior about producers over time.
Limit access to the minimum necessary users and enforce strong authentication and role-based access controls for records containing SSNs/EINs, addresses, and payment data.
Continue restricting the shared database to only the minimum set of National, State, and County Office FSA employees who need the data for their duties.
Add a data-quality review step or periodic reconciliation against SCIMS so users can correct inaccurate identity or eligibility information before it is relied on.

Apply records management controls to periodically review whether all permanently retained records remain necessary and whether any records can be archived or otherwise limited under the approved schedule.
Restrict access to payment history and earnings reports to users with a clear program need and provide handling guidance for these sensitive financial records.
The system exposes highly sensitive identifiers, including EIN and SSN, which could cause serious harm if viewed by unauthorized users or misused.
County office users can search for a specific farmer or producer using PII, which creates a risk of unnecessary access or lookup of records without a legitimate need.
Using SSN as a second authentication method creates a risk that a sensitive identifier is overused for authentication and exposed during login or verification.
Contractor access to the system creates a risk that support personnel could see or mishandle PII while assisting the application.
PII is pulled from SCIMS in another system, which creates a risk of unauthorized exposure during retrieval or of relying on data outside FSCOMS’s direct control.
Although the system says it clears memory and cache on logout, PII may still be exposed during a session if a user fails to log out properly or if the clearing fails.
Restrict access to EIN and SSN to only the minimum users and use masking or partial display where full values are not needed.
Enforce role-based access and need-to-know controls for county office searches so users can only search records necessary for their duties.
Replace SSN-based second authentication with a less sensitive verification factor or add stronger controls around its use.
Require contractor access to be time-limited, logged, and approved only for specific support tasks involving FSCOMS/FSAfarm+.
Protect requests and responses between FSAfarm+ and SCIMS with strong access controls and monitoring.
Ensure automatic logout and cache-clearing are tested and verified so session-resident PII is reliably removed.
The system collects and maintains sensitive demographic information, including ethnicity and race, which could expose producers to privacy harm if mishandled or improperly accessed.
The system stores producers' names and mailing addresses to build and send ballot mailings, creating a risk of unwanted disclosure of contact information.
The system uses producer information to determine eligibility to vote in committee elections, which could lead to unfair exclusion or inclusion if the underlying data are inaccurate.
The system maintains election results and COC member data, which could create a persistent record of individuals' participation and committee affiliation over time.
The system retains information indefinitely, increasing the exposure window for any future unauthorized access or secondary use.
County office staff enter producer data into the system, creating a risk of unauthorized internal access or improper handling during collection and entry.
Limit access to race and ethnicity fields to only staff who need them for the stated election functions, and audit access to those fields.
Protect ballot mailing lists with role-based access controls and minimize the use of mailing information to only the ballot-printing function.
Validate and periodically review committee and LAA code records against source records before eligibility decisions are made.
Apply retention and access controls to election results and COC member records so only authorized personnel can view historical participation data.
Review whether all permanent records are still required for operational purposes and, where allowed by the approved schedule, limit retention to the minimum necessary period.
Train county office staff on proper handling of producer information and require supervisory review of entered records.
The system holds highly sensitive personal identifiers and financial data, so a breach or improper access could expose individuals to identity theft, fraud, or other harm.

Consolidating data from multiple programs and source systems into a central warehouse increases the risk that information will be used or accessed beyond the original purpose for which it was collected.
Broad reporting access for national, state, and county personnel creates a risk of unnecessary internal exposure to personal data.
Batch transfers from source systems to the warehouse create a risk that personal data could be intercepted, corrupted, or improperly disclosed during transmission.
Sharing information with other federal agencies and external entities creates a risk of disclosure beyond the originating system's direct control.
Using the data for Congressional, program level, and end user reporting may reveal more personal information than individuals expect from the original collection.
Keeping the data under the NARA retention schedule without a clearly defined archiving strategy in the description creates a risk of retaining personal information longer than necessary.
Name and address validation sharing with external parties can expose personal contact information to entities that may not need the full underlying record.
Apply strict access controls and encryption for sensitive identifiers and financial data at rest and in transit.
Limit warehouse access and reporting views to the minimum data needed for each business purpose.
Use role-based access controls and need-to-know permissions for national, state, and county personnel.
Protect batch transfers with secure transport, integrity checks, and monitoring for failed or unusual loads.
Use written data-sharing agreements and confirm recipient privacy safeguards before exchanging information with other agencies or external entities.
Review reporting outputs to suppress unnecessary personal identifiers and provide only the minimum information needed for the report.
Define and enforce retention and deletion procedures so records are removed or archived when the NARA schedule allows.
Limit validation exchanges to the minimum fields needed, such as only name and address, and document the one-time purpose.

The system stores a broad mix of highly sensitive personal and financial data, so unauthorized access or misuse could expose identity, banking, payment, debt, and tax information. This includes SSNs/TINs, bank account and routing numbers, and debt-related records for producers and vendors.

Public-facing and online inquiry functions can expose detailed financial information to the wrong person if access controls or authentication are weak. The system provides producers and county office employees access to summary and detailed financial information online.

The system allows producers and farmers to update banking and assignment information, creating a risk of account takeover or fraudulent changes if identity verification is insufficient. Incorrect changes could redirect payments or alter financial instructions.

Paper, faxed, scanned, and imaged documents can expose personal data if they are mishandled during capture, storage, or retrieval. The system explicitly stores financial information images and accepts data from document storage, fax, and scanned materials.

Debt collection and delinquency functions can disclose sensitive debt status to Treasury, collection agencies, and credit bureaus, which may affect subjects beyond the original payment purpose. This includes reporting delinquent debt for creditworthiness.

Tax reporting and earnings statements expose payment history to the IRS and other recipients, which can reveal income-related information about producers. This creates privacy risk if the data is shared more broadly than necessary or if statements are intercepted.

Contractor access creates a risk that non-government personnel could view or handle sensitive records during assigned duties. Even with restrictions, contractors are still granted access to the applications and data.
Permanent retention of sensitive records increases the harm if data is later breached, misused, or accessed without authorization. The system retains the information indefinitely.
Limit access to sensitive fields by role and apply data minimization so users only see the identifiers and financial details needed for their task.
Require strong authentication and role-based authorization for FI, and restrict detailed views to users with a demonstrated business need.
Add step-up verification or dual approval before any banking or assignment updates take effect.
Encrypt stored images and enforce secure handling procedures for faxed, scanned, and document-storage inputs, including restricted access to image repositories.
Minimize debt disclosures to only the recipients necessary for collection, and keep encrypted transmission for any external debt-status sharing.
Limit tax-reporting disclosures to the minimum required by law and protect statements during generation and delivery.
Continue and strengthen contractor controls, including background investigations, Level 2 eAuthentication, NDAs, and rules prohibiting downloading, sharing, storing, or printing USDA data.
Review whether all permanent records truly need indefinite retention and dispose of records when no longer required by the approved schedule.

The system holds employee identity and contact information that could be exposed if access controls are too broad or misconfigured. Because the data is used to manage role-based access, unauthorized access could reveal who has access to which applications and how to reach them.

The system maintains authorization data about users’ roles, groups, offices, and attributes, which can reveal employees' organizational relationships and access privileges. If disclosed improperly, this could enable profiling of internal access rights or targeted attacks against users with elevated permissions.

The system retains information indefinitely, creating a long-term accumulation of personal and authorization data. Over-retention increases the amount of data available for misuse or breach and may preserve information longer than needed for the access-control purpose.

The system supports administrators who can manage security access rights in real time, which creates a risk of inappropriate role changes or insider misuse. If administrative actions are not tightly controlled and audited, users could gain or lose access improperly.
Restrict access to employee name and mailing address to only personnel with a documented need to administer access control, and log all access to those records.
Apply role-based access controls and least-privilege permissions to the authorization data itself so only authorized administrators can view or modify roles, groups, offices, and attributes.
