The system collects and processes personally identifiable information about requestors, Bureau staff, and other people in request records, creating a risk of exposure of sensitive personal data.
Request-related information is entered by Bureau staff, so improper entry, handling, or disclosure by staff could expose requestor and third-party information.

The public-facing portal allows requestors to create individual accounts, submit requests, access records, and communicate with the Bureau, which creates account and communications privacy risk if the portal is compromised.
Using Login.gov as an external authentication service introduces a privacy risk from sharing requestor identity and access data with another federal service operated outside the Bureau.
The system supports the release of information to the public, so records could be disclosed more broadly than intended if release decisions or redactions are incorrect.

The system may contain documents about Bureau business operations as well as records about individuals, creating a risk that information about non-requestors is disclosed in response to FOIA requests.
Apply strict role-based access controls, least-privilege permissions, and strong audit logging for all PII in request files and generated records.
Require staff privacy training and review procedures for entering, handling, and releasing request information.
Use secure authentication, session protection, and encrypted communications for the public portal and associated account data.
Minimize the personal information shared with Login.gov to only what is necessary for authentication and document the data exchange clearly.
Implement mandatory review and redaction checks before any records are released to the public.
Apply disclosure review procedures that identify and protect information about third parties and Bureau operations before release.
A third-party hosted cloud system could expose inquiry data if the vendor or hosting environment is compromised.
The system collects and stores names and inquiry summaries, which could reveal sensitive personal information about an individual's complaint or dealings with the Bureau.
Contact information is retained outside the case system in original formats such as email, postal mail, and voicemail notes, which can increase exposure and make access control harder.
The system supports analysis of individual inquiries and outreach activities, creating a risk that information could be used beyond simple case tracking if access or controls are insufficient.
Access by staff through a secure web interface still creates insider-risk exposure because staff can view inquiry records and outreach information.
The system supports outreach activity, which may involve collecting or retaining information about individuals beyond their original inquiry, increasing the scope of personal data held.
Because the Office receives inquiries by email, telephone, facsimile, and mail, personal information can be exposed while being transmitted or handled outside the system.
Require the third-party host to maintain strong contractual security, incident reporting, and audit obligations, and regularly assess the provider's controls.
Limit the inquiry record to the minimum necessary PII and continue allowing anonymous submissions when possible.
Move contact information into a controlled case-management repository or apply equivalent centralized access controls and retention rules to the separate records.
Restrict analytical use of inquiry data to the stated Ombudsman purpose and apply role-based access and logging to any reporting or analysis functions.
Enforce least-privilege access for staff and monitor user activity in the secure web interface.
Define and limit what outreach information is collected and retained, and separate outreach records from inquiry records where feasible.
Use secure intake procedures for email, voicemail, fax, and mail, including staff handling instructions and verification before disclosure.
Consumer complaint data may be shared with external companies or other government bodies beyond the original submission context, increasing the chance of unnecessary disclosure.
Complaints can contain sensitive personal information tied to an identifiable consumer and their financial experiences, creating a risk of exposure if accessed or used beyond the response purpose.
Physical mail is digitized by vendor staff before Bureau use, creating a risk of unauthorized access or disclosure during scanning and processing.
Vendor staff interact directly with consumers, which creates a risk that personally identifying or complaint information could be disclosed to individuals outside the Bureau.
Staff authentication relies on email used for access to the CRC system, so compromised credentials could expose complaint records and consumer information.
Voice communications may be captured and processed through call recording, IVR, and natural language processing, creating a risk of collecting more information than necessary.
Advanced analytics and operational use of complaint data may lead to secondary use of consumer information for performance assessment or process improvement beyond the immediate complaint response.
Operational metadata is generated and leveraged for administrative purposes, which may still reveal patterns about consumer interactions or complaint handling.
Limit complaint sharing to the minimum necessary recipient and purpose, and apply role-based access and disclosure controls before sending information externally.
Minimize collection and retention of complaint details to only what is needed to answer, investigate, and resolve the complaint.
Require vendor personnel who digitize mail to follow strict handling controls, including access restrictions, logging, and confidentiality obligations.
Train vendor consumer guides on privacy, limit what they can view or disclose, and monitor calls for compliance with approved scripts and procedures.
Use stronger authentication than email alone, such as multifactor authentication, and review access privileges regularly.
Provide notice before call recording or automated processing and offer a non-recorded or limited-recording path where feasible.
Constrain analytics use to aggregated or de-identified outputs whenever possible and prohibit using complaint data for unrelated purposes.
Treat operational metadata as sensitive, apply access controls, and retain it only as long as needed for complaint processing or administration.
The platform can collect and process sensitive personal data across many different CFPB uses, increasing the privacy impact if that data is misused or exposed.
The system may collect highly sensitive personal details such as military status, date of birth, sex, and race/ethnicity, which could create harm if improperly accessed or disclosed.
The system supports case management and legal matters involving consumers, employees, and external parties, which can reveal sensitive dispute or enforcement information if access is too broad.
The platform processes consumer complaints, inquiries, whistleblower tips, and other submissions, which may expose sensitive allegations or confidential reporting if not tightly controlled.
The system enables tracking, analysis, and correlation of large data sets, which can increase the risk of over-collection or profiling beyond the original purpose of collection.
The platform creates, sends, and tracks emails and texts to external stakeholders, which can expose personal information through communications channels and metadata.

Internal users authenticate through Entra ID using name and email address, and external users authenticate with email, password, and multi-factor authentication, creating account compromise risk if credentials are stolen or mishandled.
Salesforce integrates with other CFPB-authorized third-party cloud environments for storage, which increases the number of systems that could access or mishandle the data.
Records may be retained indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which can keep personal data longer than necessary and increase exposure over time.
Limit each application to the minimum PII needed for its authorized purpose and review the design and purpose before collection.
Apply stricter access controls and handling rules for sensitive attributes such as military information, date of birth, sex, and race/ethnicity.
Restrict case and legal matter records to authorized staff only and log access to those records.
Treat complaint and whistleblower submissions as confidential and limit sharing to need-to-know recipients identified in the applicable application-specific PIA.
Use privacy review and oversight before performing trend, pattern, or correlation analysis on large data sets.
Limit email and text communications to the minimum necessary content and use secure, approved messaging workflows.
Keep multi-factor authentication in place for external users and maintain access management controls for the environment.
Continue assessing every third-party cloud environment through CFPB assessment and authorization processes before data is connected or stored there.
Dispose of records according to approved NARA schedules as soon as the applicable retention period allows.

The system centralizes identity and access data for a broad workforce and external users, creating a high-value repository that could expose many people if compromised. Centralization increases the privacy impact of any unauthorized access or misuse because it manages identities and access privileges across CFPB systems.

The system collects directly supplied personal details that can reveal sensitive personal preferences and contact information, including pronouns and home-contact data. Even though the collection is limited, these fields can still expose personal characteristics and location-related information.

The system pulls identity data from multiple internal and external sources, which increases the chance of inconsistent, excessive, or outdated information being incorporated into the identity record. Aggregating data from several systems can also broaden exposure if one source is compromised or contains inaccurate records.

The use of APIs, secure transmissions, and flat text files to connect the ICAM hub to source systems creates data-in-transit and interface risks. If those connections are misconfigured or intercepted, identity information could be exposed or altered.

The system creates digital IDs and manages authentication, which means a compromise could enable identity theft or unauthorized access to CFPB resources. Because the program is used to verify identity and grant access, incorrect or stolen credentials would have significant privacy consequences.

Privileged access management exposes PII and system resources to elevated users, increasing the risk of insider misuse or overbroad access. Privileged accounts can view or manage more data than ordinary users, so misuse would have greater privacy impact.

The system maintains access rights for many categories of personnel, so stale or inappropriate access could persist if reviews are not timely and accurate. If identities or roles change and access is not updated, former users may retain access to personal data they no longer need.

The system supports access decisions and may use personal information from background, staffing, and credentialing sources, which can create fairness and notice concerns if individuals do not understand how their data is used. Even if the program says it does not make determinations about individuals, the underlying identity verification can still affect who receives access.
Limit centralized access to the identity hub to staff with a strict need to know, and enforce strong logging and monitoring for all access to the repository.
Minimize optional profile fields and collect home address or personal cell number only when necessary for work purposes, with clear notice to the individual.
Validate incoming records against authoritative sources and perform routine data quality checks to prevent stale or inconsistent identity data from being used.
Encrypt all API, file-transfer, and other transmission paths, and restrict flat text file exchanges to the minimum necessary with integrity checks and access controls.
Use strong authentication controls, periodic credential renewal, and rapid revocation procedures for compromised accounts or digital IDs.
Apply least-privilege access reviews and require documented approval for privileged access requests, with tighter monitoring of privileged account activity.
Conduct regular recertification of identities and access rights so that changes in role, employment status, or need-to-know are reflected promptly.
Provide clear privacy notices and a practical process for individuals to review and correct identity data used for access management.

The system stores consumer PII collected from supervised entities, direct consumer contacts, and complaints, creating a broad repository of sensitive financial information that could be exposed if misused or breached.
The system collects PII indirectly from supervised entities, which can limit transparency and make it harder for individuals to know what data is being gathered about them.
The CFPB may contact consumers directly to collect and verify additional information, which can reveal their involvement in a supervision activity and create privacy intrusion risk.
The system facilitates collection and sharing of relevant information, which raises the risk of over-sharing or unauthorized dissemination of PII across users and entities.

The Supervision Portal allows authorized entity representatives to view and respond to requests for information, data, and documentation from state regulators, which could expose sensitive materials to external parties if access is not tightly controlled.
Identification and provisioning of entity representatives is performed by CFPB users, creating a risk that incorrect or excessive access could be granted to the wrong external user.
The system stores compliance rating information and Examination Reports, which may affect institutions and could be sensitive if disclosed beyond intended supervisory use.
The system relies on Salesforce cloud infrastructure, which introduces vendor and cloud-hosting privacy risk if the cloud environment is not configured and governed properly.
Apply least-privilege access, strong encryption, and monitoring to all PII stored in SES, with stricter controls for consumer complaint and supervisory data.
Provide clear notice to consumers when PII is obtained indirectly from supervised entities and explain the source and purpose of the collection.
Minimize direct consumer outreach to only what is necessary, and use approved scripts or notices that explain why CFPB is contacting the consumer.
Restrict sharing to the minimum relevant information needed for supervision and enforce role-based access and audit logging for all information exchanges.
Require strong authentication, authorization checks, and periodic access reviews for all external entity representatives using the Supervision Portal.
Use a formal identity-proofing and approval workflow before provisioning entity representatives, with dual review for access grants and changes.
Limit access to Examination Reports and compliance ratings to staff with a direct supervisory need and retain them only as long as required for supervision.
Apply cloud security governance for the Salesforce environment, including configuration reviews, vendor oversight, and logging of administrative activity.
The system collects and maintains detailed consumer complaint records, including supporting documents, which can reveal sensitive personal and financial information about individuals' experiences.
The system may collect Social Security Numbers for some complaints, creating a risk of identity theft or misuse if that highly sensitive identifier is exposed or retained unnecessarily.

Complaints may be shared with companies, other government agencies, White House offices, Congressional offices, or other CFPB offices, which increases the chance of disclosure beyond the original consumer's expectations.
Consumers can submit complaints by website, phone, and physical mail, which creates multiple intake channels and a larger attack surface for interception, misrouting, or unauthorized access.
The CRS operates on a vendor-provided service and cloud platform, so consumer complaint data may be exposed through third-party hosting or service-provider security failures.
Complaint data is analyzed and shared to identify trends, which can create a risk of secondary use beyond the original complaint-handling purpose if data is not properly limited or de-identified.
Limit the complaint fields and supporting documents collected to only what is necessary for complaint handling and response, and redact unnecessary personal details before storage.
Collect Social Security Numbers only when strictly needed, mask them wherever possible, and apply enhanced access controls and encryption for any stored SSNs.
Use data-sharing limits, role-based access, and disclosure notices tailored to each recipient before sending complaint information outside Consumer Response.
Secure each intake channel with strong authentication, transport protection, and careful handling procedures for phone and mail submissions before they enter CRS.
Impose contractual security, privacy, and incident-response requirements on the vendor-provided cloud platform, including audit rights and continuous monitoring.
Use de-identified or aggregated complaint data for trend analysis whenever possible, and restrict analysts from accessing direct identifiers unless needed for a specific case.

Housing CFPB records in a contractor-owned environment creates a risk that personally identifiable information will be exposed outside direct CFPB control. This is especially sensitive because the environment is explicitly described as contractor-owned rather than Bureau-owned.

The system can store, process, and maintain a broad range of sensitive personal and case information, increasing the impact if access is mishandled. The records may include personally identifiable information and other evidence used in investigations and litigation.

Forensic collection from external entities can capture data beyond what is strictly necessary for a case, creating overcollection risk. The system is designed to extract data from storage media when immediate access is granted by a court.

Bulk ingest, analysis, and review of large volumes of records increases the risk that irrelevant or nonresponsive personal information will be processed and retained. The tools are designed to organize bureau records for search, retrieval, review, correlation, flagging, and presentation in bulk.

Metadata viewing can reveal sensitive contextual information about documents and communications, even when the content itself is not the focus of review. The system explicitly allows users to view metadata within files stored in varying file formats.

Duplicate-document identification and elimination may rely on processing multiple copies of records, increasing the spread of personal information across review sets and the chance of mishandling. The system specifically supports identifying and eliminating duplicate documents during review.

Keyword-based redaction and flagging can miss protected information if the attorney-selected keywords are incomplete or poorly chosen. The system depends on keywords input by the reviewing attorney to identify names, phrases, and terms that may indicate privileged or protected information.

Trial and investigative hearing support can expose personal information in courtroom or hearing presentations if exhibits are not properly limited or redacted. The system is used to display exhibits during investigative hearings or at trial for courtroom presentations.
Limit contractor access to CFPB records to the minimum necessary and require contractual privacy and security controls for the contractor-owned environment.
Apply strict access controls, encryption, and role-based permissions to all personally identifiable information stored or processed in the environment.
Use court-authorized collection protocols that narrowly scope forensic extraction to the records needed for the matter and document chain of custody.
Apply data minimization and relevance review before loading large record sets into the system, and purge nonresponsive material according to approved procedures.
Restrict metadata access to authorized reviewers and train staff to treat metadata as sensitive information during review.
Use deduplication controls that preserve a single controlled copy and prevent uncontrolled proliferation of duplicate records.
Require iterative validation of keyword sets and secondary human review for flagged and unflagged records to catch missed protected information.
Redact or otherwise limit personal information in exhibits before they are used in hearings or trial presentations.

The system collects user or point-of-contact contact details, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure of personally identifying business contact information. Although the beta uses only contact data, full name, business email, phone number, and mailing address are still sensitive if exposed.

The system is designed to handle small business lending application information, which could reveal sensitive business and applicant details if real data were submitted or retained. The context says only fake data is used during beta, but the system purpose shows it is intended for data about credit applications.

The system's intended use includes information about women-owned, minority-owned, and small businesses, which can create privacy risk if those characteristics are linked to identifiable entities. Even if used for fair lending analysis, such data can enable profiling or unwanted inference about business owners.

The system relies on standard privacy protections and security controls, but the context does not specify any special controls for beta testing or for preventing accidental entry of real applicant data. That leaves a risk of data quality or testing errors leading to unintended collection of real personal information.
Limit collection to the minimum contact fields needed for beta access and restrict access to those fields to authorized personnel only.
Continue enforcing the rule that only fake data may be entered beyond user or POC business contact information during beta testing.

Keep applicant and owner data de-identified or otherwise excluded from disclosures to CFPB whenever possible, consistent with Section 1071's prohibition on including applicant PII in the data collection disclosed to CFPB.
Add explicit beta-testing validation and user guidance that blocks or flags real applicant data before submission, in addition to standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls.

The system may collect and maintain sensitive personal information about consumers, respondents, counsel, officers, and other people named in covered orders, including contact details and other order-related facts. Because uploaded orders and related public records can include additional PII, the registry can expose more personal data than is necessary for registration.

The system may disclose personal information publicly through the registry, creating a risk that PII in covered orders becomes broadly accessible. Even though publication is discretionary, the system is designed to make some collected information available to the public and other regulators.

The system may retain records indefinitely because there is no approved retention schedule yet. Unschedule and permanent handling increases the amount of personal data held over time and lengthens exposure if records are misused or breached.

The helpdesk feature collects personal information from members of the public and nonbank users, including names, email addresses, and questions that may reveal sensitive issues. Those questions could disclose details about a person's regulatory or technical problem that are not needed for account support.

The system collects usernames and passwords for nonbank representatives and CFPB staff, creating a risk that account credentials could be misused if improperly accessed or handled. Credential compromise could expose all information in the registry and associated user accounts.

The system may collect unnecessary or inadvertently uploaded documents that contain sensitive information not relevant to the Orders Rule. If such documents are not promptly removed, they can expand the amount of personal data stored without a clear need.

The system shares registry information with other CFPB programs and with other regulators, which can spread personal data beyond the original collection context. Broader sharing increases the number of recipients who can access or use the information.
Require and verify redaction of all nonpublic portions of covered orders before upload, and continue limiting uploads to the minimum necessary order documents.
Publish only non-confidential information and use a format that protects confidential information, with a case-by-case review before any publication.
Obtain and implement a NARA-approved retention schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of records when authorized.
Limit helpdesk collection to structured fields where possible and instruct users not to include unnecessary personal details in questions.
Enforce strong authentication and credential protection for all user accounts, including multi-factor authentication and secure password handling.
Continue routine review of uploaded documents and promptly remove any documents that are inadvertently uploaded or not relevant to the Orders Rule.
Share registry information only under existing information-sharing agreements and protocols, and limit disclosure to what is needed for the receiving agency's mission.

The system stores and shares sensitive enforcement-matter records that can include personally identifiable information about many people, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or overexposure. This includes records about CFPB staff, members of the public, vendors, contractors, and FTC staff, plus linked legal and investigative documents.

The system collects and maintains Taxpayer Identification Numbers, which are highly sensitive identifiers and could create tax-identity misuse or breach harm if exposed. The PIA says TIN is used to identify an entity for tax reporting obligations.

The system aggregates detailed personal and professional information about individuals involved in investigations, litigation, and enforcement actions, which can create reputational and privacy harm if accessed too broadly. This includes names, contact information, roles, deadlines, legal holds, and final dispositions.

The system may collect information from consumer complaints, whistleblower tips, subpoenas, depositions, and other legal discovery, which can include highly sensitive third-party information not originally provided for this system. This creates a risk of collecting more personal information than necessary for the enforcement purpose.

The system allows internal reports that may contain PII and confidential matter status, creating a risk that reports could be distributed more broadly than intended within the Bureau. The PIA notes that some reports contain confidential information and others contain PII.

The system shares a limited set of enforcement-matter data with the FTC through a secure portal, creating a risk of cross-agency over-sharing or secondary use beyond the intended coordination purpose. The FTC can input, edit, search, and view certain CFPB matter records.

The system shares witness names, entity affiliation, opposing counsel information, and CFPB staff information with court reporting vendors, creating a risk of disclosure to third parties outside the government. This information is necessary for scheduling and documenting participants, but it still exposes identifiable individuals to vendors.

The system reports certain information to the IRS, including TIN and amounts levied against entities and individuals, which creates a risk of unnecessary disclosure if reporting is not minimized or properly secured. The PIA states this reporting is required for tax-reporting obligations.

The system includes information about CFPB staff conflicts of interest and performance records for contractors, which can create workplace privacy and personnel-file sensitivity risks if accessed by users without a business need. The ENFund application expands the types of contractor information collected and adds information pertaining to CFPB Staff.

Restrict access to matter records and linked documents to users with a demonstrated need to know, and enforce role-based permissions for viewing, editing, and reporting. This should include limiting access to only the specific data elements required for each job function.

Minimize collection and display of TIN by storing it only when required for tax reporting and masking it in views and reports whenever possible. Apply additional access restrictions and audit logging to all TIN access.

Use data minimization and report templates that exclude unnecessary personal details from routine matter reports, especially information about final dispositions, legal holds, and individual identities. Require justification before generating any report that includes PII.

Screen incoming documents and intake sources for relevance before upload, and redact or segregate extraneous personal information that is not needed for the enforcement matter. Establish retention and review procedures for source materials collected through complaints, subpoenas, and discovery.

Limit report distribution to authorized staff and classify reports containing PII or confidential matter status so they cannot be broadly shared or exported. Use logging and periodic review of report access to detect inappropriate dissemination.

Constrain FTC access in the shared portal to the minimum fields needed for coordination, and require periodic review of the Memorandum of Understanding to confirm the shared dataset remains limited. Log FTC edits and access to shared records.

Share only the minimum participant information needed for scheduling and transcription with court reporting vendors, and use contractual privacy clauses to prohibit secondary use or retention beyond the service. Require secure transmission and vendor access controls.

Transmit IRS reporting data only through approved secure channels and limit the payload to the specific fields required for the reporting obligation. Review IRS submissions for necessity before release.

Separate personnel-related information such as conflicts of interest and contractor performance records into restricted views or sub-records, with access limited to staff who manage staffing or contracting decisions. Add audit logs for access to these records.
The system can expose sensitive consumer and borrower PII through geocoding, mapping, and internal sharing, including home addresses, demographic attributes, and loan details.
Combining CFPB data with public datasets could increase the chance of re-identifying individuals from geospatial outputs or revealing more about them than intended.
Internal sharing across programs, teams, contractors, and user groups increases the risk that data will be accessed by more people than necessary for a given task.
The system stores PII on the GIS server long enough for analysis, which creates a window of exposure before deletion.
Audit logs and account information about CFPB staff create a privacy risk for employees and contractors because the system stores identifying work-related metadata.
Future integration of the online/public portals could expand access and publication capabilities before the privacy impacts are separately reviewed.
Maps, CSV files, and interactive web maps can make it easier to disseminate sensitive geospatial analysis beyond the original need-to-know audience if controls fail.

The system relies on role-based access controls, but the description does not specify stronger safeguards such as periodic access reviews or data minimization at upload, leaving room for excessive access.
Limit uploaded fields to the minimum needed for the specific geospatial task and require masking or suppression of direct identifiers before analysis where possible.
Apply disclosure review and re-identification risk checks before using layered public datasets in analyses or outputs.
Restrict shared folders and enterprise group access to the smallest set of users needed, and require approval before adding additional users.
Enforce the stated deletion timeline with automated purge controls and periodic verification that PII is removed within a week after output transfer.
Protect staff account and audit-log data with strict access limits and log review procedures so only authorized administrators can view it.
Conduct a separate privacy review and update before enabling the future online/public portal integration.
Require that any public or internal export be reviewed and approved before release, and publish only aggregated or de-identified outputs.
Add periodic access recertification and data minimization checks to complement role-based access controls.
The system stores highly sensitive identifiers, including Social Security numbers and other government IDs, which increases the harm if the database is improperly accessed or disclosed.
The system may collect personal information from third parties and federal or state databases without the individual receiving actual notice, reducing transparency to affected people.
The CFPB currently gathers information from multiple sources and does not take steps to verify the accuracy or completeness of that data, creating a risk of incorrect records.
The database is a central repository and other internal systems may connect to or derive information from it, increasing the chance that information spreads beyond the original collection purpose.
The CFPB may disclose reports externally to supervised institutions and other state and federal agency employees, which creates a risk of wider dissemination of PII outside the Bureau.

The system may incorporate information from social media, consumer inquiries or complaints, and correspondence from the public, which can introduce unverified or contextually sensitive information about individuals.
The CFPB retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which can prolong exposure of personal information beyond what is necessary.
The system includes information about CFPB employees' job functions and access levels, which could reveal internal roles and access structures if exposed.
Minimize collection and storage of sensitive identifiers and mask or truncate SSNs and similar identifiers wherever full values are not operationally necessary.
Provide direct notice to individuals when practicable whenever their information is collected from third parties or other agencies.
Implement documented data-quality checks and periodic reconciliation against authoritative sources before records are used for supervision or enforcement.
Apply strict purpose-based access controls and review any internal system connections to ensure only necessary fields are shared.
Use data sharing agreements that limit secondary use, require safeguarding, and specify destruction or return of shared reports after use.
Review third-party and public-source information before inclusion and tag it with source and confidence information so users can judge reliability.
Establish and implement a NARA-approved records disposition schedule as soon as possible and purge records when retention periods expire.
Limit visibility of employee job-function and access-level information to personnel with a bona fide need to know.
The site may collect directly identifiable personal information when users knowingly provide it, which creates a risk of exposing contact details or other identifying data.
Users may share comments, videos, links, or images that reveal sensitive or identifying information, and the site may make some of that information public.
The website may collect demographic information, which can be sensitive when combined with other data and can enable profiling or inference about individuals.
The site may collect information about consumer financial products used by the user or others, which could expose financial behavior or relationships.
Website usage data may be collected and analyzed, creating a risk of tracking users' browsing behavior and building usage profiles.
Google Analytics is used to evaluate aggregate web traffic, which introduces third-party processing of site-use data and potential disclosure to an external service provider.
ConsumerFinance.gov serves as the entry point to the online complaint intake system, so information submitted on the site may be transferred into another system and broaden access to user data.

The site allows users to limit how much information is made public, but the default public-facing nature of the website creates a risk of accidental disclosure if users do not understand the controls.
Minimize collection of directly identifiable PII and collect it only when strictly necessary for the specific interaction.
Provide clear pre-publication warnings and content-review guidance before users submit comments, videos, links, or images.
Limit collection of demographic information to what is necessary and avoid combining it with other identifiers unless required.
Restrict collection of consumer financial product information to the minimum needed for the stated public-service purpose.
Use privacy-preserving analytics settings, such as data minimization and IP truncation, for website usage measurement.
Limit Google Analytics to aggregate reporting and ensure contractual and technical controls restrict secondary use of analytics data.
Apply data-sharing controls and access restrictions when moving information from ConsumerFinance.gov to the complaint intake system.
Make the privacy controls prominent and easy to use so users can understand how to limit what they provide and what becomes public.

The system collects and stores highly sensitive identifiers, including Social Security numbers, which creates a significant risk if the data is mishandled or exposed. This is especially sensitive because the system uses the data for user registration and vehicle purchase credit checks.

The system collects and processes detailed third-party accident information, including health records, race, birth date, home address, and driver’s license numbers, which increases privacy impact if shared beyond the claim purpose. The context shows this data is gathered for accidents involving non-government third parties.

The system aggregates accident reports and related documents from police reports, SF91 forms, and insurance claims, which can create a more complete profile of an individual than any single source alone. The PIA explicitly says the system will create or aggregate new data about the individual.

The system transmits Social Security numbers to Experian to assess creditworthiness for vehicle purchases, which creates a disclosure risk to a private-sector recipient. This use extends the data beyond internal GSA processing.

The system transmits accident-related PII to OCFO and FMESB, and may further send it to GSA IG in cases of fraud or court action, which broadens access to sensitive personal data. The more recipients involved, the greater the chance of unauthorized disclosure or secondary use.

The system stores police reports and accident files in external document management storage, which creates a risk of retention and access beyond the immediate transaction. The PIA says the documents are stored in EDMS and accessible only by authorized users, but that still means sensitive records persist outside the main application.

The system logs GSA employees and contractors who can log into system transactions, which can reveal user activity and potentially sensitive case handling behavior. Audit logs are a form of monitoring even though the system is not designed to monitor the public.

The system relies on police reports and self-reported information for accuracy, and the PIA says no other cross verification is done for some non-government third-party information. This creates a risk that inaccurate or incomplete personal data will be stored and shared.

Limit collection and storage of Social Security numbers to the minimum necessary cases and apply stronger access controls and encryption for SSN fields. Review whether SSNs are required for each workflow before collection.

Restrict access to accident-related sensitive fields such as health records, race, and driver’s license numbers to authorized accident-management staff only, and use role-based access controls for those records. Provide privacy training for staff handling these cases.

Apply data minimization and separate incident records so only the data needed for the specific accident or sale workflow is combined or displayed. Review whether aggregated fields can be masked or suppressed in routine views.

Use a formal data-sharing agreement with Experian that limits use of SSNs to the stated credit-worthiness purpose and requires secure handling and deletion after use. Add a periodic review of the sharing arrangement.

Minimize the data sent to OCFO, FMESB, and GSA IG by transmitting only the fields needed for the specific recovery, fraud, or court purpose. Maintain documented access controls and recipient-specific handling rules for each transfer.

Set and enforce retention limits for police reports and accident documents in EDMS, and periodically purge records that are no longer needed. Review EDMS access lists regularly to ensure only authorized users retain access.

Limit audit log content to what is necessary for security and administration, and restrict log access to a small set of administrators. Retain logs only as long as needed for security and oversight purposes.

Add a formal correction workflow that flags disputed accident data and requires review before the information is reused in downstream processes. Where feasible, corroborate key fields against source documents before sharing them.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers, so unauthorized access or disclosure could cause significant harm to constituents and staffers.
The system links together all inquiries submitted by or on behalf of the same constituent, which can create a more complete profile than any single inquiry and increase privacy exposure.
The system stores communications and documents that may contain additional non-public and sensitive information beyond the original inquiry, expanding the amount of protected data at risk.
Staffer accounts could be misused if identity verification or approval controls are bypassed, allowing unauthorized users to submit or view inquiries.
The system routes inquiries to multiple OPM program offices and may involve other federal agencies, which increases the number of parties that can see sensitive information.
Because the portal allows staffers to submit messages and documents about inquiries, sensitive information could be exposed during transmission or through improper file handling.
Cloud-based processing and storage can expose the system to vendor or platform-related privacy risk if the cloud services are misconfigured or accessed improperly.
The system tracks and stores the status and response history of inquiries, which could reveal sensitive information about a person's benefits, health care, or employment-related issues.
Restrict access to sensitive identifiers by role and minimize collection to only what is necessary to resolve each inquiry.
Limit cross-case linking to authorized staff and document the business need for linking inquiries to the same constituent.
Apply strict retention limits and review procedures for communications and attachments so non-public records are deleted when no longer needed.
Continue multifactor authentication and manual account approval, and periodically review active accounts for appropriateness.
Limit routing of inquiries and attached records to only the specific program office or external party needed to answer the inquiry.
Use secure transmission and attachment controls for portal submissions, including encryption in transit and validation of uploaded files.

Automated matching and integrity checks can produce false positives that may wrongly flag eligible participants as ineligible, duplicate, or fraudulent.
The system shares information across federal and state systems and with state agencies, which can broaden access beyond the original collecting agency and increase secondary-use risk.
The system includes immigration status checks, which can expose highly sensitive information and create stigma or harm if handled improperly.
The system performs identity and SSN validation, which increases the risk of identity-related harm if those identifiers are exposed or misused.
The system includes household composition and age validation, which may reveal family structure and other personal details beyond what is needed for a narrow eligibility check.
Restrict database access to authorized personnel only, enforce strong authentication and auditing, and keep the AWS environment secured under the existing ATO.
Limit retention to the minimum period needed for integrity checks and purge older records that are no longer necessary.
Require human review before any adverse action is taken based on an automated match and provide a process to correct mismatches.
Limit sharing to only the data elements needed for each permitted integrity check and document each disclosure to state and federal recipients.
Apply heightened access controls and purpose limitation to immigration-related data and restrict its use to the stated eligibility check.
Protect SSNs and identity data with encryption in transit and at rest, and mask or truncate them where full values are not required.
Collect only the minimum household and age information needed for validation and avoid broader use of those details outside the eligibility check.
The system stores identifiable personal and contact information about non-employees, which creates a privacy risk if that data is exposed or misused.
NRCS employees manually enter affiliate information provided by the affiliate, which creates a risk of inaccurate or incomplete records being used for access decisions.

The records may be retained for long periods, increasing the chance that outdated personal information remains stored longer than necessary.
Retention tied to whether a person qualifies for conservation programs could leave records in the system for the full duration of that relationship, extending privacy exposure over time.
Limit stored fields to the minimum needed for access-control administration and review whether any contact details can be reduced or omitted.
Require a verification step before records are saved or used for authorization, such as confirming the affiliate's details with the source submission.
Implement periodic review of linked accounts and assigned roles to confirm that access remains appropriate.
Apply strict role-based access controls and audit logging to all internal transfers between Affiliates and zRoles.
Use least-privilege access for NRCS employees and monitor employee activity for unauthorized viewing or changes.
Apply retention schedules that remove records as soon as the approved records schedule permits and purge inactive records on schedule.
Conduct periodic reviews to determine whether each record still needs to be retained for the person's current program status.

The system stores and makes available highly sensitive personal and financial information about producers, policyholders, agents, and adjusters, creating a risk of harm if the warehouse is breached or improperly accessed.
The system combines multiple datasets into a single production warehouse, which can increase re-identification and aggregation risk by linking identity, farm, crop, and policy details.
The warehouse contains tax IDs, social security numbers, and precise location data, which are especially sensitive if exposed or misused.

Authorized external users such as AIPs can access only their policy data, but the system still exposes information through a web application on the RMA Extranet, so unauthorized access or overbroad access could disclose records to the wrong party.

The system uses weekly loads and data cleansing steps that alter source files, which creates a risk that personal data could be changed incorrectly or that privacy-relevant details could be lost during processing.
The system retains information for the life of the project, which increases the duration of exposure and the chance that data will be used beyond the original collection context.
The system uses weather and crop loss data to support fraud and abuse analysis, which could lead to adverse effects on individuals if analytic outputs are inaccurate or over-interpreted.

The system relies on validation and reporting copies of results being available to project staff and the RMA project manager, which can expose more information than necessary if reports are broadly shared or retained.
Restrict access to the warehouse and HyDRA to authorized users only, with strong authentication and least-privilege permissions.
Segregate datasets and limit cross-dataset linking to the minimum necessary for approved business purposes.
Mask or redact tax IDs, social security numbers, and precise location data in user-facing reports unless those fields are strictly required.
Enforce role-based access controls so AIPs can view only their own policy records and periodically review entitlements for all external users.
Add automated data-quality checks and exception review for cleansing and standardization steps before data is loaded into the production warehouse.
Apply a shorter retention schedule for identifiable records when historical analysis does not require full identifiers, and purge or return data promptly when the project ends.
Require human review before any fraud-related action is taken from analytic outputs, and document the limits of the analysis in reports and training materials.
Limit validation logs and report files to operational staff who need them, and remove unnecessary timestamps or record-level details from stored outputs.
The system stores names, email addresses, phone numbers, and company addresses, which could expose employees or affiliates if the application is improperly accessed or mishandled.
CoLab relies on USDA eAuth identity information to create and manage user profiles, so errors or misuse of that identity data could affect access and profile accuracy.
Authorized contractors and partners can access the system, which increases the number of people who may view profile PII and raises insider misuse risk.
Users can modify their own profiles, so inaccurate or excessive personal information may be entered and retained if users update fields incorrectly.
PII is retained for as long as the application remains in production, which may keep personal data longer than necessary if deletion is not timely.
Although deletion is authorized when data is no longer needed, the system depends on administrative judgment, which could delay removal of obsolete personal information.
Limit profile fields to the minimum contact information needed for authorization and access management, and restrict who can view those fields.
Verify eAuth-derived identity information before creating or updating a profile, and require periodic review of profile accuracy.
Apply least-privilege role assignments and periodically review contractor and partner access to ensure it remains necessary.
Add validation and field-level guidance for self-service profile edits so users can only change approved fields and are discouraged from entering unnecessary data.
Implement periodic review and automated deletion of inactive or no-longer-needed profiles before the application is retired.
Use a documented retention schedule with scheduled deletion checkpoints so records are removed promptly once they are no longer needed for operational, legal, or audit purposes.
IDEA retains vendor names and contact information in the DataMart, creating a risk of unauthorized access to stored PII if the repository is compromised.
IDEA uses read-only web service calls to pull vendor PII from SCIMS, which creates a risk of overexposure or interception during data retrieval.
Because IDEA produces reports using selectable criteria from drop-down menus, there is a risk that users could generate reports exposing more vendor PII than necessary for a given task.
Contractors have access to the system, which creates a risk that personnel beyond core employees may view vendor PII without sufficient need to know.
PII is retained while the application remains in production, which creates a risk that vendor data may persist longer than necessary if deletion is not timely.
Restrict access to the DataMart PII to only authorized roles and log all access to stored vendor records.
Encrypt SCIMS web service traffic and validate the source and destination endpoints for every read-only call.
Apply role-based report controls and default the selectable criteria to the minimum necessary fields for each report.
Enforce least-privilege access reviews for contractors and periodically recertify their need to know.
Implement a scheduled deletion process that removes retained vendor PII as soon as it is no longer needed for administrative, legal, audit, or operational purposes.

Core Services can expose sensitive customer identifiers and financial details if its API responses or internal data flows are accessed improperly. The system handles names, addresses, SCIMS IDs linked to SSNs or tax IDs, and bank account digits.

The system relies on a shared customer database view and replicated access paths, which increases the chance that more users or systems can see customer data than necessary. NRCS users do not have direct access to SCIMS, but they do access a copy of the database through Core Services and related systems.

The system transmits PII between client applications, gateways, and databases, creating interception or misuse risk if transport protections or endpoint controls fail. Requests and formatted data move over HTTPS through a single entry point and internal gateway services.

Returning data in JSON format to client applications may expose more personal information than necessary if responses are not tightly limited. Core Services gathers requested information and returns it to the user in JSON format.

Contractors with need-to-know access may still create insider privacy risk if access is not tightly limited and monitored. The system allows contractors to access Core Services as part of their regular duties.

Administrative and transactional records stored in Core Services may still reveal user activity and client interactions even though the system does not store PII. The system explicitly stores administrative and transactional information for the services only.

The system supports sharing of data across multiple USDA internal systems, which can increase the number of places personal information is copied or exposed. Core Services shares and transmits USDA application data and metadata between several USDA internal systems.

The system can support reports on sensitive demographic characteristics, which raises the risk of profiling or improper secondary use if those reports are not strictly controlled. SCIMS access allows NRCS managers to generate reports on race, sex, national origin, and disability.
Limit API responses to the minimum fields needed for each business function and mask or redact sensitive identifiers before returning them.
Enforce role-based access controls and eAuth-based authorization on every view and replicated data path, with periodic access reviews.
Maintain strong HTTPS-only transport, gateway inspection, and monitoring at the external-facing and internal CA API Gateway points.
Apply response filtering and field-level data minimization so each JSON response contains only the data needed by the requesting client.
Require need-to-know approval, background investigations, and audit logging for contractor access, with regular review of contractor activity.
Define a retention schedule for administrative and transactional records and purge them when no longer needed for the service.
Restrict internal data sharing to documented business needs and minimize metadata shared between systems.
Limit demographic reporting to authorized personnel and log/report access to protected-characteristic data.

DamWatch stores records for long periods, so personal information may remain available longer than needed for the specific emergency purpose.
The system uses publicly accessible information resources and voluntary submissions, which may lead to collecting more personal information than is necessary for EAP execution.
Telephone numbers may be collected even when they are not publicly listed, creating a privacy risk for individuals whose contact information is not otherwise public.
Limit access to EAP PII to authorized users with a documented need-to-know and require secure communications for any disclosure.
Use secure handling procedures for both hardcopy and electronic EAP distribution, including tracking, encryption, and controlled delivery.
Periodically review and recertify user access for NRCS staff, contractors, and emergency responders to ensure only current site-assigned personnel retain access.
Apply a records schedule that minimizes retention of EAP PII once it is no longer needed for the dam owner or participant's eligibility and emergency planning purpose.
Collect only the specific personal data elements required to execute an EAP and document why each element is necessary.
Treat nonpublic telephone numbers as more sensitive than publicly available information and restrict their use and disclosure to emergency execution only.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and business identifiers, so a breach or misuse could expose SSNs, tax IDs, bank account details, and ownership information.
Bulk scanning and metadata extraction create a risk of collecting or indexing more information than necessary from paper records.

Scanning paper records into databases and using metadata stores creates a risk that source documents or metadata could be inaccurately indexed, leading to incorrect retrieval or disclosure of the wrong record.
Restrict access to sensitive fields and documents using least-privilege controls, strong authentication, and audit logging for all record access.
Validate scanned records and extracted metadata before ingestion, and minimize any fields that are not required for records management.
Apply cloud hardening, configuration management, and periodic security assessments to the shared AWS environment hosting DRMS.
Require background investigations, need-to-know approval, and periodic access reviews for contractor accounts.
Provide a documented request-and-correction process that lets individuals obtain their records and submit corrections without needing direct system access.
Apply records schedules consistently and delete or transfer records as soon as the approved retention period ends.
Harden and patch PDF viewing components and restrict plug-in use to approved, updated versions.
Perform quality checks on scanned documents and metadata, including sampling and reconciliation against source records before records are finalized.

The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers in documents, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or harm if those documents are exposed. The repository may include SSNs, tax IDs, bank routing numbers, and deposit account numbers.

Users can upload documents directly into DMS, which creates a risk that inappropriate or excessive personal data may be added without sufficient review. The system stores documents rather than structured fields, so sensitive content may be embedded in PDFs unexpectedly.

Sharing with contractors and technical service providers creates a risk of broader disclosure of PII outside USDA if access is not tightly limited to the authorized purpose. The system explicitly allows external disclosure when written authorization is received.

Conservation district employees and contractors with access may expose records beyond what is necessary if role-based limits are not enforced precisely. The system says access is restricted, but still permits multiple non-owners to handle the documents.

Using PII from FSA SCIMS to identify the correct producer creates a risk of mismatched or unnecessary access to another person's record if the matching process is wrong. The system relies on name and address data for this determination.

Individuals do not have direct access to DMS, which creates a risk that they may be unable to promptly see or correct inaccurate records affecting them. The process depends on requests routed through staff or a district conservationist.

Long retention periods increase the amount of time sensitive records remain available for misuse or breach. Records may be kept for many years or for as long as a participant qualifies for conservation programs.

The system is built around PDF documents and Adobe PDF plug-ins, which can increase the risk of hidden metadata, embedded content, or document-viewing vulnerabilities exposing PII. The use of a document viewer means the security of the files and viewer matters directly to privacy.
Encrypt the stored documents and apply strict access controls and auditing to all records containing sensitive identifiers.
Require review or validation of uploaded documents before they are accepted into the repository, so unnecessary personal data can be removed or rejected.
Limit external disclosure to only the specific records and purposes covered by the written authorization, and log each disclosure to contractors or technical service providers.
Enforce least-privilege, role-based access reviews for NRCS employees, conservation district employees, and contractors so users can only see the records needed for their assigned duties.
Use a more reliable identity-matching workflow and verify matches before associating SCIMS data with a producer record in DMS.
Provide a clear, timely correction and access request process for individuals so they can obtain or correct their records without unnecessary delay.
Apply and periodically review retention schedules so records are deleted or archived as soon as they are no longer needed for the participant's program eligibility or legal obligations.
Harden the PDF viewing environment and strip unnecessary document metadata before storage or viewing.

The system stores sensitive borrower financial and loan information that could harm individuals if exposed. The data includes loan status, financials, and security property, along with direct identifiers like name and tax ID.

The system retains borrower PII permanently, increasing the long-term exposure window for records. Indefinite retention raises the chance that outdated information remains available longer than needed.

The system relies on manual data entry by field agents, which creates a risk of inaccurate or incomplete borrower records. Errors in manually entered financial or identity data could affect debt restructuring decisions and borrower privacy.

The system uses borrower data to make restructuring determinations, so inaccurate or excessive data collection could lead to unfair or incorrect servicing outcomes. Because the system performs complex calculations on borrower cash flow and loan status, any bad input can affect the result.

The system is an intranet web-based application that accesses other internal web applications and databases, which broadens the number of places borrower data may be exposed. Each connected system increases the chance of unauthorized access or overcollection if access controls are weak.

The system description does not state any internal or external sharing, but it also does not describe specific transmission safeguards for the intranet application. Without explicit safeguards, borrower PII may be vulnerable during access or processing.
Limit access to borrower loan, financial, and security-property data to authorized field office employees with a need to know, and enforce strong authentication and role-based access controls.
Apply a records review schedule to purge or archive records when no longer needed for operational or legal purposes, even if the retention schedule allows permanent records.
Add validation and quality checks for manually entered borrower data, including review of key identifiers and financial fields before the record is used.
Require a human review step for restructuring outputs before they are relied upon for borrower servicing decisions.
Document and test access controls for all connected internal systems, and limit data exchange to only the fields needed for the restructuring task.
Document encryption and secure transmission controls for the intranet application and any system-to-system access paths.
The system stores borrower data indefinitely, which increases the risk of unnecessary long-term exposure or misuse of sensitive personal and financial information.
The system collects highly sensitive identifiers and financial records, including tax ID numbers and credit reports, creating a risk of harm if the data is exposed or mishandled.
Sharing name and Tax ID with Microbilt for creditworthiness checks creates a disclosure risk to an external organization.
Using Microbilt and commercial or publicly available data to determine credit worthiness may create a risk of inaccurate or incomplete decisions affecting borrowers.
County office staff enter borrower data, which creates a risk of unauthorized access, transcription errors, or inconsistent handling during collection.
The system maintains detailed financial and business plan information about agricultural customers, which could reveal sensitive business conditions and operating plans if accessed improperly.

The system’s interaction with multiple loan-related systems expands the number of systems receiving business data, increasing the risk of broader exposure or secondary use beyond the original collection purpose.
Apply a documented retention schedule and delete records when they are no longer needed for the approved records schedule.
Restrict access to sensitive borrower fields such as Tax ID numbers and credit reports to staff with a need to know and protect them with strong access controls.
Use a written data-sharing agreement with Microbilt that limits use of the name and Tax ID to the stated creditworthiness purpose and requires appropriate safeguarding.
Implement a process to review and correct disputed or outdated credit and financial data before it is used in loan decisions.
Provide staff training and validation checks for county office data entry to reduce errors and unauthorized handling.
Limit access to completed Farm Business Plans and related financial summaries to personnel involved in loan eligibility, making, and servicing.
Document and review data exchanges with the other loan systems so only the minimum business data necessary is shared.

The system stores highly sensitive borrower identifiers and account data, creating a risk of unauthorized access or misuse of personally identifiable information. Because access is based on online queries and batch processing using name or Social Security Number, exposure could directly affect borrowers.

The system shares borrower information, including loan account information, with many external entities, increasing the risk of over-disclosure or secondary use beyond the original purpose. The breadth of recipients raises the chance that data could be exposed outside the agency boundary.

Using name or Social Security Number for online queries and batch processing creates a risk that users can retrieve or process records with insufficient need-to-know controls. If access is not tightly restricted, the system could enable broad viewing of borrower status and detailed transaction history.

The system maintains detailed borrower status information and transaction history, which creates a risk of excessive internal visibility into borrowers' financial affairs. Even if used for accounting, the level of detail could reveal more than necessary to staff or contractors who access it.

Indefinite retention of borrower records increases the risk that personal data will remain available longer than necessary and be exposed in future incidents. Permanent retention also increases the amount of historical information available for secondary use.

Reporting delinquent borrower information to Treasury, IRS, and credit bureaus can negatively affect borrowers if inaccurate or outdated data is shared. Because the system supports offsets and credit reporting, errors could have direct financial consequences.

The system's reporting to credit bureaus and HUD creates a risk of sensitive financial information being disseminated to organizations that may not need the full underlying record. This can broaden the impact of any disclosure and make borrower behavior more visible than necessary.

The mention of future public-facing Customer Self Service introduces a risk that borrower information could be exposed through an externally accessible interface if not securely designed. Public-facing functionality typically increases the attack surface for privacy incidents.
Limit access to borrower PII to only authorized roles that require it, and enforce strong authentication and audit logging for every lookup or batch action.
Apply data-sharing agreements and data minimization rules so each external recipient receives only the specific borrower information needed for its stated process.
Restrict SSN-based search and batch processing to approved users, and require role-based justification or dual approval for sensitive record retrieval.
Provide users with only the minimum borrower status and transaction history needed for their job function, and mask or suppress unnecessary fields in routine views and reports.
Periodically review whether permanent retention is still required for each record type and, where legally permitted, archive or dispose of data according to an approved schedule.
Implement data quality checks and correction workflows before delinquency, offset, or credit-reporting data is sent externally.
Limit credit-reporting disclosures to the minimum fields required by the receiving bureau and document the exact data elements shared for each reporting purpose.
Perform a privacy and security review before launching any public-facing Customer Self Service capability, including testing for authentication, authorization, and exposure of borrower data.

The system retains PII indefinitely, which increases the chance that personal data will be exposed, misused, or become stale over time. Long-term retention also expands the impact of any future security incident or unauthorized access.

PII is entered manually by County, State, Regional, and National FLP staff, which creates a risk of incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent records. Manual entry can also lead to accidental disclosure or overcollection if users enter more information than necessary.

The system stores names, mailing addresses, and phone numbers, which are direct identifiers that can be used to contact or locate individuals if exposed. Because the system supports loan appraisals, this information may be linked to sensitive financial or property-related records.

The system centralizes appraisal information for County, State, Regional, and National staff, creating a broader internal access footprint than a local or siloed system. Broader access increases the risk of unauthorized viewing or use by personnel who do not need the information for their duties.

The system maintains case file storage, document management, and action alerts, which can concentrate personal information in a single application and make it more attractive if compromised. Centralized storage also increases the consequences of any access-control failure.
Apply a records disposition schedule that deletes or archives PII when it is no longer needed for the appraisal and loan program purpose.
Require validation checks and supervisory review for manually entered records before they are finalized.
Minimize collection to only the contact fields required for appraisal processing and prohibit unnecessary notes or extra identifiers.
Enforce role-based access controls so County, State, Regional, and National users can only view the records needed for their specific duties.
Protect the centralized case files and document management functions with strong authentication, logging, and periodic access reviews.

The system collects highly sensitive personal and financial data, including SSNs/TINs, race, ethnicity, gender, credit card numbers, credit reports, and employment history, creating a risk of harm if that information is exposed or misused.

The system includes race, ethnicity, and gender data in loan processing, which creates a risk of sensitive demographic information being used or disclosed inappropriately.
Restrict access to sensitive fields such as SSNs, TINs, credit reports, and demographic data to only staff with a documented need to know, and log all access to those fields.
Implement validation and reconciliation checks across source systems and external records before the data is used in loan processing.
Require dual review or supervisory verification of manually entered borrower data before it is used in servicing or eligibility decisions.
Provide clear notices and an administrative review path for borrowers affected by credit-worthiness or eligibility determinations based on FLD CAS data.
Periodically review permanent records to confirm they remain necessary and apply archival controls that limit routine access to older records.
Separate demographic fields from operational loan data where possible and limit their use to authorized program purposes only.
The system retains PII indefinitely, which increases the chance of long-term privacy harm if the records are later misused, breached, or kept longer than needed for the original purpose.

The system collects and maintains identifiable information about individuals involved in loan oversight, trainee monitoring, and directives workflows, creating a risk of unnecessary exposure of names and mailing addresses across multiple applications.
SDMS collects information from the public on directives or policies that have not yet been approved by OMB, which could expose predecisional or sensitive policy information if improperly disclosed.

The system relies on manual entry by County Offices, State Offices, and State personnel, which creates a risk of inaccurate or outdated personal data being entered and then used for oversight or workflow decisions.

Because the applications are web-based and used for oversight and tracking, unauthorized access could reveal identifiable information about District Directors, trainees, and state personnel if access controls are weak.
Apply a records review and disposal schedule to remove or archive records when they are no longer needed for operational, legal, or archival purposes.
Limit access to each application's PII to only the users who need it for their assigned duties and log access to the records.
Withhold or redact pre-OMB directives and policies until they are approved for release, and restrict access to staff with a legitimate need to know.
Use validation and supervisory review for manually entered records before they are relied on in oversight or training workflows.
Enforce strong authentication and role-based access controls for the web applications, and periodically review user permissions.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and business identifiers that could expose individuals to identity theft or misuse if improperly accessed or disclosed.
The system maintains a very large population-scale dataset, increasing the impact of any unauthorized access or disclosure.

Sharing farm and business partner data across multiple USDA agencies creates a risk of broader disclosure than necessary for the original collection purpose.
Geospatial farm, tract, and field boundary data can reveal sensitive location information about producers' operations and holdings.
The system centralizes employee access and roles, so incorrect role assignments could expose records to users who do not need them.
County Office access to update customer and farm information may expose records to more locations and personnel than a single point of service model.
The system relies on data provided on forms during application processes, so inaccurate or outdated records could affect program decisions and create privacy harm to affected individuals.
Restrict access to sensitive identifiers with least-privilege controls and strong authentication, and monitor access to detect misuse.
Apply stronger breach-prevention controls, including continuous monitoring and incident response planning, to protect the large record set.
Enforce data minimization and archive protection for older records, and limit access to historical data to users with a documented need.
Use formal sharing agreements and role-based restrictions so each USDA agency receives only the data needed for program delivery.
Treat geospatial boundary data as sensitive and limit its disclosure and internal access to personnel who need it for program administration.
Review and periodically recertify employee roles and permissions in the centralized organizational structure to prevent excessive access.
Limit County Office access to the minimum necessary records and log all updates made from any County Office location.
Implement a data quality process for participant-submitted records so individuals can correct inaccurate or outdated information.
The system retains producer information indefinitely, which creates a long-term exposure risk if the data is later misused, breached, or requested for purposes beyond the original program need.

Some components disclose information to external systems, which creates a privacy risk from broader data sharing and possible downstream misuse or overexposure.
The system generates producer name and street address for printed forms and mailed letters, creating a risk of disclosure through physical mail handling or misdelivery.

County office staff can access and enter producer information directly in several applications, which creates a risk of unauthorized internal access or errors by personnel with broad operational access.

Establish and periodically review a records disposition schedule so information is not kept longer than required for the program and legal obligations.
