Apply strict data-sharing controls and data minimization before any transfer to external systems, with logging and review of disclosures.
Use address suppression or masking where possible and require secure mailing procedures for any printed producer notices.
Provide role-based access controls and periodic access reviews for county office users who enter or view producer data.
Limit retention and access to payment-history and overpayment records to only those staff who need them for program administration and audits.

Document and enforce purpose limitations so producer information collected for eligibility and sign-up is not reused for unrelated purposes without authorization.
Validate and scan imported XML files before they enter SWIMS, and restrict export capabilities to authorized users with logging of file transfers.
County Office users can search for a specific farmer or producer using sensitive personal identifiers, which creates a risk of unauthorized lookup or overbroad access to farmer records.

Vet and train contractors on privacy requirements and limit their access to the minimum necessary for support.

The system creates a COC Directory showing all members and information related to their terms, which may expose governance and membership details beyond what is necessary.
The system tracks election results and COC member data, which can create a persistent record of individuals' election participation and status over time.
Information is retained indefinitely as permanent records, which increases the duration of exposure if access controls fail or records are later no longer needed for active operations.
Restrict access to producer records to authorized users only and apply encryption for data at rest and in transit.
Validate committee and LAA codes against authoritative source data before determining voter eligibility.
Use role-based access and data-entry validation for county office staff who collect and enter producer information.
Limit distribution of county-specific eligible-producer lists to the minimum necessary recipients and apply secure handling procedures for ballot mailers.
Minimize the personal information retained in ballot and election reports and restrict access to election records.
Limit the COC Directory to the minimum member and term information needed for official purposes and review it for unnecessary personal details.
Apply retention and access controls to election results and member tracking records so only authorized personnel can view historical records.
Conduct periodic records reviews to confirm that permanently retained information is still required and that archival protections remain in place.

The warehouse stores highly sensitive personal and financial data, creating a risk of unauthorized access or exposure of PII at scale. Because the system centralizes many program datasets, a single breach could affect many individuals.

The system consolidates data from multiple source systems, which increases the risk that data are used or combined beyond the original collection context. This can create broader profiling or secondary-use concerns for producers and other subjects.

PII is collected from county offices and other federal agencies and then extracted into the EDW, creating a risk of inaccurate or outdated data being propagated across systems. Errors in source data could affect reporting and decisions.

The system uses batch processes to share information, which can increase the risk of unintended disclosure if transfer controls, file handling, or recipient restrictions are weak. Batch sharing also makes it harder to limit exposure to only the minimum necessary records.

Information is shared internally with multiple organizations, increasing the number of users and systems that can access sensitive records. Broader internal sharing raises the risk of unauthorized access or over-collection.

Information is shared externally with IRS, Treasury, a university, and Dunn and Bradstreet, which creates disclosure risk outside the agency. Even limited external sharing can expose personal data to third parties with different controls and retention practices.

The system uses name and address validation with Dunn and Bradstreet, which may expose personal identifying information for matching or validation purposes beyond the original collection purpose. This creates a risk of unnecessary disclosure of identity data.

The retention strategy follows the NARA schedule, but deviations are allowed when the strategy is defined, creating a risk that records may be kept longer than necessary if exceptions are not tightly controlled. Longer retention increases exposure over time.
Enforce least-privilege access controls and strong authentication for EDW DV, with role-based restrictions for sensitive fields such as SSN, account numbers, and employment history.
Apply purpose-based access controls and data minimization so users can only view the specific data elements needed for reporting or inquiry resolution.
Implement data quality checks and reconciliation controls at ingest to detect and correct source errors before records are loaded into the EDW.
Use secure transfer controls for batch processes, including encryption in transit, file integrity checks, and restricted transfer accounts.
Document and limit internal sharing to the minimum necessary organizations and datasets, and periodically review internal access and sharing agreements.
Establish data-sharing agreements and disclosure controls for external recipients, including limits on use, re-disclosure, and retention.
For validation exchanges, share only the minimum fields required and avoid sending full identifiers when a partial or tokenized match will work.
Require documented approval and periodic review for any retention deviation, and automate deletion or archival according to the approved schedule.

The system stores highly sensitive financial and identity data for a very large population, creating a broad exposure if access is misused or the system is compromised. The system supports payments for approximately 1.4 million customers annually and contains names, SSNs/TINs, bank account numbers, routing numbers, and debt information.

Public-facing components let producers update banking and assignment information and view detailed financial information online, which increases the risk of unauthorized account access or exposure of detailed financial records. The FI application provides producers access to summary and detailed financial information, and FSAFS is public facing.

Contractors have access to the system, which creates insider and mishandling risk even though they are subject to controls. The PIA says contractors with a need to know will have access as part of their regular assigned duties.

The system retains information indefinitely, so sensitive personal and financial records may remain exposed long after they are needed for operations. The retention applies to all listed applications and is permanent records.

Debt and delinquency information is used to report creditworthiness and is shared with commercial credit bureaus, which can affect individuals' financial reputation. The system also sends delinquent debt status via encrypted e-mail attachment.

The system generates letters and statements about payments and debt, which can reveal sensitive financial status to anyone who intercepts or receives the mail. NRRS and NRRS Notes generate letters to customers and producers concerning debt and collections.

The system collects and stores bank account and routing information for direct deposit and payment processing, creating risk if that information is improperly displayed, copied, or accessed. Several components explicitly include bank account number and routing number data.

The system processes SSNs/TINs and other identifiers across multiple applications, increasing the risk of identity exposure through cross-system transfers and storage. Several components list SSN/TIN as collected or maintained information.
Limit access to sensitive financial and identity data to the minimum necessary roles and monitor privileged access for unusual activity.
Require strong multi-factor authentication and hardened session controls for all public-facing producer access, especially for banking and assignment updates.
Apply enhanced contractor oversight, including periodic access reviews and least-privilege role assignment, for all contractor accounts.
Implement a records review and deletion schedule for any data not required to remain permanent, and periodically verify that indefinite retention is still justified.
Validate delinquent debt data before any external reporting and provide a correction process for individuals affected by credit-related disclosures.
Use secure mailing and statement handling controls, such as address verification and suppression of unnecessary details, for debt and payment letters.
Encrypt bank account and routing data at rest and mask it in user interfaces except where full display is operationally required.
Minimize the use and display of SSNs/TINs across applications by substituting internal identifiers where possible and restricting full-identifier visibility.
The system retains employee information permanently, which increases the long-term privacy impact if the data is later misused, breached, or no longer needed for the original purpose.

The system stores personally identifiable information about employees, including names and mailing addresses, which can expose staff to identification or contact-related privacy harm if accessed inappropriately.

The system maintains authorization data tied to users’ roles, groups, offices, and specially defined attributes, which could reveal internal organizational relationships or job-related details if improperly accessed.
Administrators can manage security access rights in real time, so excessive administrative access or misconfiguration could expose or alter employee authorization data.

Apply records management minimization by periodically reviewing whether any retained authorization records can be archived, redacted, or disposed of sooner when no longer needed for the access-control purpose.
Limit collection and display of employee PII to only the fields necessary for role-based access control, and restrict access to those fields to authorized personnel only.
Implement strict role-based permissions and audit logging for authorization records so only approved users can view or change role, group, office, and attribute data.
Require change review or approval workflows for administrative updates to roles, groups, and attributes, especially for high-impact access changes.

The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial records, so unauthorized access could expose identities, account details, and other confidential information. The data types include PII, financial data, health data, biometric data, criminal history, and employment history.

Indefinite retention of records increases the amount of sensitive information exposed over time and raises the impact of any future breach or misuse. The system states that information is kept permanently.

The system accepts data from faxed and scanned materials, which can include misdirected, incomplete, or poor-quality documents that may expose the wrong person's information. This creates a risk of collecting or indexing information that should not be in the record set.

Because the system controls workflows for financial information, users may be able to see more records than needed for their job, creating unnecessary internal exposure of sensitive information. Workflow access can broaden visibility beyond the original document submitter.

The system allows desktop browser access to stored images on a network device, which could expose records if authentication, session handling, or endpoint security is weak. Browser-based access increases the attack surface for unauthorized viewing.

The use of a SQL database to manage document indexes and workflow process creates a risk that metadata about documents and cases could be exposed even if the image files are protected. Index data can reveal sensitive associations and search terms.

The system imports Federal Reserve Bank images, so any weakness in the import or retrieval process could expose externally sourced records beyond the intended audience. Imported archival images may contain sensitive financial or identity information.

Read-only historical archives still contain sensitive personal information, and broad retrieval access can enable unnecessary viewing of legacy records. Systems used to research historical archives may expose old records to users who do not need them.
Restrict access to the system and its records to authorized users only, with role-based permissions for each subsystem and record type.
Apply a records management review to determine whether all permanently retained records truly require indefinite retention, and segregate or archive inactive records with stricter access controls.
Add document intake validation and quality checks for faxed and scanned submissions to confirm the correct subject, completeness, and readability before indexing.
Limit workflow visibility to the minimum necessary set of users and steps, and review workflow permissions regularly.
Require strong authentication and secure session controls for browser-based access, including timeout and device hardening for users accessing stored images.
Protect the SQL index database with access controls and encrypt sensitive metadata at rest, with monitoring for unauthorized queries or exports.
Use controlled import procedures and integrity checks for Federal Reserve Bank image imports, including verification that only authorized files are loaded.
Apply stricter read-only access rules for historical archive systems and periodically review who can search or retrieve archived records.
The system makes PII available in work lists and via links to additional details, which could expose more personal information than necessary to users who only need to triage work items.
Client-side filtering, sorting, and Excel export can increase the chance that PII is copied, retained, or shared outside the controlled system environment.
E-mail alerts containing work-list data may disclose PII through a less controlled channel and create repeated copies of records in users' inboxes.
The system uses replicated customer data from SCIMS, so any replication or synchronization issue could expose inaccurate or outdated personal information in FA Tracker.
Because contractors may access the system, there is a risk that non-government personnel could view sensitive customer and eligibility information beyond what they need.
The system includes data about race, sex, national origin, and disability in the source SCIMS repository, which raises sensitivity and potential discrimination concerns if exposed or misused.
The system retains information for long periods, increasing the amount of time that personal data remains available for unauthorized access or secondary use.
Limit the work-list display to the minimum fields needed for PSS intervention and gate access to additional details behind stricter role checks.
Restrict or disable local export and enforce controls such as watermarking, audit logging, and approved-device-only export for any Excel downloads.
Offer e-mail alerts only for the minimum necessary fields and require users to opt in with clear warnings about inbox storage and forwarding risk.
Implement routine reconciliation and data-quality checks between PT-FM and the SCIMS source copy to detect stale or inconsistent records.
Apply least-privilege access reviews for contractors and periodically recertify that access remains need-to-know.
Treat the sensitive demographic fields in the source system as heightened-risk data and restrict reports or views that expose them unless explicitly required.
Apply records schedules aggressively and purge data as soon as the approved retention period expires.

The system collects and maintains personally identifiable contact and banking information for exporters, financial institutions, importers, and foreign banks, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of sensitive business contact and payment data.

External users can enter and review their own program information through the public interface, which creates a risk that weak authentication or authorization could expose another participant's program records.
The system sends nightly files to a data warehouse and produces ad hoc and canned reports, which increases the risk that data may be overexposed through downstream reporting and query access.
Reports are submitted to auditors and other departments, creating a risk that information could be shared more broadly than necessary for program administration and oversight.
Department contractors have access to the system, which creates a risk of insider misuse or excessive access to sensitive program and contact information.
Information is retained indefinitely as permanent records, which creates a risk that personal and financial data will remain accessible longer than necessary and be exposed in future incidents.
The system uses tax identification numbers and payment bank information, which creates a risk of financial fraud or identity-related harm if those records are exposed.
The system tracks claims, defaults, and collections owed to CCC, which creates a risk that financial and compliance information about participants could be exposed through reports or access logs.
Restrict access to contact and banking data to users with a documented need to know and encrypt the data in transit and at rest.
Enforce strong authentication and object-level authorization so each external user can access only its own records.
Apply role-based access controls and minimize fields in ad hoc and canned reports to only what each user group needs.
Limit external report distribution to the minimum necessary recipients and use disclosure review procedures before sharing reports outside the core program team.
Require contractor access approvals, least-privilege roles, and periodic access reviews for all contractor accounts.
Reassess whether all records need permanent retention and, for records that can be separated, remove or archive nonessential personal data earlier in accordance with the approved schedule.
Mask or tokenize tax identification numbers and bank account information in user-facing screens and reports.
Apply report filters and access controls so claims, defaults, and collections information is visible only to staff who need it for program administration and oversight.

The system stores documents that may contain highly sensitive personal data, so a compromise could expose names, identifiers, financial data, criminal history, and signatures. Because the system is a shared cloud repository, the privacy impact of unauthorized access is significant.

Users can upload and share files with other users, including external partners and customers, which increases the chance of unauthorized disclosure or over-sharing. The collaborative design makes it easier for a user to share PII beyond the intended audience.

External contractors and partners have access to the system, so PII may be exposed to a wider set of non-employee users than in a purely internal system. This raises the risk of misuse or access beyond the minimum necessary.

The system allows PII to be updated by users themselves, which can create integrity and privacy risks if users change profile data incorrectly or maliciously. Incorrect profile data could then be used for administration or access decisions.

PII is manually stored from FPAC web applications and other sources, which can create handling errors during ingestion and storage. Manual processes increase the chance that sensitive information is placed in the wrong file or shared improperly.

The system retains information for long periods, including up to ten years or as long as program participation continues, which increases the amount of time sensitive records remain exposed to risk. Longer retention also increases the volume of data that could be affected by a breach.

The system does not periodically purge PII made available through third-party applications, so stale records may accumulate and remain accessible longer than necessary. This can increase privacy risk if outdated data is no longer needed for the intended purpose.

The platform supports internal and external collaboration through a third-party cloud service, which means a vendor maintains PII on the agency’s behalf. This creates a vendor dependence risk if the vendor’s security or handling practices are insufficient.
Limit access to sensitive files to only users with a documented need-to-know and enforce strong role-based authorization for all file access.
Require sharing permissions to be reviewed before external sharing is enabled and provide user guidance to prevent over-sharing of files.
Apply least-privilege access reviews for contractors and partners and remove access when their role no longer requires it.
Add validation and approval controls for user profile changes so self-service updates to PII are checked for accuracy and appropriateness.
Use standardized ingestion procedures and staff training for manually stored documents to reduce misfiling and accidental disclosure.
Apply retention schedules consistently and delete records as soon as the approved retention period ends.
Implement periodic purge processes for PII in third-party applications so outdated records are removed on a regular schedule.
Strengthen vendor oversight with contractual security requirements and periodic assurance reviews of the third-party provider’s handling of PII.
The system transmits user information to external agencies, so sensitive application data could be exposed if those transfers are intercepted or mishandled.
The system stores a DOL case number for 90 days, which creates a retention and unauthorized-access risk even if the number is not itself full PII.
Users may enter and save an inquiry in the system, which could expose case-related information if the saved inquiry is accessed by an unauthorized party.
The system relies on a single common entry point for multiple agencies, which increases the impact of account compromise or authentication failure.
Data is collected by third-party services rather than directly by FPAC CASP, so users may not have clear visibility into how their information is handled across systems.
The system depends on external agencies and Login.gov, which means privacy protections outside USDA could affect the confidentiality of user information.
Continue to enforce HTTPS for all communications and add certificate validation and periodic transport-security testing for the integrations with DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov.
Limit retention of the stored DOL case number to the minimum needed and apply strict access controls and audit logging to any stored record.
Minimize what can be saved in the inquiry function and provide clear user notice before saving any inquiry content.
Require multi-factor authentication and session timeout controls for the common entry point used to reach external agencies.
Provide a consolidated privacy notice that explains which external systems collect the data and how it is used across the workflow.
Establish and review data-sharing and security agreements with DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov to ensure equivalent privacy safeguards.

The system stores highly sensitive personal and business information in long-lived records, including tax IDs, SSNs, bank routing numbers, deposit account numbers, and farm ownership details. If access controls fail or are misused, this could expose extensive sensitive PII and financial data.

DRMS allows broad internal searching and specialized unconstrained searching for records managers and legal staff, which increases the chance of overexposure of personal information to users who do not need all records. This creates a risk of excessive internal access beyond the minimum necessary for a given task.

TeamMate+ contains audit documents that may come directly from customers or be uploaded by auditors, so incorrect or unnecessary personal data could be added to the system. Because the system is used as proof of findings, inaccurate or excessive data could be retained and propagated in audit records.

The system retains information for long periods, including records that may be permanent, which increases the duration of privacy exposure. Longer retention increases the chance that old records will be accessed, disclosed, or used beyond the original need.

The system is accessible to department contractors with a need-to-know, which expands the number of people who may encounter sensitive records. Contractor access can increase privacy risk if role assignment or oversight is not tightly controlled.

DRMS stores scanned documents and metadata across multiple databases, including PDF files, SQL, Alfresco, and Elasticsearch, which creates multiple repositories of the same sensitive information. More copies and indexes can increase the chance of unintended exposure if one repository is accessed improperly.

The system uses indexing and search capabilities over record metadata, which can make it easier to locate personal information quickly and at scale. This raises the risk that a user with access could retrieve more records than intended.

The system supports FOIA and legal discovery use cases, which can lead to disclosure of personal information outside the normal operational context if requests are mishandled. Such disclosures could reveal records about individuals contained in DRMS.
Enforce strong encryption and field-level access restrictions for the most sensitive identifiers and financial account data, with monitoring for access to those records.
Limit broad search capabilities for records managers and legal staff to only the minimum records needed for the approved task, and log all unrestricted searches for review.
Require validation and privacy review before customer- or auditor-uploaded documents are accepted into TeamMate+, including checks for unnecessary personal data.
Apply and periodically verify records retention schedules so records are deleted or archived when no longer required, rather than relying on indefinite retention by default.
Use role-based approval and periodic recertification for contractor access, with heightened monitoring of contractor activity in the system.
Minimize redundant copies of scanned records and metadata across databases, and ensure each repository has the same access controls and encryption protections.
Restrict search and indexing functions to authorized roles and apply query logging to detect bulk or unusual retrieval of records.
Use a documented disclosure review process for FOIA and legal discovery requests to ensure only responsive personal information is released.
The system retains most application records indefinitely, which increases the chance that PII will be exposed or misused long after it is needed.
The system collects and stores highly sensitive identifiers such as SSNs and EINs, creating harm if those identifiers are improperly accessed or disclosed.
PII is shared outside USDA with Approved Insurance Providers, which creates a disclosure risk if those external recipients mishandle the data.
PII is shared internally with a data-mining function that searches for fraud, waste, and abuse, which creates secondary-use and overcollection risk if access is broader than necessary.
The system relies on contractors, which may increase the number of people with access to PII and the risk of unauthorized use or disclosure.
The system uses manual hard-copy forms and e-forms submitted through multiple parties, which creates a risk of collection or transmission errors and unnecessary exposure during handling.
The system uses common office tools such as Excel to analyze data, which can increase the risk of uncontrolled copies or accidental disclosure of PII.
The system hosts many applications within a single security boundary, so a compromise of the platform could expose PII from multiple RMA applications at once.
Apply records minimization and purge or archive records according to a defined schedule instead of retaining most records permanently.
Limit collection and display of SSNs and EINs to cases where they are legally required, and mask them in user interfaces and reports whenever full values are not needed.
Use data-sharing agreements and periodic access reviews for AIPs, and require them to follow documented privacy and security controls for any received PII.
Restrict forensic data-mining access to the minimum necessary records and log each query or export for review.
Require contractor access to be role-based, time-limited, and subject to the same authentication and monitoring controls as federal users.
Standardize secure submission procedures for hard-copy and e-form intake, including validation checks and secure handling requirements for AIPs, agents, and adjustors.
Use controlled, access-restricted analysis environments instead of general-purpose spreadsheets for PII-bearing data, and prohibit local exports unless approved.
Segment the hosted applications and enforce least-privilege access between them so a compromise of one application cannot readily expose all others.
Using social media can expose users' personal information because the platforms are controlled by third-party companies outside CFPB's direct control.
CFPB may collect personally identifiable information from social media interactions, creating a risk of disclosure or misuse of identity-related data.
PII collected through social media may include contact, device, location, or demographic details, which can increase the sensitivity of the information collected.
Information shared through social media may be retained in a system of records, creating a risk of longer-term storage beyond the immediate interaction.
Public-facing social media interactions can reveal information about consumers' engagement with CFPB or consumer finance issues to others on the platform.
Use of social media may create expectations of privacy that are not fully met unless users receive clear notice about how their information is handled.
Apply CFPB privacy protections and security controls when using social media.
Limit collection and use of PII to only what is necessary for public interaction.
Provide notice to users about what kinds of PII may be collected, including identifiers such as name, username, email address, IP address, geographic information, and demographic information.
Apply the Social Networks and Citizen Engagement System of Records Notice and its associated handling rules to any PII collected through social media.
Offer appropriate opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress before or during social media interactions.
Publish clear privacy notices explaining how CFPB uses social media and what protections apply.

The system republishes a public dataset that includes personally identifiable contact details for individuals associated with housing counseling agencies, which can expose them to unwanted contact or profiling.
The dataset may include sensitive identifiers and other sensitive personal information, increasing harm if the public release is broader than necessary.
ZIP codes entered by locator tool users are collected and retained, which can reveal where a user is searching from and potentially infer housing-related interests or circumstances.
User analytics and ZIP codes are being held as permanent records until NARA approves a disposition schedule, creating a retention risk of keeping search data longer than necessary.
The tool collects non-identifying operational data such as visit timestamps, browser version, pages viewed, and time on site, which can still be used to profile or link user activity across visits.
The API and locator tool allow users to download, share, and reuse the dataset in other applications, which increases the risk of downstream misuse or re-identification through aggregation.
There is no authorization process for read-only access, so anyone can access the dataset and locator tool without gatekeeping or identity verification.
Limit the public-facing fields to the minimum needed for locating a counselor, and suppress any unnecessary personal contact details where an organizational contact point is sufficient.
Apply a strict data-minimization review to ensure sensitive elements are excluded from the public dataset and from any downloads or API outputs.
Shorten retention for ZIP codes and make user search analytics aggregate-only where possible, rather than storing individual-level ZIP code entries.
Establish and publish a NARA-approved disposition schedule for consumerfinance.gov analytics and ZIP code records, and dispose of them promptly when the schedule allows.
Limit telemetry collection to what is needed for security and usability, and avoid retaining detailed page-view histories longer than necessary.
Add anti-scraping, rate-limiting, and clear reuse terms to discourage bulk harvesting and downstream misuse of API and download functions.
Implement throttling or other lightweight abuse controls for public read-only access to reduce automated collection while keeping the tool public.
The system may include direct identifiers and sensitive personal data, creating a risk of re-identification or misuse if the data is exposed or handled improperly.
Matching records across datasets can create more complete profiles of individuals than any single source, increasing the risk of privacy intrusion.
Using record locators and updates from source entities can enable persistent linkage of records over time, increasing the risk of tracking individuals across datasets.
The system uses demographic information such as race, gender, age, education, and income, which can expose sensitive characteristics and create profiling risks.
The CFPB relies on third parties, commercial sources, and public databases for notice, which may leave individuals unaware that their information is being collected or shared.
The system collects information about consumers from sources other than the individuals themselves, which can create accuracy and fairness risks if source data are incomplete or outdated.
The CFPB retains computer and paper records indefinitely until a NARA-approved disposition schedule exists, increasing the risk of unnecessary long-term retention.

Sharing research results with the general public, source data providers, and federal financial regulators could still create disclosure risk if de-identification fails or if contextual details allow re-identification.
The system may contain biometric information and health or medical information, which are highly sensitive and would cause greater harm if disclosed.
Limit access to only CFPB personnel with a need to know and keep direct identifiers separate from analytical datasets whenever possible.
Use only the minimum necessary fields for record matching and delete or de-identify matched linkage keys after the matching is complete.
Apply strict controls to record locators and purge or replace them with non-linkable tokens once updates are incorporated.
Apply heightened review and minimization for sensitive demographic fields, and use them only when necessary for proxying, weighting, or analysis.
Require documented notice obligations and data-sharing terms from third-party sources before ingesting their data.
Perform source-data quality checks and allow correction or annotation of inaccurate records before they are used in research.
Finalize and implement a NARA-approved retention schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to that schedule.
Apply disclosure review and statistical suppression rules before releasing any research outputs outside the internal team.
Treat biometric and health-related records as highly sensitive data and apply enhanced access controls and minimization.

Even though direct identifiers are removed, users may still isolate a single loan record and infer information about a specific borrower or applicant. This creates a re-identification risk from the combination of loan and property details.

The dataset includes sensitive financial, location, and loan outcome information that can reveal private details about mortgage applicants and borrowers. Public release increases the chance of unwanted profiling or discrimination based on these details.

Republishing the dataset on consumerfinance.gov broadens access beyond the original public source and makes mass download, sharing, and reuse easier. That increases the risk of large-scale secondary use or linking with other datasets.

The API allows users to query, filter, visualize, download, and share the data in multiple formats, which can facilitate automated extraction and re-identification attempts. Those capabilities can also enable profiling at scale.

The CFPB does not independently verify the accuracy and completeness of the republished dataset before posting it, so any upstream errors or over-disclosure could be carried forward. If redaction or source data are imperfect, privacy protections may be weakened.

The dataset is available to the public, including federal and state agencies and private sector organizations, which allows broad downstream use outside the original disclosure context. This creates a risk of secondary use that may not align with the applicant’s expectations.

The system retains the dataset until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA, which may extend the period during which the data remains available. Longer retention increases the window for misuse, linking, or re-identification.
Continue and strengthen the existing redaction of fields before publication, with periodic review of whether the released fields could enable single-record identification.
Limit publication to the minimum necessary fields and keep higher-risk attributes rounded or generalized where possible.
Provide clear user guidance on privacy-safe use of the republished data, including warnings against attempting to identify individuals or combine the dataset with other sources for identification.
Add technical safeguards to the API, such as rate limiting, query constraints, and download controls, to reduce bulk extraction and automated re-identification attempts.
Implement a quality-review step before republication to check for over-disclosure, redaction failures, or anomalies that could increase identifiability.
Publish the dataset with prominent notice that it is already public and that users should comply with applicable privacy and anti-discrimination laws when reusing it.
Establish and publish a retention schedule for the republished copy as soon as feasible, and remove or archive the dataset when no longer needed for public access.

The system collects highly sensitive personal data, including SSNs, financial information, biometric information, health or medical information, and sensitive demographic or benefits-status information, which creates a high impact if exposed or misused.
The system creates new combined datasets by matching records such as credit score to response data, which can reveal more about individuals than any one source alone.

The system may collect information from third parties and use administrative data to identify survey recipients and support analyses, which raises the risk of collecting or using data beyond what respondents expect.
The system may track an individual's behavior during research and use administrative data for nonresponse bias and control group analysis, which can create monitoring concerns.
The system can disclose direct identifying information in external products such as case studies or quotes, which could expose participants if consent or de-identification is incomplete.
The system shares research outputs publicly and with other entities, so re-identification or disclosure of individual-level information remains possible even when direct identifiers are removed.
The system retains records indefinitely until a NARA disposition schedule is approved, which increases the duration of exposure for sensitive data.

The system uses non-automated transfers through encrypted tunnels and encrypted email between contractor, vendor, and CFPB systems, which still creates transfer and handling risk across multiple environments.
Limit collection and storage of sensitive fields to only those strictly needed for a specific research task, and keep direct identifiers stored separately from analysis data.
Use de-identified copies for analysis after matching and avoid retaining linked datasets longer than needed for the research purpose.
Limit third-party data collection to cases covered by respondent consent and document the standards for accuracy and completeness in contracts.
Obtain consent before following an individual's behavior and use administrative data for bias analysis only under defined research controls.
Require explicit consent before any external publication of direct identifying information and review all external products for disclosure risk before release.
Continue applying disclosure-protection procedures such as aggregation, rounding, exclusion of some variables, and exclusion of observations before public release.
Approve and implement a NARA records disposition schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
Standardize and minimize manual data transfers between contractor, vendor, and CFPB systems, and restrict transfers to encrypted channels only.

The system can contain highly sensitive direct identifiers, including Social Security numbers, financial account numbers, home addresses, and phone numbers, creating a risk of unauthorized identification or misuse.
The system may include biometric and health or medical information, which raises the sensitivity of any disclosure or secondary use.
The CFPB generally collects the data from third parties rather than directly from consumers, so individuals may not know their information is being collected or used.
Individuals generally will not be informed when their information is collected through supervisory or enforcement activity, including how it will be used or disclosed.
The system can match records across datasets and update or supplement records, which can create more detailed profiles about individuals than any single source contains.
The CFPB may use direct identifying PII to contact potential survey recipients, which can reveal a person's relationship to consumer financial products and services.
The system may use demographic and financial data to make generalized inferences, which can still produce sensitive conclusions about individuals or groups.
Market research outputs may be shared with the general public and federal financial regulators, creating a risk of disclosure if aggregation or de-identification is insufficient.
The CFPB retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which increases the period during which the data could be exposed or repurposed.
Minimize collection and storage of direct identifiers, and remove or tokenize them before analysis whenever possible.
Apply stricter access controls and handling rules for biometric and health or medical information, including limiting use to cases where it is necessary for the research purpose.
Provide clearer public-facing notice about third-party collection and downstream uses whenever notice can be given, including through the PIA and related disclosures.
Limit supervisory and enforcement data use to the purposes authorized by law and document each disclosure under the applicable legal authority.
Use privacy-preserving record linkage methods and re-identification review before combining datasets, and keep the matched dataset de-identified for analysis.
Restrict outreach to survey recipients to the minimum necessary contact information and separate contact files from analytic files.
Review aggregate outputs for small-cell or other disclosure risks before release, especially when demographic and financial variables are combined.
Apply a formal disclosure review and de-identification standard before sharing research products with the public or regulators.
Set and enforce a records disposition schedule as soon as practicable, with periodic reviews to dispose of records that are no longer needed.

The system collects highly sensitive personal data, including Social Security numbers, financial information, and even biometric and health or medical information, which increases the harm if the data are misused or exposed.
The system may use personal identifiers to retrieve records and to match data across sources, which can create a richer profile of a participant and increase re-identification or misuse risk.

Consumer Education may combine response data with administrative data such as credit scores, account balances, payment histories, and fees, which can reveal detailed financial behavior beyond what participants expect.
The project relies on information from third parties, so participants may not fully control what is collected about them or how accurate that third-party information is.
Website and online tool usage data such as IP address, timestamps, browser version, and pages viewed can enable tracking or profiling of a person's online behavior.
Some information may be retrievable by personal identifier, which creates a risk of broader internal access or disclosure than participants may expect from a research program.
The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a records disposition schedule, which increases the long-term exposure of personal information.
The system may share response data with the general public or external researchers, which can create disclosure risk even when direct identifiers are removed.
Data transfers between contractor systems and CFPB internal systems, even when encrypted, create an exposure point where information could be intercepted or mishandled.
Limit collection to only the specific sensitive fields needed for the Consumer Education purpose and keep direct identifying PII stored separately from response data.
Use matching only when participants have given informed consent, and keep the matched dataset de-identified after matching is complete.
Separate direct identifying PII from response and administrative data, and use only de-identified data for research analysis.
Continue to obtain participant consent before collecting information from third parties and make the third-party collection notice clear.
Collect website and tool usage information only in aggregate form and avoid retaining direct identifiers in the analytics dataset.
Restrict retrieval by personal identifier to cases needed to facilitate delivery of Consumer Education and limit access to personnel with a need to know.
Adopt and implement a NARA-approved records disposition schedule as soon as possible and dispose of records according to the applicable schedule.
Apply disclosure-protection techniques such as aggregation, generalized sentiments, rounding, and exclusion of variables or observations before any public release.
Keep contractor-to-CFPB transfers encrypted and pair them with formal access restrictions and confidentiality controls for collaborating researchers.
The CFPB may collect information from people in real-world consumer financial settings, which can expose participants' financial behavior and experiences to privacy intrusion.
The system may involve collaboration with outside organizations, increasing the chance that participant information is shared more broadly than necessary.
Third-party collaborations may create unclear roles and accountability for protecting participant information.

Research participants may not fully understand how their information is used, because the system is designed for research rather than individual decision-making and relies on general privacy protections.
The system may retain information long enough to support longer-term field research, increasing the duration of privacy exposure.
If the research involves disclosure testing or other interventions, participants may be exposed to information collection they did not expect in ordinary consumer transactions.
The system may involve data collection from traditionally underserved consumers, who could be more vulnerable to privacy harms if their information is mishandled.
Apply the stated standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls to all primary data collection, and minimize collection to only what is necessary for the research purpose.
Limit third-party access to only the data needed for the specific collaboration and require confidentiality and use restrictions in agreements.
Document data-handling responsibilities in written agreements and require periodic compliance review of each collaborator.
Provide clear, plain-language notice describing what information is collected, how it will be used, and that it will not be used to make determinations about individuals.
Set and enforce retention limits so field-research data is deleted or de-identified when no longer needed for the research purpose.
Use privacy reviews before any disclosure or intervention study to ensure the collection is proportionate and that participants receive appropriate notice and consent.
Apply heightened safeguards for studies involving underserved consumers, including tighter access controls and additional participant-facing explanations.
The system collects detailed mortgage application and loan data that can be sensitive because it relates to individuals' housing and lending activity.
The platform may receive information about applicants and borrowers from financial institutions even though individuals are not directly participating in the system.
The collected HMDA data may be shared with multiple federal agencies, increasing the number of entities that can access the information.
The system is designed to support public disclosure of mortgage lending data, which can expose information about institutions' lending patterns and potentially related individual-level records.
The system collects data that may be used to identify possible discriminatory lending patterns, which implies the data can support profiling or inference about protected characteristics.
The system relies on electronic submission of loan/application registers, which creates exposure to transmission or filing errors if the submission process is not secure and validated.
Limit collection and retention to the specific HMDA fields required for the reporting purpose and apply access controls to the submitted records.
Provide clear filer guidance and notices about what data is reported and how it is used, since there is no public participation component.
Apply role-based access, logging, and data-sharing agreements to ensure each federal recipient receives only the data needed for its authorized HMDA function.
Use disclosure review and de-identification rules before any public release to reduce the chance that records can be tied back to specific individuals.
Limit analytical use of the data to authorized fair-lending and oversight purposes and prohibit secondary use for unrelated profiling.
Require secure electronic submission with validation checks and error handling for loan/application registers.

The system collects and reports sensitive mortgage application data, including age, credit score, and self-identified race and ethnicity, which can expose applicants to privacy harm if improperly disclosed or combined with other records.
The system discloses certain mortgage data to the public, creating a risk that applicants' information will be broadly accessible beyond the original collection purpose.
The system shares HMDA data with multiple federal agencies, increasing the number of entities that can access the information and the chance of unauthorized disclosure or inconsistent protections.

The expansion of required reporting to more institutions, transactions, and data fields increases the amount of personal information collected and therefore the privacy impact on more borrowers and applicants.
Annual and, for some institutions, quarterly reporting creates repeated transfers of HMDA data, which increases the chance of transmission or handling errors over time.
The system relies on financial institutions to submit data in electronic format, which can expose the information to cyber or transmission risks during collection and submission.

Because HMDA data are used to identify possible discriminatory lending patterns, the data may indirectly reveal information about protected-class treatment or community-level lending patterns tied to individuals or neighborhoods.
Minimize the collection and disclosure of sensitive fields to the smallest set permitted by HMDA and apply strict access controls to those fields.
Continue to disclose only the data elements required by Regulation C and suppress or aggregate any fields that are not necessary for public release.
Apply the stated CFPB privacy protections and security controls consistently across all recipient agencies and data-sharing channels.
Limit collection to the HMDA fields actually required for each reporting period and phase in new data elements only when needed.
Use secure submission procedures and validation checks for annual and quarterly filings to reduce transmission and processing errors.
Require encrypted electronic submission and authenticated access for institutions filing loan/application registers.
Limit dissemination of analysis outputs so that discrimination reviews use aggregated or de-identified results whenever possible.
The tool collects contact PII for entity representatives, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of identifiable business contact information.
Free-text responses and attachments may inadvertently capture additional contact PII beyond the limited fields, increasing the amount of personal data stored and the chance of overcollection.
Entity contacts must submit PII to gain access to the system, which creates a risk that access onboarding collects more personal information than is necessary for the assessment process.
The system imports Bureau employee and contractor information, creating a risk of exposing internal personnel data through the assessment tool.
Aggregated data will be used in internal dashboards and an annual report to Congress, creating a risk that reporting or analytics could reveal sensitive information if aggregation is insufficient.
Voluntary assessments submitted by regulated financial entities may contain sensitive organizational information that could be exposed if shared beyond the intended Bureau uses.
Limit access to contact PII to authorized personnel only and apply the stated CFPB privacy and security controls consistently.
Add submission guidance and field validation to discourage or block unnecessary PII in free-text responses and attachments.
Minimize onboarding data to the smallest set needed to authenticate entity contacts and document why each element is required.
Apply the same access controls and retention limits to imported Bureau employee and contractor data as to other personal data in the tool.
Review aggregated dashboards and congressional reporting outputs to ensure they cannot be used to identify individual entities or contacts.
Limit use of submitted assessments to the stated purpose and enforce role-based access for processing and reporting.

The portal lets requestors create accounts, submit requests, access requested records, and communicate about request status, so unauthorized access could expose sensitive request and case information.
Documents retrieved and generated during processing may contain PII about requestors, Bureau staff, and others, creating a risk of overexposure of third-party personal information.
The system stores information entered by Bureau staff for request processing, so staff errors or misuse could lead to inaccurate, excessive, or improperly disclosed information.
The use of a third-party vendor-created system and a connection to Login.gov/GSA creates a risk that personal information could be shared across systems beyond the Bureau's direct control.
The system supports the full lifecycle of FOIA and Privacy Act requests, so retained request records may persist longer than necessary if retention is not tightly managed.
Because the portal allows communication about request status, it may reveal the existence or details of a request to someone who is not the intended recipient if messages are misdirected.
Require strong authentication and role-based access controls for account holders and Bureau users, with session timeouts and audit logging for all record access.
Review and redact third-party and staff PII before release, and apply disclosure minimization rules to limit what is returned in response to a request.
Use data entry validation, training, and supervisory review for staff-entered request information to reduce inaccurate or excessive collection.
Limit vendor and Login.gov data sharing to the minimum necessary, and document contractual and technical safeguards governing external processing.
Apply a retention schedule that deletes or archives request records when no longer needed for FOIA or Privacy Act processing.
Use secure messaging controls and recipient verification for request-status communications, and avoid including unnecessary personal details in status updates.
A third-party hosted cloud system could expose inquiry data if the service provider is compromised or mishandles the information.
Inquiry records contain personally identifiable information that could be exposed if access controls fail.
The system retains inquiry summaries and names, which could reveal sensitive details about a person's dealings with the Bureau.
Contact information is stored outside the case system in original formats, creating a risk of inconsistent protection and accidental disclosure.
Receiving inquiries by email, telephone, facsimile, and mail increases the chance that personal information will be intercepted or mishandled during intake.
Anonymous inquiries can still be linked to a person through the separate contact information or submission context, reducing anonymity.
The Office's ability to analyze and process inquiry information could lead to secondary use beyond the original contact request if controls are weak.
Independent outreach activity managed in the system may create privacy risk if outreach records are combined with inquiry records in ways users do not expect.
Because staff access the system through a secure web interface, compromise of staff credentials could expose all stored inquiry information.
Require the third-party host to maintain strong contractual security, incident reporting, and privacy obligations, with CFPB oversight and periodic review.
Restrict access to inquiry records to authorized Ombudsman Office staff and enforce least-privilege permissions.
Minimize the content of inquiry summaries and redact unnecessary personal details before storage.
Apply the same retention, access, and encryption protections to separately stored contact information as to the Entellitrak case record.
Use secure intake procedures for each channel, including secure email handling, controlled fax and mail processing, and privacy training for staff handling voicemail notes.
Treat anonymous inquiries as non-identifying by avoiding linkage to separate contact records unless strictly necessary.
Limit analysis and processing of inquiry data to the stated purpose of managing inquiries and outreach, with documented role-based approvals for any secondary use.
Segregate outreach records from inquiry records unless a specific operational need requires linkage, and document any such linkage.
Require multi-factor authentication, session timeout, and audit logging for the secure web interface.

Consumer complaints and inquiries may contain sensitive personal details, and the Bureau receives them through multiple channels that increase the chance of disclosure or misuse. These submissions can identify both the consumer and the financial entity involved.

Physical mail complaints are digitized by vendor staff before being used by the Bureau, creating a risk that third-party processing could expose personal information. The scanning step also expands the number of people and systems that can access the material.

Consumers may be exposed to privacy risk when their complaints are sent to the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint, because the complaint content may disclose their identity and personal circumstances. This sharing is part of the complaint-handling process.

Complaints may be referred to other government agencies or other Bureau offices, increasing the number of recipients that can access consumer information. Each transfer creates a further disclosure risk beyond the original collection purpose.

The system uses interactive voice response and automatic processing of human language, which can capture and process voice communications that may contain personal information. Voice interactions can reveal identity and complaint details even when the caller is only seeking help.

Advanced data analytics and complaint analysis may create privacy risk if the Bureau uses complaint data to infer patterns or insights beyond the original consumer interaction. Aggregation and analysis can increase the sensitivity of the information even when individual fields are not obvious.

Operational metadata generated by the system can still be used to process complaints or for administrative purposes, which may enable tracking of staff or consumer activity. Even when not labeled PII, metadata can be privacy-relevant when combined with other records.

Bureau staff identity information is used for authentication, so compromise of staff credentials could expose access to complaint records and related consumer information. Authentication data is a sensitive control point because it governs who can enter the CRC system.
Limit complaint collection to the minimum information needed to handle the inquiry and redact unnecessary personal details before broader sharing.
Require vendor staff to process digitized mail under strict access controls, confidentiality obligations, and monitoring, with prompt deletion or secure transfer of any temporary copies.
Review complaints before sending them to companies and remove or mask unnecessary personal identifiers unless disclosure is essential to resolve the complaint.
Use formal data-sharing rules and data-sharing agreements that limit referral content to what each recipient needs for the specific case.
Provide callers with a way to avoid automated voice processing when feasible and disclose when voice interactions are being captured or analyzed.
Apply privacy review and access restrictions to analytics outputs so that performance analysis uses aggregated or de-identified data whenever possible.
Treat operational metadata as sensitive administrative data and restrict its use to authorized purposes with retention limits.
Strengthen staff authentication with multi-factor authentication and periodic access reviews for CRC users.
The platform can hold highly sensitive personal and case information about many different people, so a compromise could expose a broad range of PII and related records.
The system processes authentication data, including names, email addresses, passwords, and multi-factor authentication, creating risk if access controls are weak or credentials are misused.
The platform supports emails, texts, web forms, phone, and uploaded mail submissions, which can lead to overcollection or inconsistent collection of personal data across different applications.
Salesforce is a third-party cloud environment, so CFPB data depends on vendor-managed infrastructure and maintenance, which creates a risk of unauthorized exposure through the vendor environment.
Data is integrated with other CFPB-authorized cloud environments for storage and archiving, which increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure during transfers or in connected systems.
The system supports automated workflows, faster analysis, and decision making, which can create privacy risk if data is used to make decisions without adequate human review.
The platform enables trend, pattern, and correlation analysis of large data sets, which can reveal more about individuals than the original records alone.
The system can collect, organize, sanitize, and share data for public consumption, which creates a risk of releasing personal information if redaction or review is incomplete.
Records may be retained indefinitely until NARA approves disposition, increasing the risk that personal information is kept longer than necessary.
Limit each application to the minimum PII needed for its specific use case and separate sensitive case records by function and access role.
Enforce least-privilege access, strong authentication, and periodic access reviews for both internal and external users.
Standardize intake forms and review collection fields so each channel collects only approved information needed for the stated purpose.
Use contractual security requirements, service-level obligations, and ongoing vendor oversight to ensure Salesforce protects CFPB data.
Assess each connected cloud environment before use and continue security logging and monitoring of transfers and access between systems.
Require human review of automated workflow outputs before decisions or case actions are finalized.
Apply data minimization and purpose checks before running large-scale analysis, and restrict analytical outputs to authorized staff.
Review and redact public-facing data before release and use approval steps for any data prepared for public consumption.
Dispose of records according to approved schedules as soon as the applicable NARA disposition authority allows.

The system centralizes identity and access data for a broad workforce, which creates a high-value target if compromised and could expose staff and external users' personal information and access privileges.
The system collects sensitive personal details directly from individuals, including preferred pronouns, job title, phone number, and potentially home address, which could be exposed or misused.

The system relies on indirect collection from multiple internal and external sources, which can expand the amount of personal data shared across systems and increase the chance of unnecessary exposure.
Transferring data through APIs, secure data transmission methods, and flat text files creates a risk of interception, misconfiguration, or unauthorized access during data exchange.
The system creates digital IDs based on identity verification, so errors or weak verification could lead to incorrect identity records or unauthorized access being granted.
Privileged access management means some users may receive elevated access to systems and PII, increasing the privacy impact if those accounts are misused or compromised.

The system provides insight into who has access to systems and PII based on role and responsibility, which could expose internal access patterns if that information is inappropriately accessed or shared.
The system supports authorized external individuals, so external provisioning expands the set of people and organizations with access-related personal data and may increase disclosure risk.
Limit access to the centralized identity and access repository to only personnel with a documented need to know, and enforce strong monitoring and audit logging for all privileged access.
Minimize optional profile fields and clearly separate any home address or personal phone number from required identity data, retaining only what is necessary for access administration.
Apply data-sharing agreements and field-level minimization rules to ensure only the identity attributes needed for ICAM are imported from each source.
Encrypt all data transfers and phase out flat text file exchanges in favor of stronger authenticated transfer methods with integrity checks.
Require multi-factor identity proofing and periodic revalidation of digital IDs before granting or maintaining access.
Use least-privilege role design, time-limited privileged access, and mandatory review of privileged access requests and rules of behavior.
Restrict reports or dashboards showing who has access to systems and PII to authorized administrators only, and log all viewing of that information.
Apply the same privacy and security controls to external users as to internal users, including vetting, least privilege, and regular access recertification.
The system stores consumer and employee PII in a cloud-based platform, creating a risk of unauthorized access or exposure if cloud controls are misconfigured or breached.
The system collects PII directly from consumers, complaints, and CFPB employees, which creates a risk of collecting more personal information than is necessary for supervision.
The system may contact consumers to collect and verify additional information, which can reveal their involvement in a supervisory matter and create privacy intrusion risk.

The system contains PII about employees of supervised entities serving as points of contact, creating a risk that their personal information is retained and shared beyond what is needed for supervision.
The system contains PII about CFPB staff, contractors, detailees, consultants, volunteers, and interns, creating a risk of internal overexposure if access is not restricted to need-to-know users.

The CFPB Supervision Portal lets external entity representatives view and respond to requests for information, data, and documentation, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure if representative access is not tightly controlled.
The system facilitates collection and sharing of relevant information across supervision activities, creating a risk that data could be shared more broadly than necessary.
The system tracks document reviews during the examination process, which may create detailed activity records that expose sensitive supervisory or personal information if improperly accessed.
The system serves as an information repository for compliance rating information, which may create a risk that sensitive organizational assessments are retained longer than necessary.
Apply and regularly test cloud-specific access controls, encryption, logging, and configuration management for SES data stored in Salesforce.
Minimize collection to only the PII needed for supervision and continue using publicly available or other-agency information before collecting directly from individuals.
Limit consumer outreach to cases where it is necessary for supervision and provide a clear privacy notice at the time of contact.
Restrict access to entity point-of-contact PII to staff who need it for the specific examination and apply retention limits after the supervisory need ends.
Limit access to CFPB staff records to authorized users supporting supervision and review those permissions periodically.
Use strong identity proofing, role-based access, and session logging for external representatives using the Supervision Portal.
Apply data-sharing rules that limit disclosure to the minimum information needed for the supervisory purpose and record each sharing event.
Protect document-review logs with the same access restrictions as the underlying case materials and retain them only as long as needed.
Define and enforce a retention schedule for compliance rating information and purge it when no longer needed for supervision or legal requirements.

Consumer complaints can contain highly sensitive personal details about a person's financial situation and alleged misconduct, creating a risk of over-collection or exposure of more information than is necessary to handle the complaint.
Social Security Numbers may be collected in some cases, which increases the harm if the system is misused or breached because SSNs are highly sensitive identifiers.

The system stores complaints, details, and supporting documents in a centralized record system, which creates a risk of retaining more personal information than needed for complaint handling and analysis.
Complaints may be sent to the company named in the complaint or to other government offices, which can disclose consumer information to additional parties beyond the CFPB.

Complaints can be submitted by phone, mail, and the CFPB website, which creates a risk that consumers may disclose personal information through channels with different security or privacy protections.
The CRS operates on a vendor-provided cloud platform, which introduces third-party and cloud-hosting privacy risks for complaint data.

The CFPB analyzes and shares complaint data and insights, which can create a risk that consumers are re-identified or that their complaint information is used beyond the original complaint-handling purpose.
Collect only the complaint details needed to investigate and resolve the issue, and provide clear prompts that discourage unnecessary personal information in submissions.
Make SSN entry optional only when identity validation is truly needed, and apply strong masking and access controls to any SSN that is submitted.
Apply a retention schedule that deletes or archives complaint records, details, and supporting documents once they are no longer needed for the CFPB's operational or legal purposes.
Before sending complaint information to companies or other agencies, disclose only the minimum necessary information and use formal data-sharing agreements that restrict further use and redisclosure.
Standardize privacy and security controls across web, phone, and mail intake so all channels handle complaint data consistently and securely.
Impose vendor oversight, cloud security requirements, and role-based access controls on the vendor-provided CRS platform.
Use de-identification or aggregation before analyzing or sharing complaint data and insights whenever individual identification is not necessary.
Housing CFPB records in a contractor-owned environment creates a risk that personally identifiable information will be exposed or mishandled outside direct CFPB control.
The system processes and stores large volumes of sensitive litigation and investigation material, increasing the risk of overcollection or unnecessary retention of personal information.
Metadata and bulk document analysis can reveal sensitive personal details beyond the content of the documents themselves.
The redaction workflow risks accidental disclosure if protected information is not correctly identified by keyword searching or attorney review.
Forensic extraction from external entities can collect more personal information than is necessary for the legal purpose if scope is not tightly controlled.
Storing and transmitting evidence in cloud-based or vendor-owned tools creates a risk of unauthorized access during processing or transfer.
Trial and investigative hearing support tools can expose sensitive exhibits to a wider audience if presentation materials are not properly restricted.
Limit contractor access to CFPB records through strict contractual privacy, security, and handling requirements, with CFPB oversight of compliance.
Apply data minimization and matter-specific retention limits so only information needed for the litigation or investigation is stored.
Restrict metadata viewing to authorized reviewers and redact or suppress nonessential metadata before sharing outside the review team.
Require human review of all automated redaction results before any production or disclosure of records.
Use court-authorized collection protocols that narrowly define the data sources, date ranges, and file types to be collected.
Encrypt sensitive records in transit and at rest and enforce role-based access controls for all vendor-owned or cloud-based tools.
Limit courtroom and hearing displays to approved exhibits and use redacted presentation copies when possible.
The system collects user profile contact information, which creates a privacy risk if that personal data is exposed or misused.

The system is designed to handle small business lending application data, which could reveal business and owner-related financial and demographic information if real data were collected outside beta testing.
Because the system supports fair lending analysis and public-facing community uses, there is a risk of secondary use or disclosure beyond the original collection purpose.
Even though beta testing says only fake data should be used, there is still a risk that real applicant information could be entered accidentally and processed.
The system relies on Login.gov access and then creates a user profile, so account compromise could expose the profile information collected in the system.
Limit the user profile to the minimum contact fields needed and protect them with standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls.
Apply strict data minimization and de-identification controls so any lending data handled by the system remains non-PII and limited to what the statute requires.
Use role-based access, purpose limitations, and disclosure controls for any downstream sharing or publication of data.
Clearly label the beta environment and block submission of real applicant data through validation, warnings, and testing procedures.
Require strong authentication and account security monitoring for Login.gov-linked users and the SBL user profile.

The registry may disclose personal information from covered orders to the public, including names and contact details of individuals listed in those orders. This can expose consumers, respondents, and other individuals to broad public visibility beyond the original legal proceeding.

The system collects usernames and passwords for authorized representatives, attesting executives, and CFPB staff, creating account-credential compromise risk. If credentials are exposed, an unauthorized person could access registry records and associated personal information.

The helpdesk feature collects personal information from members of the public and nonbank account users, which may be retained or shared beyond the immediate support need. This creates a risk of unnecessary collection of identity and contact information for routine inquiries.

The system may collect and maintain more personal information than is necessary when documents are uploaded, because uploaded orders and related records can contain unrelated or excessive PII. This increases the chance that sensitive information is stored even when it is not needed for the registry purpose.

The system is hosted in a cloud-based Salesforce environment, which can increase exposure if cloud security or access controls fail. Because the registry contains personal and enforcement-related information, a cloud compromise could affect many records at once.

The system may share registry information with other CFPB programs and with federal, state, tribal, and local regulators, creating secondary-use and re-disclosure risk. Information could be used in ways that are broader than the original registration purpose if sharing is not tightly limited.
