The registry may publish information on a public website, which can make nonbank and individual information searchable and persistent. Public posting increases the risk of aggregation, profiling, and long-term exposure of names and related order information.

The system has no NARA-approved retention schedule yet and treats records as permanent until approval is obtained, increasing the risk that personal information will be kept longer than necessary. Long retention raises the chance of later misuse, breach impact, and continued exposure of outdated data.

CFPB staff can review uploaded documents and remove items that were inadvertently uploaded or not relevant, which indicates a risk that irrelevant sensitive information may enter the system before detection. If review is delayed or incomplete, unnecessary personal information may remain accessible in the registry.
Redact nonpublic portions of covered orders before submission and publish only information the Orders Rule allows in a protected format.
Require multi-factor authentication and strong password controls for all user accounts that access the registry.
Limit helpdesk collection to only the contact information and issue description needed to respond, and delete support submissions when they are no longer needed for the inquiry.
Screen uploaded documents for relevance before storage and reject or remove documents that contain unrelated personal data not needed for the registry.
Apply cloud-specific security controls, including least-privilege access, encryption, and continuous monitoring of the Salesforce-hosted environment.
Use formal information-sharing agreements and verify that recipient offices only receive data necessary for their mission purpose.
Publish only non-confidential information and use a publication format designed to protect confidential information.
Obtain and implement a NARA-approved retention schedule as soon as possible, and dispose of records according to that schedule once approved.
Continue routine staff review of uploads and add automated checks to flag likely irrelevant or accidentally uploaded documents before they are stored.

The system aggregates sensitive personal and business information about many people involved in enforcement matters, creating a risk of overcollection and broad internal exposure if access is not tightly limited.

The system stores highly sensitive investigative materials such as complaints, whistleblower tips, subpoenas, transcripts, and legal filings, which could expose confidential allegations or sensitive case details if mishandled.
The collection of Taxpayer Identification Numbers creates a risk of unnecessary exposure of tax-related identifiers if the information is not strictly limited and protected.
The system tracks potential conflicts of interest for CFPB staff, which could reveal sensitive employment or relationship information if accessed beyond a need-to-know basis.

The system includes information about witnesses, consumers, judges, and other members of the public, creating a risk that people who are only indirectly involved in matters will have their data retained and shared.
The system shares limited matter information with the FTC and allows FTC staff to input and edit records, creating a risk of expanded interagency access beyond what is necessary for a given matter.
The system may generate reports containing PII, confidential matter status, or monetary amounts, which could disclose sensitive enforcement information if reports are distributed too broadly.
The system uses and shares information in response to FOIA requests, creating a risk that records could be disclosed publicly unless properly reviewed and redacted.

The ENFund application collects contractor performance records and detailed spending information, which could reveal sensitive operational or personnel-related information if accessed inappropriately.

Because the system integrates with a document storage system and links to other systems, there is a risk that duplication or linkage of records could expand access to sensitive documents across systems.
Enforce role-based, need-to-know access controls for all matter records and documents, with periodic access reviews.
Restrict access to sensitive investigative documents and apply document-level permissions for complaints, tips, transcripts, and legal filings.
Collect TINs only when required for tax reporting and mask them in displays and reports wherever full values are not needed.
Limit visibility of staff conflict-of-interest information to designated ethics or supervisory personnel and log each access event.
Minimize retention of contact information for witnesses, consumers, and other third parties to what is needed for the matter, and remove it when no longer needed.
Constrain FTC portal access to the limited fields required for coordination and maintain audit logs of FTC user edits and views.
Apply report templates that default to de-identified or aggregated data unless named-person or case-detail reporting is specifically approved.
Use a formal FOIA review process with redaction and exemption checks before any release of enforcement matter records.
Restrict contractor performance and spending reports to authorized operations and finance staff, and separate them from broader matter views.
Apply interface and integration controls so linked documents inherit the same access restrictions as the source system and are not duplicated unnecessarily.

The system can combine home or business addresses with loan, demographic, and other sensitive borrower data, creating a risk of re-identification or exposure of individuals through geospatial analysis and maps.
The system stores PII on the GIS server until analysis is complete, so a longer-than-necessary retention or delayed deletion could expose data beyond the intended analysis window.
Broad internal sharing of geocoded data across Bureau users, programs, employees, and contractors can expose borrower information to more people than necessary if access is not tightly limited.

Users can request additional access to private folders and the Enterprise instance supports multi-user sharing, which creates a risk that sensitive outputs may be shared too widely or with the wrong collaborator.
Staff account and audit-log data are retained for the life of the user account, which can create a long-term privacy risk if those records contain detailed identifiers or activity history.

The system can display relevant case data on maps during trials and publish maps or web-apps internally or publicly where appropriate, creating a risk that more information than intended could be revealed in visual form.

The GIS technology uses data sourced from multiple CFPB systems and AWS-hosted environments, which creates a risk of unauthorized access or exposure during transfer, storage, or integration across systems.

Require de-identification or aggregation before any map, report, or exported output is shared beyond the smallest necessary internal audience, and suppress fine-grained location details when they are not essential.
Enforce automated deletion of PII from the GIS server within the stated one-week window and monitor compliance with alerts for overdue deletion.
Apply least-privilege access reviews for all Bureau users and contractors, with periodic revalidation of the business purpose or need to know for geocoded datasets.
Require documented approval for any additional user added to a private folder or team workspace, and log those changes for review by GIS administrators.
Minimize staff account and audit-log fields to the least information needed and apply a defined retention limit for logs where possible instead of keeping them for the full life of the account.
Review all maps, PDFs, web-maps, and web-apps for disclosure risk before release, especially trial exhibits and public publications, and remove unnecessary identifiers or sensitive layers.
Use strict access controls and secure transfer protections for data moved from source systems into GIS, and limit the datasets loaded into the tool to only those needed for the specific analysis.
The system stores highly sensitive personal identifiers, including Social Security numbers and other government ID numbers, which creates a risk of identity theft or misuse if exposed.
The system collects personal information from third-party and public sources, so it may contain inaccurate or outdated records about individuals.
Individuals may not receive actual notice when the CFPB collects information about them from third-party sources.
The Directory Database is a central repository and may be used by other CFPB systems, which increases the impact of any unauthorized access or secondary use.
The CFPB may share personally identifiable information externally with institutions and other state and federal agency employees, creating disclosure risk beyond the Bureau.
The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which can keep personal data longer than necessary.
The system does not currently verify the accuracy or completeness of data collected from federal, state, and local sources, which can lead to erroneous records.

Access is granted to employees and contractors with bona fide need, but the system still contains broad internal access pathways and connected internal systems that could expose PII if need-to-know controls are imperfect.
Mask or tokenize Social Security numbers and other government ID numbers by default, and reveal them only when strictly necessary for an approved business purpose.
Implement routine data-quality review and source reconciliation before records are used for operational decisions.
Provide direct notice to individuals whenever practicable when their information is collected from third-party sources.
Apply strict purpose-based access controls and logging for any internal system that connects to or derives data from the Directory Database.
Limit external disclosures to the minimum necessary data elements and require documented sharing agreements before release.

Users may knowingly provide directly identifiable personal information, which creates a privacy risk if that information is exposed or misused on a public-facing website. The system says it can collect contact information and that users can submit comments, videos, links, or images.

User submissions may be made public, which can expose personal details beyond what the user intended. The system says users can limit how much information is made public, implying some submitted content may be publicly visible.
The website collects demographic information, which can reveal sensitive attributes or allow profiling of visitors. This creates a privacy risk even when the information is not directly identifying.

The site may collect information about consumer financial products used by the visitor and others, which is highly sensitive and could reveal financial circumstances. Such information can be privacy-invasive if disclosed or linked back to a person.

Website use information is collected and analyzed, which can create tracking or behavioral profiling risks for visitors. The system says Google Analytics is used to evaluate aggregate web traffic and that a snippet of code is added to each page.

ConsumerFinance.gov interacts with other internal and external systems, which can expand sharing of user information beyond the original website context. This raises the risk of secondary use or disclosure across systems.

The site serves as the method by which most consumers reach the online complaint intake system, so information entered on the website may be routed into a complaint process with its own privacy implications. This creates a risk of unexpected downstream disclosure or use.

Collect directly identifiable personal information only when it is necessary for the specific function the user is using, and clearly warn users before submission when they are about to provide contact or other identifying information.
Provide clear controls that let users choose whether their submitted content is public, and default to the least public setting possible for comments, videos, links, and images.
Minimize demographic data collection to only what is needed for the stated public-service purpose, and avoid retaining or exposing unnecessary demographic details.
Limit collection of consumer financial product information to what is necessary for the website's educational and service functions, and separate it from direct identifiers where possible.
Use analytics in an aggregate, privacy-preserving way and limit the data collected by the page-level analytics code to what is necessary for traffic analysis.
Apply formal data-sharing controls, including access restrictions and review of any information exchanged with internal or external systems, before information leaves ConsumerFinance.gov.
Provide a clear notice at the point where users enter the complaint intake process explaining what information will be used and how it will be handled.
The system collects and transmits Social Security Numbers for vehicle purchases, creating a high-impact identity theft risk if those numbers are exposed or mishandled.
Accident cases can include highly sensitive personal and health information about non-government third parties, including race, birth date, home address, health records, and credit card information.
The system creates and aggregates new data about individuals by combining accident reports, police reports, insurance data, and case records.
Accident information is transmitted to OCFO and may later be sent to GSA IG for fraud or court matters, creating a sharing risk beyond the original collection purpose.
Accident records are stored in EDMS and accessible to authorized users, so unauthorized access or overbroad internal access could expose third-party PII.
The system logs GSA employees and contractors who can log into system transactions, which creates a monitoring and behavioral tracking risk for workers.
Individuals involved in accidents may have limited ability to refuse collection, because a case cannot be entered without the third party's information.

The system relies on police reports and source-provided information with limited cross-verification for non-government third-party data, creating an accuracy risk that can affect individuals' records.
Vehicle sales records include names, addresses, amounts paid, and Social Security Numbers, which can expose buyers to financial and identity risks if the sales data is mishandled.
Limit SSN collection to cases where it is strictly required, mask SSNs in user interfaces and reports, and encrypt SSNs in storage and transit.
Apply data minimization to accident intake by collecting only the specific third-party fields needed for the claim and omitting sensitive fields unless required for the case.
Restrict secondary use of aggregated accident and sales data to the stated business purpose and require role-based access for any combined records.
Use data-sharing agreements and purpose-specific access controls for OCFO and any IG referrals, with logging of every transfer.
Enforce least-privilege access reviews for EDMS and periodically audit who can view accident files.
Limit audit-log access to security personnel, protect logs from alteration, and define a short retention period consistent with security needs.
Provide clear notice to third parties at the point of collection and a streamlined process to access or amend their records after the claim is opened.
Add a verification step for accident records, such as requiring a second review of police-report-derived data before it is finalized.
Remove SSNs and payment-related details from sales records unless a legal or operational requirement makes them necessary, and store the remaining sales data separately from other sensitive records.

The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers, which creates a significant risk of harm if the records are exposed or misused. The stored data can include SSNs, claim numbers, birth dates, and bank account information.

The system aggregates and links inquiries by the same constituent, which can create a more complete profile of a person than any single inquiry alone. This increases the privacy impact if the linked case history is accessed without authorization.

The system stores communications and documents from multiple parties, including non-public agency records, which increases the risk of collecting or retaining more information than is necessary. These records may contain additional PII about the respondent, constituent, and others.

Congressional staffers can submit inquiries and documents through the portal, so unauthorized or overly broad access could expose constituent information to the wrong external user. The portal is used to track status and exchange messages and documents about inquiries.

Staffer account creation depends on identity verification and approval, so weak account vetting could allow an unauthorized person to gain access to inquiry data. The portal requires registration, multifactor authentication, and staffer account review and approval.

The system is cloud-based and uses multiple Microsoft services, which may increase exposure from misconfiguration, integration, or vendor-side security issues. Sensitive case files are processed through Dynamics 365, Dynamics Portal, Dataverse, and SharePoint Online.

The system tracks and stores communications and records over the full case lifecycle, which raises the risk of retaining personal information longer than needed if retention controls are weak. The portal itself does not retain data, but OLA Tracking does retain case files and related records.
Encrypt sensitive records at rest and in transit, and restrict access to only staff who need the data to work the case.
Limit constituent-linking to cases with a documented business need and provide role-based access controls for linked case histories.
Apply data minimization and document intake rules so only records necessary to resolve the inquiry are stored, and purge irrelevant attachments and non-public records promptly.
Use strong authorization checks, session controls, and audit logging for all portal submissions, messages, and document access.
Keep multifactor authentication mandatory and require documented approval of each staffer account before access is granted.
Perform regular security reviews of the cloud configuration and vendor-managed services, including access controls and sharing settings across Dynamics 365, Dataverse, and SharePoint Online.
Define and enforce retention schedules for case files and related communications, and delete records when they are no longer needed for the inquiry or required by law.

ROVR stores large volumes of identifiable health and enrollment data about millions of enrollees, family members, and eligible non-enrollees, creating a broad privacy exposure if the repository is misused or breached.
The repository contains detailed medical, pharmacy, encounter, provider, and cost information that can reveal highly sensitive health conditions and utilization patterns.
ROVR creates person-level longitudinal records that link data over time, which increases the risk of re-identification and deeper profiling of individuals.
Enrollment data may be used to identify and address possible erroneous or duplicate coverage, which could affect an individual's benefits if the data are inaccurate or misinterpreted.
The system analyzes data across population groups, geographic areas, health plans, providers, and disease conditions, which can enable sensitive group profiling beyond individual administration.
ROVR may be used to detect fraud, waste, and abuse and to analyze specific individuals when fraud is suspected or confirmed, creating a risk of expanded investigative use of health data.
ROVR receives data from multiple external systems and agencies, which increases the risk of inconsistent data handling or unauthorized disclosure during sharing and reconciliation.
The system includes Medicare-related health claims for dual enrollees, which can expose additional sensitive coverage and utilization information across programs.
The repository may be used to assess policy and legislative initiatives, creating a risk that data collected for administration will be repurposed for broader analytical uses.
Limit access to ROVR to authorized personnel with a need to know and enforce strong access controls and auditing.
Minimize the amount of detailed claims and provider data stored or shared when non-identifiable data will suffice.
Use record-level identifiable data only when necessary to create longitudinal records and apply de-identification or pseudonymization for routine analysis.
Verify suspected duplicate enrollments through a separate review process before any enrollment-related action is taken.
Apply aggregation and disclosure controls to population-level analyses so individual identities are not revealed unnecessarily.
Use fraud, waste, and abuse data only for the stated investigative purpose and restrict further disclosure unless permitted under the Privacy Act.
Use data sharing agreements to specify permitted uses, retention, and storage protocols for all incoming data.
Limit Medicare-linked analyses to the minimum necessary data needed for reconciliation and statistical review.
Document and review any policy or legislative analysis to ensure it remains tied to FEHB plan performance and does not expand into unrelated uses.

The system stores Social Security numbers and uses them as debtor identifiers, creating a high-impact risk if the data is exposed or misused. This is especially sensitive because the same identifier is also embedded in another tracking number.

Individuals do not have direct access to ABCO data, which can limit their ability to review or correct information about their debts. This may increase the risk that inaccurate records persist and affect billing or collection actions.

The system sends debt-related notices based on agency-provided personal data, but no prior notice is provided to the individual before collection. This creates a transparency risk because people may not know their information is being used in ABCO until after billing or collection activity begins.

ABCO exchanges data with multiple internal and external systems, including Treasury systems and a digital records contractor, increasing the number of places where personal data may be exposed or mishandled. More sharing expands the attack surface and the chance of unauthorized disclosure.

Contractors at a local facility convert Payroll reports into PDF files and transmit them to Iron Mountain, which creates a risk of exposure during contractor handling or file conversion. This is a privacy risk because contractors may see personal debt information in the course of processing it.

ABCO retains data on the mainframe indefinitely, which increases the long-term risk of unauthorized access, secondary use, or breach over time. Keeping debt records forever also means sensitive information remains available long after it may be needed.

The system allows authorized agency users to run predefined and custom reports and access data elements based on privileges, which could enable broader internal disclosure than necessary if access controls are misconfigured or overbroad. This creates a risk of internal misuse or excessive access.

Access is managed through requests from agency functional managers and security officers across approximately 35 USDA agencies and about 160 Federal agencies payroll by the NFC, which creates a risk of inconsistent access approvals and privilege creep. Large-scale delegated access increases the chance that users retain access they no longer need.
Mask SSNs in user-facing views and reports, and use a surrogate identifier that does not embed the SSN for routine processing.
Provide a controlled individual access and correction process, such as a secure request channel for debt record review and amendment through the responsible agency.
Add a notice step before data is collected or used for billing, explaining that agency-provided personal data will be used in ABCO for debt billing and collection.
Limit sharing to the minimum necessary data fields for each recipient and document recipient-specific access rules for every interface and exchange.
Require contractor handling of reports to occur under strict role-based access, logging, and confidentiality controls, with periodic review of contractor access.
Apply a finite retention schedule to mainframe records and delete or archive data when no longer needed for the stated financial purpose, consistent with approved records rules.
Restrict custom reports and sensitive data elements to the minimum necessary and require approval for elevated reporting access.
Perform periodic access recertification for all agency users and remove dormant or unnecessary accounts promptly.
The system may collect more personal information than is needed because correspondence can include extra details voluntarily provided by the public beyond basic contact information.

Role-based access may still allow too many users to view correspondence records, exposing PII across business units that review and approve packages.

Limit intake and retention to the minimum PII needed to process correspondence, and redact or remove unnecessary personal details from the record.
Restrict access to contact information to staff with a documented need to know and protect it with role-based controls.
Apply least-privilege permissions and separate review/approval access so users only see the correspondence needed for their assigned task.
Configure dashboards and reports to suppress or mask PII unless a user is specifically authorized to see it.
Govern NLP and ML search results so they return only necessary excerpts and exclude or mask personal information where possible.
Limit audit and workflow tracking data to operational needs and protect logs and metadata with access controls.
Verify and periodically update contact information before outreach, and use approved contact procedures to avoid misdirected communications.
Provide handling guidance and review procedures for correspondence that may contain sensitive or politically significant personal information before it is shared for approval or response.
The system stores sensitive civil rights complaint information and complainant personal details, creating a risk of harm if the data is improperly accessed or exposed.

Document a precise records schedule and automated deletion or destruction process tied to the approved retention period.

User photos combined with names create identifiable profile data that may increase privacy exposure if accessed or disclosed improperly.

Maintain and test tenant-isolation controls so data from one tenant cannot be accessed by another tenant or customer.

Restrict access to Social Security numbers, bank account numbers, and check information to only staff with a documented need to know, and encrypt these fields at rest and in transit.
Apply role-based access controls and interagency data-sharing agreements that limit personnel and payroll access to authorized users only.
Minimize disclosure of delinquent debt information to only the minimum necessary fields and recipients needed for debt collection.
Implement data minimization and periodic review to remove personal identifiers that are not necessary for the administrative function.

Use aggregation or de-identification for statistical reporting so individuals cannot be readily identified from the statistics.
The system retains case-related information, including personally identifiable information and audio files, forever, which creates a long-term exposure risk if the data is no longer needed.

Public users can submit appeals and then view their own appeal transaction details and submitted documents, which increases the risk of unauthorized disclosure if account access is compromised.

Reports generated from the system may expose personally identifiable information to management, creating an internal disclosure risk even when no external sharing occurs.

Establish and enforce a records retention schedule that limits storage to the minimum period necessary and disposes of data when no longer required.
Restrict access to direct identifiers and contact details to only personnel with a documented need to know.
Apply stronger access controls and review procedures for audio files and determinations, with separate handling for especially sensitive case content.
Use strong account authentication and session protection for appellant portal access, and require secure password reset and account recovery procedures.
Limit contractor access to the minimum necessary functions and periodically review contractor permissions.
Keep the PII warning on reports and add handling rules that require users to verify need before opening or sharing reports containing PII.
Minimize and protect case-process metadata by collecting only what is needed for tracking and reporting and limiting who can view it.

WebTA shares customer data with multiple other USDA systems, which increases the risk that information will be disclosed beyond the original collection purpose if downstream access or use is not tightly controlled.

Enforce strict access controls, encryption, and monitoring for SSNs, payroll data, and teleworking agreement information.
Require individuals to review and confirm records entered on their behalf, or provide a correction workflow before records are finalized.
Restrict predefined and custom reports to the minimum data elements needed and approve report access only for authorized roles.
Apply system-to-system data-sharing agreements, access controls, and logging for each downstream USDA system that receives WebTA data.
Limit external disclosures to documented routine uses and agency-approved purposes, and verify that each recipient has an appropriate legal basis and safeguards.
Use formal role-based access reviews to ensure each user receives only the minimum access needed for their job.
Apply the same least-privilege and periodic access review requirements to contractors as to federal staff.
Require all agencies and systems to use approved secure transmission methods, such as SFTP over VPN or HTTPS, for every exchange of PII.
Apply retention and disposal controls that automatically purge records when the approved NARA schedule or customer agency retention period expires.
The system collects and stores direct contact information and inquiry details, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data if the case system is compromised or misused.
PII is shared internally by email to mission area subject-matter experts, which increases the chance of accidental misdelivery or interception during transmission.
PII is accessible to all USDA users with valid Linc Pass credentials in the Salesforce Government Cloud environment, which may create overbroad access if roles are not tightly limited.
Contractors have access to the system, which raises the risk of unnecessary exposure of PII beyond federal staff.

The system uses multiple channels, including chat, email, webform, and telephony integration, which increases the risk of inconsistent collection practices and accidental disclosure across channels.

Limit collection to the minimum contact and case details needed to resolve the inquiry, and avoid storing unnecessary fields in the case record.
Use a more secure approved transfer method than ordinary email for PII, or encrypt and restrict emailed records to named recipients only.
Narrow role-based access so users can view only the records needed for their assigned duties, with periodic access reviews.
Apply the same least-privilege controls and access approval process to contractors as to federal staff, and review contractor access regularly.
Implement a records schedule that deletes or archives records as soon as the approved retention period expires.

The system records identifiable images of employees, contractors, and visitors as they move through USDA buildings, creating a broad surveillance risk. The footage can capture facial images and track people across entrances, exits, parking lots, and secured areas.

The cameras may capture highly sensitive personal details beyond general video, including license plates and information from driver’s licenses. This increases the chance that the system collects more personal data than is strictly needed for security monitoring.

The use of pan/tilt/zoom, manual tracking, and automatic tracking can enable persistent monitoring of specific individuals. That creates a risk of intrusive observation of people in public and workplace settings.

The system may record people on public streets and around federal facilities, expanding surveillance beyond USDA-controlled interior spaces. This can affect bystanders who are not entering the buildings or otherwise expecting monitoring.

Video footage can be shared outside USDA with federal agencies and local law enforcement, creating a disclosure risk. Once shared, the footage may be used for investigations, prosecutions, or other purposes beyond the original security monitoring context.

Contractors and select non-employees may access the system, which creates insider access risk. Even with background checks and security clearances, broader access increases the chance of unauthorized viewing or misuse.

Footage may be retained longer than the intended six months depending on storage, camera counts, and other factors. Extended retention increases the period during which people can be monitored or identified from historical footage.

Recordings retrieved for suspected criminal activity can be retained until investigative or enforcement action is completed, which may extend retention well beyond routine deletion. This creates a risk that footage linked to many people will remain available for an open-ended period.
Limit camera placement and viewing angles to areas necessary for security, and continue avoiding locations where people have a reasonable expectation of privacy.
Mask or blur license plates and other nonessential identifying details in routine views, and restrict access to unredacted footage to authorized investigative staff only.
Require supervisory approval and documented justification before using manual or automatic tracking on an individual.
Configure cameras to minimize capture of public streets and other areas outside USDA facilities unless a specific security need exists.
Use written sharing procedures that limit disclosures to formal requests and document the purpose, recipient, and footage released.
Apply role-based access controls and periodic access reviews for employees and contractors with VSS access.
Enforce the six-month deletion schedule automatically and require approval for any extension beyond that period.
Require periodic review of criminal-activity holds to confirm the footage is still needed for an active investigation or enforcement action.

NAP notifications are centralized and sent to a print shop, creating an additional disclosure point for producer information outside the originating application.
NAP data is disclosed to external systems such as CARS and LFP, which creates a risk of broader internal dissemination than the producer may expect.
The system allows access by producer identifiers and last name for NAP payment processing, which could enable unauthorized lookup if access controls are weak.
The system processes overpayments and payment history, which can reveal financial and eligibility information about producers over time.
Establish and enforce a records disposal schedule so permanent retention is limited to records that must truly be kept indefinitely, and review whether any fields can be shortened or minimized.
Minimize collection and storage of names and street addresses to only the fields needed for each specific program workflow.
Apply role-based access and quality checks for county office data entry, with periodic review of user actions.
Limit contractor access to the minimum necessary and conduct regular access recertification for all contractor accounts.
Use secure mailing processes and suppress printed address details unless a paper notice is required for the program.
Limit the data sent to the KC Print Shop to the minimum needed for mailing and apply contractual privacy requirements to the print vendor path.
Document and review each internal disclosure to external systems, and ensure only the minimum NAP data needed is shared.
Require stronger authentication or multi-factor controls for NAP payment lookup functions that accept producer ID or last name.
Restrict access to payment history and overpayment records to staff with a direct business need and log all access to those records.
The system maintains highly sensitive identifiers and financial data, which could expose producers to identity theft or financial harm if mishandled or breached.
ARCPLC displays producer PII retrieved from another system, creating a risk of unnecessary exposure to users who only need limited eligibility information.
SWIMS uses a shared database accessible to a limited set of employees, which creates a risk that more users than necessary can access producer PII.
The system retains information indefinitely, increasing the amount of time producer PII remains available for unauthorized access or misuse.

PII is obtained from SCIMS rather than directly from the individual, which can make it harder for producers to understand what data are being used and to correct inaccuracies in the displayed information.
The system processes farm tract numbers and payment amounts along with identity data, which could reveal detailed financial and operational information about producers if accessed inappropriately.
Restrict access to the minimum set of users who need producer identifiers and payment data, and enforce strong auditing of access to those records.
Display only the minimum PII necessary for the task and mask or truncate identifiers where full values are not required.
Apply role-based access controls to the shared database so each employee can access only the records needed for their duties.
Establish and enforce periodic review of permanent records to confirm that indefinite retention remains necessary and that records are protected throughout their lifecycle.
Provide a clear notice to producers explaining that ARC/PLC uses SCIMS-maintained data and a process for requesting correction of inaccurate source records.
Separate payment and tract information from direct identifiers in user views and reports unless the full combination is required for an approved business purpose.
County office users can search for a specific farmer or producer using personal information, which creates a risk of unauthorized lookup or overbroad access to sensitive identity data.
The system uses SSN as a second authentication method, exposing highly sensitive identifiers to misuse if accessed or handled improperly.
FSAfarm+ pulls PII from SCIMS, so any weakness in access controls or data handling during retrieval could expose personal data to county office users.
Contractor access to the FSCOMS/FSAfarm+ environment creates a risk that contractors could view or mishandle PII while supporting the system.
Although the system says memory and cache are cleared on logout, transient PII could still be exposed if the clearing process fails or is incomplete.
The system relies on the statement that it does not store PII, so any unexpected persistence of data would create a privacy risk because there is no stated retention control for stored records.
Enforce role-based access controls and need-to-know restrictions for county office searches, with audit logging of each lookup.
Minimize SSN use for authentication by masking the SSN on screen and using an alternative second factor where possible.
Restrict retrieval from SCIMS to only the minimum fields needed for the specific user task and protect the transfer with strong access controls.
Limit contractor access to specific support functions and require backgrounded privileged access approval for any contractor account that can reach PII.
Test logout and cache-clearing behavior to confirm that no PII remains in memory or cache after session end.
Continuously monitor the application to verify that no PII is being stored unexpectedly and alert on any deviation from the no-retention design.

The system collects and maintains personally identifiable information about producers, including name, mailing address, ethnicity, and race, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure of sensitive identity and demographic data.

The system uses producer information to determine who is eligible to vote in committee elections, which creates a risk of profiling or unfair treatment if eligibility decisions are inaccurate or improperly applied.
County office staff collect data from producers and enter it into the system, creating a risk of human error or unauthorized entry that could compromise accuracy and privacy.

The system builds and sends county-specific lists of eligible producers for ballot printing, which creates a risk that election-related mailing lists could be exposed or misused if not tightly controlled.

The system collects and reports election data from returned ballot forms, creating a risk that ballot-related records could reveal participation or voting-related information beyond what is necessary.
The system creates and stores a directory of COC members and information related to their terms, which creates a risk of unnecessary retention and exposure of member records over time.
The system retains information indefinitely as permanent records, which increases the risk that personal data will persist longer than needed and be exposed in future incidents.

Because the system is a major application on DISC Midrange Systems, it concentrates election and producer data in a central environment, which increases the impact of any unauthorized access or breach.
Restrict access to producer records containing name, address, ethnicity, and race to only personnel with a documented need to know, and monitor access to those fields.
Validate committee and LAA code-based eligibility determinations before ballots or lists are generated, and provide a correction process for producers who are misclassified.
Use role-based access, staff training, and data-entry validation checks for county office collection and entry of producer information.
Limit distribution of county-specific eligible-producer lists to authorized election staff and use secure handling procedures for ballot printing files.
Apply access controls and minimization to returned ballot records so only the information needed for election reporting is retained and viewed.
Review the COC Directory contents periodically and remove any member-term information that is no longer required for the system's stated election purposes.
Apply a records review and archival control process for permanent records so only approved records are retained indefinitely and inactive data is protected.
Harden the DISC Midrange Systems environment with strong authentication, least-privilege access, and logging for all access to FSFOSS records.

The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial data, so a breach could expose identities, account details, and employment history. The breadth of data increases the privacy impact if access controls fail.

Consolidating data from multiple source systems into a central warehouse creates a larger single point of exposure if the warehouse is misused or compromised. Centralized reporting can reveal more about individuals than any one source system alone.

The system uses reporting tools and web-based access, which can increase the risk of unauthorized internal access to detailed personal data if permissions are too broad. Reporting environments often expose more records than are needed for a user's job.

Batch transfers from source systems to the warehouse can expose personal data in transit or during loading if the transfer process is not securely protected. Repeated automated transfers also increase the chance of accidental disclosure or interception.

The system receives data from multiple agencies and source systems, so inaccurate or mismatched records could lead to incorrect reporting or decisions about individuals. Errors in identity or eligibility data can affect privacy and fairness.

Information is collected from producers at county offices and from other federal agencies, which creates a risk that individuals may not fully understand how their data will be reused across the warehouse. Secondary use for reporting may exceed the context in which the data was originally provided.

The system supports Congressional, program-level, and end-user reporting, which can create privacy risk if reports disclose more detail than necessary. Broad reporting use may make it harder to limit personal data to the minimum needed.

The system shares information with other organizations and external entities, creating a risk of disclosure beyond the originating purpose. Even limited validation or one-time sharing can expose personal identifiers to additional parties.

Retention tied to the NARA schedule means personal data may be kept for a long time, increasing the window for misuse or breach. Longer retention also increases the amount of historical information available for profiling or secondary use.
Limit access to sensitive fields such as TIN/SSN, account numbers, and employment history to only those users with a documented need to know, and enforce strong auditing of access to those fields.
Apply data minimization in the warehouse by retaining only the fields needed for reporting and by segregating especially sensitive datasets where feasible.
Use role-based access controls and least-privilege permissions for OBIEE and web-based reporting tools, with report-level restrictions for sensitive datasets.
Protect batch processes with encryption in transit, secure service accounts, and integrity checks to prevent interception or tampering during transfers.
Implement data quality validation and reconciliation rules during ETL to detect mismatches, duplicates, and stale records before they are used in reporting.
Provide clear privacy notices and purpose limitations for data collected at county offices and from other agencies, so individuals understand how their information will be used in the warehouse.
Review and approve report templates to ensure Congressional, program-level, and end-user reports disclose only the minimum personal information needed.
Use formal data-sharing agreements and disclosure controls for all internal and external recipients, including validation-only exchanges, to limit further use and redisclosure.
Apply records management rules that delete or archive personal data as soon as the approved retention period expires, and periodically review whether all retained fields remain necessary.

The system stores and processes highly sensitive financial and identity data for a very large population, creating a broad exposure risk if access controls fail or the data is mishandled. This includes bank account details, SSNs/TINs, and payment and debt information for approximately 1.4 million customers annually.

The public-facing self-service functions increase the risk of unauthorized access or account misuse because producers and farmers can update banking and assignment information online. If authentication or authorization is weak, an attacker could change payment instructions or other financial details.

County office employees can view the same detailed financial information that producers see, which increases the risk of overbroad internal access to personal financial records. This shared visibility could expose more information than is necessary for each employee's task.

The system maintains permanent records, which increases the long-term privacy impact if sensitive information is later accessed inappropriately or retained longer than needed for operational purposes. Indefinite retention also expands the window for compromise over time.

The system generates and stores document images that may contain SSNs, bank account numbers, and signatures, creating a risk that scanned or faxed documents expose more data than necessary. Image repositories can be especially sensitive because they may contain unstructured personal information.

Debt and delinquency information is used to report creditworthiness and is supplied to commercial credit bureaus, which can affect individuals beyond the original payment purpose. This creates a risk of reputational or financial harm if debt data is inaccurate or improperly disclosed.

The system shares payment and debt information with the Department of the Treasury for offset, garnishment, and collection actions, which increases the privacy impact of interagency data use. Even when permitted, these disclosures can expose sensitive financial status to another agency.

The system produces letters and statements about payments and debt, which creates a risk that mailed or printed outputs could be seen by unintended recipients. This is especially sensitive because the letters concern receivables, delinquency, and tax reporting.

Contractors have access to the system, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure if contractor handling is not tightly controlled. Even with need-to-know access, contractors can still expose sensitive USDA data through misuse or error.
Limit access to sensitive financial and identity data to role-based, need-to-know users and log all access to customer records for review.
Require strong authentication and transaction controls for self-service changes to banking and assignment information, including review of high-risk edits before they take effect.
Restrict county office employee visibility to only the fields needed to assist the producer, rather than full producer-view parity.
Apply a records review and minimization process to determine whether all permanent records must remain fully identifiable, and segregate or archive inactive records with tighter controls.
Redact or mask SSNs, bank account numbers, and signatures in document images unless the full values are operationally required, and restrict image access to authorized staff only.
Validate delinquency and debt data before any credit-related reporting and provide a correction process for affected producers when errors are found.
Limit interagency disclosures to the minimum data needed for offset and collection, and document the specific authority and purpose for each transmission.
Use privacy-protective mailing controls for letters and statements, such as envelope sealing, address verification, and suppression of unnecessary details in printed notices.
Continue and strengthen contractor vetting, training, and enforcement of the prohibition on downloading, sharing, storing, or printing USDA data.

The system retains employees' PII indefinitely, which increases the chance that personal data will be exposed or misused over time. Long-term retention also expands the amount of information that could be affected by future incidents or unauthorized access.

The system stores name and mailing address information, which can identify and locate employees if disclosed improperly. Even limited PII can create privacy harm when combined with role and access information.

The system maintains fine-grained role, group, office, and attribute data used to control access, which could reveal internal organizational structure and employee responsibilities. If exposed, this information could help an attacker target users or infer sensitive access patterns.

Administrators can manage access rights in real time, so unauthorized or mistaken changes could grant or remove access incorrectly. Such changes could expose employee information to the wrong people or block legitimate access.

The system is an online application for submitting and tracking security requests, which means PII is handled through a web-based interface and could be exposed if the application is compromised. Online access broadens the attack surface compared with offline handling.
Implement periodic records reviews to confirm that permanent retention is still required for each record category and limit access to archived records to only those with a documented need.
Restrict access to name and mailing address fields to personnel with a verified business need and log all access to those records.
Apply least-privilege controls to authorization metadata and separate administrative views from general user access.
Require strong administrative authentication and maintain audit logs for every role, group, and attribute change made in the system.
Harden the web application with secure coding, vulnerability management, and access controls appropriate for a system that handles security requests and tracking.

The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial records, including PII, financial data, health data, biometric data, and criminal history, creating a substantial harm if the repository is exposed or misused.
The system retains information indefinitely as permanent records, which increases the amount of sensitive data exposed over time and prolongs the impact of any breach or misuse.

The system ingests data from faxed, scanned, emailed, and electronically stored documents, which can lead to inaccurate, incomplete, or misfiled records if source documents are poor quality or improperly indexed.
The system allows desktop browser access to stored images on a network device, so unauthorized internal access or overbroad access could expose sensitive records to users who do not need them.
Workflow processing in FileNet can expose sensitive financial information to additional users or steps beyond simple storage and retrieval, increasing the risk of unnecessary internal disclosure.

The system imports Federal Reserve Bank check images and historical treasury-check archives, so it may hold legacy records that are no longer actively managed but still contain sensitive personal or financial information.
County and state employees can search and retrieve claim images, which creates a risk that users with broad operational access could view records beyond their legitimate case responsibilities.
The system supports fax capture and email/desktop scanner ingestion, which increases the chance that sensitive records could be intercepted or mishandled before they are stored.
Enforce least-privilege access controls and strong authentication for all users who can view or manage the repository.
Apply a records review process to confirm that indefinite retention is still necessary for each record class and to dispose of records when the approved schedule allows.
Add validation and quality-control checks for scanned, faxed, and manually entered documents before they are indexed into FileNet.
Restrict browser access by role and log all retrieval activity for monitoring and review.
Limit workflow routing to only the minimum necessary roles and configure workflow steps to avoid exposing full images when partial information is sufficient.
Apply the same access controls, monitoring, and retention review to historical archives as to active records.
Use case-based authorization so state and county employees can retrieve only the claims assigned to their work.
Secure fax, email, and scanner intake channels with approved transmission protections and controlled intake procedures.

The system exposes PII in work lists and allows users to export those lists to Excel on their device, which can lead to unauthorized local storage or onward sharing of sensitive customer data. This is especially risky because the work lists contain names, addresses, and contract-related status information.

The system sends the same data and fields as work lists through e-mail alerts, creating a risk that sensitive information will be disclosed through email interception, misdelivery, or forwarding. The alerts also include deltas, which can reveal ongoing changes in a person's program status over time.

Users can filter and sort the data on the client side, which means PII is processed in the browser or device and may be exposed through local caching, screenshots, or browser artifacts. This expands the number of places where the data may persist beyond the controlled server environment.

The system allows access to additional details through a link to PT-FM, increasing the chance that users will view more PII than the minimal work list data needed for their task. Broader access raises the risk of unnecessary exposure if access controls are not tightly enforced.

The system depends on a replicated copy of SCIMS data, so any weaknesses in replication, access controls, or synchronization could expose a broader set of customer information than intended. Because NRCS users do not access SCIMS directly, the copy becomes a sensitive intermediary repository.

The system includes race, sex, national origin, and disability information in the underlying SCIMS source, which are highly sensitive attributes if exposed or used inappropriately. Even if FA Tracker only displays minimal information, the data source contains information that can increase privacy harm if accessed.

Contractors may have access to the system, which increases the number of people who can view PII and raises the risk of misuse or accidental disclosure. The system relies on background investigations, eAuthentication, NDAs, and rules of behavior, but contractor access still expands the attack and mishandling surface.

The system retains information for long periods, potentially for many years or as long as program participants remain eligible, which increases the duration of exposure if records are breached or improperly accessed. Long retention also increases the chance that data will outlive its original operational need.
Disable device-side export by default or require strong justification, logging, and manager approval before Excel export is allowed.
Require users to opt in to email alerts and send only the minimum necessary data, with a warning against forwarding or storing the messages outside approved systems.
Move filtering and sorting to the server side where feasible, or ensure client-side results are not cached and are cleared when the session ends.
Enforce least-privilege access to PT-FM details and display only the minimum fields needed for the work list by default.
Apply strict access controls, monitoring, and integrity checks to the replicated SCIMS copy and the PT-FM-to-FA Tracker data flow.
Restrict access to demographic and disability-related data to only those users with a documented need, and audit any access to those fields.

Continue and strengthen contractor onboarding controls, including need-to-know role approval, background checks, eAuthentication, NDAs, and enforcement of the rules against downloading, sharing, storing, or printing USDA data.
Apply records schedules consistently and periodically review whether retained records are still needed for the stated program purpose.
The system stores contact and financial identifiers for external business partners, which could expose individuals if the data is mishandled or accessed inappropriately.
External users can access the online application to enter and review their own program information, creating a risk of unauthorized viewing or alteration if access controls fail.
The system generates nightly files and ad hoc reports for multiple users, increasing the risk that more information than necessary is exposed through reporting outputs.
Reports are submitted to auditors and other federal agencies, which creates a disclosure risk if shared data is broader than needed for the receiving purpose.
Department contractors have access to the system, which raises the risk of insider misuse or overbroad access to sensitive program and contact information.
The system retains information indefinitely, which increases the long-term risk of stale data exposure and cumulative misuse over time.
The system collects tax identification numbers and payment bank information, which are highly sensitive and could cause financial harm if exposed.
Limit access to contact and banking data to personnel with a documented need to know and log all access to those fields.
Enforce strong authentication and per-record authorization so external users can view and edit only their own program information.
Apply data minimization and field-level redaction in ad hoc and canned reports so only necessary information is included.
Use formal disclosure review and sharing agreements before sending reports to auditors or other agencies, and strip out any nonessential personal or business identifiers.
Require contractors to receive role-based access, privacy training, and periodic access reviews.
Implement records management controls that periodically review whether permanent retention is still necessary for specific data elements and archive or segregate older records.
Encrypt tax identification numbers and payment bank information at rest and in transit, and mask them in user interfaces and reports.
The system stores documents that may contain highly sensitive personal data, so unauthorized access or disclosure could expose names, identifiers, financial data, criminal history, and other PII.
The system supports internal and external sharing of files, which increases the chance that PII is disclosed beyond the intended audience.
Authorized users, including contractors and partners, can access PII manually, so misuse or overbroad access by legitimate users could expose information.
PII may be maintained for long periods, which increases the amount of sensitive data available if records are no longer needed or if an account is disabled but content remains retained.
PII shared through third-party applications is not periodically purged, which can leave stale sensitive data available longer than necessary.
The system relies on a third-party cloud vendor to maintain and secure PII, which creates dependency on the vendor’s privacy and security controls.
User profile PII can be updated from LDAP and by users themselves, so inaccurate or excessive profile data could be stored and used for administration.
The system allows mobile access to stored data, which can increase the risk of exposure if devices are lost, stolen, or used in insecure environments.
Limit file access to users with a documented need-to-know and enforce strong role-based access controls on all sensitive repositories.
Require explicit sharing permissions and approval workflows for external sharing of files containing PII.
Review and log all access to PII files so that authorized-user access can be audited for inappropriate use.
Apply records disposition rules promptly and disable or remove access when retention is no longer required.
Implement periodic purge or expiration controls for PII stored through third-party applications.
Conduct vendor oversight, including security and privacy reviews of Box Inc., to verify that the third-party environment protects stored PII appropriately.
Validate user profile data before use and restrict self-service edits to necessary fields only.
Require secure mobile device protections such as strong authentication and encryption for any mobile access to stored files.
Information sent through the system may be exposed while traveling between FPAC CASP and outside agencies if transport protections fail or are misconfigured.
A producer's saved inquiry and DOL case number are retained for 90 days, creating a limited but real persistence of user-linked information in the system.
The system serves as a pass-through to DOL and USCIS, so user information is sent outside USDA and privacy protections depend on those external systems as well.

Although the system says it does not store PII, it is expected to have PII inside its boundary because it is used to access Login.gov, DOL, and USCIS, which creates a risk of accidental collection or logging of more data than intended.
The system relies on external third-party websites and applications, so users' privacy depends on those services even though FPAC CASP itself does not control their internal practices.
Enforce modern TLS configuration for all external connections and periodically test certificate validation and endpoint configuration.
Keep the 90-day retention limit, but automatically delete the stored DOL case number at expiration and restrict access to it to the minimum necessary administrators.
Document and review the data-sharing boundaries with DOL and USCIS, including confirmation that only the minimum necessary information is transmitted for the stated purpose.
Configure the application to suppress request, response, and session logging of user data and to prevent any unintended storage of PII in temporary files or error messages.
Perform and maintain privacy reviews of the external services used by the application and ensure user notices explain that DOL, USCIS, and Login.gov are involved in processing.

DRMS stores scanned paper records and metadata that may include highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers, creating a risk of exposure if the stored documents or databases are improperly accessed or mishandled.

TeamMate+ contains audit documents provided by customers and auditors that may include PII from many FPAC programs and external parties, so audit records could reveal personal, financial, or operational details beyond what is necessary for the final audit output.

DRMS allows broad internal searching and special roles for records managers and legal staff to perform unconstrained searches for audit, legal discovery, litigation holds, or FOIA inquiries, which increases the risk of overexposure or secondary use of records beyond the original business need.

TeamMate+ permits customer uploads and, in rare cases, auditor uploads, which creates a risk that incorrect, excessive, or sensitive information may be submitted into the system without strong pre-upload review.

DRMS ingests scanned documents into multiple databases, including metadata stored in Elasticsearch for instant retrieval, which increases the number of places where PII exists and therefore the attack surface for unauthorized access or disclosure.
Department contractors may have access to Pipeline FPAC Mod, which creates a risk that non-federal personnel can view or handle sensitive records if contractor access is not tightly controlled.

Individuals do not have direct access to DRMS or TeamMate+, so they must rely on a written Privacy Act request process to obtain or correct their records, which can make it harder for them to notice or remedy inaccurate or excessive information.

The system retains information for long periods, including records kept indefinitely or as long as a program participant qualifies, which increases the duration of privacy exposure and the impact of any future breach or misuse.
Restrict access to DRMS documents and databases to only users with a documented need-to-know and monitor access to sensitive document sets.
Apply least-privilege access and strong authentication to TeamMate+ audit records, and limit administrative access to a very small number of users.
Limit unconstrained searching in DRMS to specifically authorized records-management and legal workflows, and log and review those searches for appropriateness.
Require pre-upload validation and content review for TeamMate+ submissions so that customers and auditors only upload information necessary for the audit purpose.
Minimize replicated metadata and apply the same access protections to Elasticsearch, Alfresco, and SQL storage as to the source documents, with regular security review of each datastore.
Require documented contractor need-to-know approval and periodic review of contractor access to Pipeline FPAC Mod.
Provide a clear, timely Privacy Act request and correction process so individuals can request access to records about them and update incorrect information.
Apply records minimization and scheduled disposition reviews so records are retained only for the approved NARA period and not longer than necessary.
The system stores highly sensitive identifiers such as SSNs and EINs, which creates a risk of harm if the data is exposed or misused.
The system retains most application records indefinitely, increasing the amount of personal data exposed over time and the impact of any future breach.
PII is shared with the RMA Strategic Data Analysis Division for forensic data mining, which creates a risk of secondary use beyond the original collection purpose.
PII is shared externally with Approved Insurance Providers, creating a risk of disclosure outside USDA to entities that collect and use the information themselves.
The system includes contractor access, which raises the risk of unauthorized access or misuse by non-federal personnel.
The system transmits PII over network links to internal and external recipients, so interception or misrouting during transfer is a privacy risk.
The system uses hard copy forms and e-forms collected from producers, agents, and adjusters, which creates a risk of collection or handling errors before data reaches the system.
The system relies on COTS office automation tools such as Excel for analysis, which can increase the risk of uncontrolled copies or inadvertent disclosure.
Limit access to SSNs and EINs to the smallest set of users and roles needed, and apply strong encryption and logging for those fields.
Apply a records minimization and disposition review to reduce indefinite retention where legally allowed and ensure permanent records are truly necessary.
Document and enforce a purpose limitation and access controls for forensic data mining so the division only receives the minimum data needed for fraud, waste, and abuse review.
Use a data-sharing agreement with each AIP that requires privacy safeguards, role-based access, audit logging, and prompt breach reporting.
Require contractor background screening, least-privilege access, and periodic review of contractor accounts.
Continuously verify encryption and secure configuration for all transfers, and test that the VPN and encrypted tunnel are correctly implemented.
Standardize secure submission procedures for hard copy forms and e-forms, including validation, secure handling, and error checking before ingestion.
Restrict spreadsheet exports, use protected storage for working files, and require deletion of local analysis copies when no longer needed.

The CFPB may collect personally identifiable information from people who interact with the agency on social media, which can expose identity-linked data such as names, usernames, email addresses, IP addresses, geographic information, or demographic information.
Social media platforms are operated by third parties, so information shared with the CFPB may be subject to the platform’s own collection and privacy practices outside CFPB control.
Public interactions on social media may make consumers expect privacy protections that are not fully visible or understood in the platform environment.
The system’s purpose to engage the public and increase transparency could encourage broader sharing of personal information than is necessary for the agency’s mission.
Limit collection to the minimum PII necessary for each social media interaction and avoid collecting sensitive or unnecessary identity-linked details.
Apply CFPB privacy protections and security controls to social media activity and ensure covered information is handled under the stated system of records notice.
Provide clear notice, consent, access, and redress information before or during social media interactions so users understand what privacy protections apply.
Use social media only for public engagement and transparency purposes, and avoid using the information to make determinations about individuals.

The system republishes a publicly accessible dataset that includes names and detailed contact information for individuals associated with HUD-approved housing counseling agencies, which can expose those individuals to unwanted contact or profiling.
The system may disclose user ZIP codes entered into the locator tool, which can reveal a user's approximate location and interest in housing counseling services.
The system retains user analytics and ZIP codes as permanent records until a disposition schedule is approved, creating a long-term accumulation of user activity data.

The locator tool collects non-identifying operational data such as visit timestamps, browser version, operating system, pages viewed, and time on site, which can still be used to profile users' browsing behavior over time.

The API and locator tool allow users to download or share dataset data in multiple formats, which can facilitate bulk reuse, repackaging, and broader dissemination of the publicly available information.
Users who develop programs using the HUD API can present the data in a variety of formats outside CFPB, which may reduce CFPB's control over downstream privacy protections.
The public has unrestricted read-only access to the dataset and locator tool with no authorization process, increasing the risk of automated scraping or mass collection.
The system uses ZIP codes entered by users to evaluate tool use, which creates a risk that search behavior could be analyzed beyond the immediate service need.
Limit the public dataset to the minimum contact details needed for locating counseling agencies and review whether all listed fields must remain publicly exposed.
Minimize retention and use of entered ZIP codes, and avoid linking them to other user analytics unless necessary for the stated service.
Approve and implement a NARA disposition schedule for consumerfinance.gov analytics and locator ZIP codes as soon as practicable, and delete the records once the schedule is in effect.
Limit analytics collection to what is necessary for functionality, security, and usability evaluation, and avoid retaining detailed browsing telemetry longer than needed.
Provide clear restrictions or guidance on bulk downloading and sharing of the dataset to discourage unnecessary redistribution.
Publish API usage terms or technical controls that require downstream developers to preserve the public-purpose limits and avoid adding new personal data to the dataset.
Add anti-scraping and rate-limiting controls to the public interface to reduce automated mass harvesting.
Use ZIP codes entered for search only to return nearby agencies, and separate or aggregate any analytics derived from those inputs.

The system may include direct identifiers such as names, contact details, SSNs, and financial account numbers, which increases the risk of unauthorized identification or misuse if exposed. Even though the data often lacks direct identifiers, the PIA says they can be included in some circumstances.

Matching records across datasets can create richer profiles and increase the chance of re-identification or unintended secondary use. The system explicitly combines data from different sources and uses unique record locators to update or supplement individual records.

The system may use demographic and financial data to proxy population characteristics, which can create privacy concerns if individuals are inferred from group-based attributes. The data includes race/ethnicity, gender, age, education level, income, credit score, balances, and market share information.

The system relies on third parties, commercial sources, and public databases, so inaccurate or outdated information may be collected and used without the individual’s direct involvement. That can affect the privacy and fairness of any research conclusions drawn from the data.

Individuals may not receive direct notice from CFPB when their information is collected or shared, because the Bureau says notice is the responsibility of the third parties. This can leave people unaware that their data is being used for research.

The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which increases the duration of privacy exposure. Longer retention raises the chance of unauthorized access or secondary use over time.

Although the system says results shared externally do not directly identify individuals, sharing results with the general public, data sources, and federal regulators still creates a residual disclosure risk. Aggregated outputs can sometimes be combined with other information to infer details about underlying records.

Access is limited to CFPB personnel with a need to know, but the system still contains sensitive administrative data and research records that could be exposed through insider misuse or overbroad access if controls fail. The presence of biometric and health or medical information heightens the sensitivity of any access issue.
Minimize direct identifiers by stripping names, contact details, SSNs, and account numbers before analysis whenever possible, and keep any necessary identifiers in a separately protected environment.

Limit record matching to the minimum necessary datasets and use unique record locators only for the specific update or supplementation task, then remove or isolate linkage keys after matching is complete.

Apply stronger controls or suppression rules when using sensitive demographic and financial variables for proxying, so outputs cannot be used to infer information about specific individuals or small groups.
Validate and document external-source data before use, including checks for accuracy, timeliness, and relevance, and correct or exclude records that are clearly unreliable.
Provide direct CFPB notice or a public-facing notice about the data sources and research use whenever practicable, rather than relying only on third parties to notify individuals.
Adopt and implement a retention schedule as soon as possible, and delete or archive records according to the shortest lawful retention period consistent with research needs.
Review public and external reports for disclosure risk before release, including aggregation thresholds and suppression of small cells or rare combinations that could enable re-identification.

Enforce role-based access reviews, logging, and periodic audits for personnel with access to Market Research data, with extra safeguards for highly sensitive fields such as biometric or health information.

Even without direct identifiers, users may be able to isolate a single loan record and infer details about an individual applicant or borrower from the public dataset. This creates a re-identification or singling-out risk from highly granular loan-level and property data.

The dataset includes sensitive application and outcome details that could expose financial circumstances, credit behavior, and denial reasons for individual mortgage applicants. Public release of these fields increases the risk of harm from unwanted disclosure.

The dataset includes location information at a fine geographic level, which can make it easier to link a loan record to a specific property or household. This increases the chance of indirect identification in sparsely populated areas or for unusual transactions.
