Because the public can query, filter, download, and share the dataset, external users can combine records with other sources to re-identify people or profile borrowers. The API also enables reuse in other applications and systems, expanding downstream privacy exposure.

The CFPB republishes data that it does not independently verify, so any privacy-protective redactions or modifications made upstream could be incomplete or erroneous. If sensitive fields were not properly removed before republication, the public dataset could expose applicant or borrower information.

The system retains the public dataset until a CFPB records schedule is approved by NARA, which may prolong exposure of loan-level information. Longer retention increases the window for misuse, linkage, and repeated access over time.

Public access is read-only and requires no authorization, so anyone, including federal and state agencies and private sector organizations, can access the dataset without restriction. This broad access increases the likelihood of mass collection and secondary use beyond the original disclosure purpose.

The dataset may be combined with other public or proprietary information to infer protected characteristics or other sensitive attributes about applicants. The presence of race, ethnicity, and sex notice in the collection context highlights the possibility that the data supports sensitive inferences even if those fields are not listed in the public-use excerpt.
Continue and strengthen de-identification review before publication, including testing whether single records can be isolated in combination with other public data sources.
Limit publication to the minimum fields needed for public understanding and continue suppressing or rounding fields that could reveal sensitive financial outcomes.
Apply geographic generalization or suppression where needed to reduce the chance that a record can be tied to a specific household or property.

Provide clear reuse guidance and privacy warnings on the API and download pages, including cautions against attempting re-identification or combining the dataset with other sources to identify individuals.
Add a CFPB spot-check or validation step for privacy-protective redactions before republication, especially for fields that could indirectly identify borrowers.
Adopt and publish a CFPB records retention schedule as soon as possible, and periodically review whether continued retention of the public dataset remains necessary.
Keep access read-only for the public and maintain the non-public database layer behind CFPB access controls for operational staff only.
Perform privacy review for sensitive-inference risk before release of any new fields or formats, especially where the data could be combined with other datasets to infer protected characteristics.

The system collects highly sensitive identifiers and personal data, including SSNs, financial information, biometric information, and health or medical information, which creates a risk of harm if misused or exposed.
The system collects sensitive demographic and life-event information that could reveal vulnerable status or protected characteristics when combined with response data.
The system may create new linked datasets by matching administrative data, credit scores, and response data, increasing the risk of re-identification or expanded profiling.
The system may use administrative data to identify survey recipients and to support nonresponse analyses, which can expose individuals to unwanted outreach or profiling based on third-party data.
The system relies on third-party collection and contractor/vendor transfers, which creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure during sharing or transit.
Direct identifying PII is retained separately but still stored for scheduling, follow-up, compensation, and matching, creating a risk of unnecessary retention and exposure of identity data.
The system may share research products externally, including public dissemination, which could expose sensitive information if disclosure-protection procedures fail or are insufficient.
The system may share direct identifying PII in external products such as case studies or quotes, which risks exposing individuals if consent is incomplete or context changes.
Records are retained indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which creates a risk that personal data will remain available longer than necessary.

Limit collection of direct identifiers and sensitive fields to only what is necessary for scheduling, follow-up, compensation, or approved analysis, and keep identifiers stored separately from research data.

Apply disclosure-protection procedures before any release of response data that includes demographic or sensitive information, including aggregation, rounding, variable suppression, and exclusion of observations.
Use de-identified matched datasets for analysis after matching is complete and keep the linkage keys separate from the research dataset.
Use administrative data for survey targeting and nonresponse analysis only under documented purpose limits and consent where applicable, and restrict it to the minimum needed fields.
Continue to require encrypted transfers and add strict contractual controls and non-disclosure obligations for contractors, vendors, and collaborating researchers.
Restrict access to direct identifying PII to only staff with a need to know and keep those identifiers secured separately from analysis data.
Before external publication, apply disclosure-protection review to all research products and remove direct identifiers and other high-risk fields unless disclosure is necessary and authorized.
Require documented, informed consent and a separate approval review before any external product includes a quote, case study, or other direct identifier.
Adopt and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as possible and purge records according to the approved schedule instead of retaining them indefinitely.

The system may include highly sensitive identifiers and personal data, creating a risk of re-identification or misuse if exposed. The PIA says direct identifiers can sometimes be present, including SSNs, financial account numbers, home addresses, and email addresses.

The system may collect biometric and health or medical information, which is especially sensitive and could cause significant harm if improperly disclosed or analyzed. The overview explicitly lists these categories among the information included in the system.

Individuals generally are not notified when their information is collected or shared, limiting transparency and their ability to understand or challenge use of their data. The PIA says notice is generally not provided in supervisory or enforcement contexts.

The CFPB may combine records across datasets and create new data about individuals, which can expand what is known about them beyond the original source. The system explicitly uses direct identifying PII to match across datasets and update records.

The CFPB may contact potential survey recipients using direct identifying information, which can reveal that a person is associated with a supervision, enforcement, or market research inquiry. The PIA states direct identifying PII may be used to contact potential recipients of surveys.

The system retains records indefinitely until a NARA disposition schedule is approved, which increases the chance of long-term exposure, secondary use, or stale data remaining accessible. The retention section states the CFPB maintains records indefinitely for now.

Products of market research may be shared with the general public and federal financial regulators, creating a risk that aggregate outputs could still reveal sensitive information if not carefully suppressed. The PIA says these products are shared externally.

Access is limited to CFPB personnel with a need to know, but the system still depends on internal access controls to prevent unauthorized viewing or use of sensitive SEFL Data. The PIA indicates personnel access to the data is granted.
Minimize and mask direct identifiers before analysis, and use de-identified copies whenever possible.
Apply heightened handling controls and strict minimization for biometric and health or medical information, including limiting access to only cases where such data are essential.
Provide notice whenever feasible and, where direct notice is not possible, maintain clear constructive notice describing collection, use, and disclosure practices.
Use record matching only when necessary, and require validation checks before and after linkage to reduce incorrect joins and unintended profiling.
Limit survey outreach to the minimum necessary contact information and separate outreach lists from analytic datasets after contact is complete.
Establish and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as practicable, with periodic reviews to dispose of records that are no longer needed.
Review all public and regulator-facing outputs for disclosure risk before release, including suppression or aggregation of small cells and other potentially identifying details.
Enforce role-based access controls, logging, and periodic access reviews for all personnel who can reach SEFL Data used for Market Research.

The system collects highly sensitive personal data, including Social Security numbers, financial information, and even biometric or health information, which could cause significant harm if misused or exposed.
The system may retrieve information by personal identifier, which increases the risk of re-identifying participants and linking their responses to their identity.

The system can match response data with administrative data such as credit scores, balances, payment histories, and other product-use information, creating new information about participants and increasing the sensitivity of the combined profile.
The system collects website and online tool usage data, including IP address and visit timestamps, which can enable tracking of participant behavior across sessions or services.
The system relies on information collected from third parties, so participants may have less visibility into what is shared and how it is used.
The system may share response data or products with the general public, which could expose participant information if de-identification is incomplete or re-identification becomes possible.
The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which can prolong exposure and increase the chance of unauthorized access over time.
The system shares data through non-automated transfers and encrypted email, which can create operational handling risks if transfer procedures are not tightly controlled.
Limit collection to only the minimum sensitive data needed for the specific Consumer Education purpose and keep direct identifiers separated from response and administrative data.
Restrict retrieval by personal identifier to cases where it is necessary for delivery of Consumer Education and maintain the separation of identifying data from research data.
Require informed consent before any record matching and use a de-identified copy of the matched dataset for research and analysis.
Continue collecting website and online tool data in aggregate form and avoid direct identification in analytics outputs.
Obtain the individual’s consent before collecting information from third parties and document those disclosures clearly.
Apply disclosure-protection techniques such as aggregation, rounding, exclusion of variables, and exclusion of observations before any public release.
Finalize and implement a NARA-approved records disposition schedule so records are not retained longer than necessary.
Continue using encrypted tunnels and encrypted email for transfers and add strict handling controls for non-automated transfers.

The CFPB may collect information from people in real-world settings over a longer period of time, which can create a risk of broader exposure of consumer information than a one-time transaction would.
The CFPB may share or receive consumer information through collaborations with third parties, creating a risk that data will be disclosed beyond the Bureau.
The system may involve contractors or third-party collaborators handling the information, which increases the risk of unauthorized use or disclosure if roles are not tightly controlled.
The system may use primary data collection in consumer financial markets, which can capture information from individuals who may not expect research collection in everyday market activity.
The system may collect information about consumer awareness, decision-making, experiences, and risks, which can be sensitive because it reveals financial behavior and vulnerabilities.
The system may collect information about the effect of disclosures, education, and technology on consumer behavior, which can enable profiling or inference about individuals' financial behavior.

The system relies on standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls, but the input does not describe any field-specific limits on access, sharing, or retention, leaving a residual risk of over-collection or over-retention.
The input says there are generally applicable opportunities for notice, consent, access, and redress, which implies participation may not always be individualized or fully informed in every case.
Minimize collection and retention to only the data needed for the specific research question, and de-identify or aggregate data as early as possible.
Use written data-sharing agreements that limit third-party access, prohibit secondary use, and require privacy and security controls for any collaborator.
Require role-based access controls and explicit handling instructions for contractors and third parties, with oversight and auditability.
Provide clear notice to participants before or at the point of collection about what data is being collected, why it is being collected, and how it will be used.
Limit the collection of sensitive financial behavior details to what is necessary and, where possible, use aggregated analysis instead of individual-level reporting.
Apply privacy review to any analysis that infers behavior or outcomes, and suppress outputs that could identify or unfairly characterize individuals.
Publish system-specific privacy and retention limits for field research rather than relying only on general CFPB controls.
Ensure participants receive meaningful consent and access/redress processes tailored to the field research setting.
The platform collects detailed mortgage application and loan data from financial institutions, which can expose sensitive consumer financial and housing information if mishandled.
The system receives data from multiple financial institutions and agencies, increasing the chance that information could be shared more broadly than intended.

Because the data are used to identify possible discriminatory lending patterns and enforce antidiscrimination statutes, individuals may be subject to profiling or adverse attention based on their mortgage records.
The platform supports reporting of information that will be disclosed to the public under Regulation C, creating a risk that personal information becomes publicly accessible.
The system depends on electronic submission of loan/application registers, which creates a risk of unauthorized access or interception during transmission or storage.
The data are collected by and shared among several federal HMDA agencies, so a broader set of recipients may increase the number of points where privacy controls could fail.
Limit access to HMDA data to authorized personnel only and apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls.
Use role-based access controls and sharing restrictions so only authorized users and agencies can view the data they need.
Minimize the data used for analysis and reporting to only what is necessary for HMDA purposes.
Apply disclosure review and suppress or aggregate fields before any public release of HMDA data.
Encrypt electronic submissions and stored loan/application registers.
Require consistent privacy and security requirements across all Federal HMDA agencies that receive the data.

The system collects and reports sensitive mortgage data, including age, credit score, and self-identified race and ethnicity, which could expose applicants to privacy harm if mishandled or disclosed too broadly.
The system requires annual and, for some institutions, quarterly submission of HMDA data, increasing the volume and frequency of transfers and the chance of unauthorized access or disclosure.
The data are disclosed to the public, which can create a re-identification risk even though HMDA does not require direct identifiers.
Although direct identifiers are not required, institutions may still include them in identification numbers or submissions, which could directly identify applicants or borrowers.
The CFPB receives data from many covered financial institutions and multiple federal agencies, expanding the number of entities that handle the information and the risk of inconsistent safeguards.
Loan/application registers are submitted electronically, which creates a risk of interception, unauthorized access, or transmission errors during submission.
Apply strict access controls, minimization, and security protections to sensitive fields such as age, credit score, race, and ethnicity, and limit use to authorized HMDA purposes.
Use secure transmission, validation, and monitoring controls for annual and quarterly submissions, with heightened review for high-volume filers.
Limit public disclosure to the minimum data elements required and apply disclosure review or suppression rules to reduce re-identification risk.
Continue to prohibit direct identifiers in HMDA submissions and validate incoming files to detect names, Social Security numbers, or similar identifiers before acceptance.
Apply consistent privacy and security controls across all Federal HMDA agencies that receive the data, including role-based access and sharing restrictions.
Require encrypted electronic submission and secure agency endpoints for loan/application registers.

The tool collects contact PII from regulated entities, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of names, phone numbers, and email addresses. Even though the collection is voluntary, the system still stores identifiable contact information for onboarding and assessment submission.

Free-text assessment responses and attachments may contain additional personal information beyond the limited contact fields, increasing the chance of over-collection and accidental disclosure. Because the content is optional and open-ended, submitters may include more PII than intended.

The system captures Bureau employee and contractor information, which creates a risk of internal personnel data exposure if the imported identity data is accessed inappropriately. This includes work contact details and organizational information.

Entity contacts must submit PII to be onboarded, so there is a risk that access to the system depends on providing personal information that may be more than necessary for the assessment itself. The onboarding step could also create a larger repository of contact data than users expect.

Aggregated data used for reporting and analytics could still reveal sensitive information if the aggregation is too granular or if small groups are identifiable. Internal dashboards can increase the chance of re-identification or secondary use beyond the original submission context.
Restrict access to contact PII to only authorized staff with a need to know and apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls.
Add validation, warning text, and reviewer procedures to discourage submission of unnecessary personal information in free-text fields and attachments.
Limit imported Bureau employee and contractor data to the minimum needed for system administration and protect it under the same access controls as other PII.
Collect only the specific onboarding fields needed for access and clearly explain why each PII element is required before submission.
Apply disclosure review and aggregation thresholds before using data in the annual report and dashboards to reduce the risk of re-identification.

The system stores and processes personally identifiable information about requestors, Bureau staff, and other people in request files and generated documents, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure of sensitive personal data.

The public-facing portal allows requestors to create accounts, submit requests, access requested records, and communicate with the Bureau, which creates a risk of account compromise or unauthorized access to request materials.
Using a third-party vendor-created system and an external identity service introduces a risk that personal data could be exposed through inter-system integration or vendor handling.

The same process is used for Privacy Act requests and FOIA requests, which creates a risk that records about a person could be processed or disclosed in a way that is broader than intended for a self-request.
The system supports the full lifecycle of requests, so request-related information may be retained and accumulated over time, increasing the amount of personal data available in one place.
Apply strong role-based access controls, least-privilege permissions, and logging for all request records and generated documents containing PII.
Require multi-factor authentication and session protections for PAL accounts and restrict access to records and communications to authenticated requestors only.
Use a formal vendor risk-management process for FOIAXpress and Login.gov integration, including security reviews, data-sharing limits, and contractual privacy requirements.
Provide workflow checks that distinguish Privacy Act requests from FOIA requests and train staff to route and release records under the correct process.
Minimize retention of request data to the shortest period needed for legal and operational purposes and regularly purge inactive records.
The system stores inquiry records in a third-party hosted cloud application, which creates a risk of unauthorized access or disclosure by the hosting provider or through the cloud environment.

The system collects and retains personally identifiable information about inquirers, including names tied to summaries of their issues, which could expose sensitive concerns if the record is breached or misused.

Even when contact details are kept outside the system, the office still maintains them in original email, mail, or voicemail formats, which creates additional exposure points for personal information.
The system supports analysis and outreach activities, which could lead to use of inquiry information beyond the original purpose if internal controls are weak.

Because the system is used to collect, track, manage, process, and analyze inquiry information, there is a risk of overcollection or retention of more information than is needed for the Ombudsman’s mission.
The system may expose information through administrative or development activities if privacy controls are not consistently applied during changes and security reviews.
Although the Office says it preserves confidentiality, the system still creates records about people contacting a federal office, which could chill participation if confidentiality is not maintained.
Require strong vendor security controls, contractual privacy requirements, and regular oversight of the third-party host.
Limit the inquiry record to only the minimum PII needed and continue allowing anonymous submissions when possible.
Protect the separate email, mail, and voicemail sources with the same access controls, handling rules, and retention limits used for the system record.
Enforce role-based access and purpose-based use restrictions so outreach and case information can be used only for authorized Ombudsman functions.
Apply data minimization and retention limits so the system keeps only the information needed to manage the inquiry and outreach activity.
Continue requiring privacy review and security authorization for system changes before deployment.
Maintain and publicize the confidentiality safeguards and provide clear notice about how inquiry information is used and protected.

The system collects and processes consumer complaints and inquiries that may contain sensitive personal details about a consumer’s financial experiences. Because complaints can be submitted by multiple channels and may include identifiable entities and personal experience, there is a risk of unnecessary exposure or misuse of those details.

Physical mail is digitized by vendor staff before being scanned into the system, creating a risk that third-party processors could improperly view, mishandle, or retain complaint documents during intake. This expands access beyond Bureau staff and increases the chance of unauthorized disclosure.

Vendor staff work directly with consumers and process complaints and inquiries on behalf of the Bureau, which creates a risk of overbroad access to consumer information by non-Bureau personnel. If access is not tightly controlled, vendor staff could see more information than needed to provide service.

The system uses enhanced voice processing such as IVR and automatic computational processing of human languages, which may capture or analyze callers' spoken information in ways consumers do not expect. This creates a risk that voice content could be retained or used beyond the immediate service interaction.

Advanced data analytics are used to assess performance and distill operational improvements, which can create a risk of secondary use of complaint data beyond the original complaint-handling purpose. Even if intended for operations, analytics may still reveal patterns about individual consumers or their complaints.

The Bureau may send complaints to the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint, to another government agency, or to other offices in the Bureau, which creates a disclosure risk if only the minimum necessary information is not shared. This can expose consumer complaint details to multiple recipients.

Consumer complaints and inquiries are received by phone, physical mail, and email, which creates a risk that information could be intercepted or misdirected during transmission. These channels can expose consumer data if safeguards are not consistently applied across all intake methods.

The system uses staff identity verification and authentication for access, which indicates that unauthorized access is a relevant risk if credentials are stolen or misused. Because staff email is used for authentication, compromised accounts could expose complaint and inquiry data.
Limit complaint and inquiry data collection to the minimum information needed to resolve the matter and apply role-based access controls to restrict viewing to staff who need the information.
Require vendor staff handling physical mail to follow strict handling, confidentiality, and immediate-destruction or secure-transfer procedures, with audit logs for mail intake and scanning.
Impose least-privilege access, confidentiality obligations, and periodic oversight for Consumer Guides so they can access only the consumer information needed to process complaints and inquiries.
Provide clear notice to callers when voice communications are processed and limit retention of voice recordings or transcripts to what is necessary for service delivery and quality assurance.
Use de-identified or aggregated data for performance analytics whenever possible and prohibit analytics from being used to make decisions unrelated to complaint processing or administration.
Share only the minimum necessary complaint information with companies, other agencies, or internal offices, and document the basis for each disclosure.
Use secure transmission methods for all intake channels, including encrypted web, email protections, and controlled mail handling, and provide guidance to consumers on safer submission options.
Strengthen authentication with multi-factor authentication, periodic credential review, and access logging for staff accounts used to reach the CRC system.
The platform can hold a broad mix of sensitive PII and case-related information, so a compromise could expose consumers, staff, legal participants, and financial institution data in one place.
The system processes highly sensitive personal attributes such as military information, date of birth, place of birth, sex, and race/ethnicity, which increases the harm if misused or exposed.
The platform supports case management and legal matters, so unauthorized access could reveal information about supervisory, enforcement, litigation, whistleblower, or other legal proceedings.
The system creates, sends, tracks, and analyzes emails and texts, which can expose communication content and metadata to unauthorized viewers or the wrong recipients.

The platform collects information through web forms, website submissions, mail, email, and phone, which creates a risk that data may be entered or uploaded without adequate validation or minimization.
The platform processes PII for authentication, so account compromise could expose user identity data and allow unauthorized access to CFPB applications.
External users authenticate with email, password, and multi-factor authentication, so weak credential management or phishing could still lead to unauthorized access to external-facing applications.
Applications may share information with external entities on a need-to-know basis, which creates a disclosure risk if sharing is broader than necessary.
Records may be retained indefinitely until NARA approves disposition, which increases the risk of keeping personal data longer than necessary.
The platform supports trend, pattern, and correlation analysis of large data sets, which can create privacy risks from profiling or secondary use beyond the original collection purpose.
Apply strict role-based access controls, field-level restrictions, and segmentation so users only see the specific records and attributes needed for their duties.
Minimize collection of sensitive attributes and require program-level review before adding military, birth, sex, or race/ethnicity fields to an application.
Restrict legal and case records to authorized case staff and log all access and changes for audit review.
Use recipient validation, message review, and content controls before sending emails or texts containing personal information.
Standardize intake forms to collect only required fields and validate submitted data before Bureau staff upload it.
Protect authentication data with strong identity governance, including least-privilege provisioning and periodic review of access rights.
Keep multi-factor authentication mandatory for external users and add account monitoring for suspicious login activity.
Document each external sharing case in the relevant application PIA and limit sharing to specific approved recipients and purposes.
Enforce records disposition schedules and archive only the records that must be retained, with periodic disposal reviews.
Require privacy review of analytic use cases to ensure trend and correlation analysis is limited to authorized purposes and appropriately de-identified where feasible.

The system centralizes identity and access data for a very broad population, creating a single repository whose compromise could expose sensitive personal and access information about many staff and external users.

The system collects personal contact and identity-profile details that could be sensitive or revealing, including preferred pronouns, a personal cell number, and a personal address for work-from-home users.

The system relies on indirect collection from multiple internal and external sources, which increases the chance that more information than necessary is pulled into ICAM or that users are unaware of how their data is being combined.

Data is transferred between systems through APIs, secure data transmission methods, and flat text files, which creates privacy risk if transfer interfaces or file handling are misconfigured or intercepted.
The system creates and maintains digital identities for access control, which could enable tracking of individuals' system activity and access patterns beyond what they expect.
Privileged access management increases the impact of any misuse or unauthorized access because elevated accounts can reach sensitive systems and PII.
The system's role-based monitoring of who has access to systems and PII may itself create detailed records about employees and contractors' access rights and responsibilities.
Limit access to ICAM identity and access records to staff with a strict need to know and segment the data hub by function or population where feasible.
Minimize optional profile fields and make personal contact details and pronouns clearly optional with just-in-time notice before collection.
Provide clear source notices and data-sharing disclosures that explain which upstream systems supply data to ICAM and why each source is used.
Apply strict interface security controls and file-handling controls, including encryption in transit, integrity checks, and restricted processing of flat files.
Implement short retention for access logs and digital identity records that are no longer needed for authentication, auditing, or incident response.
Require stronger approval, periodic review, and least-privilege enforcement for privileged accounts, with immediate removal when elevated access is no longer needed.
Restrict access to role-and-responsibility reports to authorized administrators and audit their use to prevent unnecessary internal exposure.
The system collects and stores consumer PII for supervision, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure or misuse of sensitive personal information.
The system collects PII directly from consumers and from complaints, which can include information gathered outside the supervised entity’s original relationship with the consumer.
The CFPB may contact consumers to collect and verify additional information, which can intrude on privacy and reveal their involvement in a supervision matter.
The system facilitates collection and sharing of relevant information, creating a risk that PII will be shared more broadly than necessary among internal and external parties.
The Supervision Portal allows external entity representatives and state regulators to exchange files, which creates a risk of unauthorized access or accidental disclosure to external users.
Entity representatives are identified and provisioned by a limited set of CFPB users, creating a risk of improper access if provisioning is mistaken or abused.
Because SES is a cloud-based system, there is a risk that cloud hosting or configuration weaknesses could expose stored PII or supervisory records.
The system stores compliance rating information and examination reports, which could unfairly affect institutions if inaccurate or outdated information is used or disclosed.
Limit access to consumer PII to staff with a demonstrated need to know and enforce strong role-based access controls and audit logging.
Minimize direct collection from consumers and complaints to only what is necessary for supervision and prefer other-agency or publicly reported sources first.
Provide clear notice before contacting consumers and limit outreach to the minimum information needed to verify supervision-related facts.
Apply data-sharing restrictions so only relevant information is shared for the supervision purpose and only with authorized recipients.
Require strong authentication, least-privilege permissions, and secure file-transfer controls for all portal users, including external representatives and state regulators.
Use a formal identity-proofing and approval workflow before provisioning entity representatives, with periodic review and removal of stale accounts.
Ensure the cloud deployment is hardened with configuration reviews, encryption, and continuous monitoring of the Salesforce environment.
Implement record-quality review and a process for correcting or annotating disputed compliance ratings and examination reports.

The system collects and stores consumer complaints that can include detailed personal experiences, supporting documents, and other sensitive information, creating a risk of overexposure if access is not tightly controlled.
Social Security Numbers may be collected for some complaints, creating a heightened risk of identity theft or misuse if those identifiers are exposed.
Complaint data may be shared with the company or financial service provider that is the subject of the complaint, which can expose a consumer's allegations and personal information to a third party.
Complaint data may be referred to other government agencies or other CFPB offices, creating a risk of broader secondary use and disclosure beyond the original submission context.
The system is operated on a vendor-provided cloud platform, which creates a risk that a third-party service provider could access or mishandle complaint data.

The CFPB analyzes complaints to identify trends and share complaint data and insights, which can create a risk of re-identification or unintended secondary use if data are not properly minimized or aggregated.
Complaints can be submitted by phone, physical mail, website, and referrals from other entities, which creates a risk of inconsistent collection and authentication controls across channels.
Limit access to complaint records and supporting documents to staff with a need to know and apply role-based permissions and audit logging.
Minimize SSN collection by making it optional only when needed for identity validation, and mask or encrypt SSNs wherever stored or transmitted.
Before sending a complaint to the subject company, redact unnecessary personal information and provide only the minimum information needed to resolve the complaint.
Use written data-sharing agreements and purpose limits for referrals to other agencies or CFPB offices, and track each disclosure for accountability.
Impose vendor security and privacy requirements, including encryption, access controls, monitoring, and regular assessments of the cloud provider.
Publish only aggregated or de-identified complaint insights and apply re-identification review before sharing complaint data externally.
Standardize intake procedures across website, phone, mail, and referrals so that identity verification, notice, and privacy safeguards are consistent in every channel.

Placing CFPB records containing personally identifiable information in a contractor-owned environment creates a risk of unauthorized access, misuse, or loss of control over sensitive records. The appendix specifically says it documents privacy risks from housing CFPB records outside CFPB-owned systems.

The system processes and stores large volumes of highly sensitive investigative and litigation materials, increasing the impact of any privacy incident. The tools ingest, analyze, process, format, and organize bureau records for search, retrieval, review, correlation, flagging, and presentation.

Metadata exposure is a privacy risk because users can view metadata within files, which may reveal information beyond the document content itself. Metadata can disclose authorship, timing, routing, or other contextual details about individuals.

Automated keyword searching for names, phrases, and terms can over-collect or flag protected information, creating a risk that sensitive information is exposed to reviewers more broadly than necessary. The system automatically flags files containing reviewer-supplied keywords for attorney review.

Forensic collection from external entities can sweep in personal data from third parties who are not the target of the investigation or litigation. The system is designed to forensically collect data from storage media when immediate access is granted by a court.

The system handles both electronic and non-electronic information, including paper records, which increases the chance of mishandling during storage, transport, or review. The PIA says the tools gather and store information in a secure and forensically sound manner, implying sensitivity to handling integrity.

Trial and investigative hearing support can expose exhibits during courtroom presentations, creating a risk that more information is shown than is necessary for the proceeding. The system is used to display exhibits during investigative hearings or at trial.
Limit contractor access to the minimum necessary records and enforce contractual security, confidentiality, and audit requirements for the contractor-owned environment.
Apply role-based access controls and need-to-know review permissions for all processed bureau records.
Restrict metadata visibility to authorized reviewers and suppress or redact unnecessary metadata before broader sharing or production.
Require attorney validation of keyword hits before any protected information is shared or produced, and tune keywords narrowly to each case.
Use collection scoping rules and court-authorized collection protocols that limit forensic acquisition to data reasonably necessary for the matter.
Maintain secure chain-of-custody procedures and separate handling controls for paper and electronic records throughout collection, storage, and review.
Redact or limit sensitive exhibit content before courtroom presentation whenever disclosure of the full exhibit is not necessary.

If the beta environment is used with real small business loan application data, it could expose actual applicants' sensitive lending information even though the system says beta-testing should use fake data only.
The system collects identifiable user profile contact information, which could be exposed if improperly handled or breached.

The system is designed to handle small business lending data that can reveal business characteristics and financial details, creating risk of overcollection or unnecessary exposure if more data than needed is collected.
The system may enable re-identification or linkage of small business applicants through location and business profile data, especially when combined with other available information.

Because the system supports fair lending enforcement and public or interorganizational identification of business needs, there is a risk that data could be used in ways that affect individuals or businesses beyond the stated non-determination purpose if controls fail.
Enforce a hard validation rule in beta-testing that blocks submission of real applicant data and requires test-data-only confirmation before records can be saved.
Apply standard CFPB privacy protections and security controls to the user profile fields and restrict access to staff with a need to know.
Limit collection to the data elements required for the statutory purpose and review any additional fields before they are added.
Use de-identification or aggregation for reporting and analysis whenever possible, especially for location and business profile attributes.
Limit access to authorized users and document role-based use restrictions so the data is used only for the stated fair lending and community analysis purposes.

The system may collect more personal information than necessary if users upload documents that contain inadvertently included or irrelevant PII.

The helpdesk feature collects identifying information and questions from members of the public and account users, which may reveal sensitive issue details in the text of the question.
The system stores usernames and passwords for nonbank representatives and CFPB staff, creating account compromise risk if credentials are misused or exposed.

The system shares registry information with other CFPB programs and other regulators, which creates a risk of secondary use or disclosure beyond the original collection context.
Require redaction of nonpublic portions of covered orders before upload and block publication of any non-confidential information that could identify individuals unnecessarily.
Have CFPB staff routinely review uploaded documents and remove files that are inadvertently uploaded or not relevant to the Orders Rule.
Use sole discretion to publish only non-confidential information and publish it in a format designed to protect confidential information.
Minimize helpdesk submissions by limiting the information requested to what is needed to answer the question and by handling support requests through secure web forms.
Protect account credentials with multi-factor authentication and password creation requirements for user accounts.
Limit access to the system to authorized personnel and require staff and contractors to follow privacy and acceptable-use obligations.
Obtain and implement a NARA-approved retention schedule so records are disposed of when no longer needed.
Apply data-sharing agreements and protocols that limit disclosures to what is necessary for the receiving agency’s stated purpose.
The system stores a wide range of personally identifiable information about many people involved in enforcement matters, creating a risk of unauthorized access or overexposure of sensitive case data.

Sharing limited enforcement matter data with FTC staff and other external recipients creates a risk of secondary use or disclosure beyond the original collection context.
Sharing information in response to FOIA requests creates a risk that personal or sensitive matter information may be disclosed publicly if exemptions are not applied correctly.
Generating reports that include PII, confidential matter status, or monetary amounts can create a risk of unnecessary internal exposure if report access is not strictly limited.
The system links to other CFPB systems and a separate document storage system, which can increase the risk of duplicating records and expanding access paths to sensitive information.
Restrict access to matter records and documents to authorized users with a demonstrated need to know, and enforce role-based access controls and logging.

Apply stricter document classification and access controls for investigative files, with separate permissions for sensitive legal materials such as consumer complaints, whistleblower tips, and legal memoranda.
Minimize collection and sharing of TINs to cases where tax reporting requires them, and mask or redact TINs in views and reports unless explicitly needed.
Treat whistleblower tips and consumer complaints as sensitive source information and restrict access to staff working on the matter.
Limit access to conflict-of-interest information to staff who need it for ethics and assignment decisions, and avoid using it for unrelated purposes.
Restrict contractor performance records and spending reports to authorized procurement and operations staff, and separate vendor contact data from performance evaluations where possible.
Use a written data-sharing agreement with FTC that limits use, retention, onward sharing, and access to the specific enforcement purposes described in the module.
Apply FOIA review procedures that redact exempt personal and investigative information before any release.

The system can expose sensitive consumer loan and demographic data to a wider set of internal users through Bureau-wide and team sharing, increasing the risk of unauthorized internal access or overexposure.
Maps, geocoded outputs, and case data displayed for internal use or trials may reveal individuals' locations and related attributes if shared too broadly or mishandled.

Staff account data used for authentication, billing, support, and audit logs create a privacy risk if those records are retained longer than needed or accessed beyond their purpose.

Because GIS data can be uploaded from existing CFPB systems and stored on the server before final output is moved, there is a risk that PII remains in the GIS environment longer than intended or is not deleted on schedule.
Future integration of the online/public portals could increase the risk of public disclosure if anonymized or aggregated outputs are not properly de-identified before publication.
The system's ability to combine CFPB data with public datasets may enable re-identification or inference of sensitive attributes from location patterns even when no new PII is formally generated.

Keep role-based access controls tightly enforced so users only access the system and information necessary and relevant to their assigned duties.
Restrict internal maps and case displays to authorized staff and use private folders or team-specific sharing only when collaboration is necessary.
Use the secure browser-based enterprise system and keep data stored in controlled CFPB or FedRAMP Moderate AWS environments with access limited to authorized users.
Limit staff account and audit-log retention to the minimum necessary and review logs only for privacy and security compliance purposes.
Delete PII from the GIS server within the stated one-week window after final output is transmitted and verify deletion through routine checks.
Before any public release, apply disclosure review and data-release standards to ensure only aggregated or de-identified outputs are published.
Apply additional de-identification and disclosure testing when layering CFPB data with public datasets, especially for small geographies or unique patterns.
Require documented approval and periodic review for user requests to access geocoded data, with access granted only when the need to know is confirmed.
The system stores highly sensitive identifiers, including Social Security numbers and other government ID numbers, which increases the harm if the directory is misused or exposed.
The CFPB may collect personal information from third parties without individuals receiving actual notice at the time of collection.

The CFPB may disclose reports externally to employees at supervised institutions and other state or federal agency employees, creating a risk of unnecessary sharing if access is not tightly limited.
The system retains computer and paper records indefinitely until NARA approves a disposition schedule, which increases the risk that personal information will remain available longer than necessary.
The system includes information about CFPB employees' job functions and access levels, which could reveal internal roles and access structure if improperly disclosed.
Limit collection and display of SSNs and other government identifiers to cases where they are strictly necessary, and mask or redact them in reports and user interfaces by default.
Provide direct notice to individuals when PII is collected from third-party sources whenever practicable, in addition to constructive notice.
Implement routine data-quality checks and source validation before records are used in the directory.
Flag public and social-media-derived information for human review before it is incorporated into the directory.
Apply strict need-to-know access controls and logging for any connected internal systems that derive data from the directory.
Use data-sharing agreements and secure transmission for all external disclosures, and share only the minimum necessary information.
Establish and implement a records disposition schedule as soon as possible so records are not kept indefinitely.
Restrict access to employee job-function and access-level information to staff with a bona fide need and review whether it should be separated from the broader directory.

Visitors may disclose directly identifiable personal information when they use the site, creating a privacy risk if that information is collected or shared more broadly than intended. The site says users can limit how much information they give and how much is made public, but it also collects contact information and other personal content.

User-submitted comments, videos, links, and images may be publicly exposed, which could reveal personal details or sensitive opinions to other visitors. The system explicitly says users can control how much of their information is made public, implying some submissions may be public by default or through user choice.

The site collects information about a visitor's use of the website, which can create tracking and profiling risks across sessions or pages. Even if used for analytics, usage data can reveal browsing behavior and interests.

Demographic information may be collected, which can increase the sensitivity of the data set and support inference about individuals or groups. Combined with other information, it may enable identification or categorization beyond what users expect.

Information about consumer financial products that users and others have used may reveal highly sensitive financial behavior or circumstances. Such information can expose personal financial history even when the site is used for education or feedback.

ConsumerFinance.gov serves as the path to the online complaint intake system, so information entered on the site may flow into another system and be used in a more sensitive context. This creates a risk of secondary use or broader exposure than a visitor expects when interacting with the public website.

Google Analytics is used to evaluate aggregate web traffic, which creates a third-party processing risk for visitor data. Even if the stated purpose is aggregate analysis, analytics tools can still collect or infer detailed browsing information.

The site may collect directly identifiable PII when a user knowingly provides it, which creates a risk of accidental over-collection if disclosures are not clearly understood. Users may not realize what counts as directly identifiable information or how it will be used.
Minimize collection of directly identifiable information and clearly warn users before they submit contact details or other identifying content.
Provide prominent pre-publication notices and clear controls that let users decide whether comments, videos, links, or images are public.
Limit analytics collection to aggregated or de-identified website-use data and restrict any detailed usage logs to what is necessary for site improvement.
Collect demographic information only when needed for a specific website function and explain why it is requested.
Avoid collecting consumer financial product-use information unless it is necessary for the specific interaction, and separate it from other identifiers where possible.
Provide a clear notice at the point of transition to the complaint intake system explaining that information will be used in another system and may be subject to different handling rules.
Use privacy-preserving analytics settings, such as limiting cookies or other identifiers and configuring Google Analytics to collect only what is needed for aggregate reporting.
Use plain-language notices that explain what counts as directly identifiable PII and when users are knowingly providing it.
The system collects and stores Social Security Numbers, which creates a high-impact risk if those identifiers are exposed or misused.
Accident records can include highly sensitive personal and health information about third parties, including race, birth date, health records, driver’s license numbers, and home contact details.
Vehicle sales processing collects Social Security Numbers and transmits them to Experian for credit-worthiness checks, creating disclosure and secondary-use risk.
The system creates or aggregates new data about individuals, which can amplify privacy impact by combining accident, sales, and account information.
Accident and claims data are transmitted to multiple internal systems and offices, increasing the risk of unauthorized access during sharing and transfer.
Accident documents are handled through email, fax conversion, and attachment workflows, which can expose personal data if messages or files are misdirected or retained outside the system.
Although the system says it does not store police reports locally, the reports are stored in EDMS, so a compromise of that connected repository could expose accident PII.
The system logs GSA employees and contractors with access to transactions, which can create employee monitoring and behavioral tracking concerns.
Individuals may have difficulty correcting inaccurate accident or sales data because verification depends heavily on police reports and user-submitted information, with limited cross-verification.
Limit SSN collection to cases where it is strictly necessary, and apply strong encryption and access controls to SSNs at rest and in transit.
Restrict accident-case access to authorized personnel only and keep sensitive third-party fields tied to the specific claim purpose.
Minimize the use of SSNs in vehicle sales and use the credit check only for the stated eligibility purpose, with strict controls on transmission to Experian.
Apply data minimization reviews before combining records so only the minimum necessary personal data is aggregated.
Use formal data-sharing agreements and restrict downstream recipients to the minimum data needed for recovery, fraud, or court purposes.
Replace email-based handling of accident attachments with a secure portal or encrypted transfer workflow and limit inbox access.
Ensure the EDMS repository uses strong encryption, role-based access control, and audit monitoring for stored accident documents.
Limit audit log content and retention to what is needed for security and accountability, and restrict who can review the logs.
Provide a stronger correction workflow that lets individuals submit supporting documentation and have disputed data revalidated.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers, creating a significant harm risk if the data is exposed or misused.
The system aggregates and links multiple inquiries to the same constituent, which can create a broader profile of a person’s interactions and issues than any single inquiry alone.
The system stores communications and documents from multiple parties, including non-public agency records, which may reveal information beyond the original inquiry.

Limit collection of sensitive identifiers to only what is necessary for each inquiry and apply strong access controls and encryption to those fields.
Restrict access to linked constituent case histories to staff with a need to know and log access to linked records.
Apply retention limits and periodic review to communications and attached documents so records are kept only as long as needed to resolve the inquiry and meet legal requirements.
Provide clear notice to staffers about what constituent information they may submit and require them to confirm they have authority to share it on the constituent’s behalf.
Harden the portal with secure session management, strong authentication, and regular security testing for the submission interface.
Keep multifactor authentication mandatory and require documented approval checks for each staffer account request.
Use least-privilege cloud access controls and configuration reviews for Dynamics 365, Dataverse, and SharePoint Online.

The repository includes pharmacy manufacturer payments and rebate information, which may expose commercially sensitive and potentially linkable benefit details if not protected.
Limit access to the repository and require de-identification or aggregation for routine analysis, using identifiable longitudinal records only when specifically needed.
Apply strict role-based access controls and data minimization so identifiable longitudinal records are available only to staff with a documented need.
Require human review and corroboration before any fraud, waste, or abuse flag is used for action against an individual.
Handle dual-enrollment findings as sensitive exceptions and disclose them only to authorized personnel for reconciliation purposes.
Ensure all data sharing agreements specify permitted uses, retention, storage protocols, and privacy safeguards before any exchange occurs.
Segregate Medicare-related data and apply enhanced access controls for dual-enrollee records.
Suppress or aggregate small groups in reports and analyses to reduce inferential disclosure from comparisons across populations, geographies, and conditions.
Treat pharmacy manufacturer payment and rebate fields as sensitive analytical data and restrict their disclosure to authorized analytic uses only.
The system retains debtor data indefinitely on the mainframe, which increases the privacy impact if records are no longer needed or if a breach occurs.
The system contains highly sensitive identifiers, including Social Security Numbers stored as debtor IDs and debtor numbers, creating a risk of identity theft or misuse if exposed.

The system maintains mailing addresses and debt information about federal employees, separated employees, retirees, and vendors, which could reveal financial distress or other sensitive personal circumstances if disclosed.
Many authorized users across approximately 35 USDA agencies and about 160 Federal agencies can access agency-specific data, creating a broad internal access surface and risk of overexposure.
Contractors may access the system, which introduces additional privacy risk from non-federal personnel handling debtor information.

The system sends personal data to external Treasury systems and Iron Mountain, creating disclosure and transmission risk outside USDA.
Payroll reports are converted to PDF, encrypted, and transmitted to Iron Mountain by contractors at a local facility, which creates handling risk during file preparation and transfer.
The system relies on data provided by agencies and employees, so inaccurate or outdated source data could lead to incorrect billing or debt collection records.
Apply a documented records review and deletion schedule for mainframe records so data is not kept indefinitely when no longer required.
Replace SSNs with a non-SSN unique identifier wherever possible and restrict access to SSN-bearing fields to the minimum necessary users.
Limit display and reporting of mailing addresses and debt amounts to only what is necessary for billing and collection functions.
Continuously review and recertify user access across USDA and Federal agencies to ensure least-privilege access remains appropriate.
Require contractor-specific access approvals, training, and periodic access reviews before and during system access.
Provide an individual access and correction process through the responsible agency even though direct ABCO access is not available.
Use data-sharing agreements and minimum-necessary disclosures for Treasury and Iron Mountain exchanges, with periodic verification of recipient safeguards.
Move file preparation and transmission to a controlled, audited automated workflow with role-based access and logging.
Strengthen validation and reconciliation with routine source-data verification against authoritative agency records before billing is generated.
The system may collect more personal information from members of the public than is necessary because correspondence can include voluntary details beyond basic contact information.
The system stores and uses contact information that could expose individuals if improperly accessed or handled.
Phone numbers may be used to contact individuals for more information, which could create an unwanted disclosure or use beyond the original correspondence purpose if not controlled.
Centralizing correspondence in a single content management system increases the impact of any unauthorized access because many users can access and interact with the records.

Tracking package movement and workflow status can create internal visibility into who submitted correspondence and how it is handled, which may expose sensitive interaction history if improperly disclosed.
Using NLP and machine learning to analyze historical correspondence and generate results from similar inquiries may surface personal information in ways users do not expect.
Search, dashboard, and report outputs may reveal correspondence status and categories tied to individuals, increasing the chance of overexposure through internal reporting.
The system may retain physical and email addresses for correspondence purposes without a clearly stated retention limit in the provided context, increasing the risk of keeping PII longer than needed.
Limit collection to only the PII needed to process the correspondence and instruct users to redact or avoid unnecessary personal details in submissions.
Apply role-based access controls so only authorized staff handling the correspondence can view identifying contact information.
Use phone numbers only when necessary for follow-up and document the purpose for each contact attempt.
Continue enforcing role-based controls and limit access to correspondence records to business units that need them for ingestion, review, or approval.
Restrict metadata editing and workflow-tracking views to authorized personnel and log all changes to package records.
Review and test NLP and ML search results to ensure they do not surface unnecessary personal information from historical correspondence.
Limit dashboard and report access to authorized users and suppress personal identifiers in routine reporting where possible.
Establish and enforce a retention schedule that deletes correspondence PII when it is no longer needed for processing or records obligations.
The system stores highly sensitive discrimination and employee complaint records, which could cause significant harm if improperly accessed or disclosed.
The system collects direct personal contact and identifying information, creating a risk of identity exposure if the records are breached or misused.
Information is entered from mail, email, telephone, and interviews, which increases the risk of collecting inaccurate or incomplete data.
Because approved users manually input the information, there is a risk of insider mishandling or unauthorized disclosure by staff with access.
Contractor access creates a risk that non-government personnel could access complaint PII beyond what is necessary.
The system is connected to the public Internet, which increases exposure to external cyber threats.
Because the system is co-located at a contractor site and the contractor provides security services, there is a risk of reduced direct government control over the data environment.
The system retains files until destruction based on judicial regulations, which may keep complaint data longer than necessary if retention is not tightly managed.
The system collects information when individuals contact OASCR and states they cannot decline to provide it, which limits individual control over their personal data.
Limit access to complaint records to only personnel with a demonstrated need to know and enforce role-based permissions with logging and periodic review.
Minimize the personal identifiers collected and mask or truncate identifiers such as case numbers where full values are not needed for daily work.
Validate intake data against source documents and use standardized entry checks before records are finalized.
Train approved users on privacy handling and require disciplinary controls for improper access or disclosure.
Limit contractor access to the minimum necessary functions and require the same privacy and security controls that apply to federal users.
Harden the Internet-facing gateway with strong authentication, continuous monitoring, and regular vulnerability management.
Conduct regular government oversight of the contractor-hosted environment, including security reviews and access audits.
Periodically review retention schedules and destroy records as soon as the approved retention period ends.
Provide a clear privacy notice at intake explaining what information is required and why it is needed for the investigation.
Users can enter unrestricted free-text in the "About Me" section, which may lead to collection of unnecessary or highly sensitive personal information beyond what the system needs.
The system stores personally identifiable information that is not required for operation, increasing the impact if the data is misused or exposed.

Sharing data through Tableau dashboards and reports across multiple administrative domains can expose personal information more broadly than necessary.
Moving data into the USDA Data Lake creates a centralized repository that could increase the impact of unauthorized access or secondary use.
Contractors with access to the system may pose a privacy risk if their authorization or clearance is not tightly limited to the minimum necessary.
Collecting information by email to create accounts may expose personal data during transmission or through misdirected messages.
Restrict the "About Me" field with validation, guidance, or removal so users can only enter approved, minimal information needed for the system.
Make PII collection optional only where needed and clearly minimize the fields collected to the smallest set required for the stated purpose.
Keep profile photos optional and provide clear notice that photos are PII when combined with a name.
Limit access to names, addresses, and permit numbers to staff who need them for parking permits or request handling.
Apply role-based access controls and report-level filtering so Tableau dashboards show only the minimum personal information necessary for each audience.
Enforce strict access controls and data governance in the USDA Data Lake to prevent secondary use beyond the approved reporting purpose.

The system sends employee name and status information to the Credit Card Service Center by email, which creates a privacy risk if email is intercepted, misaddressed, or retained improperly.

The system stores and disseminates personal identity data through a staging table and multiple databases, which creates additional internal handling points where unauthorized access or leakage could occur.

Replace email transmission of the Fleet report with a more secure delivery method or encrypt the report end-to-end and limit distribution to approved recipients only.
Apply role-based access controls, periodic access reviews, and contractor-specific least-privilege permissions for all users and contractors.
Periodically review archived records and purge or de-identify data that is no longer needed before the full retention period ends when allowed by records rules.

Classify emergency responder fields as sensitive and limit their display to personnel who need them for emergency operations or access administration.

Apply the approved NARA and USDA retention schedule consistently and delete records when the retention period ends.
Restrict use of preference data to travel convenience functions and avoid secondary use or sharing of predictive preference profiles.
Continue validating Authorization and Voucher data with audit checks before transmission and encrypt the transfer end to end.
Enforce least-privilege access reviews so enterprise-wide users only receive the minimum roles needed for their duties.
Maintain strong multi-factor authentication and session protection for eAUTH and the cloud application, including monitoring for abnormal logins.

Enforce the approved records schedule and periodically review stored records to delete or archive data when the retention period expires.
Limit traveler preference and predictive-profile data to what is necessary for booking, and provide users a way to review and clear saved preferences.
Apply strict data-minimization and field-level review before transmitting authorization and voucher data to FMMI so only the information needed for budget and accounting validation is shared.
Require strong endpoint security and session protections for browser and mobile access, including device hygiene checks and session timeout controls.
Continuously test tenant and role separation to ensure restrictive roles prevent unauthorized access across users and organizational boundaries.
Require multifactor authentication for all users accessing the system and monitor for anomalous login activity.

Apply role-based access controls and audit logging to debt and accounts receivable records, with periodic review of who can view delinquent debt information.
Limit payroll and personnel data sharing to the minimum necessary fields and recipients for each business function.
Document and enforce purpose limitations for each ADMIN application so data used for one administrative function is not reused for unrelated purposes.

Aggregate or suppress statistical outputs so individuals cannot be identified from document-processing statistics.
