The system allows human resources staff to enter information on an individual's behalf, which creates a risk of inaccurate or incomplete records being associated with the wrong person or entered without the individual's direct review.
The system shares and transmits PII among multiple internal USDA systems and customer agencies, increasing the risk of unauthorized disclosure or over-sharing beyond the minimum necessary.

Authorized users can run predefined and custom reports and access data elements based on access privileges, which creates a risk that users may see more personal information than is necessary for their duties.
Contractors may access the system if authorized, which increases the risk of privacy misuse or mishandling by non-federal personnel.
Individuals are given access to their own data only at the customer agency's discretion, which could limit timely correction or review of inaccurate personal information.

The system retains records for varying periods under agency requirements and memoranda of understanding, which can increase the privacy risk of keeping PII longer than necessary across different agencies.
Limit collection and display of SSNs and other sensitive fields to only what is strictly required for timekeeping and payroll functions, and mask them wherever full values are not needed.
Require employee review and approval of HR-entered records before they are finalized, with an auditable correction workflow for disputed entries.
Apply data minimization and field-level access controls to each inter-system transfer so only the specific data needed by EmpowHR, Insight, eAuth, and TIME is shared.
Enforce role-based access reviews and report restrictions so custom and predefined reports cannot expose data elements outside each user's job need.
Subject contractor access to the same least-privilege, training, and monitoring controls as federal users, with periodic recertification of contractor roles.
Provide a standard self-service mechanism for individuals to view their records and request corrections, subject to identity verification.
Apply a uniform retention and disposal schedule across customer agencies where possible, and automatically purge records when the approved retention period ends.

The system collects and maintains directly identifying contact information, so a compromise could expose names, addresses, phone numbers, and email addresses. This creates a privacy risk because the system links identity data to inquiry and case history records.

PII is shared internally with all USDA Mission Areas for escalated inquiries, which broadens access beyond the original contact center staff. This raises the risk of unnecessary exposure if mission area personnel do not need the full set of PII to respond.

PII is transmitted by email to SME contacts, which can expose data to misdelivery or interception if email is not handled carefully. This is especially sensitive because the transmitted information includes contact details and inquiry content.

The system uses Cisco telephony integration and a browser-based connector, which can create additional technical pathways for PII exposure. If those integrations are misconfigured or compromised, contact information and call-related data could be disclosed.

The system retains information for at least seven years, which increases the amount of time personal data remains available. Long retention raises the risk that outdated or unnecessary PII will persist longer than needed.

No purging or archiving is currently set up, so retained PII may accumulate without routine deletion. This increases the chance that more personal data than necessary will remain accessible over time.

Customers can provide contact information through multiple channels, including webform, email, chat, and phone, which increases the chance of inconsistent collection practices across channels. Different channels can create uneven privacy handling and user expectations.

The system supports reporting and analytics on case information and contact statistics, which can create secondary privacy risk if reports reveal patterns about individuals or their inquiries. Even aggregate tools can expose sensitive operational details if access is too broad.
Restrict access to contact and case records to only staff who need the data for a specific case, and review those permissions regularly.
Limit internal sharing of PII to the specific mission area contacts needed for the escalation, rather than all mission areas by default.
Replace routine email transmission of PII with a secure case-management workflow or encrypted secure messaging, and require verification before sending any PII by email.
Conduct security testing and configuration reviews for the Cisco and B+S integration points before and during operation.
Define and enforce a shorter retention schedule for records that are no longer needed, and delete or archive them on schedule.
Implement automated purging or archiving for records that reach their retention limit.
Apply the same privacy notice, data minimization, and secure handling rules across all intake channels.
Restrict reporting access and ensure analytics are aggregated so they do not identify individual customers or specific inquiries.

The system captures and stores identifiable video of employees, contractors, and visitors as they enter and move through USDA buildings, creating broad surveillance of routine activity. This can reveal where people go and when they are present at federal facilities.

Cameras may capture facial images and license plates, allowing individuals to be identified and tracked across locations. The system also records textual information from documents or belongings when zoom is used.

Some footage includes highly sensitive personal data from driver's licenses, including names, addresses, and dates of birth. This creates a risk of collecting more personal information than needed for security monitoring.

The cameras can monitor passersby on public streets and use zoom, pan/tilt/zoom, manual tracking, and automatic tracking, which may enable persistent observation of individuals not suspected of wrongdoing. This can chill ordinary movement near federal facilities.

Video may be exported and used later for criminal or disciplinary actions, which creates a risk of secondary use beyond real-time security monitoring. Footage can also become evidence in criminal prosecution.

Footage can be shared outside USDA with federal agencies and local law enforcement, which increases the risk of wider dissemination of identifiable images and related information. Once shared, the agency may have less control over further use.

Contractors and select non-employees can access the system, creating a risk of insider misuse or unauthorized viewing of surveillance footage. Access by non-employees expands the number of people with access to sensitive recordings.

Footage may be retained longer than the intended six months depending on storage, camera counts, and other factors, which can prolong exposure of personal data. Longer retention increases the amount of historical movement and identity information available for review.
Limit camera placement and viewing to security-relevant areas and avoid unnecessary coverage of routine public movement. Continue excluding locations with a reasonable expectation of privacy.
Restrict use of zoom, pan/tilt/zoom, and tracking functions to authorized security purposes and document when they are used. Apply the minimum necessary field of view for each camera.

Configure cameras and operator procedures to avoid capturing driver's license details or other close-up personal documents unless needed for a specific incident. Review camera angles and zoom settings to minimize incidental capture of identity documents.

Use manual or automatic tracking only when responding to a specific security concern and log each use of tracking features. Limit real-time monitoring of public-street passersby to circumstances tied to a legitimate security need.

Require supervisory approval and a documented justification before exporting footage for criminal or disciplinary use, and limit exports to the specific incident at issue. Preserve chain-of-custody records for any exported footage.
Share footage externally only in response to formal requests and only the minimum footage necessary for the stated investigation or prosecution. Record each disclosure and the receiving organization.
Limit contractor and non-employee access to named users with role-based permissions and periodic access reviews. Revoke access promptly when a contract or need ends.

Enforce the six-month deletion schedule through automated controls and alerts when footage is approaching the retention limit. Require documented approval for any exception and periodic review of exceptions.
The system may collect limited personally identifiable information, creating a risk that customers can be identified from survey responses or free-form comments.
The system could infer or reveal identity because it can collect feedback across many channels, including unstructured and unsolicited inputs such as social media and free-form comments.
Cross-mission-area aggregation and expansion increases the privacy impact by combining feedback from many USDA programs into one system.
A small number of users with access to all data across all mission areas creates a risk of overly broad internal access to sensitive feedback and any included PII.
Contractors may access the system, which creates a risk of access by non-employees to customer feedback and any PII in the platform.
The system uses real-time analytics and dashboards to analyze large volumes of data, which may increase the chance that users can identify individuals from detailed feedback patterns.
The retention period has not been approved by the component records officer and NARA, creating uncertainty about whether data is retained longer than necessary.
The system migrates data from existing USDA tools into one cohesive product, which can concentrate personal information and increase the impact of any access or misuse event.
Because the system may collect demographic and geographic insights, there is a risk of profiling or sensitive segmentation of customers.
Minimize collection of direct identifiers and require users to collect name, email, and zip code only when a follow-up contact is specifically requested.
Apply review and redaction procedures to free-form and unsolicited feedback before broader internal use.
Use aggregation and de-identification rules before combining data across mission areas, and suppress small cells in dashboards.
Restrict all-data access to the minimum number of users needed and periodically review those elevated permissions.
Require contractors with access to complete the same privacy and security training and limit their permissions to mission need.
Implement query and dashboard controls that prevent users from drilling down to overly small or identifiable groups.
Obtain formal records approval for the retention schedule and document the approved disposal rules before relying on the schedule.
Complete a privacy review before migrating data from legacy tools and map only the data elements needed for the VoC purpose.
Limit demographic and geographic analysis to the minimum level needed for improvement and avoid reporting on small or highly specific groups.

The system requires users to provide personally identifiable information to create an account, so people cannot avoid giving up their name, email address, username, and contact information if they need access.
The system stores USDA email addresses in a third-party cloud service outside the ACFO-SS-FMS boundary, which creates a privacy risk from cloud-hosted PII exposure.
The system is used to collaborate on documents that are described as publicly accessible, so users may accidentally place more personal information into documents than intended for public release.
Contractors can access the system, which broadens the number of people who may view or handle user information and increases insider-access risk.
Access is granted through customizable workflows and supervisor or higher-level approval, so inconsistent access decisions could result in users receiving more access than needed.
The system retains information for 75 months, which extends the period during which PII remains exposed to potential misuse or breach.
Because access transactions are fully logged, the system may collect detailed records about who accessed or changed accounts, creating additional privacy-sensitive audit data that must be protected.
Limit account fields to the minimum required for provisioning and use role-based alternatives where possible for non-PIV users.
Restrict the cloud-hosted email data to the minimum needed and apply strong access controls and encryption for the hosted solution.
Provide clear user guidance and review controls to prevent personal information from being entered into documents intended for public release.
Apply least-privilege access reviews for contractors and periodically revalidate contractor access.
Require documented, minimum-necessary access approvals and periodic access recertification to verify that granted permissions remain appropriate.
Review whether the full 75-month retention period is necessary for all account and access records, and purge records as soon as the approved schedule allows.
Protect audit logs with strict access controls and limit retention of logs to what is needed for accountability and compliance.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial data, including SSNs, TINs, handwritten signatures, salary data, and award details, which creates a risk of harm if exposed or misused.
GIMS data may be shared with external parties outside the Department, including organizations and entities outside the US, which creates disclosure risk beyond the original collection context.
Information may be disclosed in common office formats or on paper, which increases the chance of accidental forwarding, loss, or unauthorized copying.
Contractors have access to the system for backup, support, and account management, which creates insider-access and privilege-misuse risk.
Users can manually enter information into the system, which creates a risk of collecting or maintaining inaccurate, incomplete, or unnecessary personal data.
The system transfers data from external applications and systems, so there is a risk that data could be intercepted or altered during transmission if controls fail.
The system maintains records for long periods, which increases the amount of time personal data remains exposed to breach, misuse, or outdated retention.
Review panelists may receive encrypted PII, but the system still shares personally identifiable information outside the core processing environment, creating residual disclosure risk.
Limit access to the sensitive fields to only staff and contractors with a documented need to know, and keep the existing encryption and password protections enforced.
Continue requiring Grants Director approval for any external disclosure and apply the same approval gate to all non-Department sharing.
Use controlled distribution methods for Excel, Word, PDF, and hard-copy disclosures, including recipient verification and secure handling procedures.
Apply least-privilege access for contractors and review their access regularly for the specific support tasks they perform.
Add validation and review steps for manually entered records before they are saved or used for processing.
Maintain strong encryption and mutual authentication for all inbound transfers and verify that encrypted databases remain properly configured.
Enforce retention and archival schedules so records are deleted or archived only for the approved period and no longer.
Keep redacting EIN/TIN and encrypting other PII before any distribution to review panelists or other authorized recipients.
The system centralizes detailed SNAP participant information from every state, creating a high-impact repository that could expose many people if it is misused or breached.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial data, which raises the privacy impact if those records are accessed or disclosed improperly.
The system collects historical data from 2000 to the present, which increases the amount of information retained about individuals over a long period.
The system performs automated matching and integrity checks, which can produce false positives and wrongly flag eligible participants as ineligible, duplicate, or fraudulent.
The system shares information across federal and state systems and with state agencies, which increases the number of entities that may receive or use participant data.
The system includes immigration status checks, which may expose especially sensitive information about participants and their households.
The system validates identity, SSN, age, and household composition, which means it processes multiple direct identifiers and household details that could be misused if not tightly controlled.

The system uses secure file transfer tools and an AWS environment, but any centralized transfer and cloud storage environment still creates a risk of unauthorized access if configuration or access controls fail.
Limit database access to the smallest set of authorized personnel and systems needed for integrity checks, and log all access and queries for review.
Apply field-level protections for sensitive identifiers and financial data, including encryption at rest and in transit and stronger role-based access controls.
Establish a retention schedule that limits how long historical participant data is kept and delete records that are no longer needed for integrity checks.
Require human review and an appeal or correction process before adverse action is taken on the basis of an automated match.
Use data-sharing agreements and data-minimization rules so each recipient receives only the information necessary for the specific fraud or eligibility check.
Restrict immigration-status data to personnel and systems with a documented need to know, and separate it from unrelated participant records where feasible.
Validate identity and household-related data against authoritative sources and limit use of SSNs, age, and household composition to the minimum needed for the stated checks.
Continuously monitor the AWS environment and managed file transfer services for misconfiguration, unauthorized access, and anomalous transfers, and remediate issues promptly.

The system stores personally identifiable information about affiliates, including names, business addresses, contact information, and affiliate IDs, creating a risk of unauthorized disclosure of sensitive identity and contact data if the database is compromised or improperly accessed.
NRCS employees manually enter affiliate information provided by the affiliate, which creates a risk of inaccurate or incomplete records being stored and then used for access control decisions.

The system is used to assign specific roles in eAuth and grant access to NRCS applications, so a mistaken or unauthorized record could lead to inappropriate access to government systems and information.
The application is only accessible by NRCS employees, so insider misuse or overbroad employee access could expose affiliate records beyond a need-to-know basis.

The system retains affiliate records for long periods, potentially for years or as long as the person qualifies for conservation programs, which increases the amount of time the data remains exposed to breach or misuse.

The system links affiliate records to Level 2 eAuthentication accounts and shares information with zRoles, creating a risk that linked identity and access data could be misassociated or exposed through the integration.
Limit access to affiliate records to authorized NRCS employees with a documented need to know and enforce strong authentication and auditing for all database access.
Implement a verification step for affiliate-submitted information before it is saved or used for access decisions, such as confirmation with the affiliate or a second employee review.
Require supervisory approval or periodic recertification for role assignments that are driven by affiliate records.
Apply role-based access restrictions and logging within the NRCS employee user base so only staff with an operational need can view or edit affiliate records.
Retain affiliate records only for the minimum period required by the applicable records schedule and SORN, and delete or archive records when eligibility ends and retention is no longer required.
Validate the affiliate-to-account linkage before role assignment and periodically reconcile linked records between Affiliates and zRoles to detect mismatches.

The system stores and exposes a large amount of personally identifiable information, including names, addresses, phone numbers, tax IDs, policy details, and agent and adjuster Social Security numbers, creating a significant confidentiality risk if the warehouse or web application is breached or misused.

The system’s web application access path creates a risk of unauthorized disclosure if authentication or extranet access is compromised. HyDRA is an online resource used to disseminate information, and access is granted through an RMA Extranet URL.

Because access is provided to multiple organizations and external users, there is a risk that users will view information beyond what they need for their role. The system shares data with FSA, RMA, OIG, and AIPs, and AIPs are only limited to data associated with their policies.
The system retains data for the life of the project, which increases the amount of time sensitive personal and policy information remains exposed to privacy risk.

The system combines data from multiple years and sources into a single production database, which can increase the privacy impact of any unauthorized access and make individuals more exposed through aggregation.

The system uses data cleansing and standardization steps that alter source records, which creates a risk that personal information could be changed incorrectly and then used or disclosed in inaccurate form.
The system stores and uses location-linked crop unit information, including latitude and longitude, which can reveal precise property or field locations and increase re-identification risk.
The system includes tax IDs and Social Security numbers for agents and adjusters, which are highly sensitive identifiers that increase harm if exposed.
Encrypt the warehouse data at rest and in transit, and restrict database and application access to only authorized users with strong role-based controls.
Require multi-factor authentication for all HyDRA users and continuously monitor access to the RMA Extranet and application logs for suspicious activity.
Apply least-privilege access reviews for FSA, RMA, OIG, and AIP users and periodically recertify that each user still needs the specific records they can access.
Implement and periodically review retention and disposal controls so data is returned to RMA or securely destroyed as soon as the approved retention period ends.
Separate data by year or subject area where feasible and limit cross-year access to users who need historical aggregation for approved analysis.
Add quality controls that preserve original source values and flag any cleansing or standardization changes for review before the data is used in reports.
Mask or generalize precise latitude and longitude values in user-facing reports unless exact coordinates are required for an approved business purpose.
Minimize exposure of tax IDs and Social Security numbers by suppressing them in reports and limiting their display to users with a documented need to know.
The system stores identifiable user profiles with names and work contact details, creating a privacy risk if those records are exposed or misused.
Some profiles may include personal contact information beyond basic work details, increasing the sensitivity of the stored PII.
CoLab relies on eAuth identity information to create and authorize access, so any weakness in identity proofing or access request handling could expose profiles to unauthorized users.
Authorized contractors and partners have access to the system, which creates a risk of overbroad access or insider misuse of user PII.
Users can modify their own profiles, which creates a risk that inaccurate or unnecessary personal information could be entered and then retained.
PII is retained while the application remains in production, which can keep personal data longer than needed and increase exposure over time.
The system depends on account disabling when a user leaves, so stale accounts could remain a privacy risk if deprovisioning is delayed or incomplete.
Limit profile fields to the minimum required for authorization and business operations, and periodically review whether each field is still needed.
Restrict collection of personal contact information to only cases where it is necessary and document why those extra fields are needed.
Require strong eAuth authentication and periodic access reviews for CoLab project membership and profile access.
Apply least-privilege role assignments and routinely audit contractor and partner access to ensure it matches current duties.
Add validation and user guidance for profile edits so users can only change approved fields and are warned not to enter unnecessary personal data.
Set and enforce a defined deletion schedule for inactive or unneeded profiles instead of retaining them for the full production life of the application.
Automate offboarding so accounts are promptly disabled when users leave and verify completion through periodic account reconciliation.
The system stores vendor names and contact information in the IDEA DataMart, which creates a risk of unauthorized access to identifiable personal data if the data store is compromised or misused.
The system processes transitory PII through read-only web service calls, creating a risk that personal data could be exposed during retrieval or processing even if it is not stored long term.
The system uses selectable criteria from drop-down menus to produce reports, which could allow users to infer or assemble more personal information than intended from report outputs.
Contractors have access to the system, so vendor PII could be viewed or handled by personnel beyond direct government staff if access controls are not tightly enforced.
PII is refreshed periodically from SCIMS, so outdated or incorrect vendor contact information may persist between refreshes and be used in reports.
Application-specific information is retained while the application remains in production, which can extend the exposure period for any PII stored in the DataMart.
Minimize the amount of vendor PII stored in IDEA DataMart and apply strict role-based access controls and encryption to the stored records.
Keep the read-only SCIMS integration limited to the minimum necessary fields and log or suppress any temporary copies of vendor PII during web service processing.
Restrict report criteria and outputs to approved business needs and review report templates to prevent unnecessary disclosure of vendor PII.
Enforce least-privilege access reviews for contractors and verify that only users with a documented need to know can access vendor PII.
Shorten the refresh interval or validate report data against SCIMS at the time of use to reduce the chance of stale vendor information being reported.
Apply a defined retention schedule that deletes vendor PII from IDEA DataMart as soon as it is no longer needed for reporting, legal, audit, or operational purposes.
Core Services handles identifiable customer data that can be linked to highly sensitive identifiers, creating a risk of improper disclosure or re-identification if access controls fail.
The system transmits PII between multiple internal systems and client applications, increasing the chance of exposure during data exchange or integration failures.
A single external-facing gateway serves as the entry point for requests, so a compromise or misconfiguration there could expose data or allow unauthorized access to the service.
Contractors have access to the system, which creates a risk of insider misuse or overbroad access to customer information.
Core Services returns requested information to users in JSON format, which could expose more data than necessary if responses are not minimized or filtered.
The system relies on replicated or copied access to SCIMS data, which raises the risk that stale or duplicated customer information could be exposed beyond its source system controls.
Core Services accesses race, sex, national origin, and disability data for reporting, which creates a risk of sensitive demographic information being exposed or used beyond the intended purpose.
Although Core Services says it does not store PII, it stores administrative and transactional information, which may still reveal user activity or customer interactions if improperly accessed.
Restrict access to only the minimum fields needed for each request and mask or tokenize customer identifiers wherever possible.
Apply strict API authorization, field-level filtering, and encrypted transport for all system-to-system exchanges.
Harden and continuously monitor the API gateway, including intrusion detection, rate limiting, and configuration review.
Enforce least-privilege contractor access with periodic access reviews and audit logging of contractor activity.
Implement response minimization so APIs return only the specific fields required for the requesting application.
Synchronize replicated SCIMS data with source-system controls and regularly validate that copied data remains current and authorized for use.
Limit access to demographic reporting to authorized personnel and separate reporting datasets from operational client data when possible.
Minimize retention of administrative and transactional records and apply retention and disposal controls to those records as well.

Emergency Action Plans contain personally identifying details that could expose emergency responders and property owners if the documents are mishandled or disclosed beyond the intended emergency context.

Limit EAP access to only the specific responders and officials who need the information for a particular dam and require secure handling for all copies.
Apply a records review and purge schedule so EAP PII is removed or updated when no longer needed, rather than relying only on maximum retention periods.
Use encrypted secure communications and controlled distribution procedures for both hardcopy and electronic EAP disclosures.
Limit responder access to only those assigned to the relevant dam site and review access periodically to confirm the need-to-know still exists.
Maintain background investigations for contractors and add periodic access recertification and audit logging for contractor accounts.
Verify publicly sourced and voluntarily submitted contact information with the originating organization or individual before storing it in an EAP.
Encrypt stored EAP files and restrict access with role-based controls so the centralized contact information is protected if the system is compromised.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers in scanned documents, creating a risk of harm if the records are exposed or mishandled.

Allowing contractors access to records creates a risk of unauthorized viewing or misuse of sensitive records by non-federal personnel.
Storing records in a cloud system on shared infrastructure increases the risk of misconfiguration or unauthorized access to the records repository.

Validate scanned documents and extracted metadata before they are accepted into the system, with quality-control checks for misclassification and indexing errors.

Apply least-privilege access reviews, enhanced background screening, and periodic auditing for contractor accounts.
Harden the cloud environment with configuration baselines, segmentation, and continuous security assessment of the host environment.
Enforce records schedules and dispose of records when no longer required under the approved retention schedule.
Use secure PDF handling practices, including patching viewer software and restricting plug-in use to approved, managed devices.
The system stores highly sensitive personal and financial identifiers in documents, creating a significant harm if the repository is exposed or mishandled.
Users can upload documents directly into the system, which increases the chance that sensitive information is added without adequate review or minimization.
The system relies on PDF files and Adobe PDF plug-ins for viewing, which can increase exposure if documents are opened on insecure endpoints or if plugin vulnerabilities are exploited.
DMS uses name and address information from FSA SCIMS to identify the correct producer, which risks misidentification or inappropriate association of records if the matching is wrong.
The system permits disclosure to contractors and technical service providers, which creates a risk of secondary use or over-disclosure beyond the original purpose.
Conservation district employees and contractors have access to the system, so there is a risk of unauthorized viewing or misuse by non-federal personnel with broad operational access.
Individuals do not have direct access to DMS, which can make it harder for them to see, verify, or correct their own information promptly.
